## 7. Pakiṇṇaka Section
## For Those Aspiring for Buddhahood
## Miscellaneous Meanings to be Noted Regarding the Pāramīs
At this point, pausing the account of the hermit Sumedha, I shall present the miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) meanings to be noted regarding the ten Pāramīs (as found in the Cariyāpiṭaka Aṭṭhakathā), so that noble sons who aspire for and strive towards Sammāsambodhi-ñāṇa (Omniscience) may become exceptionally skilled in understanding and practicing the meritorious deeds that constitute the foundation of Sammāsambodhi.
The points and meanings to be included in this Pakiṇṇaka section are:
(1) The states called Pāramīs,
(2) The reason for being called Pāramīs,
(3) The classification of Pāramīs,
(4) The order of Pāramīs,
(5) The characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes of Pāramīs,
(6) The foundational causes of Pāramīs,
(7) The factors that defile Pāramīs,
(8) The factors that purify Pāramīs,
(9) The opposing factors of Pāramīs,
(10) The detailed practice of the ten Pāramīs,
(11) The detailed classification of Pāramīs,
(12) The summary of Pāramīs,

## (1) The States Called Pāramīs
It should be asked: "Which states are called Pāramīs?"
(The answer is:) Virtues such as giving (dāna) and morality (sīla), which are performed based on Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) and Skillful Means (upāyakosalla-ñāṇa), and are not oppressed or destroyed by craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi), are called Pāramīs.
To explain further: In the matter of giving (dāna), if there is attachment through craving (taṇhā) as "my dāna," or the misconception through conceit (māna) as "I am the dāna," or the wrong view (diṭṭhi) as "dāna is my self (atta) or soul," then that dāna is called dāna oppressed and destroyed by craving, conceit, and wrong view. Only when it is not so oppressed and destroyed can it be called a Pāramī. (The same applies to the observance of morality, etc.)
Even if not oppressed by craving, conceit, and wrong view, it cannot yet be called a Pāramī; it is only when the acts of giving, morality, etc., are performed based on Great Compassion and Skillful Means that they are called Pāramīs. Therein:
Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) means: A noble son who wishes to become a Bodhisatta must be able to develop intense kindness and pity toward all beings, whether present or absent, near or far, as if they were his own children born from his breast.
3:
105
Without distinguishing between friend and foe, one should develop intense compassion by contemplating all beings as suffering creatures in the round of rebirth (saṃsāra), who are being scorched and consumed by the blazing fires of lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), birth (jāti), aging (jarā), death (maraṇa), sorrow (soka), lamentation (parideva), pain (dukkha), grief (domanassa), and despair (upāyāsa). One should maintain great compassion, wishing to rescue beings from saṃsāra without even regarding one's own life. Such compassion is called Mahākaruṇā, the foundation of the Pāramīs. Although the Bodhisatta Sumedha was already endowed with the conditions to attain liberation during the dispensation of Dīpaṅkara Buddha if he so desired, because he was possessed of this Mahākaruṇā, he endured suffering in saṃsāra for four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons to fulfill the Pāramīs in order to save beings. (This means that if he had wished to escape alone, he could have done so since his life as Sumedha.)
Skillful Means (Upāyakosalla-ñāṇa) is the proficient wisdom that acts as the supporting condition (upanissaya) and foundation for Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) through one's deeds of giving, morality, etc. A noble son who wishes to become a Buddha must aspire only for the single fruit of Omniscience through all his acts of giving, morality, etc. (He must not aspire for worldly happiness included within the suffering of the round of rebirth.) The wisdom that is proficient in knowing and aspiring only for the fruit of Omniscience for all the merits one performs is called Upāyakosalla-ñāṇa.
These two factors, Great Compassion and Skillful Means, are the great primary foundations for becoming a Buddha and for being able to

fulfill the Pāramīs. Noble sons who wish to aspire for Buddhahood should first strive to be endowed with these two primary foundational factors. It is meant that only the virtues such as giving and morality performed based on these two factors can truly be Pāramīs.
Free from the three proliferations (papañca) of "I," "mine," and "my soul,"
With compassion for infinite beings as the basis,
With the desire and aspiration for Omniscience to become a Buddha,
Those ten deeds beginning with giving (dāna) are called Pāramīs.

## (2) The Reason for Being Called Pāramīs
It should be asked: "Why are the ten virtues such as giving, morality, etc., called Pāramīs?"
(The answer is:) In the Pali term 'Pāramī', one should first note that according to grammatical rules, the root word 'Parama' is combined with the suffix 'ī'. Between that root and suffix:
Because they are supreme (ukkaṭṭha) individuals, peerless and noble, being endowed with special virtues such as giving and morality, the Great Bodhisattas are called 'Parama'. (Alternatively) They are called 'Parama' because they accumulate, fulfill, and protect special virtues such as giving and morality; and because, being endowed with these special virtues, they are like those who bind other beings (para) to themselves with loving-kindness; and because they exceedingly wash and cleanse other beings from the stains of defilements; and because they go especially to the noble Nibbāna called 'Para';
5:
107
and because they clearly perceive the world beyond (para) with wisdom just like the present world; and because they practice by instilling in their own continuity the collection of special virtues such as morality in an incomparable and exceeding manner; and because they can oppress and abandon the group of thieves called defilements (kilesa) which are external (para)—for these reasons, the Great Bodhisattas are called 'Parama'.
Based on their peerless and abundant fulfillment of special virtues such as giving and morality, the sound (word) and the knowledge arise in the mouths of those who hear and see them: "This person is a Bodhisatta, a great supreme (parama) person." Thus, those special virtues such as giving and morality are called Pāramī because they are the cause for the sound (word) and the knowledge that says they are indeed the great supreme Bodhisattas (deriving from the analysis: paramānaṃ bhāvo pāramī). (Alternatively) Only the Great Bodhisattas can perform those virtues of giving, morality, etc., in such an exceeding manner. Thus, those acts of giving, morality, etc., are called "the work of the Great Bodhisattas, the property of the Great Bodhisattas." Therefore, those virtues of giving, morality, etc., are called Pāramī because they are the work and property of the supreme (parama) Great Bodhisattas (deriving from the analysis: paramānaṃ kammaṃ pāramī, or paramānaṃ ayaṃ pāramī).
In summary: Because they are the cause for the sound (word) and knowledge that refers to them as Great Bodhisattas, (Alternatively) because they are the work and property of the Great Bodhisattas, the acts of

giving (dāna) and so forth are called Pāramīs.
Because they cause the two—the word and the knowledge—to say "These are the Supreme Bodhisattas,"
Or alternatively, because they are the property and the work
That only those supreme noble beings can perform,
Those ten beginning with giving (dāna) are called Pāramīs.

## (3) The Classification of Pāramīs
It should be asked: "How many classifications of those Pāramīs are there?"
(The answer is:)
Dānaṃ sīlañca nekkhammaṃ, paññā vīriyena pañcamaṃ.
Khanti sacca madhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettupekkha ti te dasa.
According to this teaching, those Pāramīs are classified into ten in brief: Dāna-pāramī, Sīla-pāramī, Nekkhamma-pāramī, Paññā-pāramī, Viriya-pāramī, Khanti-pāramī, Sacca-pāramī, Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī, Mettā-pāramī, and Upekkhā-pāramī.
(The respective ultimate realities of these ten Pāramīs will be presented when reaching section 5 on Characteristics, Functions, Manifestations, and Proximate Causes.)
Dāna, Sīla, Nekkhamma, Paññā, Viriya,
Khanti, Sacca, Adhiṭṭhāna, Mettā, Upekkhā.
These ten Pāramīs, in brief, were taught by the Most Exalted One.

## (4) The Order of the Ten Pāramīs
Five Types of Ordering
The ordering of various states as first, second, third, etc., is of five types:
(Occurrence, Abandonment, Practice, Planes, and the Order of Teaching—these five are the sequence.)
7:
109
(1) Order of actual occurrence (Pavatti-kkama)
(2) Order of abandonment (Pahāna-kkama)
(3) Order of practice (Paṭipatti-kkama)
(4) Order of planes (Bhūmi-kkama)
(5) Order of teaching by the Buddha (Desanā-kkama)
Among these five:
(1) In the teaching such as "Paṭhamaṃ kalalaṃ hoti, kalalā hoti abbudaṃ," for beings who are womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka), first at the moment of conception there is the kalala (clear drop) for seven days, then the abbuda (foam) for seven days, then the pesi (lump of flesh) for seven days, and so on. Such an ordering according to how things actually occur is called Pavatti-kkama (Order of Occurrence).
(2) In the teaching such as "Dassanena pahātabbā dhammā, bhāvanāya pahātabbā dhammā," states to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga) and states to be abandoned by the three higher Paths are ordered as first and second. Such an ordering according to the sequence of abandonment is called Pahāna-kkama (Order of Abandonment).
(3) In the sequence of the seven Purifications (visuddhi) such as Sīla-visuddhi, Citta-visuddhi, Diṭṭhi-visuddhi, etc., one must first practice to achieve Sīla-visuddhi, then practice to achieve Citta-visuddhi, and so on. Because they are ordered according to the sequence of practice as first, second, etc., it is called Paṭipatti-kkama (Order of Practice).
(4) In teachings such as "Kāmāvacarā dhammā, rūpāvacarā dhammā," states are ordered as Kāmāvacara, Rūpāvacara, and Arūpāvacara according to the sequence of planes as first, second, etc. This is called Bhūmi-kkama (Order of Planes).
8: (5) Apart from the four previous types of sequences, the sequence of the Perfections such as "Rūpakkhandha, Vedanākkhandha," etc., found in the teachings is called desanākkama (the sequence of teaching), as it was taught by the Buddha with regard to a specific reason. In the four preceding sequences, specific reasons are given: "Because it arises in this order, the discourse is thus; because it is abandoned in this order, the discourse is thus; because it is practiced in this order, the discourse is thus; because it exists in this order in the planes, the discourse is thus." However, in the fifth type, desanākkama (the sequence of teaching), various specific reasons are given as appropriate: one reason for the order of the five aggregates, another for the twelve sense-bases, and so on. The order of the ten Perfections in this section on Perfections is not according to the sequences of arising, abandoning, practice, or planes; it is solely the desanākkama (sequence of teaching) taught by the Buddha with regard to a specific reason. Therefore, one might ask: "Why did the Buddha teach the ten Perfections in this specific order—Dāna, Sīla, Nekkhamma, and so on—rather than in any other way?" (The answer is:) When the Bodhisatta, the hermit Sumedha, had just received the prophecy, he first resolved upon the Perfection of Generosity (Dāna-pāramī), then secondly upon the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī), and so on. Because he resolved upon them in this order from the very beginning...
9: ...he taught them in this order. If it is asked again, "Why did he resolve upon them in this order?" the answer is: "When he reflected with the knowledge of investigating the Perfections (pāramī-pavicaya), they appeared in this order within the range of his knowledge; therefore, he resolved upon them in this order." The point is: when the Bodhisatta Sumedha reflected on the Perfections just after receiving the prophecy, they appeared in his knowledge in this order. Because they appeared in this order, he resolved upon them in this order. Because he resolved upon them in this order, now that he has become the Buddha, he teaches them in this very same order. Here, I shall present the detailed reasons for their appearing in this order when the Bodhisatta Sumedha reflected, his resolving upon them in this order, and his teaching them in this order upon becoming the Buddha, all together. Among those ten Perfections, Generosity (Dāna) especially supports Virtue (Sīla). (Even a person who is naturally immoral, when becoming a donor for a son's novitiation, easily undertakes virtue.) Among the ten Perfections, the act of generosity is easy to perform. (Even for one who finds it difficult to undertake virtue, the act of generosity is often easy.) For these reasons, Generosity is taught first.
10: 112  Generosity (dāna) is taught followed by virtue (sīla) because dāna is more fruitful only when it is encompassed by virtue (dāna with a foundation of basic virtue). Virtue is taught followed by renunciation (nekkhamma) because virtue is more fruitful only when it is encompassed by renunciation (virtue with a foundation of renunciation). Similarly, renunciation is more fruitful only when it is encompassed by wisdom (paññā). (Even if one goes to the forest and ordains, if one does not practice wisdom, the benefit is not great; it is like a large investment with little profit.) Wisdom is more fruitful only when it is encompassed by energy (viriya). (Even if one has wisdom, if one is lazy and lacks energy, the benefit cannot be great.) Energy is more fruitful only when it is encompassed by patience (khanti). Patience is more fruitful only when it is encompassed by truthfulness (sacca). Truthfulness is more fruitful only when it is encompassed by determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Determination is more fruitful only when it is encompassed by loving-kindness (mettā). Loving-kindness is more fruitful only when it is encompassed by equanimity (upekkhā). Therefore, after nekkhamma, paññā is taught; after paññā, viriya; after viriya, khanti; after khanti, sacca; after sacca, adhiṭṭhāna; after adhiṭṭhāna, mettā; and after mettā, upekkhā. Equanimity is more fruitful only when it is encompassed by compassion (karuṇā). The Great Beings (Bodhisattas) are those who are already endowed from the beginning with the great foundational cause of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā).  ## Question regarding Great Compassion and Equanimity  There is a question: How do the Great Bodhisattas, who are possessors of Great Compassion and are extremely kind and sympathetic towards beings, practice equanimity (looking on with indifference)?
11: 113  (Answer by some teachers): Some teachers (Keci) answer that although it is said they practice equanimity, they do not do so in every matter or at all times; they only practice equanimity in matters where it is appropriate and at times when it is appropriate.  (Answer by other teachers): Other teachers (Apare) answer, “It is not equanimity towards beings, but equanimity towards the wrongdoings committed by beings. Thus, there is no conflict between Great Compassion and the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī).”  ## (Another way) Detailed Order of the Ten Perfections  (1) Generosity (dāna) is taught first because it can occur even among many common people and thus concerns all beings; also because it is not as fruitful as higher perfections like virtue; and because it is easy to perform.  (2) Virtue (sīla) is taught next because only when there is virtue can both the giver and the receiver be pure (and the benefit be great); also because after teaching the practice of supporting others (giving), the Buddha wished to teach the practice of refraining from harming others (abstaining from taking life, etc.); furthermore, dāna is a practice that points out what should be done, while sīla is a practice that points out what should be avoided or refrained from. Thus, after teaching the practice to be followed, he wished to teach the practice of restraint; also, dāna is the cause of the fulfillment of wealth (bhoga-sampatti), while sīla is the cause of the fulfillment of existence (bhava-sampatti) such as human or celestial life.
12: ...thus, after teaching the cause of wealth, he wished to teach the cause of existence; for these reasons, Virtue is taught after Generosity. (3) Renunciation (Nekkhamma) is taught after Virtue because the perfection of Virtue can be accomplished through Renunciation; because after teaching bodily and verbal good conduct (through Virtue), he wished to teach mental good conduct (through Renunciation); because for one pure in virtue, the attainment of absorption (jhāna or Renunciation) is easy; because through Virtue, the offense of action (kammāparādha)—which is unwholesome kamma—can be abandoned, and by such abandonment, the purity of effort (payoga-suddhi)—the purity of all bodily and verbal endeavors—is achieved; while through Renunciation, the offense of defilement (kilesāparādha) can be abandoned, and by such abandonment, the purity of inclination (āsaya-suddhi)—the purity of the internal disposition of wisdom such as insight and knowledge of the ownership of kamma, free from internal tendencies of eternalism and annihilationism—is achieved. Thus, after showing the purity of effort through Virtue, he wished to teach the purity of inclination through Renunciation. Furthermore, he wished to show that one who has abandoned transgressive defilements (vītikkama-kilesā) through Virtue can then abandon obsessive defilements (pariyuṭṭhāna-kilesā) through Renunciation. (4) Wisdom (Paññā) is taught after Renunciation because the accomplishment of Renunciation can be purified by Wisdom; because he wished to teach that without absorption (which is included in Renunciation), there can be no wisdom; because after teaching the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta) through Renunciation, he wished to teach the sign of equanimity (upekkhā-nimitta) through Wisdom; because...
13: ...he wished to show that only when one can focus on and reflect upon the welfare of others through Renunciation can the skill in means (upāya-kosalla-ñāṇa)—the wisdom that can act for the benefit of others—arise; for these reasons, Wisdom is taught after Renunciation. (5) Effort (Viriya) is taught after Wisdom because the task of wisdom can be completed through the exertion of effort; because after teaching the wisdom that observes the ultimate reality of phenomena void of a person or being, he wished to show the marvelous nature of effort exerted for the welfare of beings; because after teaching the sign of equanimity, he wished to teach the sign of exertion (paggaha-nimitta); because only after reflecting with wisdom and putting forth strenuous effort can a special benefit be obtained—thus, after teaching the act of investigation, he wished to teach the act of exertion. (6) Patience (Khanti) is taught after Effort because only one with effort can endure whatever suffering is encountered; because the endurance of a lazy person who lacks effort and is unable to act is not beautiful, whereas the endurance of an energetic person who is capable but chooses to endure is truly beautiful—thus, effort is like an ornament for patience; because after teaching the sign of exertion, he wished to teach the sign of serenity; because excessive effort can lead to restlessness (uddhacca), and only the patience of reflecting on the Dhamma (dhammanijjhānakkhanti) can abandon that fault of restlessness—thus, he wished to teach the principle that can abandon the fault of restlessness arising from excessive effort; because only one with much patience can practice wholesome deeds continuously without restlessness...
14: ...thus, he wished to show the cause for the continuous practice of an energetic person; because if one strives for the benefit of others without the quality of dhammanijjhānakkhanti,* greed (craving) for a return of gratitude from them can arise, and only with this patience can one perform pure service without greed; thus, he wished to show that for one who holds heedfulness as a guide, craving and greed for a return of gratitude from the recipient of the service will not arise while striving for the benefit of others; because (considering the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka, etc.) he wished to show that the Great Bodhisattas endure the suffering inflicted by others even when they are not actively striving for the benefit of others; for these reasons, Patience is taught after Effort. (7) Truthfulness (Sacca) is taught after Patience because patience can be maintained for a long time only through truthfulness; because (considering the Mahākapi Jātaka, the 6th in the Tiṃsanipāta, where the Bodhisatta monkey king saved a brahmin who had fallen into a pit, and while the monkey king was resting trustfully in the brahmin's lap, the wicked brahmin struck him with a stone, yet the monkey king endured it without anger and even saved the brahmin from the danger of wild beasts like tigers and lions by leading him to the edge of the forest, guiding him with drops of blood as he leaped from tree to tree), even when someone acts ungratefully, the Bodhisattas endure that wrong and do not deviate from the resolution and thought they had when receiving the prophecy: "I will save all beings." *The wisdom that can observe the nature of things as they truly are is called dhammanijjhānakkhanti.

He is accustomed to doing good even to those who wrong him. Thus, after preaching the virtue of patience (khanti) towards those who wrong others, He taught Truthfulness (sacca) immediately after Patience because He wished to show that He was unfailingly true to His intention of benefiting the wrongdoer (as He had resolved when aspiring for Buddhahood). Furthermore, He wished to show that Great Bodhisattvas, through the virtue of patience, do not waver or become agitated even when others speak falsely or wrongly to them, and they never abandon their nature of speaking only the truth for themselves. Having taught the patience of reflecting on the Dhamma (dhamma-nijjhāna-khanti), which is capable of focusing on the ultimate reality devoid of a person or being, He wished to teach the Truth of Knowledge (ñāṇa-sacca) developed through that patience; thus, Sacca is taught after Khanti.

(8) Only one who is unshakably determined, thinking, 'I will speak only the truth even if it costs me my life,' can fulfill and complete truthful speech (sacca-vācā). Since Truthfulness can be fulfilled and completed through determination, and after teaching the unfailing nature of Truthfulness, He wished to show that Great Bodhisattvas do not waver or shake in that truthfulness. Furthermore, only one who possesses the knowledge of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇa) can firmly undertake the Perfections (pāramīs) and fulfill them to completion as undertaken. Therefore, after teaching the Truth of Knowledge, He wished to show the virtue that can bring about the foundation of the Perfections, which is the result of that Truth of Knowledge, and lead them to completion; thus, Determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is taught after Truthfulness.

(9) Only by developing the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) can the determination to work for the benefit of others be fulfilled and completed.

(Great Bodhisattvas who undertake the Perfections usually dwell primarily in loving-kindness.) Therefore, after teaching Determination, He wished to show the virtue of carrying out the welfare of others according to one's determination. Furthermore, for one who is firmly established in determination, the acquisition of wholesome states through loving-kindness becomes possible; thus, Loving-kindness (mettā) is taught after Determination.

(10) (If one develops only loving-kindness without equanimity, craving and greed (taṇhā-lobha) may deceive one by masquerading as loving-kindness. Only by practicing and developing equanimity from time to time can greed be prevented from entering and deceiving.) Thus, because pure loving-kindness can be achieved through equanimity; (Great Bodhisattvas carry out the welfare of beings through loving-kindness, and through equanimity, they remain indifferent and do not take offense at whatever wrongs those beings commit against them.) Therefore, after teaching the virtue of carrying out the welfare of beings, He wished to teach the virtue of being able to remain indifferent to the wrongs committed by those beings. Furthermore, only after developing the meditation on loving-kindness can the meditation on equanimity (upekkhā-bhāvanā) be successfully developed. Thus, after teaching the meditation on loving-kindness, He wished to show the consequence of that loving-kindness. Moreover, He wished to show the marvelous quality of being able to remain indifferent even towards beings whose welfare one desires; thus, Equanimity (upekkhā) is taught after Loving-kindness.

The ten Perfections, the nectar of wholesome deeds,
Connected and supported as appropriate,
Following the sequence of cause and effect,
Without teaching in a confused or disorderly manner,

## (5) Characteristics, Function, Manifestation, and Proximate Cause of the Perfections
In this section, we shall first explain the nature of Characteristic (lakkhaṇa), Function (rasa), Manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), and Proximate Cause (padaṭṭhāna). Then, we shall present these four aspects both collectively for all Perfections and individually for each, along with the identification of their ultimate realities (paramattha).

In the two ultimate realities of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa), only when one can comprehend and contemplate each state through these four aspects—Characteristic, Function, Manifestation, and Proximate Cause—can the knowledge that is pure from the view of self (atta-diṭṭhi), known as the Purification of View (diṭṭhi-visuddhi), arise. Similarly, in the case of these Perfections, knowledge regarding the Perfections will only be purified when one comprehends and contemplates all ten Perfections collectively and each one individually through these four aspects. This is why these four aspects are explained in the scriptures. Among them:

Characteristic (lakkhaṇa) means... (According to the verse in the Commentaries: 'Sāmaññaṃ vā sabhāvo vā, dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ mataṃ'—The general mark or the individual essence of states is known as the characteristic.) The general mark that is common to many states is called a general characteristic (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa), and the specific mark that is not common to others but is the unique property of a particular state is called a specific characteristic (visesa-lakkhaṇa). (For example, in the materiality known as the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), the marks of being subject to change, impermanence, suffering, and non-self are general marks common to many, while...
18:
120
the nature of hardness is a specific characteristic that is the unique property of the earth element alone, not common to others.)

If it is not common, it is the true individual essence;
If it is common, it is the general nature;
These two are to be taken as Characteristic.

Function (rasa) means... (According to the Commentary: 'Kiccaṃ vā tassa sampatti, rasoti paridīpaye'—The task of that ultimate reality or its achievement should be illustrated as Rasa.) The distinct task (kicca) of various ultimate realities or their achievement (sampatti), which is their occurrence in a complete and perfect manner, are both called Rasa.

The manifestation of the task and the achievement,
These should not be lacking;
Take these two as Rasa.

Manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) means... (According to the Commentary: 'Phalaṃ vā paccupaṭṭhāna-mupaṭṭhānākāropi vā'—The fruit of various ultimate realities or the mode in which they appear to the knowledge of the yogi is known as Paccupaṭṭhāna.) When a yogi penetrates and deeply contemplates ultimate realities with knowledge, the nature, function, cause, or fruit of that ultimate reality may appear. Any one of these four—nature, function, cause, or fruit—as it appears in the yogi's knowledge is called Manifestation.

Nature, function, or cause—
These three that appear,
And the one fruit that appears;
Take these as Manifestation.

Proximate Cause (padaṭṭhāna) means... (According to the statement: 'Āsannakāraṇaṃ yaṃ tu, padaṭṭhānanti taṃ mataṃ'—That which is the immediate cause is known as Padaṭṭhāna.) While there are two kinds of causes for various ultimate realities—proximate and remote—the proximate cause is called Padaṭṭhāna.

Only for the fruit,
The powerful and immediate cause;
Take that as Proximate Cause.

In this context, one should ask: "What are the Characteristic, Function, Manifestation, and Proximate Cause of the ten Perfections?"
19:

(The answer is:) The Characteristic, Function, Manifestation, and Proximate Cause common to all ten Perfections are: (1) All ten Perfections have the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of supporting others. (2) They have the function (rasa) of benefiting others; (alternatively) they have the achievement (sampatti-rasa) of unshakability. (3) They have the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of appearing in the yogi's knowledge as the nature of desiring the welfare of beings; (alternatively) they have the manifestation of the fruit (phala-paccupaṭṭhāna) which is Buddhahood. (4) They have Great Compassion (mahā-karuṇā) or (alternatively) the two states of Great Compassion and Skill in Means (upāya-kosalla-ñāṇa) mentioned earlier as their proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

For each individual Perfection:

(1) The volition (cetanā) that consists of giving away one's own possessions to others, based on Great Compassion and Skill in Means, is called the Perfection of Generosity (dāna-pāramī). That Perfection of Generosity has: (a) the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of relinquishing; (b) the function (rasa) of destroying greed (lobha) which is attached to the objects of donation; (c) the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of appearing in the yogi's knowledge as the nature of non-attachment to those objects of donation; (alternatively) it has the manifestation of the fruit (phala-paccupaṭṭhāna) which is the...
20:
122
production of the result, namely the perfection of existence and the perfection of wealth. (d) Since generosity can only occur when there is an object to be given, the Perfection of Generosity has the object of donation as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

Just as if one wishes to study and know the details of a person or an object, one must thoroughly study and know these four points: (a) the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), which is the mark common to many or the unique mark belonging to that one alone; (b) the function (rasa), which is the task of that person or object or the completeness of its causes; (c) the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), which is the result of that person or object or the mode that is memorable in the mind; (d) the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), which is the most immediate cause of that person or object—only then is it said that one has studied them completely. Similarly, in the case of the Perfection of Generosity: Generosity is a state that has the characteristic mark of relinquishing. It is a state that performs the task of destroying greed that is attached to objects of donation. When a yogi contemplates it minutely, it appears in his knowledge as the nature of non-attachment to objects of donation; (alternatively) it appears in his knowledge as a state that produces the results of success in life (bhava-sampatti) and success in wealth (bhoga-sampatti). It is a state that can only arise when there is the cause known as the object of donation. Only when one studies and knows it from these four sides, through these four major points, is it said that one knows the Perfection of Generosity completely and purely. (The same method applies to the Perfection of Morality and the others.)

(2) The states of bodily good conduct and verbal good conduct based on Great Compassion and Skill in Means (specifically, in terms of their ultimate nature...
21:
123
the mental factors of abstinence (virati-cetasikas) which refrain from misconduct that should not be done, and the states such as volition (cetanā) which cause the performance of duties, great and small, that should be done) are called the Perfection of Morality (sīla-pāramī). That Perfection of Morality has: (a) the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of composing, in the sense of not allowing bodily and verbal actions to occur as misconduct but making them occur as good conduct; and the characteristic of being the root cause of wholesome states. (b) The function (rasa) of discarding and destroying immorality (dussīlya), namely the three types of bodily misconduct and four types of verbal misconduct; (alternatively) the achievement (sampatti-rasa) of being complete in excellence as a faultless state that is not to be blamed or loathed. (c) The manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of appearing in the yogi's knowledge as the pure nature of bodily and verbal actions. (d) The two states of shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

(3) The group of mental states, preceded by the knowledge that sees the faults in the objects of desire (vatthu-kāma), the defilements of desire (kilesa-kāma), and various existences, and which desires to be liberated from that existence of desire, based on Great Compassion and Skill in Means, is called the Perfection of Renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī). That Perfection of Renunciation has: (a) the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of departing from the existences of desire. (b) The function (rasa) of clearly exposing the faults of those existences of desire. (c) The manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of appearing in the yogi's knowledge as the nature of turning away from those existences of desire (the nature of turning one's back on the existences of desire). (d) The knowledge of spiritual urgency (saṃvega-ñāṇa) as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

(4) The mental factor of wisdom (paññā-cetasika) which is capable of penetratingly knowing the general characteristics and specific characteristics of various states, based on Great Compassion and Skill in Means, is called the Perfection of Wisdom (paññā-pāramī). That Perfection of Wisdom has: (a) the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of penetrating the true nature; (alternatively) it is very skillful...
22:
It has the characteristic of penetrating the general and specific natures of objects without error, just as an arrow shot by an archer hits the target without fail. (b) It has the function (rasa) of illuminating the object like a lamp (destroying the darkness of delusion that conceals the true nature of the object). (c) It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of non-confusion regarding the object, appearing to the yogi's insight like a man pointing out the right path to one who is lost and suffering in the middle of a forest. (Alternatively) It has the manifestation of the effect (phala) of removing the delusion of confusion regarding the object. (d) It has concentration (samādhi) as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). (Alternatively) It has the Four Noble Truths as its proximate cause.

(5) Viriya Pāramī (The Perfection of Energy) is the effort exerted for the welfare and benefit of others, both physically and mentally, based on Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) and Skillful Means (upāyakosalla). (The cause that produces benefit is called 'hita' in Pali and 'asī-apwā' in Burmese). This Perfection of Energy has: (a) the characteristic of exerting effort (enduring hardship); (b) the function of supporting and encouraging its associated mental states so they do not slacken in wholesome deeds; (c) the manifestation of non-collapse, appearing to the yogi's insight as the opposite of sloth and torpor (thina-middha) which cause regression in wholesome deeds; (d) the proximate cause of the sense of urgency (saṃvega) or (alternatively) the eight grounds for arousing energy (vīriyārambhavatthu).

(The insight dominated by moral dread (ottappa) that fears the dangers of birth, aging, sickness, death, and the woeful states is called the sense of urgency or saṃvega-ñāṇa.)
23:
The eight grounds for arousing energy (vīriyārambhavatthu) are as follows:

"Work, travel, illness, and alms food—each of these four has two aspects. These are the eight grounds for arousing energy to be noted here."

According to this mnemonic verse from the Paramatthasarūpa (section on meditation) by the Most Venerable Mahāvisuddhārāma Sayadaw: one should know the eight grounds for arousing energy (vīriyārambhavatthu) as two related to new work (navakamma), two related to traveling, two related to illness, and two related to alms food. Among them:

Regarding the two related to new work: (1) Reflecting, "I will have to perform new work such as sewing robes. While doing such work, it will not be easy to attend to the instructions of the Buddhas; I will strive in advance starting from now." (2) After completing the work, reflecting, "I have finished the new work. While I was doing it, I could not attend to the instructions of the Buddhas at all. Now I must strive with double effort to make up for it."

Regarding the two related to traveling: (1) When one has to go on a journey, reflecting, "I will have to go on a journey. While traveling, it will not be easy to attend to the instructions of the Buddhas; I will strive in advance starting from now." (2) After completing the journey, reflecting, "I have finished the journey. While I was traveling, I could not attend to the instructions of the Buddhas at all. Now I must strive with double effort..."
24:
...to make up for it." These are the two.

Regarding the two related to illness: (1) When a slight illness occurs, reflecting, "A slight illness has come upon me. There is a possibility that this illness might increase. Before it gets worse, I will strive in advance starting from now." (2) During convalescence, reflecting, "It has not been long since I recovered from illness. There is a possibility that the old illness might recur. Before it recurs, I will strive starting from now." These are the two.

Regarding the two related to alms food: (1) When not receiving enough alms food, reflecting, "I did not receive enough food from the village. Since I have eaten only a little, my body is light and strong, and I am not oppressed by sloth and torpor; thus I am capable of working. I will strive right now." (2) When receiving sufficient alms food, reflecting, "Because I received sufficient food from the village, I am strong and capable of working. I will strive right now." These are the two.

These eight types of reflection (to prompt the exertion of energy) are called the eight grounds for arousing energy (vīriyārambhavatthu).

(In these same eight situations—after finishing work, after traveling, after recovering from illness, or when not getting enough food—thinking wrongly, "I am very tired, I should sleep," or when having work to do or a journey to make, thinking, "I will be tired, I should sleep," or when illness first begins...
25:
...thinking, "I am very weak, I should sleep," or when receiving sufficient food, thinking, "My stomach is very heavy, I should sleep"—these eight types of wrong thinking that prevent the exertion of wholesome effort are called the eight grounds for laziness (kusītavatthu). These eight grounds for arousing energy and eight grounds for laziness were taught by the Buddha in the Saṅgīti Sutta, Pāthika Vagga of the Dīgha Nikāya.

(6) Khanti Pāramī (The Perfection of Patience) is the endurance of the faults of beings and formations, based on Great Compassion and Skillful Means. (In terms of ultimate reality, it is the group of consciousness and mental factors led by non-hatred (adosa) manifesting as the quality of patience). This Perfection of Patience has: (a) the characteristic of endurance; (b) the function of overcoming both desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) that are wished for and undesirable objects (aniṭṭhārammaṇa) that are not wished for. (One who lacks patience is carried away by greed when encountering desirable objects and by anger when encountering undesirable objects. Such a person is said to be overcome by objects. One who possesses patience can withstand both without succumbing to greed or anger; thus, it is said that patience overcomes the objects). (c) the manifestation of allowing desirable and undesirable objects to be present within oneself (the ability to give them space), appearing as such to the yogi's insight. (Alternatively) It has the manifestation of non-opposition. (d) the proximate cause of seeing things as they truly are.
26:
(7) Saccā Pāramī (The Perfection of Truthfulness) is the nature of not failing or deviating from one's own promise or intention, based on Great Compassion and Skillful Means. (Under this Saccā Pāramī, the mental factors of abstinence (virati), volition (cetanā), and wisdom (paññā) are to be taken as the ultimate realities according to the context). This Perfection of Truthfulness has: (a) the characteristic of non-deviation; (b) the function of manifesting the nature of truth; (c) the manifestation of being sweet, noble, and pleasant, appearing as such to the yogi's insight; (d) the proximate cause of purity in body, speech, and mind.

(8) Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī (The Perfection of Determination) is the unwavering undertaking of wholesome deeds based on Great Compassion and Skillful Means. (It is the group of consciousness and mental factors occurring in the manner of such undertaking). This Perfection of Determination has: (a) the characteristic of standing firm in the perfections, relinquishment (cāga), and conduct (cariya), which are the requisites for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) and the foundation of omniscience; (b) the function of overcoming unwholesome states that are contrary to the requisites for enlightenment; (c) the manifestation of being unshakable in the task of fulfilling the requisites for enlightenment; (d) the proximate cause of the requisites for enlightenment themselves.

(9) Mettā Pāramī (The Perfection of Loving-kindness) is the mental factor of non-hatred (adosa), also known as non-ill-will (abyāpāda), which promotes the welfare and happiness of the world of beings, based on Great Compassion and Skillful Means. This Perfection of Loving-kindness has: (a) the characteristic of occurring in the manner of desiring the welfare of beings; (b) the function of promoting welfare as desired.
27:
(Alternatively) It has the function of removing the nine grounds of resentment and nine grounds of malice. (c) It has the manifestation of being cool, appearing as such to the yogi's insight. (d) It has the proximate cause of viewing beings in a lovable manner. (If one views beings in a hateful manner, loving-kindness cannot be developed).

(10) Upekkhā Pāramī (The Perfection of Equanimity) is the mental factor of neutrality (tatramajjhattatā) which, based on Great Compassion and Skillful Means, discards both love and hatred toward desirable and undesirable beings and formations, remaining impartial. This Perfection of Equanimity has: (a) the characteristic of occurring in a neutral manner, without love or hatred; (b) the function of viewing things with impartiality; (c) the manifestation of subsiding hatred and love, appearing as such to the yogi's insight; (d) the proximate cause of reflecting on the fact that beings have kamma as their own property (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa).

In describing the ultimate realities of these ten perfections, the qualifying phrase "based on Great Compassion and Skillful Means" is placed at the beginning of every perfection because, in the mental continuum of Great Bodhisattvas, only those acts of giving, virtue, etc., that arise based on Great Compassion and Skillful Means are called 'Perfections' (Pāramīs).

When the ten perfections, deep in Dhamma,
And their fourfold aspects are truly understood,
Contemplated repeatedly with the eye of wisdom,
And fully developed within one's own continuum,
Then indeed, suffering will surely come to an end.
28:
## (6) The Causes of the Perfections
If it is asked, "What are the fundamental causes of these perfections?"

(a) The Resolve (abhinīhāra),
(b) Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) and Skillful Means (upāyakosalla),
(c) The four Buddha-grounds (buddhabhūmi),
(d) The sixteen noble inclinations (ajjhāsaya),
(e) The reflective insights (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) that contemplate the faults of not giving, etc., and the benefits of giving, etc.,
(f) The fifteen types of conduct (caraṇa) and five supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) along with their attendant causes—
Briefly, it should be said that these are the fundamental causes of the perfections.

To answer in detail:

## (a) Abhinīhāra (The Resolve)
(Abhi = towards omniscience; nīhāra = directing the mind; it means the aspiration to become an Omniscient Buddha.)
One should reconsider the eight factors for receiving a prophecy mentioned in the section on the rarity of a Buddha's appearance. When reaching a life where these eight factors are fully present (such as the life of Sumedha), due to the prompting of the fulfillment of these eight factors, in the mental continuum of Great Bodhisattvas like the wise Sumedha, without anyone else having to suggest it—
29:
131

“Having crossed the great ocean of Saṃsāra by my own strength, I shall also help other beings (Veneyya) to cross. Having striven to be free from the great prison of Saṃsāra by my own strength, I shall also liberate other beings. Having striven to tame my own faculties, I shall also discipline and tame other beings. Having striven to extinguish the heat of my own defilements (Kilesa), I shall also cool the defilements of other beings. Having striven to attain Nibbāna, the state of supreme peace, I shall also lead other beings to attain that Dhamma. Having striven to extinguish the great flames of the three rounds of existence (Vaṭṭa), I shall also extinguish them for other beings. Having striven to become one who is purified from the dust of defilements, I shall also purify other beings. Having striven to realize the Four Noble Truths, I shall also make other beings realize them. (In short: Having striven to become a Buddha, I shall save other beings.)”

In this manner, the great wholesome consciousness (Mahā-kusala citta) and its mental factors (Cetasika) desiring to become an Omniscient Buddha arose continuously and repeatedly. Such great wholesome consciousness and mental factors that aspire to become an Omniscient Buddha are called the Great Resolve (Abhinīhāra-kusala). This extraordinary merit of Abhinīhāra is the fundamental root cause of all Ten Perfections (Pāramīs).

Indeed, it is because of the arising of this extraordinary merit of Abhinīhāra that the Great Bodhisattas receive the Definite Prophecy (Niyata-byādita). After receiving it, they systematically reflect upon the Perfections with their own wisdom, undertake them, and fulfill them to the highest pinnacle.
30:
132

This extraordinary merit of Abhinīhāra has: (a) the characteristic (Lakkhaṇa) of directing the mind towards Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa); (b) the function (Rasa) of aspiring, “Having become an Omniscient Buddha, may I be able to accomplish and carry out the welfare and happiness of beings up to the attainment of Nibbāna”; (c) the manifestation (Paccupaṭṭhāna) appearing in the yogi’s knowledge as the fundamental root cause of the requisites of enlightenment (Bodhi-sambhāra); (d) the proximate cause (Padaṭṭhāna) of Great Compassion (Mahā-karuṇā) (or, alternatively, the fulfillment of the special sufficing conditions (Upanissaya) to be mentioned later).

Because it arises with a view toward the inconceivable attributes of a Buddha and the incomparable welfare of the world of beings, this extraordinary merit of Abhinīhāra should be understood as the primary root cause of the entire collection of Perfections (Pāramī), Relinquishments (Cāga), and Conduct (Cariya), and as a great merit endowed with excellent and incomparable power. To briefly show its special potency:

As soon as this extraordinary merit of Abhinīhāra arises, the Great Being (Bodhisatta) is considered one who has entered the field of practice (Paṭipatti) to attain Omniscience. Furthermore, because the Great Being who possesses this merit of Abhinīhāra will certainly attain Buddhahood without fail, and because after reaching and attaining this extraordinary merit, there is no turning back (no changing the aspiration to another type), he receives the title ‘Bodhisatta’ (Buddha-to-be). (Until this great merit arises, one cannot yet be called a Bodhisatta.) From that time onwards, the Great Being possesses the mental disposition to attain Omniscience and the capacity to fulfill the Perfections, Relinquishments, and Conduct to the highest pinnacle. That Abhinīhāra—
31:
133

Because he was a possessor of that merit of Abhinīhāra, the hermit Sumedha reflected on the Perfections accurately and without error through the Knowledge of Investigating the Perfections (Pāramī-pavicaya-ñāṇa), also known as the Knowledge of the Self-Enlightened (Sayambhū-ñāṇa), which is the precursor to Omniscience. Having done so, he undertook them firmly and practiced them for four incalculable periods (Asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (Kappa).

Furthermore, that extraordinary merit of Abhinīhāra has:
(I) Four supporting causes (Pccaya),
(II) Four direct causes (Hētu),
(III) Four powers (Bala). Among them:

(I) The four supporting causes (Pccaya-hetu) are as follows:
(1) When a noble man who will aspire for Buddhahood personally sees a living Buddha performing a miracle with great Buddha-majesty, he reflects: “How great is the majesty of Omniscience! Because of attaining Omniscience, the Blessed One possesses such wonderful and extraordinary qualities and inconceivable majesty.” Based on that personally witnessed Buddha-majesty, his mind inclines toward Omniscience.
(2) Even if he does not see it himself, his mind may incline toward Omniscience based on hearing from others that “The Blessed One is endowed with such and such majesty.”
(3) Even if he neither sees the Buddha’s majesty himself nor hears it from others, his mind may incline toward Omniscience—
32:
134

—by hearing the Dhamma concerning the Buddha’s majesty as taught by the Blessed One.
(4) Even without the preceding three causes, because the noble man who wishes to aspire for Buddhahood himself possesses a very noble disposition, he reflects: “I shall protect the lineage and traditional nature (Dhammatā) of those Blessed Ones so that it does not disappear.” Thus, respecting and honoring the Dhamma exceedingly, his mind inclines toward Omniscience based on that spirit of Revering the Dhamma (Dhamma-garu).

Therefore:
1. Personally beholding the majesty of a living Buddha; (or)
2. Hearing about it from another who has personally seen it; (or)
3. Hearing the Dhamma concerning the Buddha’s majesty as taught by the Blessed One; (or)
4. Cultivating a spirit of Revering the Dhamma due to having a very noble disposition (Āsaya) oneself—
These four are called the supporting causes (Pccaya) of the extraordinary merit of Abhinīhāra.

(II) The four direct causes (Hētu) are as follows:
(I) The perfection of sufficing condition (Upanissaya-sampadā), which is having performed extraordinary merits (Adhikāra) in the presence of previous Buddhas. (II) The perfection of compassion (Karuṇā-sampadā), which is having a naturally great foundation of compassion and the desire to remove the suffering of beings even at the cost of one’s own life.
33:
135

(III) The perfection of zeal (Ussāha-sampadā), which is not becoming weary (not being discouraged) and not being afraid of practicing the difficult practices for the sake of the welfare of beings and the suffering of the round of existence, even if one must strive for a very long time to complete the great state of Buddhahood one desires. (IV) Good friendship (Kalyāṇamittatā), which is associating with a good friend who restrains one from what is not beneficial and connects one with what is beneficial—these are the four. (It is because of these four direct causes that one can aspire for Buddhahood; without these four causes, one cannot make the aspiration.)

Among those four, regarding (I) Upanissaya-sampadā: the Great Bodhisatta has previously made aspirations to become a Buddha in the presence of former Buddhas, both mentally and verbally. (The number of Buddhas is not specified.) Therefore, the Great Bodhisatta’s inclination and disposition (Ajjhāsaya) are always leaning and inclining toward Omniscience. He is also always leaning and inclining toward practicing for the welfare of beings. Because of the presence of this Upanissaya-sampadā, Bodhisattas possess: (1) faculties (Indriya) that are superior to those of prospective Paccekabuddhas and prospective Disciples (Sāvaka); (2) the ability to practice for the benefit of others more exceptionally than they; (3) skillfulness in practicing for the benefit of others more exceptionally than they, and the possession of the Knowledge of What is Possible and Impossible (Ṭhānāṭhāna-kosalla-ñāṇa). (By considering these three points, one should know that the Great Bodhisattas have accumulated extraordinary merit in the presence of previous Buddhas.)

Regarding (IV) Kalyāṇamittatā, the Good Friend whom the Bodhisatta associated with and relied upon is—
34:
136

—a person endowed with these eight qualities: Faith (Saddhā), Virtue (Sīla), Learning (Suta), Generosity (Cāga), Effort (Vīriya), Mindfulness (Sati), Concentration (Samādhi), and Wisdom (Paññā).

Faith, virtue, learning, and generosity,
Effort, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—
These eight are the true attributes of a Good Friend (Kalyāṇamitta).

That Good Friend, being endowed with faith, believes in the Omniscience of the Buddha and the law of Kamma and its results. (One without faith cannot believe in Omniscience and Kamma and its results.) Through that belief, he does not abandon the desire for the welfare of beings, which is the root cause of Omniscience. Because of being endowed with virtue, he is one who is loved and respected by beings. Because of being endowed with learning, he can preach profound Dhamma that can carry out the welfare and happiness of beings. Because of being endowed with generosity, he is one with few desires, easily satisfied, secluded from the defilements of sensual pleasure, and unmixed with defilements in various situations. Because of being endowed with effort, he is one who always strives in the practice for the welfare of beings to flourish. Because of being endowed with mindfulness, he is one who is never forgetful or negligent in wholesome deeds. Because of being endowed with concentration, he is one with an undistracted (steady) mind. Because of being endowed with wisdom, he is one who knows the truth.

That Good Friend, after reflecting on the state and tendencies of wholesome and unwholesome dhammas (with mindfulness), and knowing according to reality what is and is not beneficial for beings (with wisdom), possesses a firm and steady mind (with concentration) and strives with strong persistence to remove beings from what is not beneficial and connect them with what is beneficial (with effort).
35:
137

By associating with and relying on such a Good Friend endowed with these attributes, the Bodhisatta purifies his sufficing conditions (Upanissaya-sampatti) more and more. Being endowed with a very pure disposition (Āsaya) of wisdom and the effort (Payoga) in very pure bodily and verbal actions, and becoming one endowed with the four great strengths, he is soon able to fulfill the eight factors for receiving the prophecy simultaneously. Having made the great merit of aspiring for Buddhahood, called the Mahābhinīhāra, with great courage, he stands in the state of a true Bodhisatta. From that time on, he no longer changes his aspiration for Buddhahood to another; he becomes a Great Definite Person (Niyata-puggala) who is certain to become a Buddha without fail.

(III) The four great powers (Bala) are as follows:
(a) Internal Power (Ajjhattika-bala): This refers to the extreme inclination of the mind toward Omniscience (Sammā-sambodhi), relying on one’s own strength through the spirit of Revering the Dhamma (Dhamma-garava), which is the fourth of the previously mentioned four supporting causes. With this internal power, the Bodhisatta, honoring himself and relying on moral shame (Hiri), fulfills his aspiration and the Perfections, and attains Omniscience.
(b) External Power (Bāhira-bala): This refers to the extreme inclination of the mind toward Omniscience, relying on the first, second, and third of the previously mentioned four supporting causes. With this external power, the Bodhisatta, honoring the external world and relying on the uplifting pride that “I am a noble man fully endowed with the capacity to become a Buddha,” becomes endowed with the extraordinary merit of Abhinīhāra, fulfills the Perfections, and attains Omniscience.
36:
138
(c) Upanissaya-bala: (This refers to the intense inclination toward Omniscient Knowledge, based on the attainment of strong dependence (upanissaya-sampadā), which is the first of the four root causes previously mentioned.) Through this power of strong dependence, the Bodhisatta possesses sharp faculties and a pure nature; being mindful and endowed with the extraordinary merit of aspiration (abhinīhāra), he fulfills the perfections (pāramīs) and attains Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa).
(d) Payoga-bala: (This refers to being endowed with the successful effort and energy sufficient to attain Omniscient Knowledge, and the constant, respectful practice of the merits of strong dependence and special services (adhikāra).) Through this power of effort, the Bodhisatta is endowed with pure bodily and verbal actions, performs the merits of special services incessantly, and being endowed with the merit of aspiration, fulfills the perfections and attains Omniscient Knowledge.
When these four conditions (paccaya), four root causes (hetu), and four powers (bala) are fulfilled, and one reaches a state of life such as that of Sumedha the Wise, the eight factors for receiving a definite prophecy (niyata-byādika) converge. Driven by the convergence of these eight factors, as previously shown, the wholesome consciousness and mental factors of aspiration (abhinīhāra) arise, thinking: "I shall strive with unrelenting effort to become a Buddha and save the veneyya beings (those ready for guidance)." This great merit of aspiration is the fundamental root cause of the perfections.
37:
139
## The Great Wonders
Due to the arising of the great merit of aspiration, the following great wonders occur for the Great Bodhisatta: (1) Embracing all beings as if they were his own children; (2) The continuity of his mind is not defiled by the power of unwholesome states (there is no defilement caused by the agitation of kilesas); (3) All his desires, actions, and speech are solely for the purpose of carrying out the welfare and happiness of beings; (4) There is no regression in his perfections (pāramī), generosity (cāga), and conduct (cariya); instead, they only progress, increase, and mature further and further.
Because of the occurrence of these great wonders, the Bodhisatta is endowed with a great stream of merit and a flow of wholesome deeds. Thus, he becomes a noble personage worthy of the supreme offerings of beings, an incomparable field for sowing the seeds of merit, and a great object of veneration.
## (b) Great Compassion and Skill in Means
Just like the extraordinary merit of aspiration, Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) and Skill in Means (upāyakosalla-ñāṇa) are also fundamental causes of the perfections. (These two, Great Compassion and Skill in Means, have been described above.)
Because of this Great Compassion and Skill in Means, the Great Bodhisattas are always able to strive for the benefit of others without regard for their own self-interest. Even though they must practice the conducts of Bodhisattas which are difficult for ordinary people to perform, they do not count them as exhausting. Because these two qualities are established in them,
38:
140
when beings perform acts such as developing devotion and faith, paying homage, or recollecting the virtues of the Great Bodhisattas, wholesome merits that lead to welfare and happiness can arise and be fulfilled for those beings.
To describe further... among those two qualities of compassion and wisdom that arise in the Bodhisatta's continuity: through wisdom, he attains Buddhahood; through compassion, he performs the duties of a Buddha. Through wisdom, he himself is able to cross the great ocean of saṃsāra; through compassion, he is able to save the veneyya beings. Through wisdom, he clearly perceives the suffering of others; through compassion, he strives to cure and remove that suffering. Through wisdom, he is weary of suffering; through compassion, he accepts that very suffering, which should be wearying, as if it were happiness for the sake of saving veneyya beings. Through wisdom, he turns toward Nibbāna; through compassion, he returns to wander in the round of saṃsāra to save beings. In this way and others, the virtues of compassion and wisdom are many. These two, compassion and wisdom, are not only the causes of the perfections; they are also the great root causes of the aspiration for Buddhahood.
## (c) The Four Buddhabhūmi
Just like aspiration, compassion, and wisdom, these four Buddhabhūmi (grounds of a Buddha) are also root causes of the perfections: (1) Ussāha, (2) Ummanga, (3) Avatthāna, (4) Hitacariyā. Among these:
(1) Ussāha refers to the energy (viriya) of unrelenting effort in the perfections (pāramī), generosity (cāga), and conduct (cariya). (2) Ummanga refers to...
39:
141
the Skill in Means (upāyakosalla-ñāṇa) mentioned previously. (3) Avatthāna refers to the unwavering and firm stability in the qualities that lead to Buddhahood. (4) Hitacariyā refers to these two: the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) and the development of compassion (karuṇā-bhāvanā).
These four qualities are called the four Buddhabhūmi because they are the causes for the arising of Omniscient Knowledge.
## (d) The 16 Great Dispositions (Ajjhāsaya)
(Disposition (ajjhāsaya) is a type of underlying trait that dominates and dwells within the continuity of beings. This disposition is of two kinds: good disposition and bad disposition.)
Because the Great Bodhisattas see the faults in the objects of sense pleasure (vatthu-kāma) and household life (gharāvāsa), noble qualities such as non-greed (alobha) become predominant. The state of having a mind that is always inclined and leaning toward deliverance from those sense pleasures and household life is called the disposition for renunciation (nekkhamma-ajjhāsaya). These dispositions are six: the disposition for renunciation, the disposition for solitude (paviveka), the disposition for non-greed, the disposition for non-hatred (adosa), the disposition for non-delusion (amoha), and the disposition for deliverance (nissaraṇa). Including the dispositions for giving (dāna), virtue (sīla), and so on, there are ten more, making sixteen in total. Among these:
Because the Great Bodhisattas have a strong underlying trait of the disposition for renunciation, they see the faults in sense pleasures and household life. Because they have a strong underlying trait of the disposition for solitude, they see the faults in delighting in company. Because they have strong underlying traits of the dispositions for non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion,
40:
142
they see the faults in greed, hatred, and delusion. Because they have a strong underlying trait of the disposition for deliverance, they see the faults in all forms of existence. Without seeing the faults in greed and so on, and without the predominance of non-greed and so on, the perfections such as giving cannot occur. Therefore, these six great dispositions are also root causes of the perfections.
Similarly, the ten great dispositions such as the disposition for giving are also root causes of the perfections. (The state of always having a mind inclined toward giving and so on, due to seeing the faults in the respective opposite qualities and the predominance of non-greed and so on, is called the disposition for giving, etc.)
Because the Great Bodhisattas have an intense disposition for giving, they see the faults in stinginess (macchariya), which is the opposite of giving, and they fulfill the perfection of giving completely. Because they have an intense disposition for virtue, they see the faults in immoralities (dussīlya) known as misconduct, and they fulfill the perfection of virtue completely. The same should be understood for the remaining perfections.
Specifically, the opposite of the disposition for renunciation is sense pleasure and household life; the opposite of the disposition for wisdom (ñāṇa) is delusion (moha) and doubt (vicikicchā); the opposite of the disposition for energy (viriya) is laziness (kosajja); the opposite of the disposition for patience (khanti) is anger (akkhanti); the opposite of the disposition for truthfulness (sacca) is falsehood (musāvāda); the opposite of the disposition for resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) is instability (anadhiṭṭhāna) in wholesome deeds; the opposite of the disposition for loving-kindness (mettā) is ill-will (byāpāda); and the opposite of the disposition for equanimity (upekkhā) is the desirable and undesirable worldly conditions (lokadhamma).
41:
143
Because the Great Bodhisattas have an intense disposition for equanimity, they see the faults in the desirable and undesirable worldly conditions, which are the opposites of equanimity, and they fulfill the perfection of equanimity completely. Therefore, these ten dispositions such as the disposition for giving are also root causes of the perfections.
## (e) Reflective Knowledges (Paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) on the Faults of Not Giving, etc., and the Benefits of Giving, etc.
The reflective knowledges that contemplate the faults in the ten things such as not giving and not undertaking virtue, and the reflective knowledges that contemplate the benefits in the ten things such as giving and undertaking virtue, are also root causes of the perfections.
(Those who wish to aspire for Buddhahood should pay special attention to and study this section.)
(a) The detailed way of reflecting on the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) is as follows:
For beings whose minds are attached to and cannot bear to relinquish their own possessions such as land, gold, silver, cattle, buffaloes, female servants, male servants, children, and wives, those possessions such as land are objects of sense pleasure (vatthu-kāma). As such, they are things that are craved and yearned for by many... they are shared with the five enemies... they are causes of quarrels and disputes... they lack essence... if it is thought that one must oppress others to obtain or protect those possessions, one will oppress them ruthlessly... when those possessions are destroyed, one suffers greatly from sorrow (soka) and lamentation (parideva)... and for those who have a mind of stinginess (macchariya) based on attachment to those possessions,
42:
144
they must go to the woeful planes (apāya). Reflecting thus, "Indeed, these possessions bring about various and many kinds of harm; only the single act of giving, which is the relinquishing and donating of these possessions, is the cause of happiness," the one who is a Bodhisatta should maintain heedfulness (appamāda) in the act of giving.
Alternatively, when a solicitor comes to beg, one should reflect: "This person is very intimate with me, for they have openly spoken even of their shameful needs which should be kept secret for personal reasons"; or "This is a person who points out a good method and rule, saying, 'Take these possessions of mine, which I must leave behind, to the world beyond in this way'"; or "While the world is burning with the fire of death (maraṇa-aggi), blazing brightly like a house on fire, this is a great friend who helps to carry my belongings out of this burning world-mansion to escape the danger of fire"; or "This is like a great, excellent place to store and keep those belongings that have been carried out so they are not consumed by fire"; or "Because they are a companion in the merit of giving and because they are the cause for the fulfillment of the extremely rare and noble merits of the Buddhabhūmi, they are a very noble spiritual friend (kalyāṇa-mitta)."
Similarly, one should reflect: "This person has commended me in a very noble deed; therefore, I should certainly and truly perform that which has been commended"; or "My life will surely perish; therefore, even if not asked, I..."
43: "It is worthy to give; how much more so when asked? It is certainly worthy to give." ... "Great Bodhisattas with a strong inclination for giving search for recipients even if they are hard to find. By my merit, a recipient has arrived on his own." ... "Giving is, in its true nature, an act of exalting myself by means of giving to the recipient." ... "Just as I exalt myself, I should also exalt all these beings." ... "Without a recipient, how can my Perfection of Giving (Dāna Pāramī) be fulfilled?" ... "I have kept all these possessions for the sake of recipients." ... "When will recipients take my property on their own, as if it were their own, without me having to offer?" ... "How can I become dear to recipients, and they become dear to me?" ... "How can I be delighted during and after the act of giving?" ... "How can recipients and the inclination for giving arise within me?" ... "How can I give by knowing the hearts' desires of recipients without them asking?" ... "It is a great deception for me not to give when both the gift and the recipient are present." ... "How can I sacrifice my limbs and my life to recipients?" One should always incline the mind toward such generosity.
44:
(Alternatively) "Just as a cricket, when cast away, returns only to the one who cast it away without lingering, so too does the result of an action follow only the donor who gives generously without expecting a reward." Having reflected thus, one should cultivate a mind that does not desire or expect rewards. (Reward here refers to human or celestial bliss resulting from that gift, not Buddhahood.)

## Mindset When Giving
When giving, if the recipient is a loved one (piya), one should feel joy, thinking, "My beloved is asking of me." If the recipient is a neutral person (majjhatta/udāsīna), one should reflect with joy, "This person who asks of me will surely become my friend through this gift." If the recipient is an enemy, one should reflect with even greater joy, "An enemy asks of me. This enemy who asks of me will surely become my dear friend through this gift."

As mentioned, one should give by cultivating compassion preceded by loving-kindness (mettā) toward neutral persons and enemies, just as one does toward a loved one.

## If Greed is Extremely Difficult to Overcome
If greed (lobha) has been ingrained and practiced for a long time in the continuum of the one who aspires to be a Buddha,
45:
and attachment arises to the point of being unable to give or sacrifice the objects of donation, that person who professes to be a Bodhisatta should reflect as follows:

"O virtuous Bodhisatta, when you made the aspiration for Buddhahood to attain Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), did you not surrender this body, the merits gained from sacrificing it, and the fruits of those merits for the benefit of beings? This being so, your attachment to external objects (bāhira-vatthu) outside your current body is like an elephant's bath. Therefore, you should not allow attachment to any object to arise."

(While other beings bathe to wash away bodily impurities, an elephant's bath is not for washing away filth but for breaking and destroying the lotus stalks in the water. Thus, an elephant's bath is a fruitless bath. Similarly, attachment to external objects is like an elephant's bath because it cannot achieve the fruit of Buddhahood.)

As a worldly analogy, when a great medicinal tree exists, those who need the roots dig them up and take them; those who need the shoots, bark, trunk, forks, heartwood, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits take them. Even when they are taken, the great medicinal tree never has various distracting thoughts like, 'These people are taking my things.' Similarly, I, who strive
46:
for the welfare of the entire world of beings, should not harbor even an atom's weight of perverted or wrong thoughts, no matter how this miserable, ungrateful, and perpetually impure body is used for the benefit of others. All the four great elements (mahābhūta), both internal and external, have the nature of breaking apart and perishing; there is no distinction between internal and external. Despite there being no distinction, thinking 'I, mine, my soul' is merely the vanity of pure delusion (moha). Therefore, just as with external possessions, you should have a mind that has surrendered the entire body, without any lingering attachment even to internal parts such as hands, feet, eyes, flesh, and blood, letting those who desire such parts take whatever large or small limbs they wish."

When one reflects in this way, the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of that Bodhisatta—who has a mind surrendered for the sake of Omniscience and has no lingering attachment to body or life—become increasingly and easily purified. The noble Bodhisatta, endowed with such extremely pure bodily, verbal, and mental actions, becomes very pure in livelihood, stands in the good practice that leads to Nibbāna, and is endowed with the wisdom that clearly sees the causes of ruin and progress. Thus, he truly becomes a great noble being who can exalt all beings through material gifts (vatthu-dāna), the gift of fearlessness (abhaya-dāna), and the gift of Dhamma (dhamma-dāna) more than before.

(This is the detailed method of reflection on the Perfection of Giving.)
47:
(b) The detailed method of reflection on the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla Pāramī) is as follows:

"This virtue (sīla) is the pure water of Dhamma (dhamma-re-sin) that can wash away the stains and taints of defilements (kilesa) which cannot be washed away by the waters of the Ganges and so on. It is the great medicine for removing the heat of passion (rāga) and others, which cannot be removed by sandalwood, gold, and so on. It is the ornament of the wise, which has no connection at all with the common ornaments of ordinary people such as pearl strings, diadems, and earrings. It is a type of fragrance suitable for anointing at all times, which does not need to be naturally purified or prepared because it is fragrant in all directions. It is a great and noble mantra of subjugation (vasīkaraṇa-manta) because it brings about benefits such as receiving faithful homage and offerings from noble classes like kings, brahmins, and householders, as well as from devas and brahmas. It is a great stairway for ascending to the celestial and brahma realms. It is the cause for attaining meditative absorptions (jhāna) and higher knowledges (abhiññā). It is a great highway leading to the city of Nibbāna. It is the fundamental basis and foundation for the three types of Bodhi (Enlightenment). Because it can fulfill all that is desired and longed for, it is more beautiful and superior to the Cintāmaṇi jewel and the Padethā (wishing) tree." In this way, one should reflect on the virtues and benefits of Sīla.

(The commentaries state that the disadvantages of not being endowed with virtue should be reflected upon through the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta and others. Here, I shall present a summary of the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta from the Sattaka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.)

On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosala country accompanied by a large group of monks,
48:
He saw a great mass of fire in a certain place. He stepped off the main road and sat down at the foot of a tree on a seat prepared by the Venerable Ānanda, made of his outer robe folded in four. Then He addressed the monks:

"Monks, which is better: to sit or lie down embracing that great mass of fire, or to sit or lie down embracing a maiden with soft and tender touch from the khattiya, brahmin, or householder class?"

The monks (with a limited view) replied that it is better to sit or lie down embracing a maiden. Then the Blessed One said:

"For a person of bad virtue (dussīla), it is better to embrace the great mass of fire, for that can cause suffering for only one life. Embracing a maiden, however, leads to the lower realms and is not better." Then He continued in order:

(2) "Which is better: to have both calves wrapped with a strong hair-rope (woven from cow or horse hair) by a strong man and have the skin, flesh, nerves, and bones rubbed and torn, or to enjoy receiving the homage of donors?"

(3) "Which is better: to be pierced in the middle of the chest with a sharp spear by a strong man, or to receive the salutation of donors with joined palms?"
49:
(4) "Which is better: to have the body wrapped with a glowing, red-hot iron plate by a strong man, or to use the robes offered out of faith by donors?"

(5) "Which is better: to have the mouth pried open with a red-hot iron spike by a strong man and have a glowing, red-hot iron ball inserted into the mouth (burning the lips, mouth, tongue, throat, chest, stomach, and small intestines) and passing all the way through the lower exit, or to enjoy the alms-food offered out of faith by donors?"

(6) "Which is better: to be firmly grasped by the head or shoulders (so as not to struggle) by a strong man and be forced to sit or lie down on a glowing, red-hot iron couch or iron chair, or to use the couch or chair offered out of faith by donors?"

(7) "Which is better: to be held upside down by the feet by a strong man and be thrown into a large, boiling iron cauldron, or to use the monastery offered out of faith by donors?"

When asked, the monks replied as before (with a limited view), and the Blessed One said:
