152

He (the Buddha) taught in detail that for an immoral person, suffering may occur for only one lifetime, and thus the first six (types of persons) are noble, while the latter six lead to the woeful states and are not noble. At the conclusion, he taught:

In order for the merits of the donors of the four requisites to be great and fruitful, and for one's own monkhood to be worthwhile, one must develop and practice the three trainings. A monk who aspires for both his own benefit and the benefit of others must be endowed with the factor of heedfulness (appamāda). Thus, he concluded the discourse.

When this sutta was preached, sixty immoral monks vomited hot blood; sixty monks who had committed minor offenses left the order (disrobed); and sixty virtuous monks became Arahants. (This is the summary of the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta.)

Likewise... "Because of the cause of being endowed with virtue, a virtuous person experiences great joy, thinking, 'I have indeed performed the Dhamma that is blameless, excellent, and protective against danger.'"

A virtuous person can be free from the danger of self-reproach (attānuvāda-bhaya) and the danger of being blamed by the wise (parānuvāda-bhaya). The danger of punishment (daṇḍa-bhaya) and the danger of woeful states (apāya-bhaya) have no opportunity to arise at all.

Such a person is praised by the wise as one who is virtuous and of good conduct.

Unlike an immoral person, there can be no dissatisfaction of heart at all.
51:
153

Because this virtue (sīla) is the root cause of heedfulness (appamāda), and because it accomplishes great benefits by primarily removing the loss of wealth (bhoga-byasana) and so forth, and because it cuts off unwholesome states, it is the cause of the highest prosperity and happiness.

Even if one is of low birth, if one possesses virtue, one is worshipped by kings, brahmins, and others; therefore, being endowed with virtue is more beautiful and superior to being endowed with noble birth or caste.

It is not shared with the five kinds of enemies, it follows one to the next life, it is highly beneficial, and it is the cause of concentration and wisdom; therefore, the treasure of virtue (sīla-dhana) is more beautiful and superior to the collection of external wealth.

In the world, even those called rulers cannot rule over their own minds; only a virtuous person can rule over his own mind. Thus, because virtue is the cause of the highest mastery (cittissariya)—the ability to control and dominate one's own mind—it is more beautiful and superior to the power (issariya) of kings and others.

Due to the merit of virtue, one attains the quality of mastery in various future lives.

Because the Great Teacher (the Buddha) taught that one day of life for a virtuous person is more noble than a hundred years of life for an immoral person, and that even if an immoral person is alive, he is as if dead, virtue is a quality more excellent than life itself.

Even enemies must like a virtuous person. The laws of old age (jarā), disease, and failure (vipatti) cannot overwhelm or oppress a virtuous person.
52:
154

Therefore, virtue is superior even to natural physical beauty.

Since virtue is the root cause of the bliss of heaven and Nibbāna, it is superior to special dwellings such as palaces, pavilions, monasteries, and houses, as well as special ranks and positions such as king, crown prince, or general.

Because virtue certainly carries prosperity and happiness and follows closely to the next life, it is superior even to those living nearby, such as relatives and friends, who are said to desire one's welfare.

Virtue is the great guardian of the body (kāyarakkha) that specially protects this body—which is difficult to protect even with the fourfold army, medicine, or mantras—so that it is free from danger.

In this way, for one who reflects that "virtue is endowed with many noble qualities," virtues that are not yet fulfilled or purified can become fulfilled and pure.

If, in the continuum of one who has made the vow to be a Bodhisatta, unwholesome states such as anger, which are opposite to virtue, should arise intermittently due to long-standing habits, that Bodhisatta should reflect as follows:

"Have you not made the wish to attain the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and the knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)? If you are deficient in virtue, let alone supramundane attainments (lokuttara-sampatti), you cannot even reach mundane attainments (lokiya-sampatti). Indeed, the virtue that is the root cause of the Omniscience you desire—which is the most noble of all attainments—must be a most excellent virtue. Therefore, you should be one who dearly loves virtue."

"The virtue that is the root cause of the Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) must be a most excellent virtue. Therefore, you should be one who dearly loves virtue."

Alternatively... "By preaching the Dhamma, you must save beings in the three great vehicles of characteristics: impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta). You must also mature the five faculties (indriya)—faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—of those beings whose faculties are not yet mature. Just as people do not trust the treatment of a physician who gives unsuitable food, people cannot trust the words of one who lacks virtue." Therefore, after reflecting, "In what way shall I, being a trustworthy person, perform the tasks of saving beings and maturing their faculties?", you should, by your very nature, be one whose virtue is extremely pure.

Furthermore... After reflecting in this way, one should strive well to purify one's virtue.

(This is the detailed method of reflection on the Perfection of Virtue.)
54: 156 (C) The method of reflection on the Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma Pāramī)... One should reflect on the faults of household life, thinking: "Living in the household life is very cramped and narrow because the obstacles (palibodha) of wife, children, etc., are never-ending." In this way, one should reflect on the disadvantages of living in the household. Regarding monkhood: "Because all those obstacles are extinguished, it is as vast and clear as the open sky." In this way, one should reflect on the benefits of Nekkhamma, which is monkhood. Conversely, one should reflect on the benefits of Nekkhamma (departure from sensuality). (This is the method of reflection on the Perfection of Renunciation.)
55: 157 (D) The detailed method of reflection on the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā Pāramī)... One should reflect on the virtues of wisdom, thinking: "Without wisdom, perfections such as Dāna cannot be pure. The intentions of giving (dāna-cetanā), virtue (sīla-cetanā), etc., cannot even exert effort in their respective tasks like giving." (I shall further explain the detailed reflection) Just as this great mechanical body cannot be beautiful or perform its tasks without life... just as the physical sense bases like the eye, ear, and nose cannot perform their tasks of seeing, hearing, etc., without consciousness (viññāṇa)... in the same way, faculties such as faith (saddhā) and effort (vīriya) cannot effectively complete their tasks without wisdom. Therefore, wisdom is the primary and chief cause in fulfilling the perfections such as Dāna. How other perfections arise because of wisdom: (1) Because the Great Bodhisattas always keep the eye of wisdom open, even after sacrificing and giving away their own limbs, they neither exalt themselves nor disparage others. Like the great medicinal tree (mentioned before), they do not develop various kinds of wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka) and remain joyful throughout the three periods of time. Only when there is wisdom can one be endowed with the previously mentioned Skill in Means (upāyakosalla-ñāṇa) and be able to give with the intention of benefiting others. Such giving for the benefit of others is the true Perfection of Giving. (Without wisdom, one tends to give while looking only for personal benefit. Giving while looking only for personal benefit is very much like lending for interest.)
56:
158

(2) Without wisdom, states such as greed and anger dominate, so let alone becoming the cause for Omniscience, even the purity of virtue cannot be achieved.

(3) Only a wise person sees the faults in household life (gharāvāsa) and the benefits in monkhood; sees the faults in sensual pleasures and the benefits in meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti); sees the faults in saṃsāra and the benefits in Nibbāna. Then, having become a monk and developed meditative attainments, and having personally realized Nibbāna, he can establish and lead others into that monkhood, meditative attainments, and Nibbāna.

(4) Exerting effort with energy (vīriya) alone without wisdom can lead to misplaced effort and may fail to complete the required benefit. (It is even better not to exert effort than to exert it wrongly.) If energy is applied in conjunction with wisdom, it is a correct practice and can thus achieve the required benefit.

(5) Only a wise person can endure the wrongdoings and mistakes of others. For an unwise person, the faults and offenses committed by others only increase unwholesome states such as anger, which is the opposite of patience (khanti). For a wise person, however, those offenses only increase the quality of patience and serve only to strengthen that patience.

(6) Only a wise person, after knowing the three kinds of truth—truth of abstinence (virati-sacca), truth of speech (vacī-sacca), and truth of knowledge (ñāṇa-sacca)—as well as their causes and their opposites, can (by abandoning what should be abandoned and developing what should be developed) be one who does not fail others (one who is truthful).
57: (7) Only a wise person can support and encourage themselves through the power of wisdom and become endowed with concentration (samādhi). By being endowed with such concentration, there can be the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) to remain firm and unshakable in all the meritorious deeds of the perfections (pāramī). (8) Only a wise person can develop loving-kindness (mettā) equally toward all three types of individuals—the loved, the hated, and the neutral—without discrimination. (9) Only through the power of wisdom can one remain unperturbed and maintain a state of equanimity (majjhatta) when encountering the two types of worldly conditions (lokadhamma): the desirable (iṭṭha) and the undesirable (aniṭṭha). In this way, one should contemplate the virtues of wisdom, reflecting that wisdom alone is the cause of the purification of all perfections. Alternatively: Without wisdom, the perfection and purity of view (diṭṭhi) cannot be achieved; without the perfection and purity of view, the perfection and purity of virtue (sīla) cannot be achieved; without the perfection and purity of view and virtue, the perfection and purity of concentration (samādhi) cannot be achieved. A person without concentration cannot fulfill even a small amount of their own benefit, let alone the benefit of others. Therefore, you, who strive for the welfare of others, should you not diligently exert effort in respectfully increasing the quality of wisdom? Thus, a Bodhisatta should admonish himself. Indeed, by the power of wisdom, the Bodhisatta, having established himself in the four determinations (adhiṭṭhāna)—which will be described later—supports the multitude of beings through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu),
58: uplifting them and establishing them in the path of merit that leads to liberation from saṃsāra, while also maturing their five faculties (indriya): faith (saddhā), energy (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā). Likewise, through the power of wisdom, he frequently investigates and contemplates ultimate realities (paramattha) such as the aggregates (khandha) and the sense bases (āyatana). Having understood the nature of the cycle of existence (pavatti) and the cessation of the cycle (nivatti) as they truly are, he directs the meritorious deeds of the perfections he has accumulated, such as generosity (dāna), toward the attainment of the noble fruits of the Path (magga-phala). Thus, he fully practices and fulfills the path of the Bodhisattas. In this way and others, having clearly understood the many virtues of wisdom, one should repeatedly develop the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī). (This is the detailed reflection on the perfection of wisdom.) (e) The detailed reflection on the perfection of energy (vīriya-pāramī) is as follows: Even in worldly matters where the end is visible, one cannot reach the other shore (the completion) with weak or deficient energy. For one with sharp energy who does not count the exhaustion, there is nothing difficult to achieve. Indeed, "A person with weak energy cannot even begin the effort to save beings from the whirlpool of saṃsāra. One with moderate energy, though making an effort, cannot persevere to the end and tends to retreat or give up halfway. Only one with supreme energy (ukkaṭṭha-vīriya)
59: can reach the other shore of effort (omniscience/sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) without regard for physical comfort." Thus should one contemplate the fulfillment of energy. Alternatively: "Even for those striving for their own liberation from saṃsāra, such as candidates for Sāvaka-bodhi or Pacceka-bodhi, if their energy is weak, they will fail to reach their intended goals of Sāvaka-bodhi-ñāṇa or Pacceka-bodhi-ñāṇa. For a Great Being who has prayed for Buddhahood to rescue all beings, including devas and brahmas, if his energy is weak, how could he ever reach the knowledge of Right Self-Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi-ñāṇa)?" Furthermore: "Because the collection of defilements (kilesa) such as greed (rāga) and hatred (dosa) are extremely difficult to restrain, like rutting elephants; because the kammas rooted in those defilements are like executioners raising their swords to strike; because the four woeful realms (duggati) rooted in those kammas always have their mouths open; because evil friends (pāpamitta) who urge and send one toward those kammas and woeful realms are always gathered around; because the nature of ignorant worldlings (puthujjana) is to easily follow the words of those evil friends; and because the false and erroneous thoughts and statements of the sophists (vitaṇḍavādī), who are evil friends for the ignorant worldlings to follow,
60: such as 'If the nature of liberation from saṃsāra truly exists, there is no need for special effort; it should happen naturally,' can only be kept at a distance by the power of energy." Furthermore: "If Buddhahood can be attained through personal effort and energy, what difficulty could there be for a supreme person like me to exert this energy?" In this way and others, one should contemplate the virtues of energy. (This is the detailed reflection on the perfection of energy.) (f) The detailed reflection on the perfection of patience (khantī-pāramī) is as follows: This quality called patience is a great weapon for the virtuous that others cannot destroy in fulfilling virtues, because it blows away and eliminates anger (dosa), which is the opposite of all virtues. It is the great ornament of Great Beings who can rule over others. It is the perfect strength of recluses, brahmins, and holy ones. It is the stream of water that extinguishes the fire of anger (kodha). It is the excellent mantra and medicine that neutralizes the poison of the harsh words of wicked people. It is the natural custom of the wise and the most noble among those established in restraint (saṃvara-sīla). Being a deep disposition (āsaya), it is like the ocean; it is the harbor where the waves of the ocean of anger end.
61: It is the great door-leaf that shuts the gates of the woeful realms. It is the great stairway for ascending to the celestial and brahma realms. It is the great mansion where all virtues reside. It is the supreme purity of body, speech, and mind. Thus should one reflect. Alternatively: "Because these beings do not hold onto the cooling quality of patience and instead exert themselves in unwholesome states (akusala) that cause burning, they suffer in this life and will suffer in the life hereafter." Furthermore: "Although it is true that painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) arises because of another's offense, I myself have created the body (attabhāva) which is like the field for that suffering, and the kamma which is like the seed." Furthermore: "This present state of patience is the very means of paying off the debt (the practice of debt repayment) so that the original debt of suffering may be extinguished." Furthermore: "If there were no offenses by others, how could I ever fulfill the perfection of patience?" Furthermore: "Although this person commits this offense now, in the past, this person has done such-and-such a favor for me." Furthermore: "Because this person's offense is the very cause for my quality of patience, it is actually an act of doing me a favor."
62: "All these beings are like my own children. What wise person would be angry at the mistakes committed by their children?" Furthermore: "This person offends me because he is possessed by the ogre of anger (kodha). I should actually remove that possession and influence of the ogre of anger from him." Furthermore: "This suffering has arisen for me because of a certain offense; (since it could not happen if I did not exist), I am also a cause of that offense." Furthermore: "Both the mind-matter (rūpa-nāma) that offends and the mind-matter that is offended have already ceased within the moment of that offense. Now, who should be angry with whom? It is simply not appropriate." Furthermore: "Since all phenomena are non-self (anatta), in the ultimate sense, there is no one who offends and no one who is offended." By such reflections, one should repeatedly develop patience to its fulfillment. If, due to long-standing habit, the fire of anger continues to dominate one's mind based on the offenses of others, then he who claims to be a Bodhisatta should reflect as follows: "This quality called patience is a great virtue that responds with gratitude to the practices (paṭipatti) that are the opposite of all the offenses of others."
63: "The offense of another, by causing me suffering, becomes the cause for the arising of faith (saddhā) in my continuum—according to the teaching that faith has suffering as its proximate cause (dukkhūpanisā-saddhā)—and also the cause for the perception of non-delight (anabhirati-saññā) in the entire world." Furthermore: "Encountering various desirable and undesirable objects is the very nature and law of the faculties (indriya) such as the eye. In such a case, even if I wish 'May I not encounter undesirable objects,' this wish cannot be granted." Furthermore: "That person who follows the will of anger is a madman, a person with a distracted mind because of that anger. What benefit is there in retaliating against a madman?" Furthermore: "The Omniscient Buddha protects all these beings like children born from his breast. Therefore, I, who pray for the prize of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), should not feel disgust or anger toward these beings." Furthermore: "If the offender is one endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla), I should not be angry with a virtuous person." "If the offender is one without virtues such as morality, he is a person who is especially and exceedingly worthy of compassion."

“This anger, called kodha, is a great enemy that causes all harm and destroys all prosperity.”

“It is not proper for me to abandon the virtue of patience because of anger.”

“If anger, which is the opposite of all virtues, arises within me, how can I ever fulfill virtues such as morality (sīla)? Without those virtues, how can I be one who benefits beings and reach Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) as I have vowed and intended?”
“Only when there is patience can one be concentrated (samādhi) without the mind wandering among external objects. Because of being able to contemplate thus, after standing in the insight knowledge called Anulomika-khantī, one can intensely reflect that ‘All these phenomena are merely a collection of natural states (sabhāva-dhamma) that are devoid and empty of being a self or the property of a self, arising and passing away due to their respective causes. They do not come from anywhere, nor do they go anywhere, nor do they remain permanently as a solid mass anywhere. In this collection of natural states, there is no concern or activity of any person (since there is no person inherently).’ Because of knowing according to reality, one can intensely reflect that these are not the basis for the conceit of ‘I’ and ‘mine.’ Because of being able to reflect thus, the Great Bodhisattas

(g) The detailed reflection on the Perfection of Truthfulness (Sacca Pāramī) is as follows:
“If there is no truthfulness, virtues such as morality cannot arise, and the practices (paṭipatti) for becoming a Buddha as vowed and intended can no longer occur.”
“If one violates truth, all unwholesome states (akusala-dhamma) will gather and reside in them.”
“For a person whose past and future words of truth are not consistent, not only can they not be trusted by others in this life, but in every successive future life, others will not listen to their words.”
“Only when there is truthfulness can virtues such as morality flourish,” and so forth.
“Only with the foundation of truth is one able to purify and fulfill all the perfections (pāramī), acts of relinquishment (cāga), and conducts (cariya). Therefore, by being unerringly truthful in natural phenomena, one can perform all the works of pāramī, cāga, and cariya, and thus the great practice of the Bodhisattas can be completed.”
In this way and by such methods, one should reflect on the Perfection of Truthfulness.
(This is the detailed reflection on the Perfection of Truthfulness.)

(h) The detailed reflection on the Perfection of Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī) is as follows:
“If there is no firm determination in the meritorious deeds of the perfections such as giving (dāna), then when the opposites of dāna, such as stinginess (macchariya) and immorality (dussīlya), converge and fall upon one, one will no longer be able to stand unshakably and firmly in those acts of dāna and so forth. If one cannot stand thus, there can be no proficiency or courage in those meritorious deeds of dāna. If there is no proficiency or courage in those meritorious deeds of dāna, then the structures of the perfections such as dāna, which are the causes of Omniscience, can no longer exist.
Only when there is firm determination in meritorious deeds such as dāna, can one stand unshakably and firmly in those acts of dāna when the opposites such as stinginess and immorality converge and fall upon one. Only when one can stand thus can proficiency and courage in those meritorious deeds of dāna arise. Only when that happens can the structures of the perfections such as dāna, which are the causes of Omniscience, exist.”
In this way and so forth, one should reflect on the virtues of determination.
(This is the detailed reflection on the Perfection of Determination.)
(i) The detailed reflection on the Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā Pāramī) is as follows:
“Even a person who stands only for their own benefit (a selfish person), if they lack a mind of loving-kindness that desires the welfare of beings, they cannot obtain or reach

## (f) The Fifteen Conducts (Caraṇa) and Five Supernormal Knowledges (Abhiññā) with their Causes
Just like the aforementioned knowledges of reflection, the fifteen conducts (caraṇa) and five supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) along with their causes are also the fundamental causes of the perfections. To elaborate further...
Regarding the fifteen conducts (caraṇa):
According to the ancient verse: “Sī, In, Bho, Jā, Sat, Cattā, remember these as Caraṇa” —
(1) Restraint through morality (sīla-saṃvara).
(2) Guarding the doors of the sense faculties (indriyesu guttadvāratā), which is blocking the doors and restraining with mindfulness so that the thieves of unwholesome states cannot rob or destroy the six great doors of the sense faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
72:
(3) Moderation in eating (bhojane mattaññutā).
(4) The practice of wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga), which involves dividing the day into six parts—morning, afternoon, evening, the first watch of the night, the middle watch, and the last watch—and sleeping only during the middle watch, while spending the remaining five parts in meditation through the two postures of sitting and walking.
(5-11) The seven noble qualities (saddhamma), according to the mnemonic: "Sa Sa Hi O, Ca Vi Po"—Faith (saddhā), Mindfulness (sati), Moral Shame (hiri), Moral Dread (ottappa), Great Learning (bāhusacca), Energy (vīriya), and Wisdom (paññā).
(12-15) The four jhānas: the first jhāna, second jhāna, third jhāna, and fourth jhāna.
(These are the fifteen practices of conduct [caraṇa-dhammas].)
Among these fifteen caraṇa-dhammas, the supporting causes for the first four—virtue, restraint of the senses, moderation in eating, and wakefulness—are the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and qualities such as fewness of wishes and contentment.
Among the seven noble qualities:
(a) The causes for Faith (saddhā) are:
1. Repeated recollection of the Buddha's qualities (buddhānussati).
2. Repeated recollection of the Dhamma's qualities (dhammānussati).
3. Repeated recollection of the Saṅgha's qualities (saṅghānussati).
73:
4. Repeated recollection of one's own virtue (sīlānussati).
5. Repeated recollection of one's own acts of generosity and sacrifice (cāgānussati).
6. Repeated recollection of one's own faith, virtue, learning, sacrifice, and wisdom, using deities as witnesses (devatānussati).
7. Repeated recollection of the qualities of Nibbāna (upasamānussati).
8. Avoiding people who are devoid of faith (lūkha-puggala-parivajjana).
9. Associating with people who possess faith and are refined (siniddha-puggala-sevana).
10. Reflecting on the teachings that inspire confidence (pasādanīya-dhamma-paccavekkhaṇā).
11. Inclining the mind toward the development of faith in every posture (tadadhimuttatā).
These are the eleven causes.
(Mnemonic: Seven recollections, avoiding the faithless, associating with the faithful, reflecting on inspiring teachings, and inclination—these eleven are the causes for the growth of faith.)
(b) The causes for Mindfulness (sati) are:
1. Being possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven activities, such as moving forward and returning.
2. Avoiding people who are unmindful and negligent.
3. Associating with people who possess mindfulness.

4. Having a mind that is always inclined toward establishing mindfulness in every posture. These are the four causes.
(Mnemonic: Always possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding the unmindful, associating with the mindful, and inclination—these four are the causes for the growth of mindfulness. Verse by Sayadaw U Budh.)
(c-d) The causes for Moral Shame (hiri) and Moral Dread (ottappa) are:
1. Reflecting on the fault of unwholesome actions.
2. Reflecting on the suffering of the woeful states (apāya).
3. Reflecting on how wholesome qualities provide support.
4. Avoiding those who lack moral shame and dread.
5. Associating with those who possess moral shame and dread.
6. Having a mind that is always inclined toward developing moral shame and dread in every posture. These are the six causes.
(Mnemonic: Reflect on the faults of unwholesome acts and the four woeful states. Keep the support of wholesome qualities in mind. Avoid those without shame and dread, and approach those who possess them. In every posture, incline the mind toward shame—these six are the causes for shame and dread.)
(e) The causes for Great Learning (bāhusacca) are:
1. Having prior study and practice.
2. Frequently questioning and investigating.
3. Engaging in and striving for the noble qualities.
4. Studying blameless arts and sciences.
5. The maturity of the faculties (indriya) such as faith.

6. Avoiding things to stay far from defilements.
7. Avoiding those with little learning.
8. Associating with those of great learning.
9. Having a mind that is always inclined toward gaining great learning in every posture. These are the nine causes.
(Mnemonic: Prior study, frequent questioning, engaging in the Dhamma, studying pure arts, maturing the five faculties, staying away from defilements, avoiding those with little learning, associating with those of much learning, and inclining the mind in every posture—these nine are the causes for great learning.)

2. Seeing the benefits of energy.

5. Reflecting on the noble inheritance of the qualities of the virtuous.
6. Reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher (the Buddha).

(g) The causes for Wisdom (paññā) are:
1. Frequently questioning about the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), etc.
2. Cleanliness of internal and external objects.

Balancing the faculties: "If faith is excessive, one becomes biased; if wisdom is excessive, one becomes cunning; if energy is excessive, one becomes restless; if concentration is excessive, one becomes sluggish; but as for mindfulness, there is no excess, only a constant need for it." Thus, one must balance faith with wisdom, and energy with concentration.
4. Avoiding the unwise.
5. Associating with the wise.

Through these caraṇa-dhammas and the higher knowledges (abhiññā), the purification of effort (payoga-suddhi) and the purification of intention (āsaya-suddhi) can be achieved. Through the purification of effort, one is able to give the gift of fearlessness (abhaya-dāna) to beings. Through the purification of intention, one is able to give material gifts (āmisa-dāna). Through both, one is able to give the gift of the Dhamma (dhamma-dāna). In this way, one should extract the manner in which the caraṇa-dhammas and abhiññās serve as causes for the perfections (pāramīs) as appropriate.

## (7) The Defilements of the Perfections
If it is asked, "What are the factors that defile the perfections?"
The answer is: Generally, it can be said that the wrong grasping and reflection on the perfections as "mine" or "my soul" through craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi) are the causes for the defilement of the perfections. Specifically:
1. Excessive and varied thoughts regarding the objects to be given and the recipients are the defilements of the Perfection of Generosity (dāna-pāramī). (A Bodhisatta practicing the perfection of generosity should give whatever objects he has, whether good, bad, inferior, or superior, to any recipient who arrives, regardless of their status. If he hesitates, thinking, "This object is too poor to give," or "This is too excellent to give," or "This recipient is immoral and unworthy," such varied and excessive thoughts defile the perfection of generosity.)
2. Excessive and varied thoughts regarding beings and time are the defilements of the Perfection of Virtue (sīla-pāramī). (If one wishes to fulfill the perfection of virtue, it should be practiced regardless of the being or the time. If one thinks, "I will abstain from killing only for these specific beings...
78:
...but I will not abstain for those beings," or "I will keep the precepts only at this time, but not at that time"—such excessive and varied thoughts regarding beings and time defile the perfection of virtue.)
3. Thinking of the two types of sensual pleasure and the three realms of existence as delightful, and thinking of the cessation of those sensual pleasures and existences as non-delightful, are the defilements of the Perfection of Renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī).
4. Excessive wrong thoughts and false conceptions of "I" and "mine" are the defilements of the Perfection of Wisdom (paññā-pāramī).
5. Thoughts of withdrawal and distraction that give rise to sloth and torpor (thina-middha) and restlessness (uddhacca) are the defilements of the Perfection of Energy (vīriya-pāramī).
6. Excessive thoughts discriminating between oneself and others (one's own people versus others) are the defilements of the Perfection of Patience (khanti-pāramī).
7. Thinking of things not seen, heard, reached, or known as if they were seen, heard, reached, or known; and thinking of things seen, heard, reached, or known as if they were not—such wrong thoughts are the defilements of the Perfection of Truthfulness (sacca-pāramī).
8. Thinking of the perfections, sacrifice, conduct, and wholesome deeds that constitute the requisites of enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra) as faulty, and thinking of the unwholesome states that are opposite to those requisites as virtuous, are the defilements of the Perfection of Determination (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī).
79:
9. Excessive and varied thoughts discriminating between those who work for one's benefit and those who do not (those who are friendly and those who are not) are the defilements of the Perfection of Loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī).
10. Excessive thoughts discriminating between pleasant (iṭṭha) and unpleasant (aniṭṭha) objects encountered are the defilements of the Perfection of Equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī).
**********
## (8) The Factors for the Purification of the Perfections
If it is asked, "What are the factors for the purification of the perfections?"
The answer is: Not being destroyed by craving, conceit, wrong view, etc., and not having excessive and varied thoughts regarding the objects to be given, the recipients, etc. (as mentioned in the section on defilements), are the factors for the purification of the perfections.
Indeed, only those perfections such as generosity that are developed without being destroyed by defilements like craving, conceit, and wrong view, and without excessive thoughts regarding the objects and recipients, can become pure perfections.
**********
## (9) The Opposites of the Perfections
If it is asked, "What are the opposing factors (paṭipakkha) of the perfections?"
The answer is: Generally, all defilements and all unwholesome states are the opposites of the perfections.
80:
Specifically, greed (lobha) which is attachment to the objects of donation, and stinginess (macchariya) are the opposites of the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī). Misconduct (dussīlya), known as immoral deeds, is the opposite of the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī). Delighting and taking pleasure in sensual objects (vatthu-kāma), sensual defilements (kilesa-kāma), and existence (bhava) is the opposite of the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī). Intense delusion (sammoha) is the opposite of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī). The eight grounds for laziness (kusīta-vatthu) previously mentioned are the opposites of the perfection of energy (viriya-pāramī). Intolerance (attachment or resentment) towards pleasant and unpleasant objects through the power of greed and hatred is the opposite of the perfection of patience (khanti-pāramī). Not making the true nature of reality manifest is the opposite of the perfection of truthfulness (sacca-pāramī). The inability to overcome the opposites of the perfections (not practicing to conquer them) is the opposite of the perfection of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī). The nine grounds for malice (āghāta-vatthu) are the opposites of the perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī). Not viewing pleasant and unpleasant objects encountered with equanimity is the opposite of the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī).

Alternatively:
(1) Only when there is no greed (lobha) for the object of donation, no hatred (dosa) towards the recipients, and no delusion (moha) regarding the act of giving and its results, can the act of generosity be fulfilled. Therefore, greed for the object, hatred for the recipients, and delusion regarding the gift and its results—these three are the opposites of the perfection of generosity.

(2) Only when one is free from the crookedness of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct can one practice and undertake virtue. Therefore, the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha)
81:
are the opposites of the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī).

(3) Since the merit of renunciation (nekkhamma) is a noble quality that involves abstaining from sensual pleasure, from harming others, and from self-mortification, therefore, greed that pursues sensual pleasure, hatred that harms others, and delusion that leads to self-mortification are the opposites of the perfection of renunciation.

(4) Greed, hatred, and delusion are qualities that blind beings, making them unable to see. Wisdom, however, enables those blinded by greed, hatred, and delusion to see. Thus, greed, hatred, and delusion, which cause blindness in beings, are the opposites of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī).

(5) Due to greed, one shrinks from wholesome deeds. Due to hatred, one cannot remain firm in wholesome deeds. Due to delusion, one cannot strive on the right path. Through energy (viriya), one can strive on the right path without shrinking or wavering in wholesome deeds. Thus, the aforementioned greed, hatred, and delusion are the opposites of the perfection of energy (viriya-pāramī).

(6) Only when there is patience (khanti) can one remain firm without swaying toward greed in the face of pleasant objects, and remain firm without swaying toward hatred in the face of unpleasant objects. One can then look intently at the emptiness (suññatā) of phenomena from the concept of a person or being. Therefore, greed, hatred, and delusion, which prevent one from remaining firm and looking intently at pleasant, unpleasant, and empty natures,
82:
are the opposites of the perfection of patience (khanti-pāramī).

(7) Without truthfulness (sacca), one tends to follow greed when others do favors, and follow hatred when others commit offenses; at such times, things cannot happen according to the truth. Only when there is truthfulness can things happen according to the truth without following greed or hatred, even when others do favors or commit offenses. Therefore, greed that follows favors, hatred that follows offenses, and delusion that prevents things from being as they truly are, are the opposites of the perfection of truthfulness (sacca-pāramī).

(8) Only when there is determination (adhiṭṭhāna) can one overcome the worldly conditions (lokadhamma), whether pleasant or unpleasant, and remain unshakably firm in the meritorious perfections one has undertaken. Therefore, greed, hatred, and delusion, which cause the inability to overcome worldly conditions, are the opposites of the perfection of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī).

(9) Since the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) can be removed through the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā), greed, hatred, and delusion, which are included within those hindrances, are the opposites of the perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī).

(10) Without equanimity (upekkhā), one cannot destroy or restrain greed and hatred toward pleasant and unpleasant objects, and cannot remain impartial. Only when there is equanimity can one destroy and restrain greed and hatred toward pleasant and unpleasant objects and remain impartial. Therefore, greed, hatred, and delusion are the opposites of the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī).
**********
83:
## (10) How the Perfections are Fulfilled
If it is asked, "How are the perfections fulfilled? In what manner did the Bodhisattas fulfill the perfections?"

The answer is:
(1) In the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī), the Bodhisatta fulfills it by supporting the welfare of beings, by sacrificing his own body and life without hesitation, by removing dangers that may befall beings, and by pointing out and teaching the right path of Dhamma to beings, thus helping them in many such ways.

To explain in detail: Generosity (dāna) is of three types according to the object of donation: (a) material gift (āmisa-dāna), (b) gift of fearlessness (abhaya-dāna), and (c) gift of the Dhamma (dhamma-dāna). Among these three:

(a) Regarding material gifts (āmisa-dāna), the Bodhisatta's objects of donation are again divided into two: (1) internal objects (ajjhattika-vatthu) belonging to the body, and (2) external objects (bāhira-vatthu) outside the body. Among these two:

External objects of donation (bāhira-dāna-vatthu) of the second type are of ten kinds (according to the Suttanta method): food, drink, clothing, vehicles, flowers, scents, unguents, bedding, dwellings, and accessories for lighting such as oil, wicks, and lamps. Among these ten, each type, such as food, has many varieties like hard food, soft food, etc.

Similarly, there are six kinds according to the six sense objects (according to the Abhidhamma method), such as the gift of visible forms, the gift of sounds, etc. Among these six,
84:
even for a single type like the gift of visible forms, there are many varieties such as blue, yellow, etc.

Similarly, there are many varieties of gems such as rubies, gold, silver, pearls, and coral; inanimate objects such as paddy fields, farm lands, and gardens; and animate objects such as female slaves, male slaves, cattle, and buffaloes.

## How External Generosity (Bāhira-dāna) is Practiced
Among these various objects of donation, the Bodhisatta gives whatever object the recipient desires. If he knows that a recipient is in need, he gives even without being asked, having understood the need. If he is asked, there is no need to say more; he certainly gives. When giving, he gives completely and without any strings attached.

If he has a full and sufficient supply of objects, he gives them fully and sufficiently to the recipients. If they are insufficient, he divides what should be divided and gives accordingly.

In particular, although it is said he gives, he does not give things that would harm others, such as weapons, poisons, or intoxicants. Nor does he give playthings that cause negligence (pamāda) and yield no benefit.

To a sick recipient, he does not give food that is unsuitable for that person, nor does he give even suitable food in excess of the proper amount. He gives only the type of food suitable for that person, in a moderate and appropriate quantity.
85:
Similarly, when asked, he gives only what is suitable for laypeople to laypeople, and what is suitable for monks to monks. (He does not give a monk's requisites to a layperson, nor a layperson's belongings to a monk.) When giving, he does so without causing any suffering to anyone connected to him, such as parents, relatives, friends, children, wife, slaves, or workers.

He does not have the habit of promising something good and then giving something inferior. He does not give out of desire for gain, offerings, influence, or fame, nor does he expect any favor in return. He does not give hoping for the benefits of rebirth (bhava-sampatti) or wealth (bhoga-sampatti) other than the Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) known as Sammāsambodhi. He gives aiming and aspiring only for Omniscient Wisdom.

He does not give with disgust toward the recipients or the objects of donation. Even toward recipients who do not restrain their body, speech, and mind, or those who abuse and revile him, he has no feeling of disrespect or irritation (as if discarding rubbish). Instead, with a very clear mind and placing compassion (karuṇā) at the forefront, he gives respectfully. He never gives based on the belief that noisy or chaotic gatherings are auspicious (maṅgala); he gives only with strong faith (saddhā) in kamma and its results.

He never gives by making the recipients suffer, such as by making them wait upon him or prostrate before him; he gives only without causing them any hardship. He gives with a very pure mind, without any desire to deceive or cause division among others.
86:
He never gives while speaking harsh or rude words, with a frowning face or a pouting lip. He gives only with a pleasant face and a cool, calm mind, speaking endearing words (piyavācā).

If the Bodhisatta realizes that he is excessively attached to an object of donation—whether because the object is of excellent quality, because he has used it for a long time, or because of the inherent nature of greed to be attached to good things—he quickly removes that greed and gives it away, even searching for a recipient if necessary.

If he encounters a situation where (a) the object of donation is only enough for one person, (b) he is just about to consume it himself, and (c) a recipient arrives right before him, the Bodhisatta does not hesitate or deliberate. He undergoes the hardship of not consuming it himself and, like the Bodhisatta Akitti the Wise, he respectfully and honorably offers it to the recipient.

When recipients ask for his wife, children, slaves, and so on, the Bodhisatta explains the situation to them to make them understand and satisfied. Only then, with his wife and others being joyful, does he give them to the recipients. In doing so, if he knows the recipients are ogres (yakkha) or demons (rakkhasa), he does not give.

In giving away his kingship (the wealth of the kingdom), he does not give it to those who would act to the detriment, suffering, or disadvantage of the people.
87:
He does not give indiscriminately but only to those recipients who protect the people righteously. This is how the practice of giving external objects (bāhira-vatthu) should be understood.

## The Practice of Internal Giving (Ajjhattika-dāna)

There are two ways in which the Great Being (Bodhisatta) practices internal giving:

(1) Just as a man in this world might surrender himself to another for the sake of clothing, obeying and performing whatever tasks are assigned as a slave, the Bodhisatta, desiring to attain Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and having no desire for sensual pleasures or worldly existence, but wishing only for the supreme welfare and happiness of beings, surrenders his entire body to others with a wholesome desire to reach the pinnacle of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī). He obeys and performs whatever they command without refusal. (This is the type of giving the whole body.)

(2) He gives his limbs, such as hands, feet, and eyes, to those who desire them, without wavering or shrinking back. He has no attachment, clinging, or hesitation toward these limbs, just as he has none toward external objects. (This is the type of giving parts of the body.)

## Twofold Purpose

The Bodhisatta gives in order to fulfill the hearts' desires of the recipients so that they may use the gifts happily as they wish, and also to gain mastery (vasībhāva) in the meritorious practice of the perfections for his own sake, being entirely free from attachment to the objects of the gift.
88:
Knowing and believing that 'By such giving, I shall certainly attain Omniscience,' he gives his internal body or limbs just as he gives external objects. 

In such giving, he only gives internal objects that are certainly beneficial to the recipient. In particular, if he knows it is Māra or his hosts who wish to harass and oppress him, he considers, 'Let it not be to their detriment,' and does not give his body or limbs. Likewise, he does not give to those possessed by Māra or his associates, nor to the insane. To others, however, because such requests are rare and such internal giving is difficult to perform, he gives immediately upon being asked without any delay.

## (b) Abhaya-dāna (The Gift of Safety)

The Bodhisatta practices the gift of safety by protecting and rescuing beings from dangers such as the wrath of kings, thieves, fire, water, enemies, wild beasts like lions and tigers, and from nagas, ogres (yakkhas), and demons (rakkhasas), sacrificing his own life countless times to ensure their freedom from fear.
89:
## (c) Dhamma-dāna

Dhamma-dāna refers to the teaching of the true and undistorted Dhamma without a mind defiled by greed, hatred, and so on.

Among the three types of future Buddhas—the Sāvaka-bodhisatta who aspires to Disciple-enlightenment, the Pacceka-bodhisatta who aspires to Private-enlightenment, and the Sammāsambodhisatta who aspires to Universal-enlightenment—the Great Being gives the gift of Dhamma to Sāvaka-bodhisattas by praising and teaching the virtues of the Refuges (saraṇa), Morality (sīla), sense restraint, moderation in eating, wakefulness, the seven noble qualities (saddhamma), the practice of Samatha and Vipassanā meditation, the seven purities (visuddhi), the attainment of the four paths, the three knowledges (vijjā), the six super-knowledges (abhiññā), the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and the four paths of the Disciples (Sāvaka-bodhi-ñāṇa). He establishes those not yet established in these virtues and encourages those already established to practice them purely.

Similarly, he gives the gift of Dhamma to Pacceka-bodhisattas and Sammāsambodhisattas by clearly explaining the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) and functions (rasa) of the perfections (pāramī), and by demonstrating the greatness of their power throughout the three periods: while fulfilling the perfections, while attaining Buddhahood, and while performing the duties of a Buddha. He establishes them in the practices of Pacceka-bodhi and Sammāsambodhi and encourages those already established to practice them purely.
90:
## Ten Kinds of Giving according to the Suttanta Method

Likewise, when the Bodhisatta gives material gifts (āmisa-dāna) to beings, he gives the gift of food with the strong aspiration: 'By this gift of food, may I be able to bring about the various attainments such as long life, beauty, happiness, strength, and wisdom for all beings, as well as the supreme attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship.'

Similarly, he gives the gift of drinks to quench the thirst of beings' sensual defilements (kāma-kilesa).

He gives the gift of clothes to fulfill the benefit of having a golden-hued complexion and obtaining the spiritual ornaments of moral shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa).

He gives the gift of vehicles to fulfill the benefit of various psychic powers and the bliss of Nibbāna.

He gives the gift of fragrance to obtain the incomparable scent of the virtue of morality.

He gives the gift of flowers and unguents to fulfill the benefit of being adorned with the attributes of a Buddha.

He gives the gift of seats to fulfill the benefit of attaining the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka) at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

He gives the gift of beds to obtain the 'Tathāgata-sleep' (Tathāgata-seyyā), which is the dwelling in the fourth jhāna, according to the verse:
'Sleeping on the left is sensual, on the right is the lion's way,
Lying on the back is the peta's, while the Buddha's sleep is the fourth jhāna.'
91:
He gives rest houses, pavilions, and monasteries to become a refuge for the three worlds.

He gives lamps and lighting facilities to obtain the five kinds of eyes.

## Six Kinds of Giving according to the Abhidhamma Method

He gives the gift of forms (rūpa-dāna) to obtain a bodily radiance that shines eighty cubits at all times, even in the fourfold darkness of 'the new moon, heavy clouds, midnight, and the deep forest.'

He gives the gift of sounds (sadda-dāna) to obtain a voice like that of the Great Brahma.

He gives the gift of flavors (rasa-dāna) to obtain the benefit of being a noble person loved and cherished by all beings.

He gives the gift of touch (phoṭṭhabba-dāna) to obtain the benefit of the delicacy of a Buddha (Buddha-sukhumālatā).

He gives the gift of medicine to obtain the benefit of Nibbāna, where there is no aging or death.

He performs the act of canceling slave records for servants to free them from the slavery of defilements.

He gives the gift of harmless joy to enable beings to delight in the Dhamma.

He gives his children as a gift so that all beings may become the children of the Buddha through the Ariya birth.
92:
He gives wives like Queen Maddī to attain the status of the Lord of the entire world.

He gives the ten kinds of gems to be endowed with the great Marks of a Superior Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa).

He gives various ornaments to be endowed with the eighty minor marks (anubyañjana).

He gives the treasury of wealth to obtain the great treasury of the Dhamma-gem.

He gives up kingship to become the King of Dhamma (Dhamma-rāja).

He gives parks, gardens, ponds, and forests to be endowed with the superhuman states (uttari-manussa-dhamma) such as jhāna, vimokkha (liberation), samādhi (concentration), samāpatti (attainment), magga (path), and phala (fruit).

He gives his feet to a requesting recipient so that he may approach the Mahābodhi seat with feet adorned with the wheel-marks.

He gives his hands, wishing to give the hand of the Dhamma to beings so they may cross over the fourfold flood (ogha).

He gives his ears and nose to obtain the faculties such as faith (saddhindriya).

He gives his eyes to obtain the Eye of All-Knowledge (Samantacakkhu) or Omniscience.

'May my entire body serve the welfare and happiness of beings at all times—when they look at me, listen to me, remember me, or serve me.' With such a strong aspiration, he gives his flesh and blood.
93:
'May I be the one upon whom the entire world depends for its livelihood.' With such a strong aspiration, he gives his head, the supreme part of the body, to become the supreme person in the entire world.

In giving thus, he does not give through unrighteous means, nor by oppressing others, nor out of fear or shame, nor by coercing the recipient. He does not give inferior things when superior ones are available, nor does he give to praise himself and disparage others. He does not give for any goal other than Buddhahood, nor does he give with contempt, disgust, or disrespect toward the recipient. Indeed, he gives the gift with great respect. He gives with his own hands. He gives at the proper time. He gives with respect for the recipient. He gives without discriminating between the low and the high. He gives with joy in all three times: before, during, and after giving. Therefore, he has no regret after giving. He does not show pride or contempt toward the recipient. He speaks pleasant words (piyavācā) to the recipients, understands their needs, and makes himself approachable for them to ask. Whenever he performs an act of giving, he usually gives it along with various accompaniments.

For example, if he wishes to give food, he thinks, 'I will give this food along with its accompaniments,' and then gives it together with drinks, clothes, and so on.
94:
Likewise, when wishing to give the gift of clothing, he thinks, “I shall give this gift of clothing together with its accompaniments,” and then gives it along with food and so forth. The same method applies to the gift of vehicles and other such offerings.

Similarly, when wishing to give the gift of visual objects (rūpa-dāna), he makes sounds (sadda) and so forth the accompaniments of that gift of visual objects and offers them. The same method applies to the gift of sound and other such offerings.

In this context, the ten types of gifts mentioned in the Suttanta method, such as food and drink, are clear and well-known as they are conventional concepts (paññatti). However, the gifts of visual objects, sounds, and so forth, which are classified according to the six sense objects in the Abhidhamma method, are not so clear as to “how one gives a gift of visual objects” or “how one should direct the mind to make it a gift of visual objects.” Therefore, I shall further explain the manner of giving such gifts as rūpa-dāna.

## Rūpa-dāna
Among those six types of gifts according to the Abhidhamma method, what is called the gift of visual objects (rūpa-dāna) is as follows: having obtained any one of the various kinds of flowers, fabrics, or metals that possess colors such as blue, yellow, red, or white, one directs the mind toward the color itself and reflects, “I shall give the gift of color; this is indeed my gift of color.” Then, giving those flowers, fabrics, or metals—which are the bases of that color—to the recipient is called rūpa-dāna (the gift of visual objects).

The point is that a person who wishes to give a gift of color is unable to extract the color alone to give it. Therefore, taking any object that is the basis of that color, such as flowers, fabrics, or metals...
95:
...one should give it to the recipient while reflecting and contemplating only on the color, thinking, “I shall give the gift of color; this is indeed my gift of color.” Such a type of gift is called rūpa-dāna (the gift of visual objects). (The same method applies to sadda-dāna (the gift of sound) and others.)

## Sadda-dāna
The gift of sound (sadda-dāna) should be understood through the power of the sound of drums and so forth. In the matter of sadda-dāna, one is unable to extract the sound-material (sadda-rūpa) alone and give it like a lotus fiber or a lotus root, nor can one place it in the hand and give it like a bunch of lotus flowers. In truth, by giving objects such as large drums or bells which are the bases of that sound-material, one is said to give the gift of sound (sadda-dāna). Having reflected, “I shall give the gift of sound,” if one personally plays or causes others to play any kind of musical instrument such as a large drum or a clay drum as an offering to the Triple Gem; or if one personally installs or causes others to install bells, gongs, and so forth on pagoda platforms while reflecting, “This is my gift of sound”; or if one gives medicine, honey, molasses, and so forth that improve the voice to those who preach the Dhamma; or if one shouts out invitations to listen to the Dhamma; or if one preaches the Dhamma; or if one speaks welcoming words of Dhamma to those who approach; or if one personally delivers or causes others to deliver appropriate words of appreciation (anumodanā) at ceremonies for the donation of monasteries or food—this is called giving the gift of sound (sadda-dāna).

## Gandha-dāna
Likewise, if one obtains any object with a pleasant fragrance among various kinds of fragrant roots, fragrant stems, and so forth, or...
96:
...if one obtains ground incense powder, (without directing the mind toward the object itself) but directing the mind only toward the fragrance, and reflects, “I shall give the gift of fragrance; this is indeed my gift of fragrance,” and then makes an offering to the Triple Gem; or if one offers pieces of aloe wood, calamander wood, white sandalwood, or yellow sandalwood for the purpose of offering fragrance—this is called giving the gift of fragrance (gandha-dāna).

## Rasa-dāna
Likewise, if one obtains any pleasant object of taste such as delicious roots, tubers, bulbs, or fruits, (without directing the mind toward the object itself) but directing the mind only toward the taste, and reflects, “I shall give the gift of taste; this is indeed my gift of taste,” and then gives it to the recipients; or if one gives taste-objects such as grain, millet, beans, or cow’s milk—this is called giving the gift of taste (rasa-dāna).

## Phoṭṭhabba-dāna
Likewise, the gift of tangibles (phoṭṭhabba-dāna) should be understood through the power of couches, stools, beds, chairs, rugs, blankets, and clothing that are pleasant to the touch. In the matter of phoṭṭhabba-dāna, if one obtains any tangible object such as a couch, stool, bed, chair, rug, blanket, or clothing that provides a comfortable touch, (without directing the mind toward the object itself) but directing the mind and considering only the comfortable touch, and reflects, “I shall give the gift of touch; this is indeed my gift of touch,” and then gives, offers, or relinquishes any of the aforementioned tangible objects—this is called giving the gift of tangibles (phoṭṭhabba-dāna).
97:
## Dhamma-dāna
Under this heading of Dhamma-dāna, since it refers to the gift of mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) included among the six sense objects:

It should be understood through the power of nutritive essence (ojā), drinks (pāna), life-prolonging things (jīvita), and the taking of Dhamma-dāna, according to the saying: “Ojā, pāna, jīvita, take as Dhamma-dāna.”

To elaborate: if one obtains any substance rich in nutritive essence such as ghee or the cream of clarified butter, (without directing the mind toward the object itself) but directing the mind only toward the mental object of nutritive essence, and reflects, “I shall give the gift of mental objects; this is indeed my gift of mental objects,” and then gives the ghee or cream of clarified butter;

Or if one gives the eight kinds of drinks (pāna) mentioned as:
“Rose-apple, mango, grape, banana, and wild banana,
Water lily, and two types of plantain—these are the eight drinks”;

Or if, directing the mind toward the gift of life (jīvita-dāna), one gives food by tickets (salāka-bhatta) and so forth which are causes for the prolongation of life; or if one causes physicians to attend to and treat those afflicted with disease; or if one causes the destruction of nets, traps, cages, and snares; or if one causes the release of those held in bondage; or if one issues orders and beats the drum of proclamation in towns and villages saying, “Beings must not be killed, and meat must not be sold”; or if one personally performs or causes others to perform acts that protect the lives of beings—this is called giving the gift of Dhamma (dhamma-dāna).

The Bodhisatta, for the sake of all these accumulated meritorious deeds of giving, inclined his heart and made the following aspiration: “May I be able to bring about the welfare and happiness of the entire world of beings up to the attainment of Nibbāna,” and for his own part...
98:
...“May this be a supporting condition for the inexhaustible and undiminished Golden Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), and for my aspiration (chanda), energy (viriya), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), and the liberation of the fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala-vimutti).”

While fulfilling this Perfection of Giving (dāna-pāramī), the Bodhisatta developed the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), realizing the instability of his own life. He also developed the perception of impermanence regarding wealth and possessions. He reflected on how those possessions are shared and connected with many others. He also constantly aroused great compassion (karuṇā) toward all beings. By doing so, he extracted the essence of merit that should be taken from wealth and possessions. Just as a person who, from a burning house, carries out his own person and the essence of his wealth to safety, the Bodhisatta, as if carrying himself and the essence of his wealth out of the great house of the three realms which is ablaze with the eleven fires such as lust (rāga), was able to give generously and courageously without leaving anything behind. Without making divisions such as “I will eat this much, I will keep this much, and I will give only this much,” he was able to give generously and joyfully without any lingering attachment.

(This is the sequence of the practice of the Perfection of Giving.)

(2) The sequence of the practice of the Perfection of Virtue (sīla-pāramī) is as follows:

Just as one who wishes to support and protect others with wealth must first strive to become a person of wealth himself in order to provide such support, so too the Bodhisatta, wishing to adorn...
99:
...beings to be disciplined with the ornament of virtue (sīla), must first strive to make his own virtue pure.

In thus striving for the purity of virtue, there are four factors:
(1) Purity of natural disposition (ajjhāsaya),
(2) Undertaking the training rules from others,
(3) Non-transgression,
(4) Making it pure as before if a transgression occurs.

Among these:
(1) Due to the purity of natural disposition, some individuals, by respecting themselves and having a nature that loathes evil, can become persons of extremely pure virtue, based on the principle of moral shame (hiri).
(2) Likewise, if there is the undertaking of training rules from others, one can become a person of extremely pure virtue by respecting the external world and arousing moral dread (ottappa) which fears evil, thinking, “I have indeed undertaken these training rules from such and such a teacher.”
(3) Only one who maintains the two aforementioned principles of hiri and ottappa can achieve non-transgression of the training rules. By thus not transgressing the training rules, one becomes pure in virtue and able to stand firm in virtue.
(4) Even if one or two training rules are occasionally broken due to forgetfulness, because of being endowed with the aforementioned hiri and ottappa, one can quickly restore them to their original purity by means of formal confession (desanā), or by undertaking the parivāsa and mānatta penances, and so forth. (Regarding the breaking of training rules, if one is a monk...
100:
...one must restore them to the original state by undertaking parivāsa and mānatta; if one is a layperson or a novice (sāmaṇera), one must restore them by undertaking and receiving the training rules anew.)

## Vāritta-sīla and Cāritta-sīla
Virtue that is pure due to the four aforementioned factors is of two kinds: (1) Vāritta-sīla and (2) Cāritta-sīla. Between these two:
(1) Abstaining from the ten unwholesome actions such as killing living beings (pāṇātipāta), which have been prohibited by the Noble Ones such as the Buddha with the words, “This is blameworthy, it should not be done, it must be avoided,” (and guarding oneself so as not to commit those unwholesome acts) is called vāritta-sīla (virtue of avoidance).
(2) Performing acts that are faultless and clearly beneficial, such as showing respect to teachers, parents, and good spiritual friends (kalyāṇa-mitta), is called cāritta-sīla (virtue of performance).

## How the Great Bodhisattas Fulfill Vāritta-sīla
A. The Great Bodhisattas maintain great compassion toward all beings such that even in their dreams, anger and resentment do not arise; thus, they do not commit the act of killing living beings.
B. Because they always delight only in doing favors for others, they do not even perform the act of handling others' property with a mind to steal, viewing it like a venomous snake.
C. In those lives where they become hermits or monks, they avoid from afar the ignoble practice of sexual intercourse. Apart from the coarse act of sexual union, which is the coming together of pairs—
101:
203
(1) Delighting in physical care such as massage provided by a woman,
(2) Delighting in laughing and joking together with a woman,
(3) Delighting in gazing intently into a woman's eyes,
(4) Delighting in listening to the sound of a woman's laughter, talking, singing, or weeping from behind a wall,
(5) Delighting in reminiscing about laughing, talking, and playing together with a woman in the past,
(6) Delighting in envying and longing for the state of a householder who is endowed with sensual pleasures,
(7) Practicing the holy life while longing for and delighting in a certain heavenly rebirth—
He abstained from these seven types of sexual fetters (methuna-saṃyoga) mentioned in (A. ii, 438-439). Needless to say, he had already long abstained from committing adultery with the wives of others.
Even in his lives as a layman, the Bodhisatta did not commit misconduct or stray with the wives of others even in his thoughts.
(d, e, f, g) When he spoke, he avoided the four types of verbal misconduct and spoke only words that were true, words that promoted harmony and unity between friends, words that were pleasant to the ear, and words that were meaningful, considered, and in accordance with the Dhamma.
102:
204
(h, i, j) He possessed no greed that covets the wealth of others, no ill-will (byāpāda) that desires the destruction of others, and he held the correct Right View (Sammā-diṭṭhi) without distortion. He was endowed with the knowledge that beings are the owners of their actions (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) and was habitually inclined toward faith and loving-kindness for the virtuous who practice well.
By thus avoiding the unwholesome actions that lead to the four lower realms and established in the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakamma-patha) which are the path to the heavenly realms and Nibbāna, the Great Bodhisatta possessed pure intentions, pure bodily actions, and pure verbal actions. Consequently, all his heart's desires regarding the welfare and happiness of beings were quickly fulfilled and perfected. His Perfections (pāramīs) were also brought to completion.
## The Benefits of Abstaining from Misconduct
Because the Bodhisatta abstained from the misconduct of taking life (pāṇātipāta), he gave the gift of fearlessness to all beings. Thus, he could easily perfect the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) and attained the eleven benefits of loving-kindness. Along with the benefits of being free from disease, having a long life, and great happiness, he obtained the Marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa), such as long and slender fingers and toes, and was able to eradicate the habitual tendency (vāsanā) toward anger.
By abstaining from the misconduct of taking what is not given (adinnādāna), the Bodhisatta obtained wealth that is not shared with enemies (wealth that cannot be destroyed by the five types of enemies). Furthermore, without being wrongly suspected by others, he became one who is loved, cherished, relied upon, and trusted.
103:
205
He became one with a mind unattached to wealth and possessions, one who practiced generosity, and one who could eradicate the habitual tendency toward greed.
By abstaining from unchastity (abrahmacariya), the Bodhisatta became one who was not frivolous, possessed a peaceful body and mind, and was loved, cherished, and not shunned by all beings. He gained the benefit of a good reputation and fame. Furthermore, he possessed a mind unattached to women and an inclination free from lust. His innate disposition for renunciation (nekkhamma-jhāsaya) became strong, and he was able to eradicate the habitual tendency toward greed.
By abstaining from false speech (musāvāda), the Bodhisatta became one who was trusted, relied upon, and held in high esteem by beings, and his words became influential and authoritative. He was loved and cherished by the devas, possessed a fragrant breath, and was well-restrained in his bodily and verbal conduct. He obtained the Marks of a Great Man, such as having only one hair growing from each pore, and was able to eradicate the habitual tendency toward defilements.
By abstaining from slanderous speech (pisuṇavācā), the Bodhisatta obtained the benefits of having a physical body (rūpakāya) that could not be broken by the efforts of others, having an inseparable retinue, possessing firm faith in the Dhamma of the virtuous that could not be destroyed, having steadfast friends, being loved by all beings, and being one whose defilements were attenuated.
104:
206
By abstaining from harsh speech (pharusavācā), the Bodhisatta obtained the benefits of being loved and cherished by beings, being habitually calm and cool, possessing sweet speech, being praised by all, and being endowed with the eightfold Brahma-voice.
By abstaining from frivolous speech (samphappalāpa), the Bodhisatta obtained the benefits of being loved, cherished, and respected by all beings, having his words followed by everyone, being habitually wise and considered in speech, possessing great power and majesty, and being able to quickly answer problems with penetrating wisdom. Upon becoming a Buddha, he could answer the questions of beings of various languages with a single word of the Ariyan language, Māgadhī (even when he answered in a single word of Māgadhī, people of the 101 races each heard and understood the answer in their own respective languages).
By abandoning covetousness (abhijjhā), the Bodhisatta obtained the benefits of easily acquiring whatever he desired, having the opportunity to enjoy and use noble wealth, being recognized as a noble person by wealthy kings, brahmins, and householders, not being oppressed by enemies, not being deficient in the sense faculties such as the eyes, ears, and nose, and being a peerless individual.
By abandoning ill-will (byāpāda), the Bodhisatta obtained the benefits of being looked upon with eyes of love by all beings he encountered, being one who is praised, being able to easily inspire faith in beings, and possessing a nature that is not harsh.
105:
207
He obtained the benefits of being not desolate in nature, habitually dwelling only in loving-kindness, and possessing great power and majesty.
By avoiding wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) and cultivating right view (sammā-diṭṭhi), the Bodhisatta associated with noble friends (kalyāṇa-mitta). He would not perform an evil deed even if his head were to be cut off. Because he perceived that only kamma is one's own property, he did not hold the view of omens based on what is seen or heard (diṭṭha-suta-maṅgala). He remained firmly established in faith in the Dhamma of the virtuous and had unwavering faith in the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) of the Buddha. Just as a golden swan king does not delight in a place full of excrement and filth, he did not delight in false views other than right view. He was proficient and skilled in discerning the three characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self (anicca, dukkha, anatta). In his final life as a Buddha, he attained Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa), which knows all knowable things without hindrance or obstruction. In every life before becoming a Buddha, he was always a leader and obtained noble wealth. These are the benefits he received.
In this way, reflecting that this virtue (sīla) is the root of all wealth, the very beginning and origin of all the Buddha's qualities, and the foremost of all perfections, he cherished it greatly. He should fulfill virtue respectfully, being mindful and clearly comprehending in these four areas: restraint of body and speech, restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and the use of the four requisites, without being negligent, and regarding gains, offerings, influence, and fame as great enemies disguised as friends.
(This is the practice regarding the virtue of avoidance, vāritta-sīla.)
