208
## How the Great Bodhisattas Fulfilled the Virtue of Performance
The Bodhisatta constantly performed acts of salutation, welcoming, joining the hands in reverence, showing respect, and attending upon those who were true noble friends (kalyāṇa-mitta). He personally supervised and performed service (veyyāvacca) for the sick. When he heard the Dhamma, he uttered words of appreciation (sādhu). He was accustomed to praising the virtues of those who possessed them. He was patient with the offenses of others and repeatedly recollected only the favors they had done. He joyfully shared in the merits of others (anumodanā) and was inclined to dedicate his own meritorious deeds toward Omniscient Knowledge. He habitually dwelt without negligence in wholesome qualities at all times. If he had a fault, he did not hide it but viewed it as a fault and made it known as it truly was in the presence of his companions in the holy life. He fulfilled the noble practice (paṭipatti) by progressing higher and higher.
Likewise, he assisted with skill and effort in various affairs that were appropriate for him and could bring benefit to beings. When beings encountered sufferings such as disease, he arranged for their liberation from that suffering as was fitting. When beings encountered misfortunes (byasana) such as the loss of relatives (ñāti-byasana), loss of wealth (bhoga-byasana), loss through disease (roga-byasana), loss of virtue (sīla-byasana), or loss of right view (diṭṭhi-byasana), he dispelled their grief and sorrow. Intending for those who should be restrained to be free from the unwholesome and established in the wholesome,
107:
209
and remaining only in a state of saving them, he restrained with justice those who should be restrained and encouraged with justice those who should be encouraged.
When he heard of the great practices of the former Great Bodhisattas—which are the cause for the maturation of the perfections (pāramī), relinquishment (cāga), and conduct (cariya), and which are extremely noble, extremely difficult to perform, endowed with inconceivable power, and capable of definitely bringing about the welfare and happiness of beings—he was not at all terrified or afraid.
He thought: "Those former Great Bodhisattas were also true human beings like me. By gradually and completely fulfilling the practices of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā), they succeeded in reaching the Golden Omniscient Knowledge. Therefore, I too shall practice well the things to be practiced—virtue, concentration, and wisdom—just like those former Great Bodhisattas. Through this noble practice (paṭipatti), after gradually completing the practices of the three trainings (sikkhā), I will certainly reach Omniscient Knowledge."
Thus, with effort preceded by faith, he fulfilled the virtues well and completely without slackening. Likewise, the Bodhisatta did not display the meritorious deeds he performed to make them famous among people; only if he had a fault did he not hide it but made it known. He fulfilled virtue by being one of few wishes (appicchatā), being easily contented (santuṭṭhī), being secluded from defilements (paviveka), not associating with the masses through the power of defilements, enduring suffering, and not longing for various objects with greed.
108:
210

Being unshaken by the power of restlessness (uddhacca), not being conceited, not being frivolous or fickle, not being harsh in speech, not speaking incoherently, possessing calm faculties (indriya), possessing a peaceful heart, and being free from wrong livelihoods (micchā-ājīva) such as acting with pretension to impress others, he was endowed with these virtues. Furthermore, being endowed with pure conduct of body and speech and the objects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), he viewed even minor faults as great dangers and well-established himself in the practice of the training rules (sikkhāpada). Without any craving or greed that clings to the body and life, and with a mind directed only towards Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and Nibbāna, he tirelessly exerted effort in wholesome states (kusala-dhamma). He did not accept even a slight amount of craving or greed that clings to the body and life, but rather abandoned it. He abandoned the defilements (upakkilesa) such as anger and malice which cause the decline of virtue. Without being satisfied or complacent with just a small amount of extraordinary attainment, he strove for higher and higher attainments. Through such exertion, the extraordinary attainments such as jhāna obtained by the Bodhisatta never declined or remained stagnant, but only increased and flourished more and more.

Likewise, the Bodhisatta would lead the blind to their desired destination or show them the way. To those who were deaf or mute, he would give signs with his hands. (He would use hand and body gestures to help them achieve their needs.) To those who were lame (with weak legs or hands), he would donate stools or vehicles, or he would personally carry them to their destination.
109:
211

He would send them on their way. He strove to instill faith (saddhā) in those lacking faith, energy (vīriya) in the lazy, mindfulness (sati) in the negligent, concentration (samādhi) in those wandering with restlessness (uddhacca), and wisdom (paññā) in the unwise. He strove to help those overwhelmed and oppressed by the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) to abandon them. He strove to help those oppressed by sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka), thoughts of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka), and thoughts of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka) to abandon these wrong thoughts. Being grateful to those who had previously done him a favor, he would first greet them with pleasant words and honor them. He would then reciprocate their previous favor with an equal or superior act of gratitude, showing them respect and worship. In times of danger, he would act as a good friend (kalyāṇa-mitta).

Having known the natural disposition and mind of various beings, he would rouse them from unwholesome states (akusala) and establish them in wholesome states (kusala), associating and dealing with them according to their preferences. (This means he would support those who like giving with the practice of generosity (dāna-saṅgaha), those who like pleasant words with kindly speech (piyavācā-saṅgaha), those who like beneficial actions with useful conduct (atthacariyā-saṅgaha), and those who like equality with impartiality (samānattatā-saṅgaha), thereby rousing them from unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states while associating and dealing with them.)

Likewise, even with the desire for another's benefit, the Bodhisatta did not oppress others, nor did he engage in quarrels.
110:
212

He did not act in a way that would make another person's face unpleasant, nor did he cause remorse (kukkucca) in others. He did not speak words of blame by placing others in a position of being oppressed. He did not associate with those who acted humbly towards him by placing himself in a superior position. He did not avoid association entirely, nor did he associate excessively, nor did he associate at improper times; he only associated with those worthy of association according to the place and time. He did not criticize those loved by others in their presence, nor did he praise those hated by others. He did not become intimate with those with whom one should not be intimate.

He did not reject a righteous invitation from others. He did not engage in excessive begging. When receiving donations, he did not accept more than what was necessary. He gladdened and encouraged those endowed with faith (saddhā) with Dhamma talk related to the benefits and power of faith. Likewise, he gladdened and encouraged those endowed with virtue (sīla), learning (suta), generosity (cāga), and wisdom (paññā) with Dhamma talk related to the benefits and power of wisdom.

If the Bodhisatta was born as a person with psychic powers (abhiññā) and jhāna, he would use his psychic powers to show the dangers of hell and so forth to negligent beings as appropriate to terrify them. He would then establish those lacking faith and other virtues in faith and so forth, making them enter and believe in the Dispensation (Sāsana). He would cause those already endowed with virtues like faith to mature.

In this way, this incomparable stream of wholesome merit, which is the Bodhisatta's virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla),
111:
213

increased and flourished stage by stage from one life to another.

(This is the sequence of fulfilling the Perfection of Virtue - Sīla Pāramī.)

(3) The sequence of fulfilling the Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma Pāramī) is as follows:

Nekkhamma Pāramī refers to the group of wholesome mental states (kusala-citta-cetasika) characterized by the desire to escape and be liberated from sensual pleasures (kāma) and existence (bhava), based on Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) and Skill in Means (Upāyakosalla-ñāṇa) as previously mentioned, and preceded by the Knowledge of Danger (Ādīnava-ñāṇa) which sees the faults in those sensual pleasures and existences. Therefore, the Bodhisatta first saw the faults in those sensual pleasures and existences as they truly are through the Knowledge of Danger. The way he saw them was as follows:

He saw that living in a household (the life of a layperson) is the abode of all defilements (saṅkilesa); that it is extremely narrow and cramped for the arising of wholesome states due to impediments (palibodha) such as wife and children; and that it is very cluttered and confused with various affairs such as trading and farming. Thus, he saw it as a place where the happiness of renunciation (nekkhamma-sukha) and so forth cannot be attained.

He saw that the sensual pleasures enjoyed by humans are like licking a drop of honey stuck to the edge of a sword—they provide little satisfaction and result in much harm. They are like a festival or dance seen for a single moment during a flash of lightning—the time of enjoyment is very short. They are like the ornaments of a madman—things to be experienced and enjoyed only through distorted perception (saññā). Like an object used to cover
112:
214

filth, they are merely deceptive imitations. Like licking a small amount of water clinging to a wet finger, they cause lack of contentment. Like a person suffering from intense hunger eating food, they are accompanied by disease. Like bait on a fishhook, they are the cause of a mass of destruction. Like a hot fire, they are the cause of suffering in all three periods of time. Like monkey's glue, they are the cause of being bound. Like objects covering an executioner, they are merely things that cover up harm. Having seen and reflected on the faults in sensual pleasures and existence in such ways, and having reflected on the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma) which is the escape and liberation from those sensual pleasures and existence, he fulfilled the Perfection of Renunciation.

In fulfilling it, since the state of a monk is the fundamental basis for the completion of the Perfection of Renunciation, the Bodhisatta, in order to fully practice the Perfection of Renunciation, would first take up the life of a rishi or a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka) during times outside of a Buddha's Dispensation, following those who believe in action (kammavādī) and the efficacy of action (kiriyavādī) who hold that wholesome and unwholesome karma and their results clearly exist. During the time of a Buddha's Dispensation, he would take up the life of a monk within the Dispensation (he would ordain as a monk).

After becoming a monk, he would establish himself in the two types of virtue previously mentioned—the virtue of avoidance (vāritta-sīla) and the virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla)—and he would undertake and practice the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) to make that Perfection of Virtue pure and clean.
113:
215

By thus enhancing his practice with the dhutaṅga and washing away the impurities of defilements with the pure water of virtue (sīla), the Bodhisatta, possessing blameless and extremely pure conduct of body and speech, became established in the first three factors of the Noble Lineage (Ariyavaṃsa)—contentment with whatever robes are obtained, contentment with whatever alms-food is obtained, and contentment with whatever lodging is obtained. To attain the fourth factor of the Noble Lineage, which is delighting in meditation (bhāvanārāma), he developed and practiced meditation as appropriate among the forty subjects of tranquility meditation (samatha-kammaṭṭhāna), reaching access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) and absorption concentration (appanā-jhāna). When he reached absorption concentration, it is said that the Bodhisatta had well-fulfilled the Perfection of Renunciation.

(The detailed explanation regarding the forty subjects of meditation should be taken from the Visuddhimagga.)

(This is the sequence of fulfilling the Perfection of Renunciation.)

(4) The sequence of fulfilling the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā Pāramī) is as follows:

The Bodhisatta, in fulfilling the Perfection of Wisdom, realized that the light of wisdom cannot coexist with the darkness of delusion (moha). Therefore, he first avoided states such as discontent with wholesome practices, laziness, and physical lethargy, which are causes of delusion. He then exerted effort in great learning (bāhusacca), jhāna, and other states that are causes for the growth of wisdom.
114:
216

## (a) Sutamaya-paññā

To mature the wisdom based on learning (sutamaya-paññā) called great learning (bāhusacca), the Bodhisatta—with mindfulness (sati), energy (vīriya), and wisdom (paññā) preceded by skill in means (upāyakosalla-ñāṇa)—respectfully studied, listened to, memorized, recited, and investigated the fields of learning. These include the five aggregates (khandha), twelve bases (āyatana), eighteen elements (dhātu), four truths (sacca), twenty-two faculties (indriya), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and various ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma) such as wholesome and unwholesome states. He also studied various types of blameless worldly arts and sciences that can bring about the welfare and happiness of beings. Having himself become a wise person who penetrated and understood these teachings, he then generated wisdom based on learning in others by establishing them in those teachings.

Likewise, he generated the intuitive wisdom (paṭibhāna-paññā) called ready wit (ṭhānuppattika), which is the skill in means (upāyakosalla-ñāṇa) that discerns the factors for success and prosperity and the factors for failure and loss in the various affairs of beings, as appropriate in those various matters for the benefit of beings.

## (b) Cintāmaya-paññā

Likewise, he generated wisdom based on reflection (cintāmaya-paññā) by closely and penetratingly observing and reflecting on the nature of ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma) such as the aggregates.

(The act of studying, listening to, and memorizing ultimate realities such as the aggregates is wisdom based on learning. After having studied, listened to, and memorized them,)
115:
...investigating and contemplating with focused attention, preceded by thinking about the nature of phenomena, is wisdom based on thinking (cintāmaya-paññā).)

## (c) Wisdom Based on Mental Development (Bhāvanāmaya-paññā)
Similarly, by means of comprehending the individual characteristics (paccatta-lakkhaṇa) and the common characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) of phenomena such as the aggregates (khandhas), the Bodhisatta, who brings about mundane full understanding (lokiya-pariññā), also develops and fulfills the nine stages of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), such as the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa), which constitutes the preliminary stage of wisdom based on mental development.

By thus developing and fulfilling these, the Bodhisatta clearly perceives internal and external objects as mind and matter (nāma-rūpa). He understands: "This mass of phenomena, which is merely mind and matter, arises and ceases due to their respective causes. In this mass of mind and matter, there is no 'doer' or 'one who causes to do' in the ultimate sense. Indeed, these two realities of mind and matter are truly impermanent (anicca) because they arise and then perish; they are suffering (dukkha) because they are oppressed by arising and passing away; and they are non-self (anatta) because they do not follow one's will." He understands this uniformly, without distinction, for both internal and external phenomena. Having understood thus, he abandons greed and attachment to this internal and external mass of phenomena himself and causes others to abandon it. During this period before becoming a Buddha (without yet possessing Omniscience), through the power of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) alone, he works for the sake of beings regarding the three types of Enlightenment (Bodhi).
116:
He establishes those who have not yet reached the three vehicles (yānas) of practice that lead to the maturation of Enlightenment, and he matures those who have already reached them. For his own part, he attains the fivefold mastery (vasībhāva) over various mundane jhānas, attainments (samāpattis), and supernormal powers (abhiññās). Due to the special supportive influence of concentration (samādhi) associated with these mundane jhānas and supernormal powers, he reaches the pinnacle of wisdom.

(In this regard, the method of developing mundane jhānas, attainments, and supernormal powers, as well as the ten stages of insight knowledge, should be understood from the Visuddhimagga. Specifically, in the Visuddhimagga, the development of wisdom for a future Disciple (Sāvaka-bodhisatta) is explained up to the Path (Magga). Here, however, as it concerns a future Perfectly Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambodhi-bodhisatta), it differs in that all developmental practices are preceded by compassion and the knowledge of skillful means (upāya-kosalla-ñāṇa). Furthermore, as a Bodhisatta, he must halt his progress at the sixth stage, the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way (Paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), before reaching the Path Knowledge called Purification by Knowledge and Vision (Ñāṇadassana-visuddhi). Among the ten insight knowledges, he must halt the development of wisdom at the nine lower insight knowledges, up to the early stage of the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations (Saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa).)

(This is the sequence of fulfilling the Perfection of Wisdom.)

(5) The sequence of fulfilling the Perfection of Energy (Vīriya-pāramī), etc.

Just as a general who wishes to defeat an enemy must strive incessantly at all times, so too the Bodhisatta, wishing to conquer the enemy of defilements (kileas) by himself without a teacher and then...
117:
...wishing to enable venereable beings to conquer them just as he did, strives with great effort to fulfill the Perfections at all times.

Therefore, the Bodhisatta, being constantly mindful, reflects every single day: "What foundations of merit and wisdom have I developed today? What benefit have I performed for others today?" Thus reflecting, he exerts great effort for the welfare of beings.

To be of service to beings, he generously sacrifices his own possessions, his body, and his life without hesitation.

Every physical and verbal action he performs or speaks is done with a mind inclined toward Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Furthermore, for every physical and verbal merit performed, he directs his mind and makes an aspiration only for the attainment of Omniscience.

(Not to mention abundant or inferior sensual objects,) even regarding excellent sensual objects in small quantities, he possesses only a mind of detachment and a desire for renunciation.

In all matters to be performed, he acts only after generating the knowledge of skillful means (upāya-kosalla-ñāṇa).

He always exerts effort for the various benefits of beings.

He endures all kinds of pleasant (iṭṭha) and unpleasant (aniṭṭha) objects he encounters.

Even for the sake of his life, he does not commit a fault and remains firmly established in truth.
118:
He develops loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā) toward all beings without limit. Like a father who wishes to suffer the pain of his child himself, he desires to take upon himself all the sufferings that might fall upon beings.

He rejoices with sympathetic joy (anumodanā) in the meritorious deeds of all beings. He constantly reflects on the greatness and the vast majesty of the Buddhas. All his physical and verbal actions are performed with a mind inclined and directed toward Omniscience.

In this way, for the Great Being who constantly exerts effort in meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna), the immeasurable foundations of merit and wisdom increase day by day.

Furthermore, the Bodhisatta, having generously sacrificed his body and life for the use and protection of beings, seeks and employs effective methods to remove the suffering of hunger and thirst, and the suffering caused by cold, heat, wind, and sun that beings encounter. He strives with a strong mind so that every being, without limit, may obtain and enjoy the various kinds of happiness he has gained by removing the aforementioned sufferings; the various kinds of physical and mental happiness he has gained by living in delightful parks, gardens, palaces, reservoirs, and forest monasteries; and the various kinds of happiness he has heard about from others—such as the bliss of jhānas and attainments enjoyed by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Noble Disciples, and Great Bodhisattas after their renunciation.
119:
(This is the manner in which the Bodhisatta strives and exerts himself during the period before attaining jhānas and attainments.)

After attaining jhānas and attainments, the Bodhisatta, while contemplating the group of states consisting of joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, and seeing things as they truly are—which arise from the jhānas and attainments he himself enjoys—directs his mind and exerts effort so that all beings may obtain the same.

Furthermore, he sees beings who are submerged and without a savior in the great suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa), in the suffering of defilements which is the cause of that round, and in the suffering of formations (abhisaṅkhāra-dukkha) that causes one to wander in the round. His vision is as follows:

He sees clearly the beings in hell (niraya) suffering intense and agonizing pain for a long time without interruption, due to being cut, chopped, split, and crushed, and due to the fires of hell and so forth.

He sees clearly the beings in the animal kingdom suffering great distress due to mutual anger, causing each other heat, being oppressed and slaughtered, and having to endure whatever others command or force them to do.

He sees clearly the hungry ghosts (petas) whose entire bodies are covered in large sparks of fire, who are parched and consumed by hunger, thirst, wind, and sun, who live eating filth such as vomit and saliva, and who suffer great distress, weeping with their arms raised.
120:
He also sees clearly how human beings suffer: some are ruined and destroyed for the sake of their livelihood; some suffer deep misery and disfigurement, no different from beings in hell, due to receiving criminal punishments such as the amputation of hands and feet; some suffer distress no different from hungry ghosts, being oppressed by diseases such as hunger and thirst because their livelihood is insufficient; and some suffer distress no different from animals, being oppressed by the powerful because they lack material and human resources, having to carry out only the interests of those powerful ones, and having their very life and death dependent on them (having to rely only on them).

Regarding the devas in the six celestial planes of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), although ordinary people see only pure happiness, in the Bodhisatta's view, they are agitated in mind because they have swallowed the poison of sensual objects. They are burned by the fevers of passion (rāga), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha). Like large bonfires of dry wood blazing brightly when fanned by the wind, they can never find coolness at any time and live in a state of burning. Being oppressed by this inability to find peace, they must...
121:
...rely on others. This he sees clearly.

He also sees clearly the great Brahmas of the fine-material and immaterial spheres: though they live as long as eighty-four thousand great aeons (mahākappa), they are like birds thrown high into the distant sky with great effort, or like arrows shot far by a strong man; because they have impermanence (anicca) as their end, they must surely end in falling down. He sees clearly: "Alas, they cannot transcend the suffering of birth (jāti), the suffering of aging (jarā), and the suffering of death (maraṇa)."

Having seen and understood thus clearly, great spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arises in him, and he radiates loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā) without limit to the beings of the thirty-one planes.

In this way, the Great Being, who accumulates the merits for Enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra) through the three doors of body, speech, and mind without interruption, exerts himself with unflagging renewed strength through the practice of respect (sakkacca-bhāvanā), which means developing the perfections with reverence, and the practice of persistence (sātacca-bhāvanā), which means developing them constantly.

Alternatively, the energy (vīriya) that is the root cause capable of leading one to Buddhahood—the state which is the foundation of immeasurable, incomparable, extensive, and perfectly pure qualities—is so great in majesty that it is beyond thought. Let alone ordinary people being able to practice such energy of the Bodhisatta, they would not even dare to hear of it.
122: To elaborate further: The aspiration to become a Buddha is rooted in the three intentions: "Buddho bodheyyaṃ, mutto moceyyaṃ, tiṇṇo tāreyyaṃ" (Being enlightened, I shall enlighten others; being liberated, I shall liberate others; having crossed over, I shall help others cross). This involves the four great Buddha-bhūmi (stages of a Buddha) which were previously explained in the section on the causes of the perfections; the four saṅgahavatthu (bases of sympathy); having the sole task of compassion; the intense contemplation and investigation of the nature of Dhamma which is the distinguished cause for realizing the attributes of a Buddha; being unstained by craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi) in all things; being able to regard and treat all sentient beings as one's own beloved children; having no mental weariness towards the sufferings of saṃsāra encountered while practicing for Buddhahood; the complete renunciation of all gift-objects; not becoming conceited by thinking "There is no one in the world who can give like me" after such renunciation; undertaking the training of higher virtue (adhisīla), higher mind (adhicitta), and higher wisdom (adhipaññā); being unshakable and firm in practicing those teachings; being greatly delighted and joyful in meritorious deeds; having a mind inclined towards the three types of seclusion (viveka); exerting effort in the Jhanas; not being content with merely blameless states; teaching and demonstrating the Dhamma one has heard to others with a mind desiring their welfare; initiating and renewing effort in the collection of perfections and merits; exerting courageously with increasing intensity without slackening; being entirely unmoved by the accusations or harmful acts of others; standing firm in truth (sacca); being proficient and masterful in the Jhana attainments; reaching power in the higher spiritual knowledges (abhiññā); personally discerning the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa); and accumulating the requisites of the four supramundane paths by developing meditation subjects such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). These meritorious requisites of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), such as these,
123:
can only be fulfilled through the power of Viriya (effort). Therefore, from the time of making the aspiration for Buddhahood until becoming a Buddha, the Bodhisatta exerts himself with respect and constancy, without retreating, to fulfill the noble Viriya that leads to the attainment of higher and higher Dhamma.

When the aforementioned Parakkama-viriya (effort that leads to higher attainment) is fulfilled, the subsequent perfections such as Khanti-pāramī and Sacca-pāramī, as well as the preceding perfections such as Dāna and Sīla, are also fulfilled because they occur in connection with Viriya. Thus, the sequence of practice for the subsequent perfections like Khanti-pāramī should be understood in this same manner.

In this way:
Supporting beings in various ways by renouncing gift-objects, which are the foundations of happiness, is the fulfillment of Dāna (generosity). Not destroying but protecting the lives, essence of property, and wives and children of beings; not causing division; speaking endearing words; and speaking beneficial words, etc., is the fulfillment of Sīla (virtue). Likewise, through Nekkhamma (renunciation), practicing for the great benefit of beings by accepting their four requisites and giving them the gift of Dhamma, etc.; through Paññā (wisdom), being skillful and discerning in the proper means for the welfare of beings; through Viriya (effort), exerting oneself tirelessly and enduring hardship in those means; through Khanti (patience), enduring all wrongs committed by beings; through Sacca (truthfulness),
124:
not lying or deceiving beings, and not failing in the undertaking to benefit beings; through Adhiṭṭhāna (determination), remaining unshaken even if harm comes to oneself because of working for the benefit of beings; through Mettā (loving-kindness), repeatedly contemplating the welfare and happiness of beings; through Upekkhā (equanimity), not reaching a state of fluctuation due to the benefits or harms done by beings to oneself—in this way, the accumulation and development of the Bodhisatta's unique and incomparable requisites of merit and wisdom based on infinite beings, and the respectful fulfillment of the causes of the perfections mentioned earlier, should be briefly understood as the practice (paṭipatti) of fulfilling the perfections.

## (11) The Varieties of Perfections
If it is asked, "How many are the varieties of the aforementioned perfections?"

The brief answer is that there are thirty varieties: the ten perfections (pāramī), the ten secondary perfections (upapāramī), and the ten ultimate perfections (paramattha-pāramī).

(In connection with Dāna, it is divided into three: Dāna-pāramī, Dāna-upapāramī, and Dāna-paramattha-pāramī. Similarly, in connection with the other nine such as Sīla and Nekkhamma, each is divided into three, such as Sīla-pāramī, Sīla-upapāramī, and Sīla-paramattha-pāramī. Thus, when the ten perfections are expanded, they become thirty.)
125:
## The Distinction between Pāramī, Upapāramī, and Paramattha-pāramī
If it is asked, "What is called Pāramī? What is called Upapāramī? What is called Paramattha-pāramī?", the various views, statements, and doctrines of different teachers are extensively explained in this Miscellaneous Section of the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary to answer that question. However, if all those various doctrines were presented in this Chronicle of Buddhas, it might confuse the understanding and intellect of those studying this text. Therefore, only the decision favored by the noble Elder Mahādhammapāla, the author of the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary, will be presented in this work.

(1) The renunciation of external (bāhira) belongings such as children, wives, gold, silver, and property is called Dāna-pāramī. The renunciation of major and minor limbs such as hands and feet is called Dāna-upapāramī. The renunciation of life is called Dāna-paramattha-pāramī.

(2) Similarly, the secure observance of the training rules without transgression even for the sake of external belongings such as children, wives, gold, silver, and property is called Sīla-pāramī. The secure observance of the training rules without transgression even for the sake of major and minor limbs such as hands and feet is called Sīla-upapāramī. The secure observance of the training rules without transgression even for the sake of life is called Sīla-paramattha-pāramī.

(3) Renouncing the world by cutting off craving and greed attached to external belongings is called Nekkhamma-pāramī. Renouncing the world by cutting off craving and greed attached to
126:
craving and greed attached to major and minor limbs such as hands and feet is called Nekkhamma-upapāramī. Renouncing the world by cutting off craving and greed attached to life is called Nekkhamma-paramattha-pāramī.

(4) Discerning and contemplating the presence or absence of benefit for beings by removing craving and greed attached to external belongings is called Paññā-pāramī. Discerning and contemplating the presence or absence of benefit for beings by removing craving and greed attached to major and minor limbs such as hands and feet is called Paññā-upapāramī. Discerning and contemplating the presence or absence of benefit for beings by removing craving and greed attached to life is called Paññā-paramattha-pāramī.

(5) Exerting for the accomplishment and fulfillment of the perfections already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned is called Viriya-pāramī. Exerting for the accomplishment and fulfillment of the secondary perfections already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned is called Viriya-upapāramī. Exerting for the accomplishment and fulfillment of the ultimate perfections already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned is called Viriya-paramattha-pāramī.

(6) Enduring the worldly conditions (lokadhamma) that cause harm to external belongings is called Khanti-pāramī. Enduring the worldly conditions that cause harm to major and minor limbs such as hands and feet is called Khanti-upapāramī. Enduring the worldly conditions that cause harm to life is called Khanti-paramattha-pāramī.

(7) Not abandoning the truth for the sake of external belongings is called Sacca-pāramī. Not abandoning the truth for the sake of major and minor limbs such as hands and feet
127:
is called Sacca-upapāramī. Not abandoning the truth even for the sake of life is called Sacca-paramattha-pāramī.

(8) Firmly believing that "the perfections such as Dāna can only be fulfilled if they are undertaken without destruction," and thus maintaining the undertaking unshakably even when external belongings are destroyed is called Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī. Maintaining the undertaking unshakably even when major and minor limbs such as hands and feet are destroyed is called Adhiṭṭhāna-upapāramī. Maintaining the undertaking unshakably even when life itself is destroyed is called Adhiṭṭhāna-paramattha-pāramī.

(9) Not abandoning loving-kindness (not failing in the radiation of mettā) even towards beings who destroy or oppress external belongings is called Mettā-pāramī. Not abandoning loving-kindness even towards beings who destroy or oppress major and minor limbs such as hands and feet is called Mettā-upapāramī. Not abandoning loving-kindness even towards beings who would oppress or destroy one's own life is called Mettā-paramattha-pāramī.

(10) Maintaining equanimity towards beings and formations (saṅkhāra) that cause benefit or harm to external belongings is called Upekkhā-pāramī. Maintaining equanimity towards beings and formations that cause benefit or harm to major and minor limbs such as hands and feet is called Upekkhā-upapāramī. Maintaining equanimity towards beings and formations that cause benefit or harm to one's own life is called Upekkhā-paramattha-pāramī. In this way, the detailed varieties of the perfections should be understood.

(This concludes the varieties of the perfections.)

## (12) The Summary of the Perfections
If it is asked, "What are the summarized teachings of the perfections?"

The answer is: Just as the thirty detailed varieties of perfections, when grouped by similar nature, are counted as only ten (the three types of Dāna being grouped as Dāna-pāramī due to their similar nature of giving, and so on), similarly, if the ten perfections such as Dāna and Sīla are again grouped by similar nature, there are only six essential types.

"Dā, Sī, Khan, Vī, Jhāna, and Paññā; these six are the summary."

The method of grouping by similar nature is as follows: Nekkhamma (renunciation) refers to monkhood, Jhana, or wholesome states in general. Among these, Nekkhamma as monkhood is grouped with Sīla-pāramī due to their similar nature. Nekkhamma as Jhana, which is secluded from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), is indeed Jhāna-pāramī. Nekkhamma as general wholesome states can be grouped within all six.

Sacca (truthfulness) refers to these three: Vacī-sacca (truthful speech), Virati-sacca (the mental factor of abstinence, sammā-vācā), and Ñāṇa-sacca (the mental factor of wisdom). (Paramattha-sacca, which is Nibbāna, is not required here.) Among these, Vacī-sacca and Virati-sacca are grouped with Sīla-pāramī due to their similar nature. Ñāṇa-sacca, being the mental factor of wisdom, is counted under Paññā-pāramī.

Tatramajjhattatā should be classified and counted under jhāna-pāramī, while the equanimity of knowledge (ñāṇupekkhā), which is the mental factor of wisdom, should be classified under the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī). (c) Through the pair of Dāna and Viriya, the set of wholesome qualities—generosity (cāga) and learning (suta)—is fulfilled. (d) Through the pair of Dāna and Jhāna, the set of wholesome qualities—abandoning sensuality and abandoning hatred—is fulfilled. (e) Through the pair of Dāna and Paññā, both the vehicle of tranquillity (samatha-yāna) and the vehicle of insight (vipassanā-yāna) are fulfilled. (f) Through the pair of Sīla and Khanti, the set of wholesome qualities—purity of effort (payoga-suddhi) in terms of bodily and verbal actions, and purity of inclination (āsaya-suddhi) in terms of the heart's intention—is fulfilled. (g) Through the pair of Sīla and Viriya, the set of wholesome qualities—tranquillity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) meditation—is fulfilled. (h) Through the pair of Sīla and Jhāna, the set of wholesome qualities—abandoning defilements of transgression (vītikkama-kilesa) and abandoning defilements of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna-kilesa)—is fulfilled. (Defilements of transgression refer to those that cause one to overstep in bodily and verbal actions; these are abandoned through Sīla. Defilements of obsession refer to those that do not yet cause bodily or verbal overstepping but arise and rage within the mind; these are removed through Jhāna.)
131: (i) Through the pair of Sīla and Paññā, the set of the gift of safety (abhaya-dāna) and the gift of Dhamma (dhamma-dāna) is fulfilled. (Abhaya-dāna can be performed only when there is Sīla; Dhamma-dāna can be performed only when there is Paññā.) (j) Through the pair of Khanti and Viriya, the set of the quality of endurance and the quality of sharpness/striving is fulfilled. (Endurance exists only when there is Khanti to withstand both good and bad worldly conditions; striving is sharp in wholesome deeds only when there is Viriya.) (k) Through the pair of Khanti and Jhāna, the two benefits—abandoning opposition caused by hatred and abandoning compliance caused by greed—are fulfilled. (Without Khanti, one tends to oppose disagreeable worldly conditions with hatred; without Jhāna, one tends to be immersed in and comply with agreeable worldly conditions with greed.) (l) Through the pair of Khanti and Paññā, the two benefits—the ability to look intently at the emptiness of mind and matter from the concept of a being or soul (referring to dhamma-nijjhānakkhanti) and the ability to realize Nibbāna—are fulfilled. (m) Through the pair of Viriya and Jhāna, the two qualities of uplifting (paggaha) and non-distraction (avikkhepa) are fulfilled. (n) Through the pair of Viriya and Paññā, the two benefits—being a refuge for venereable beings and being a refuge for oneself—are fulfilled. (It means that through Viriya, one becomes a refuge for beings, and through Paññā, one becomes a refuge for oneself.) (o) Through the pair of Jhāna and Paññā, both the vehicle of tranquillity and the vehicle of insight are fulfilled.
132: ## Benefits Obtained by Combining Three. For the Great Bodhisattas: (1) Through the set of Dāna, Sīla, and Khanti, the three benefits of abandoning the three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—are obtained. (Greed is abandoned through Dāna, hatred through Sīla, and delusion through Khanti.) (2) Through the set of Dāna, Sīla, and Viriya, the three benefits of taking the essence of wealth, taking the essence of the body, and taking the essence of life are obtained. (Because it is associated with the five kinds of enemies, wealth has no essence; its essence is only Dāna. Because it is associated with many kinds of diseases, the body has no essence; its essence is only Sīla. Because it ends in destruction, life has no essence; its essence is only the practice of insight meditation (vipassanā). This matter is explained in the Kaṇha Jātaka Commentary of the Dasaka Nipāta.) (3) Through the set of Dāna, Sīla, and Jhāna, the benefit of completing the three types of meritorious actions (puṇya-kiriya)—giving, virtue, and mental development—is obtained. (4) Through the set of Dāna, Sīla, and Paññā, the benefit of completing the three types of giving—giving of material things (āmisa-dāna), giving of safety (abhaya-dāna), and giving of Dhamma (dhamma-dāna)—is obtained. 133: 235  In this same way, the fulfillment of three or four benefits through the remaining sets of three or four practices should be understood by combining them appropriately.  ## Classification of the Six Perfections into Four Factors  As mentioned, by grouping similar natures, the sixfold perfections—dāna, sīla, khanti, viriya, jhāna, and paññā—should be understood as being classified into the four factors of determination (adhiṭṭhāna). These four adhiṭṭhānas are:  “Truth, Relinquishment, Peace, and Noble Wisdom—these are the four determinations.” According to this:  (1) The determination of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna),  (2) The determination of relinquishment (cāgādhiṭṭhāna),  (3) The determination of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna),  (4) The determination of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna).  Among these:  (1) The determination of truth means: Nibbāna, which is the ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca), along with the path leading to that Nibbāna...
134: (Because they serve as the basis and resting place during the lives of fulfilling Pāramīs and the life of becoming Buddha, vacī-sacca, virati-sacca, and ñāṇa-sacca are called foundations. Because it serves as the basis and resting place in the life of becoming Buddha, Nibbāna, which is the ultimate truth, is called a foundation.) (2) Cāga-adhiṭṭhāna refers to the absolute and root-level relinquishment of all defilements through the Path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga). To achieve such relinquishment, the giving up and abandoning of various objective sensualities (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensualities (kilesa-kāma) through various Pāramīs such as Dāna in the preceding lives of the Bodhisatta are called Cāga-adhiṭṭhāna. (During the period of fulfilling Pāramīs in Bodhisatta lives, since defilements cannot yet be absolutely relinquished at the root, the Great Bodhisattas must rely on and rest in the relinquishment of objective sensualities as appropriate through Pāramīs like Dāna, and the abandoning of subjective sensualities through momentary abandonment (tadanga-pahāna) and abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). Only upon becoming Buddha, having reached the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship and Omniscience, do they rely on and rest in the final and absolute root-level relinquishment of all defilements. Therefore, the absolute root-level relinquishment of all defilements through the Path of Arahantship, and the abandoning of various objective and subjective sensualities through Pāramīs like Dāna in Bodhisatta lives via momentary and suppressive abandonment, are called Cāga-adhiṭṭhāna.)
135: (3) Upasama-adhiṭṭhāna refers to the absolute cooling and peace from all the heat of defilements through the Path of Arahantship, and the absolute cooling and peace from all the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha) at the time of Parinibbāna. To achieve such absolute and final peace, the cooling of the heat of various defilements such as greed, hatred, and delusion through various Pāramīs like Dāna in the preceding lives of the Bodhisatta via momentary and suppressive means is called Upasama-adhiṭṭhāna. (During the period of fulfilling Pāramīs in Bodhisatta lives, since the heat of defilements and the heat of suffering in the round of rebirths are not yet absolutely and finally cooled, the Great Bodhisattas rely on and rest temporarily in the cooling of defilements like greed, hatred, and delusion through the Pāramīs like Dāna, which are the causes for such peace, via momentary and suppressive means. Only upon becoming Buddha do they rely on and rest in the final and absolute cooling of the heat of defilements and suffering. Therefore, the aforementioned cooling of the heat of defilements and suffering is called Upasama-adhiṭṭhāna.) (4) Paññā-adhiṭṭhāna refers to the wisdom of the Fruition of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala) and the wisdom of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), along with the various types of wisdom such as skill in means (upāya-kosalla-ñāṇa) that arise in the continuum of the Great Bodhisattas in the preceding period, which lead to the attainment of those wisdoms. (In the Bodhisatta lives, they rely on and rest in the preceding types of wisdom. Only upon becoming Buddha do they rely on and rest in the wisdom of the Fruition of Arahantship and Omniscience. Therefore, the various types of wisdom mentioned are called Paññā-adhiṭṭhāna.)
136:
Blind worldlings, who are heedless, rely and rest only upon objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma); thus, those objects of sensuality become the resting place for those blind worldlings. As for the Noble Bodhisattas, because they clearly perceive the faults of those objects of sensuality, they rely and rest upon these four qualities: Truth (Sacca), Relinquishment (Cāga), Peace (Upasama), and Wisdom (Paññā), which lead to Nibbāna, the escape from sensuality. Thus, these four qualities are the great Foundations of Resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) for the Great Bodhisattas.

## How the Four Foundations of Resolution Arise in the Bodhisatta's Continuum

The Noble Bodhisatta, having aspired to Buddhahood and received the Definite Prophecy (niyata-byādita), reflects upon the perfections (pāramī) with the Knowledge of Investigating Perfections (pāramī-pavicaya-ñāṇa). According to his intention and promise to fulfill those perfections until reaching Buddhahood, he fulfills, accumulates, and masters all perfections as a way of manifesting his verbal truth (vaci-sacca). Therefore, the Foundation of Truth (Saccādhiṭṭhāna) clearly arises within the Bodhisatta's continuum.

When fulfilling the perfections, because he relinquishes the defilements that are the opposites of those perfections and also relinquishes objective sensuality, the Foundation of Relinquishment (Cāgādhiṭṭhāna) also clearly arises.

Because the faults of defilements are calmed by the virtues of the perfections, the Foundation of Peace (Upasamādhiṭṭhāna) also clearly arises.
137:
Through those very perfections, because he is skilled and proficient in the means (upāya) for the welfare of others, the Foundation of Wisdom (Paññādhiṭṭhāna) also clearly arises.

(This means that whenever the ten perfections or the six perfections are fulfilled—or whenever the wholesome merits of the perfections arise—the following four foundations clearly arise in the Bodhisatta's continuum: (1) the Foundation of Truth, which is the unwavering effort according to his promise; (2) the Foundation of Relinquishment, which is the abandoning of unwholesome states that are the opposites of the perfections; (3) the Foundation of Peace, which is the calming of the dangers of defilements; and (4) the Foundation of Wisdom, which is the proficiency in the means for the welfare of beings. Thus, if the aforementioned six perfections are further condensed, they become the four Foundations of Resolution: Truth, Relinquishment, Peace, and Wisdom.)

A person who strives in any blameless worldly business, when they personally experience the fulfillment of their objectives and the resulting profits from that work, they will repeatedly and increasingly strive with diligent effort in that business. In this case, the fulfillment of objectives and the resulting profits from the previously performed business are the cause, and the repeated and increased diligent effort in that business is the effect.

Similarly, the Noble Bodhisatta, who strives in the extremely blameless work of the merits of perfections, personally enjoys and experiences the fulfillment of objectives and the resulting profits of the four foundations: the sweet taste of verbal truth (Saccaṃ have sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ — Truth is indeed the sweetest of tastes, Yakkha Saṃyutta Pāḷi), the relinquishment (Cāga) of opposing defilements,
138:
the peace (Upasama) from the calming of the heat of those defilements, and the foundation of wisdom (Paññā) which is the knowledge of skill in means. Consequently, he strives with diligent effort in those merits of perfections, increasing them life after life. In this striving, the fulfillment of objectives and the resulting profits of the four foundations experienced when performing previous perfections are the cause, and the merits of perfections performed repeatedly and increasingly in subsequent times are the effect. It should be understood through reflection that the arising of the merits of perfections and the arising of the four foundations are identical in essence, differing only in name. To explain in detail:

(1) While accumulating the merit of the Perfection of Generosity (Dāna Pāramī), the Noble Bodhisatta personally experiences the following four profits: (a) the Foundation of Truth, which is the unwavering act of giving according to his promise and intention upon seeing a recipient; (b) the Foundation of Relinquishment, which is the abandoning of unwholesome states such as stinginess (macchariya), which are the enemies and opposites of generosity; (c) the Foundation of Peace, which is the calming of the great unwholesome dangers: greed (lobha) which clings to the object of donation, hatred (dosa) toward the recipient (which can occur in those who do not wish to give), delusion (moha) regarding the act of giving (delusion can arise if one does not give), and fear (bhaya) of not having enough to eat or use if the object is given away, which occurs in those who do not wish to give; (d) the Foundation of Wisdom, which is the act of giving led by wisdom according to the appropriate time and planning. Because he experiences these four profits, he continues to develop and fulfill the Perfection of Generosity repeatedly and increasingly in the future.
140:
the Foundation of Relinquishment, which is abandoning slackness and weakness of effort; the Foundation of Peace, which is the calming of unwholesome dangers; and the Foundation of Wisdom, which is the possession of great wisdom. Because he experiences these four profits, he continues to develop and fulfill the Perfection of Energy repeatedly and increasingly in the future.

(5) When fulfilling and accumulating the Perfection of Jhana (Jhāna Pāramī), the Noble Bodhisatta personally experiences the four profits: the Foundation of Truth, which is contemplating the welfare of the world with fixed concentration as he promised; the Foundation of Relinquishment, which is abandoning the unwholesome hindrances (nīvaraṇa); the Foundation of Peace, which is the tranquility of the mind; and the Foundation of Wisdom, which is the possession of great wisdom. Because he experiences these four profits, he continues to develop and fulfill the Perfection of Jhana repeatedly and increasingly in the future.

(6) When fulfilling and accumulating the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā Pāramī), the Noble Bodhisatta personally experiences the four profits: the Foundation of Truth, which is skillfully performing the means for the welfare of others as he promised; the Foundation of Relinquishment, which is abandoning the pursuit of wrong paths and erroneous actions; the Foundation of Peace, which is the calming of all anxieties caused by ignorance (avijjā); and the Foundation of Wisdom, which is the possession of great wisdom. Because he experiences these four profits, he continues to develop and fulfill the Perfection of Wisdom repeatedly and increasingly in the future.
141:
According to the method described, whenever the merit of the perfections arises, the four Foundations of Resolution also arise. Thus, it is said that the six perfections are included and counted within the four Foundations of Resolution.

## Mutual Inclusion of the Foundations of Resolution

Just as the six perfections are included within the four Foundations of Resolution, each of the four Foundations of Resolution also includes the other three. The method of mutual inclusion is as follows:

The Foundations of Relinquishment, Peace, and Wisdom have the nature of being unwavering, truthful, and acting according to one's promise, just like the Foundation of Truth. Therefore, the three foundations of Relinquishment, Peace, and Wisdom are encompassed by the Foundation of Truth.

The Foundations of Truth, Peace, and Wisdom have the nature of abandoning their opposites, just like the Foundation of Relinquishment, and they are also the results of total relinquishment. Therefore, the three foundations of Truth, Peace, and Wisdom are encompassed by the Foundation of Relinquishment.

The Foundations of Truth, Relinquishment, and Wisdom have the nature of calming all the heat of the round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa) and the round of defilements (kilesa-vaṭṭa), just like the Foundation of Peace. Therefore, the three foundations of Truth, Relinquishment, and Wisdom are encompassed by the Foundation of Peace.
142:
The Foundations of Truth, Relinquishment, and Peace are led by wisdom and are themselves followers of wisdom. Therefore, the three foundations of Truth, Relinquishment, and Peace are encompassed by the Foundation of Wisdom.

## The Benefits Provided by the Foundations of Resolution

In this way, all perfections first arise because of the Foundation of Truth; they appear in their distinct manifestation through the Foundation of Relinquishment; they prosper and increase through the Foundation of Peace; and they become pure and distant from all surrounding defilements through the Foundation of Wisdom.

Furthermore, at the beginning of the perfections, the Foundation of Truth is the leader; only when there is the Foundation of Truth can the work of perfections be initiated. In the middle, the Foundation of Relinquishment is the leader; after starting the work of perfections with the Foundation of Truth, one can unreservedly sacrifice one's own life for the sake of others through the Foundation of Relinquishment. At the end, the Foundation of Peace is the leader; the task of perfections is completed only when all the suffering of the round of rebirths is calmed. The Foundation of Wisdom, however, is the leader in all three stages: the beginning, the middle, and the end. Only with wisdom can one initiate the effort, sacrifice one's life unreservedly, and completely calm all the suffering of the round of rebirths.

All four Foundations of Resolution constantly work for the welfare of both oneself and others. They also make one a person who is loved and respected, and venerated like a royal stone-parasol by all people.
143:
245
Among these four foundations (adhiṭṭhāna), because they possess the two foundations of Truth (Sacca-adhiṭṭhāna) and Liberality (Cāga-adhiṭṭhāna), the Great Bodhisattas, when they are in the state of laypeople, support others through the gift of material things (āmisa-dāna). Because they possess the two foundations of Tranquility (Upasama-adhiṭṭhāna) and Wisdom (Paññā-adhiṭṭhāna), when they are in the state of homeless ascetics or monks, they support others through the gift of the Dhamma (dhamma-dāna).

## The Completion of the Four Foundations in the Final (Pacchima) Birth

Note: In the presentation of Acariyavāda (the views and doctrines of various teachers) in the scriptures, if it is the view of teachers worthy of being placed in the position of the main author's teacher, it is usually expressed as "Eke vadanti" (Some say) or "Aññe vadanti" (Others say). If it is the view of teachers equal in qualification to the main author, it is usually expressed as "Apare vadanti" (Others say). If it is the view of teachers lower in qualification than the main author, it is usually expressed as "Keci vadanti" (Some say).

Therefore:
"Eke and Aññe—refer to the teachers,
Apare—refer to those of equal status,
Keci—refer to those of lower status."

This mnemonic (niyama) has been handed down by successive generations of recorders. Thus, if one says "Eke teachers" or "Aññe teachers," they should be understood as teachers who stand in the position of the main author's teacher. If one says "Apare teachers," they should be understood as teachers equal to the main author.
144:
246
If one says "Keci teachers," they should be understood as teachers lower in qualification than the main author.

## Eke-vāda

1. Regarding the complete and final fulfillment of the four foundations in the last (pacchima) birth of becoming a Buddha, the Eke teachers say that the four foundations are already fully completed from the very moment of conception. (Just as the conception in the final birth occurs only when the task of fulfilling the perfections is entirely complete, so too the conception in the final birth occurs only when the four foundations are entirely and fully completed.)

In their explanation, the Eke teachers state: Because the Great Bodhisatta has already achieved the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom (Paññā-adhiṭṭhāna), he is possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) when descending into his mother's womb, when staying in the mother's womb for ten months, and when being born.

Ordinary worldly people do not know when they descend into the mother's womb, nor when they stay in the womb, nor when they are born. Those destined to be the eighty great disciples (asīti-sāvaka) know only the time of descending into the mother's womb, but they do not know the time of staying in the womb or the time of birth. Those destined to be the two chief disciples (aggasāvaka) and those destined to be Paccekabuddhas know only the time of descending into the mother's womb and the time of staying in the womb, but they do not know the time of birth. Indeed, for those destined to be chief disciples or Paccekabuddhas, at the time nearing birth,
145:
247
the birth-winds (kammaja-vāta) turn them upside down and cast them toward the birth canal (yoni-mukha) as if being thrown into a very deep abyss. Because they must emerge through the very narrow birth canal, like a great elephant emerging through a keyhole, they experience infinite suffering. Therefore, those destined to be chief disciples or Paccekabuddhas cannot know, "We are emerging from our mother's womb." Thus, one should reflect with great sense of urgency (saṃvega) on the dwelling and conception in the mother's womb, thinking, "Even for those who have fulfilled the perfections, they must encounter such great suffering in this situation."

As for the Bodhisattas, they know all three stages: the time of descending into the womb, the time of staying there, and the time of birth. The birth-winds cannot turn the Bodhisattas upside down. Therefore, when Bodhisattas are born, they always emerge from the mother's womb standing firmly upright, with both hands extended and eyes open (like a noble Dhamma-preacher descending calmly from the Dhamma-throne).

Apart from the Omniscient Bodhisattas, there is not a single being who knows all three stages: the time of descending into the mother's womb, the time of staying in the womb, and the time of birth. Therefore, at the time when Bodhisattas are conceived (descend into the mother's womb) and at the time they are born, the ten thousand world systems
146:
248
tremble. (From the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, Vol. 3, page 69.)

Because the Great Bodhisatta has already fully completed the causal foundation of Truth (Sacca-adhiṭṭhāna), immediately after birth, he takes seven steps toward the north, looks fearlessly at all directions, and with words following the Truth, he roars three times like a lion-king, without fear or trembling: "Aggo'hamasmi lokassa, jeṭṭho'hamasmi lokassa, seṭṭho'hamasmi lokassa = I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the most excellent in the world."

Because he has already fully completed the causal foundation of Tranquility (Upasama-adhiṭṭhāna), when he saw the four great omens—an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a monk—he deeply understood the four summaries of the Dhamma (dhammuddesa) found in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta: how this body is oppressed by the law of aging (jarā), the law of sickness (byādhi), and the law of death (maraṇa), and how, if craving (taṇhā) for wealth and possessions does not cease, one cannot escape from being a slave to the dictates of that craving. In the continuity of the Bodhisatta, the various forms of pride (māna) were calmed: pride in youth (yobbana-māda), pride in health (ārogya-māda), pride in life (jīvita-māda), and pride in prosperity (sampatti-māda).

Because he has already fully completed the causal foundation of Liberality (Cāga-adhiṭṭhāna), he renounced without hesitation or attachment the royal splendor already in his hands along with many relatives, as well as the impending splendor of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti).
147:
249
This is how the Eke teachers explained it. The Venerable Elder Dhammapāla did not offer any criticism or scrutiny of this Eke-vāda.

## Keci-vāda

The Keci teachers say that the four foundations are fully and completely fulfilled at the second stage, which is the time of becoming a Buddha.

In their explanation: At the time of becoming a Buddha (when attaining the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscience), as previously resolved, through the causal foundation of Truth practiced in previous lives, he fully realizes the Four Noble Truths; thus, the foundation of Truth is fully and completely fulfilled. Through the causal foundation of Liberality practiced in previous lives, he is able to abandon all defilements (kilesa) by the root; thus, the foundation of Liberality is fully and completely fulfilled. Through the causal foundation of Tranquility practiced in previous lives, at the time of becoming a Buddha, he reaches the element of peace called Nibbāna, which is most sublime; thus, the foundation of Tranquility is fully and completely fulfilled. Through the causal foundation of Wisdom practiced in previous lives, at the time of becoming a Buddha, he attains Unobstructed Knowledge (Anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa), which knows all knowable things (ñeyya-dhamma) without hindrance or obstruction; thus, the foundation of Wisdom is fully and completely fulfilled.

This is how the Keci teachers explained it. Regarding this Keci-vāda, the Venerable Elder Dhammapāla stated, "Taṃ asiddhaṃ, abhisambodhiyāpi paramatthabhāvato," indicating that he could not accept it as being fully complete.
148:
250
The meaning is: The statement of those Keci teachers is not yet finished or complete. This is because the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscience, called Supreme Enlightenment (Abhisambodhi), is purely of the ultimate sense (paramattha), and also because the foundation of Tranquility (Upasama-adhiṭṭhāna) must be taken to include the non-arising cessation (the cessation which is called cessation because it does not arise) of the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha). Since that non-arising cessation of the suffering of the round of rebirths is a nature attainable only at the time of Parinibbāna, the statement of those Keci teachers is not yet finished or complete.

## Aññe-vāda

The Aññe teachers say that the four foundations are fully and completely fulfilled at the third stage, which is the time of preaching the Dhammacakka Sutta (when the knowledge of teaching is produced).

In their explanation: At the time of preaching that Dhammacakka Sutta, in the Buddha who has fulfilled the basic causal foundation of Truth practiced in previous lives, the foundation of Truth is fully and completely fulfilled by preaching the Noble Truths, analyzing and explaining the three modes—Sacca-ñāṇa, Kicca-ñāṇa, and Kata-ñāṇa—for each truth. In the Buddha who has fulfilled the basic causal foundation of Liberality practiced in previous lives, the foundation of Liberality is fully and completely fulfilled by distributing the Dhamma of the virtuous and performing the Great Gift of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma-mahādāna). In the Buddha who has fulfilled the basic causal foundation of Tranquility practiced in previous lives,
149:
251
because he himself has already quenched the heat of defilements and causes those to be disciplined (veneyya) to be quenched just as he is, the foundation of Tranquility is fully and completely fulfilled. In the Buddha who has fulfilled the basic causal foundation of Wisdom practiced in previous lives, the foundation of Wisdom is fully and completely fulfilled by clearly and exhaustively knowing the inclinations (āsaya) and underlying tendencies (anusaya) of those to be disciplined.

This is how the Aññe teachers explained it. Regarding this Aññe-vāda, the Venerable Elder Dhammapāla also criticized it, saying: "Tadapi asiddhaṃ, apariyositattā buddhakiccassa = Only when the Buddha's work (Buddha-kicca) is finished can the four foundations be fully and completely fulfilled. At the time of preaching the Dhammacakka Sutta, the Buddha's work has only just begun and has not yet reached its end; therefore, the doctrine of those Aññe teachers is also not yet finished or complete."

## Apare-vāda

The Apare teachers, however, say that the four foundations are fully and completely fulfilled at the fourth stage, which is the time of attaining Parinibbāna.

In their explanation: Among the foundations of Truth, the function of the foundation of Ultimate Truth (Paramattha-sacca-adhiṭṭhāna), which is Nibbāna—the greatest of all—is not yet finished or complete merely by reaching the Path of Arahatship and attaining the Parinibbāna of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna). Only when one enters the Parinibbāna of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna), where all is ceased and the drama of existence ends, is the function finished and complete. Therefore, at that time of Parinibbāna, the foundation of Truth is fully and completely fulfilled. At that time, the acquisitions (upadhi) consisting of: the acquisition of sensual pleasure (kāmupadhi), the acquisition of the aggregates (khandhupadhi), the acquisition of defilements (kilesupadhi), and the acquisition of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārupadhi)—
150:
252
Due to the absolute abandonment of the four kinds of acquisitions (upadhi), the foundation of relinquishment (cāgādhiṭṭhāna) is fully and perfectly completed. At that time, because all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) have absolutely ceased, the foundation of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna) is fully and perfectly completed. At that time, because the fruits of wisdom have reached their ultimate conclusion, the foundation of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna) is fully and perfectly completed.

This is how the Apare teachers explained it. The Venerable Dhammapāla, without criticizing the view of these Apare teachers at all, stated his own view by merely supplementing what was needed to that Apare view: "(1) At the time of birth, it is especially evident that the foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna) is completed. (2) At the time of becoming a Buddha, it is especially evident that the foundation of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna) is completed. (3) At the time of preaching the Dhammacakka, it is especially evident that the foundation of relinquishment (cāgādhiṭṭhāna) is completed through the great gift of Dhamma. (4) At the time of attaining Parinibbāna, it is especially evident that the foundation of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna) is completed."

To summarize the views of the teachers:
(1) The Eke teachers say that at the first stage, the time of taking conception in the final existence, the four foundations reach their conclusion and are completed.
(2) The Keci teachers say that at the second stage, the time of becoming a Buddha, the four foundations reach their conclusion and are completed.
(3) The Aññe teachers say that at the third stage, the time of preaching the Dhammacakka,
151:
253
the four foundations reach their conclusion and are completed.
(4) The Apare teachers say that at the fourth stage, the time of attaining Parinibbāna, the four foundations reach their conclusion and are completed.
(5) The Venerable Mahādhammapāla, the author of this Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary, following the record that "authors show their preferred view last," presented the Apare view last as his preference and accepted the view of the Apare teachers with a supplement. His way of acceptance with the supplement is: "According to the Apare view, the four foundations reach their completion only at the fourth stage, the time of attaining Parinibbāna; however, it is especially evident that the foundation of truth is completed at the first stage, the foundation of wisdom at the second stage, the foundation of relinquishment at the third stage, and the foundation of peace at the fourth stage." He accepted it by adding these words.

## Benefits of the Foundations
Through the foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna), the purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) is fulfilled. Through the foundation of relinquishment (cāgādhiṭṭhāna), the purification of livelihood (ājīvavisuddhi) is fulfilled. Through the foundation of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna), the purification of mind (cittavisuddhi) is fulfilled. Through the foundation of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna), the purification of knowledge (ñāṇavisuddhi) is fulfilled.

Furthermore, because of the foundation of truth (as it does not deviate), one does not follow the path of hatred (dosāgati). Because of the foundation of relinquishment (as one is not attached to or greedy for sensual objects), one does not follow the path of desire (chandāgati). Because of the foundation of peace (as there is no fault or defect in oneself),
152:
254
there is nothing to fear, and thus one does not follow the path of fear (bhayāgati). Because of the foundation of wisdom (as one sees things as they truly are), one does not follow the path of delusion (mohāgati).

Furthermore, because of the foundation of truth, without getting angry, one can endure heat and cold, hunger and thirst, the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun, and reptiles, as well as harsh and abusive words spoken by others, and extremely painful bodily sensations. Because of the foundation of relinquishment, without being attached by greed, one makes use of the four requisites: robes, alms-food, dwellings, and medicine. Because of the foundation of peace, without any fear (which is a form of shrinking anger), one avoids dangers such as wild elephants, wild horses, wild bulls, and wild dogs. Because of the foundation of wisdom, without any delusion (moha), one abandons the three types of wrong thoughts—sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka), malevolent thoughts (byāpāda-vitakka), and cruel thoughts (vihiṃsā-vitakka)—along with other unwholesome states.

Through the foundation of truth, one attains the happiness of renunciation (nekkhamma). Through the foundation of relinquishment, one attains the happiness of seclusion (paviveka). Through the foundation of peace, one attains the happiness of tranquility (upasama). Through the foundation of wisdom, one attains the happiness associated with the four paths of knowledge (magga-ñāṇa).

Through the foundation of truth, one attains the happiness of the first jhāna; through the foundation of relinquishment, the happiness of the second jhāna; through the foundation of peace, the happiness of the third jhāna; and through the foundation of wisdom, the happiness of the fourth jhāna.

In this way, one should understand how all the perfections (pāramīs) are collectively categorized and counted within the four foundations, which are followed by many such noble qualities and benefits.
153:
255
## Categorizing All Perfections into Two Factors
Just as all perfections are categorized by the four foundations, they are likewise categorized by the two factors: compassion (karuṇā) and wisdom (paññā). Indeed, only the qualities such as giving (dāna), which are embraced by compassion and wisdom (having compassion and wisdom as their fundamental basis), are the requisites for the knowledge of supreme enlightenment (sammāsambodhi-ñāṇa) and yield the fruit of becoming an Omniscient Buddha.

(These are the summary principles of the perfections.)

In this section:
One should understand the summary as follows: the thirty detailed perfections are condensed into the ten perfections; those ten are again condensed into the six perfections of giving (dāna), virtue (sīla), patience (khanti), energy (viriya), meditation (jhāna), and wisdom (paññā). Those six are again condensed into the four foundations of truth (sacca), relinquishment (cāga), peace (upasama), and wisdom (paññā). Finally, all perfections are condensed into the two factors of compassion (karuṇā) and wisdom (paññā).
