## (13) Factors for Fulfilling the Perfections
If it is asked, "What are the factors that cause the fulfillment of the perfections?"
(1) Practicing with the four types of development (bhāvanā);
(2) Abandoning the opposing states of the perfections by reflecting with the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa);
(3) Dedicating oneself to the Buddhas;
154:
256
In brief:
(a) The exhaustion of love for oneself;
(b) The increase of love for sentient beings—
These factors should be briefly answered as the causes for fulfilling the perfections.

In detail:
(1) Practicing with these four types of development is a great means for the fulfillment of the perfections: the development of all requisites (sabbasambhāra-bhāvanā), which is the practice of all perfections, relinquishments, and conducts aiming solely for the attainment of omniscience without any remainder; the respectful development (sakkacca-bhāvanā), which is practicing with great esteem and respect; the continuous development (nirantara-bhāvanā), which is practicing consistently throughout existences; and the long-term development (cirakāla-bhāvanā), which is practicing for a long duration without any shrinking or regression until becoming a Buddha.

(2) Furthermore, a person who is a Bodhisatta must first relinquish his own possessions even before receiving them, at the very door of giving, thinking: "When supplicants arrive, I shall give away all my possessions and wealth along with my life that I will obtain, without hesitation; I shall use only what remains after giving to those supplicants."

When the mind is thus prepared for prior relinquishment, regarding whatever possessions arise as one's own:
(a) Having no habit of giving in the past;
(b) The scarcity of one's own possessions;
155:
257
(c) The excellence of one's own possessions making one reluctant to give;
(d) The fear and thought that one's possessions will be exhausted—
Among these four factors that hinder and block the performance of the good deed of giving (dāna-vinibandha):

(a) Even when the objects to be given are complete and the supplicant is clearly present before him, if (perchance) there is no inclination in the Bodhisatta's mind to give, that Great Being decides and knows: "I certainly did not practice the habit of giving in previous lives. That is why, even though external factors are complete now, the wholesome desire to give does not stay or arise in my mind." Having so decided, he reflects with the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa): "Even if there is no desire to give, only by giving will I gain the habit, and my mind will then delight and find pleasure in the good deed of giving. Come now, from now on I shall give boldly and generously. Have I not already relinquished all my possessions to supplicants beforehand?" and then he gives freely and joyfully. When he gives in this way, the first hindrance to giving mentioned in point (a)—having no habit of giving—is severed from the Bodhisatta's mind.

(b) If the objects to be given are scarce or deficient, the Bodhisatta reflects as follows:
156:
258
"Because I did not give in the past, I am now deficient and poor in possessions. Therefore, now, whether it be little or inferior, I should give with whatever objects I have, even if I have to endure hardship and suffering myself. Through this gift, I shall bring the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) to its pinnacle in the future."

Thus he reflects. After reflecting in this way, the Bodhisatta gives freely and joyfully with whatever objects of giving he obtains. When he gives in this way, the second hindrance to giving mentioned in point (b)—the scarcity of one's own possessions—is severed from the Bodhisatta's mind.

(c) If a mind reluctant to give arises because the objects to be given are of very high quality, he reflects as follows:

"O virtuous Bodhisatta, do you not desire the great and most noble Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)? Therefore, to attain that most noble Golden Omniscience, you should give only the very best objects of giving."

Thus he reflects. After reflecting in this way, the Bodhisatta gives freely and joyfully the objects of giving that are very excellent and desirable. When he gives in this way, the third hindrance to giving mentioned in point (c)—the excellence of one's own possessions making one reluctant to give—is severed from the Bodhisatta's mind.
157:
259
(d) When the Bodhisatta sees the exhaustion of offerings while performing acts of generosity, he reflects as follows:
“The nature of depletion and exhaustion is indeed the inherent characteristic of wealth and possessions. In fact, it is because I did not perform acts of generosity in the past that would prevent such exhaustion that I now personally witness the depletion of offerings. Come now, I shall perform acts of generosity even with whatever little or much I have as offerings. Through this gift, I shall reach the pinnacle of the Perfection of Generosity (Dāna Pāramī) in the future.”
Having reflected thus, the Bodhisatta gives away whatever offerings he has with a free and clear mind. When he gives in this manner, the fourth obstacle to generosity mentioned in point (d)—the fear and anxiety that one’s own possessions will be exhausted—is severed within the Bodhisatta’s continuum.
In this way, reflecting upon and abandoning the obstacles to generosity through the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) as appropriate is a skilful means for the fulfillment of the Perfection of Generosity. This should be understood for the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla Pāramī) and others as well.
(3) Furthermore, a person who is a Bodhisatta must, from the very beginning, dedicate and surrender himself to the Buddhas, saying: “Imāhaṃ attabhāvaṃ buddhānaṃ niyyādemi = I dedicate and offer this physical personality to the Buddhas.” Thus, having previously dedicated himself to the Buddhas in advance—
158:
260
—dedicating and offering oneself to the Buddhas is a great skilful means for the fulfillment of all perfections.
Indeed, a Bodhisatta who has dedicated and surrendered himself to the Buddhas, while striving with diligence to fulfill the perfections in various lives, may encounter difficult and hard-to-endure tasks that could destroy his body and life, or meet with great harms caused by beings and formations (sattava-saṅkhāra) that are so sharp and violent they could take his life. At such times, he reflects: “I have already surrendered this physical personality to the Buddhas; let whatever happens in this matter happen.” Having reflected thus, he remains absolutely unshaken and undisturbed by those tasks and harms that could even threaten his life; instead, he stands firm and resolute only in the cultivation of the mass of merit that constitutes the perfections.
In this way, dedicating and offering oneself to the Buddhas is also a skilful means for the fulfillment of the perfections.
Furthermore, in brief, for the Great Being who is a Bodhisatta:
(a) The exhaustion of the affection of craving (taṇhā-sineha) for oneself,
(b) The increase of the affection of loving-kindness and compassion (mettā-karuṇā-sineha) for those to be disciplined (veneyya)—
These two are the causes for the fulfillment of the perfections.
159:
261
To elaborate further: In the continuum of the Great Being who has a strong aspiration and inclination of mind to attain Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), because he sees the nature of phenomena (sabhāva-dhamma) as they truly are, he is not attached to or smeared by those phenomena through craving, conceit, and wrong view (taṇhā, māna, diṭṭhi). Consequently, the affection of craving and love (taṇhā-pema-sineha) for his own self, which is merely a collection of natural phenomena, diminishes day by day until it is exhausted.
Because he looks upon all beings as if they were his own beloved children, having repeatedly cultivated the momentum of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā), the affection of loving-kindness and compassion—namely, love through the power of mettā and love through the power of karuṇā—only grows and flourishes more and more within the Bodhisatta’s mind.
Therefore, the Great Bodhisatta, having removed the opposing factors of the perfections such as stinginess (macchariya) by being free from greed, hatred, and delusion in his own continuum and the continua of others as appropriate to the moment, performs acts of favor for all beings through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu)—namely, Generosity (Dāna), Kindly Speech (Piyavācā), Beneficial Conduct (Atthacariyā), and Impartiality (Samānattatā)—which follow the four foundations (adhiṭṭhāna) previously mentioned. He brings those beings who have not yet entered the three vehicles of practice leading to the three types of Bodhi to enter them, and he nurtures those who have already entered to reach maturity.
Indeed, the compassion and wisdom of the Great Bodhisattas are adorned by the base of sympathy known as Generosity. (This does not mean compassion and wisdom exist in isolation or are dry without generosity;
160:
262
it means that compassion and wisdom arise while repeatedly giving gifts.) When giving, there is no harshness or shouting at the recipients and their attendants; the gift is given only after speaking pleasant and sweet words. Thus, the Great Bodhisattas’ base of sympathy of Generosity is adorned by the base of sympathy of Kindly Speech. In speaking pleasant words, it is not merely a superficial sweetness of the tongue to please the ear; it is a practice and speech for the benefit of the other party with a heart that truly desires their welfare. Thus, the Great Bodhisattas’ base of sympathy of Kindly Speech is adorned by the base of sympathy of Beneficial Conduct. (The fulfillment of the perfections, sacrifices, and conducts which are the requisites for Enlightenment is the practice for the benefit of beings; this is the base of sympathy of Beneficial Conduct.) For the Great Beings who practice the requisites for Enlightenment, they can maintain a mind that treats all beings as equal to themselves in every situation, sharing both suffering and happiness. Thus, the Great Bodhisattas’ base of sympathy of Beneficial Conduct is adorned by the base of sympathy of Impartiality (Samānattatā).
When they become Buddhas, because of the fulfillment of the four foundations (adhiṭṭhāna), they perform only the single task of favoring all beings through these four bases of sympathy which have increased to the utmost, thereby completing the work of liberation and discipline. To elaborate: The Buddhas’ base of sympathy of Generosity is increased and fulfilled by the Foundation of Liberality (Cāgādhiṭṭhāna). The base of sympathy of Kindly Speech is increased and fulfilled by the Foundation of Truth (Saccādhiṭṭhāna). The base of sympathy of Beneficial Conduct is increased and fulfilled by the Foundation of Wisdom (Paññādhiṭṭhāna). The base of sympathy of Impartiality is increased and fulfilled by the Foundation of Peace (Upasamādhiṭṭhāna).

## (14) The Duration for the Fulfillment of the Perfections
If it is asked, “For how long a duration are the perfections fulfilled? (How long must one fulfill the perfections to become a Buddha?)”
It should be said that after receiving the definite prophecy (niyata-byādita) upon aspiring for Buddhahood, the perfections are fulfilled in a minimum of four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa), a medium of eight asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons, and a maximum of sixteen asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons. (One becomes a Buddha only after fulfilling the perfections for this long.)
These three types of duration differ according to the three types of Bodhisattas: the Wisdom-led (Paññādhika) Bodhisatta, the Faith-led (Saddhādhika) Bodhisatta, and the Energy-led (Viriyādhika) Bodhisatta. (The perfections are fulfilled only after four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons for a Paññādhika Bodhisatta, eight asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons for a Saddhādhika Bodhisatta, and sixteen asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons for a Viriyādhika Bodhisatta; thus, it is meant that the duration varies according to the three types of Bodhisattas.)
If it is asked, “Why are there three different durations for fulfilling perfections when all are equally Bodhisattas?”
The answer is: In a Wisdom-led (Paññādhika) Bodhisatta, faith is weak while wisdom is sharp. In a Faith-led (Saddhādhika) Bodhisatta, faith is sharp while—
164:
Wisdom is moderate [for the second type]. The Bodhisatta who is predominant in energy (viriyādhika) has weak wisdom. One reaches Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) through the power of wisdom; if wisdom is sharp, one reaches Omniscience quickly; if wisdom is weak, one reaches Omniscience slowly. Due to these differences in the strength of wisdom, there are three distinct periods for fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs). (This is the answer from the Commentaries.)

Other teachers (Apare), however, say that the three periods for fulfilling perfections vary according to whether the Bodhisatta's energy (viriya) is sharp, moderate, or weak.

Some teachers say it is appropriate that the three periods vary according to whether the fifteen factors that mature liberation (vimutti-paripācanīya-dhamma) are sharp, moderate, or weak.

[Mnemonic:] The Commentary distinguishes by wisdom; the Other Teachers by energy; and the [other] Teachers by liberation.

Among these three views, the appropriateness of the Commentary's view will be explained in the section classifying the three types of Bodhisattas.

## Three Types of Bodhisattas
To elaborate... at the very moment of receiving the definite prophecy (niyata-byākaraṇa), such as in the life of the hermit Sumedha, Great Bodhisattas are divided into three types: (1) Ugghaṭitaññū Bodhisatta, (2) Vipañcitaññū Bodhisatta, and (3) Neyya Bodhisatta.

Among these three, if a Bodhisatta, in the life he receives the definite prophecy, were to incline his mind toward the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvaka-bodhi-ñāṇa) (i.e., if he wished to enter Nibbāna as a disciple), then in the presence of a Fully Enlightened Buddha...
165:
...while listening to a four-line verse (catuppādika gāthā), the Bodhisatta who possesses the extraordinary supporting merit (upanissaya-kusala) capable of reaching the Fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala) along with the six higher powers (abhiññā) and four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) before the third line (tatiya-pāda) of that verse is finished, is called an Ugghaṭitaññū Bodhisatta. This Ugghaṭitaññū Bodhisatta is also known as a Wisdom-led (paññādhika) Bodhisatta. An Ugghaṭitaññū Bodhisatta is one whose wisdom is of the highest degree.

If a Bodhisatta, in the life he receives the definite prophecy, were to incline his mind toward the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvaka-bodhi-ñāṇa), then in the presence of a Fully Enlightened Buddha, while listening to a four-line verse, the Bodhisatta who possesses the extraordinary supporting merit capable of reaching the Fruit of Arahatship along with the six higher powers before the fourth line of that verse is finished, is called a Vipañcitaññū Bodhisatta. This Vipañcitaññū Bodhisatta is also known as a Faith-led (saddhādhika) Bodhisatta. A Vipañcitaññū Bodhisatta is one whose wisdom is of a moderate degree.

If a Bodhisatta, in the life he receives the definite prophecy, were to incline his mind toward the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvaka-bodhi-ñāṇa), then in the presence of a Fully Enlightened Buddha, while listening to a four-line verse, the Bodhisatta who possesses the extraordinary supporting merit capable of reaching the Fruit of Arahatship along with the six higher powers exactly when that verse is finished, is called a Neyya Bodhisatta. This Neyya Bodhisatta is also known as an Energy-led (viriyādhika) Bodhisatta. A Neyya Bodhisatta is one whose wisdom is weak.
166:
All three types of Bodhisattas mentioned have prayed for Buddhahood for an incalculable number of aeons (asaṅkheyya-kappa) prior to receiving the definite prophecy. After receiving the definite prophecy, they fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) as described and attain Omniscient Buddhahood according to the specified timeframes.

## Buddhahood Cannot Be Attained Earlier
Just as varieties of grain or rice that naturally bloom, fruit, and ripen according to a specific timeframe (bīja-niyāma) cannot bloom, fruit, or ripen earlier than their natural period no matter how much effort is made in watering them, etc.; similarly, before the specified timeframes are complete, even if those Bodhisattas strive excessively every day in the perfections (pāramī), sacrifices (cāga), and conducts (cariya), they cannot become a Buddha in the intervening period because their wisdom is not yet mature and the factors that produce Buddhahood are not yet completed.

Therefore, the fulfillment of perfections according to the stated timeframes should be clearly understood.

## (15) The Consequences and Benefits of the Perfections
“What are the consequences and benefits of the perfections?” If such a question is asked—

“Not being reborn in the Avīci hell and so forth are the consequences and benefits of the perfections.” This should be the brief answer.
167:
The detailed answer is as follows:

The 18 impossible states (abhabbaṭṭhāna), such as not being reborn in the Avīci hell (these 18 impossible states will be described following this miscellaneous section); the practice for the benefit of the world of beings; the twenty wonders (found in the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta of the Suññata-vagga, Uparipaṇṇāsa-pāḷi, Majjhima-nikāya); furthermore, the fulfillment of all the Bodhisatta's wishes; proficiency and mastery in verbal and manual arts; and all the benefits mentioned in various Jātaka stories and the Buddhavaṃsa text, etc., are the consequences and benefits of the perfections. (The benefits shown by the 15 pairs [duka] mentioned in the previous section on the summary of the 12 perfections are also the benefits of the perfections.)

Furthermore, because the Bodhisatta desires the welfare of all beings from the time he makes the aspiration for Buddhahood, he is like a great father to the world of beings. Because he is endowed with special virtues, he is worthy of noble offerings and is one to be highly respected. He is like a fertile field for sowing the seeds of the most noble merit. He is loved and respected by humans and devas. Because his heart is suffused with the momentum of loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā), he cannot be harmed by lions, leopards, tigers, or other wild beasts. Because he possesses extraordinary merit in every life he is born into, he can surpass and rule over others with the qualities of noble appearance, retinue, happiness, strength, and sovereignty. He is free from disease. He possesses extremely pure faith (saddhā), energy (viriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā). He has few defilements (kilesa). Because he has few defilements...
168:
...he is easy to admonish. He is patient. He delights in meritorious deeds. He does not get angry or harbor malice. He does not negate the gratitude owed to others. He does not compete [with others]. He is free from envy and stinginess. He is not crooked or deceitful. He is not harsh or arrogant. He is peaceful. He is not negligent in wholesome dhammas. He endures the suffering caused by others but does not cause suffering to others himself. The towns, villages, and regions where the Bodhisatta resides are free from danger. If, due to some unfortunate kamma, he occasionally falls into the minor Ussada hells (as in the life before becoming King Temiya), he does not develop anger due to the suffering like other denizens of hell, but instead, his sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) increases more and more. These are also the consequences and benefits of the perfections.

Furthermore, the group of six: Āyu-sampadā, Rūpa-sampadā, Kula-sampadā, Issariya-sampadā, Ādeyya-vacanatā, and Mahānubhāvatā are also benefits of the perfections. Among them:

Āyu-sampadā: This is longevity in every life. Through this Āyu-sampadā, the Bodhisatta strives to complete the meritorious deeds he has undertaken and increases many wholesome dhammas.

Rūpa-sampadā: This is having a beautiful, inspiring, and graceful physical appearance. Through this Rūpa-sampadā, the Bodhisatta inspires faith in beings who are influenced by physical beauty (rūpa-pamāṇa).

Kula-sampadā: This is being born into a noble family. Through this Kula-sampadā, even beings intoxicated with pride of birth (jāti-māna), etc., approach the Great Being. Thus, he can admonish them to be free from pride.
169:
Issariya-sampadā: This is having great wealth, great power, and a large retinue. Through this Issariya-sampadā, he is able to support those who should be supported through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgaha-dhamma) and to justly restrain those who should be restrained.

Ādeyya-vacanatā: This is being a person whose words are trusted by all. Through this Ādeyya-vacanatā, he becomes a refuge and reliance for beings, like a great pair of scales, and no one dares to transgress the Bodhisatta's authority.

Mahānubhāvatā: This is having great majesty (the objects he uses are incomparably grand). Through this Mahānubhāvatā, he is not dominated or ruled by anyone else, but he alone rules over others in accordance with the Dhamma.

In this way, the virtues such as Āyu-sampadā are the benefits of the perfections, and they themselves are the cause for the growth and prosperity of an immeasurable foundation of merit. They are the cause for leading beings who have not yet entered the three vehicles of enlightenment (bodhi-yāna) to enter them, and for maturing those who have already entered.

(This concludes the benefits of the perfections.)

## (16) The Primary Fruit of the Perfections
If it is asked, "What is the primary fruit (phala) of the perfections?"

The answer is: The state of being a Buddha, which is the infinite virtue and grace of the Buddha led by the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) and the Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), is briefly the primary fruit of the perfections. (This means becoming a Buddha is the primary fruit of the perfections.)

In detail: The glory of the physical body (rūpa-kāya), which is brilliant and beautiful with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa), the eighty minor marks (anubyañjana) (which will be detailed in the Chronicle of Gotama Buddha), and many other virtues such as the bodily aura that shines up to eighty cubits even in fourfold darkness; together with the collection of the glory of the Dhamma body (dhamma-kāya), which is beautiful with the infinite virtues residing in that physical body, such as the ten powers (dasabala-ñāṇa), the four intrepidities (vesārajja-ñāṇa), the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), and the eighteen special qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadhamma). Furthermore...

“Buddho'pi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,
Kappam'pi ce aññam'abhāsamāno.
Khīyetha kappo cira dīgham'antare,
Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassa” —

According to this verse cited by the Commentators, even if one Buddha were to speak the praises of another Buddha for an entire aeon (āyu-kappa) without speaking of anything else, the aeon would come to an end over a long period, but the praises of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.
171: 273 Even if an entire aeon (āyu-kappa) were to pass, the qualities of the Buddha would not be exhausted; this collection of Dhamma is the fruit (phala) of the perfections (pāramīs). In this regard, so that people may develop faith and devotion in the infinite and immeasurable qualities of the Buddha, and so that those who study this text may increase their merit that leads to wisdom (paññā-saṃvattanika), I shall conclude this Miscellaneous Section (Pakiṇṇaka) by presenting the text and meaning of the three verses (gāthā) spoken in praise of the Buddha Anomadassī by the hermit Suruci, the future Elder Sāriputta. (1) Sakkā samudde udakaṃ, pametuṃ āḷhakena vā. Na tveva tava sabbaññu, ñāṇaṃ sakkā pametave. Samudde: In the great ocean. Udakaṃ: The entire mass of water residing therein. Āḷhakena vā: By means of a bucket (āḷhaka). Aññena vā: Or by any other measuring vessel. Pametuṃ: To measure it with the intent of knowing 'it is this much' or 'it has this extent'. Eighteen Impossible States (Abhabbaṭṭhāna)  ## 18 States in which Bodhisattas who have received the Definite Prophecy are not born  In the commentary to the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta, the eighteen states are described along with their specific enumeration, stating that Bodhisattas who are endowed with the eight factors for receiving a prophecy (as mentioned in the section on the rarity of a Buddha's appearance) and who, like the hermit Sumedha, have received the Definite Prophecy (niyata-byākaraṇa) after their prayer is fulfilled, do not encounter these eighteen states while wandering through saṃsāra.  The eighteen are:  (1) Not being born blind from birth.  (2) Not being born deaf from birth.  (3) Not being born insane.  (4) Not being born mute.  (5) Not being born crippled (unable to walk).  (6) Not being born a barbarian.  (7) Not being conceived in the womb of a slave woman.  (8) Not being a person with fixed wrong views (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi).  (9) Not undergoing a change of gender (meaning not changing from male to female).  (10) Not committing the five heinous crimes (anantariya-kamma).  (11) Not being a leper (having leprosy).
174: 276 (12) Even if born in the animal kingdom, not being an animal smaller than a quail (or alternatively, smaller than a tailor-bird). (A note on this will be provided later.) (13) Not being born as a Khuppipāsika Peta (hungry ghost), a Nijjhāmatanhika Peta, or a Kāḷakañjika Asura. (A Khuppipāsika Peta is a type of hungry ghost that is always famished because they never get to eat or drink. A Nijjhāmatanhika Peta is a ghost that is constantly suffering from being consumed by fire, such as the monk-ghosts seen by Venerable Moggallāna on Vulture Peak. The Kāḷakañjika Asura is the name of that specific ghost-asura; their bodies are about three gāvutas in size, with very little flesh and blood, resembling the color of a withered leaf. Their eyes protrude like those of a crab and are situated on top of their heads; their mouths are as small as the eye of a needle and are also on top of their heads, so when they find food, they must bend down to take it.) (14) Not being born in the Avīci Hell or the Lokantarika Hell. (The Lokantarika Hell is the empty space where three world systems meet. This space is a place of punishment for those who commit evil deeds and is called Lokantarika Hell as a type of purgatory.) (15) Not being born as a Māra in the sense-sphere heavens (kāmāvacara). (16) In the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), not being born as an unconscious being (asaññasatta) or in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa).
175: 277 (17) Not being born in the immaterial brahma realms (arūpa-brahma). (18) Not being born by migrating to another world system (cakkavāḷa). These are the eighteen. Regarding the 12th point, 'not being an animal smaller than a quail,' this is stated according to the Pali: 'Na tiracchānayoniyaṃ vaṭṭakato pacchimattabhāvo hoti.' Tiracchānayoniyaṃ: In the animal species. Vaṭṭakato: Than a quail. Pacchimattabhāvo: An animal having a smaller body. Na hoti: Does not become. This is how it should be translated. Similarly, in the Dhammarāsī Pyo, it is composed as: 'Does not reach the Kāḷakañji ground, not smaller than a quail, and even among elephants, not excessively large.' People also commonly say, 'The smallest of all is the quail.' However, in the manuscript of the Sutta Nipāta Commentary held by the Monywe Jetawun Sayadaw, it seems the text was 'Na tiracchānayoniyaṃ vatakato pacchimattabhāvo hoti.' He wrote extensively (in the Samantacakkhudīpanī, Volume II) that the Pali word 'vatakato' should be translated as 'tailor-bird.' According to Monywe Jetawun Sayadaw, it should be translated as 'not being an animal smaller than a tailor-bird.' His reference to the tailor-bird is based on the Sakunagghi Jātaka of the second vagga of the Duka Nipāta. A summary of that Jātaka is as follows: The Bodhisatta was once born as a small bird called 'lāpa' and used to live and feed among the clods of earth in a plowed field. One day, at the edge of the forest,
176: 278 while he was out feeding, he was snatched up by a hawk. While still in the hawk's talons, he lamented, 'Because I did not stay in my ancestral territory, I have suffered this oppression by an enemy. If I had stayed in my own place, I would not have suffered like this.' Then the hawk asked, 'What is your ancestral territory?' When the bird replied that it was the clods of earth in a plowed field, the hawk said, 'Very well, I will release you now. Go to your own place and resist me if you can.' After being released, the little 'lāpa' bird went to his place, stood on top of a large clod of earth, and challenged the hawk, 'O hawk, come if you have the courage!' When the hawk swooped down with great speed and force, the little 'lāpa' bird suddenly ducked under the clod of earth. The hawk could not control its momentum nor catch the bird, and died from striking its breast against the edge of the clod. (Teachers translate the word 'lāpa' in this story as a buttonquail. Monywe Sayadaw, however, translates it as a tailor-bird.) Furthermore, he also relies on the (1) Siṅgila Sakuṇa Jātaka (also known as Piṅgala Sakuṇa Jātaka) of the (3) Kuṭidūsaka Vagga in the Catukka Nipāta. A summary of that Jātaka is as follows: The Bodhisatta was once born as a species of bird called 'siṅgila.' When he reached maturity, he built a pleasant, rain-proof
177: 279 nest (a weaver bird's nest) and lived on the border of the Himālaya. One day during the rainy season, while it was raining continuously, a monkey, suffering greatly from the cold, sat on a tree branch near the Bodhisatta, grinding its teeth. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the verse beginning with 'Manussasseva te sīsaṃ—' and asked, 'Friend monkey, your head, hands, and feet are like those of a human; why then do you have no house?' The monkey replied, 'Although I have a head, hands, and feet like a human, I have no house because I lack the wisdom to reflect.' Then the Bodhisatta (with two verses beginning with 'Anavaṭṭhitacittassa—') explained that one with an unsteady and frivolous mind, who wrongs friends and lacks good habits, cannot find happiness. He spoke with loving-kindness, saying, 'Friend monkey, strive to develop wisdom, try to overcome your lack of virtue, and build yourself a home.' However, that monkey, being a betrayer of friends, became angry and destroyed the Bodhisatta's nest, tearing it into pieces. (In this Jātaka, the commentary explains 'piṅgala sakuṇa' as a type of house sparrow whose body and feathers are bright yellow like turmeric. Therefore, Monywe Jetawun Sayadaw considers that it should be a 'weaver bird'.)

In the Atthasālinī Commentary, however, the size is not specifically marked as a quail, but it is stated as 'na honti khuddakā pāṇā,' meaning they are not born as minute creatures. Regarding those minute creatures— According to the verse in the third part of the Sāratthavilāsinī (Pañcikā-ṭīkā): 'Khuddajantu siyā naṭṭhi, atha vā khuddako va yo. Sataṃ vā pasato yesaṃ, keci ānakulā api'—it should be understood as referring to insects or creatures whose bones and flesh cannot be distinguished, or creatures of which a hundred would fit in a single handful. In some manuscripts of the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, the Pali 'hatthito adhika-attabhāvo' is present. According to this phrase, it must be translated as 'even if born in the animal kingdom, not being an animal larger in body than an elephant.' Just as it is translated this way, it is composed in the Dhammarāsī Pyo as: 'Not smaller than a quail, and even among elephants, not excessively large.' In this regard, in the Paṇḍara Nāga Jātaka of the Tiṃsa Nipāta, the Bodhisatta—

There is a mention of being a Garuda King. A Garuda must be much larger in physical size and strength than an elephant. Evidence of this size is found in the Bhūridatta Jātaka: when a Garuda snatched a Nāga and flew into the sky, reaching a large banyan tree near a hermit's leaf-hut, the Nāga, seeking a way to escape, coiled its tail around a branch of the banyan tree. Because the Garuda was so powerful, the entire banyan tree was uprooted along with its roots. This clearly shows that the Garuda's physical size and strength are greater than an elephant's. Therefore, in the Chatthasaṅgāyana edition and some versions of the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, the Pali phrase 'hatthito adhika-attabhāvo' (having a body larger than an elephant) is not included.

In explaining these 'Abhabbaṭṭhāna' (impossible states), the descriptions in the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary and the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary are partly similar to and partly different from the Sutta Nipāta Commentary. Among the 18 states mentioned in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary:
1. Not being insane,
2. Not being crippled in limbs,
3. Not being a barbarian,
4. Not being born from the womb of a slave woman,
5. Not changing from a male to a female,
6. Not being a leper,
7. Not being Māra,
8. Not being born in another universe—
These eight states are not included in the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary. While the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary does not explicitly list the number of states, the states it mentions that are additional to those in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary are:
180:
282
1. Not being a woman,
2. Not being a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka),
3. Not being a eunuch (paṇḍaka).
These are the three. (The account in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary is the same as the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary.) Among these three states, the state of being a woman is clear.

The term 'Ubhatobyañည်း' (Ubhatobyañjanaka) is derived from the Pali word 'Ubhatobyañjanaka'. (It means a person who has both gender signs because of the kamma that produces the female sign and the kamma that produces the male sign.) There are two types of Ubhatobyañjanaka: the female hermaphrodite and the male hermaphrodite.

In a female hermaphrodite, the female sign is normally prominent and the male sign is hidden. In a male hermaphrodite, the male sign is normally prominent and the female sign is hidden.

When a female hermaphrodite desires to perform the role of a male with other women, her female sign disappears and the male sign becomes prominent. When a male hermaphrodite desires to take the role of a woman with other men, his male sign disappears and the female sign becomes prominent.

A female hermaphrodite can both become pregnant herself and make others pregnant. A male hermaphrodite cannot become pregnant himself; he can only make others pregnant. This is the distinction between these two types of Ubhatobyañjanaka. (From the Vinaya Mahāvagga Commentary, Vol. 3, page 306.)
181:
283
The term 'Paṇḍuက်' (Paṇḍaka) is derived from the Pali word 'Paṇḍaka'. (It means a person with deficient gender.) It refers to a person who, though male, is deficient and unlike other men. Those Paṇḍaka are:
1. Āsittapaṇḍaka: One whose sexual passion is only relieved by sucking the male organ of another and having the semen discharged into their mouth. (Nowadays commonly called 'pan-soke'.)
2. Ussūyapaṇḍaka: One whose sexual passion is only relieved by spying on others committing sexual acts and feeling envy or jealousy.
3. Opakkamikapaṇḍaka: One whose testicles have been removed through effort (such as the eunuchs in royal palaces).
4. Pakkhapaṇḍaka: One whose sexual passion is intense and unbearable during the waning moon, but whose passion subsides during the waxing moon.
5. Napuṃsakapaṇḍaka: One who was conceived without the gender-determining matter (bhāva-rūpa) from the moment of conception. (Since the bhāva-dasaka-kalāpa-rūpa was absent at conception, they later have neither female nor male organs. It means they are neither female nor male. Following this Pali term 'Napuṃsaka', they are called 'Napone' in the Burmese language.)
Thus, these five types of Paṇḍaka should be noted. (Vinaya Mahāvagga Commentary, Vol. 3, page 297.)

The explanation of the 18 Abhabbaṭṭhāna is finished.

182:
284
## 9. Section on the Chronicle of the Twenty-Four Buddhas
## 1. Chronicle of Dīpaṅkara Buddha
Just as the Burmese term 'Mahāwin' comes from the Pali 'Mahāvaṃsa' and 'Rājawin' from 'Rājavaṃsa', the Burmese term 'Buddhawin' comes from the Pali 'Buddhavaṃsa', and 'Dīpaṅkara Buddhawin' comes from 'Dīpaṅkara Buddhavaṃsa'.

Regarding the meaning of Buddhavaṃsa (Chronicle of Buddhas):
'Ito heṭṭhā kappasatasahassāmikesu catūsu asaṅkheyyesu uppannānaṃ pañcavīsatiyā buddhānaṃ uppannakakappādiparicchedavasena paveṇivitthārakathā buddhavaṃso nāma.'
Based on this statement from the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, it should be understood as: "The detailed discourse that explains the lineage of the twenty-five Buddhas who appeared during the period of four incalculables (asaṅkheyya) and one hundred thousand aeons (kappa), categorized by the aeons in which they appeared, their names, their lineages, their castes, and so on, in thirty-two successive aspects—this is called the Buddhavaṃsa."

Although the succession of aeons and other details of the Buddhas' appearances is called the Buddhavaṃsa, when extracting and speaking about the aeon of appearance and other details of a single Buddha from that succession, the original term 'Buddhavaṃsa' can still be used. For example, although 'Saṅgha' is the
183:
285
proper name for the collective of Noble Ones (Ariya), an individual from that collective can also be called 'Saṅgha' if one wishes to do so.

Therefore, this section called the 'Dīpaṅkara Buddhavaṃsa' should be understood as the section describing the biography (the aeon of appearance, etc.) of Dīpaṅkara Buddha.

In the Buddhavaṃsa Pali, there is no detailed preaching of the events that occurred during the conception and birth of the Bodhisatta Dīpaṅkara. Only in the Sumedhakathā is it mentioned that the Bodhisatta, the hermit Sumedha, said:

'Evaṃ me siddhipattassa, vasībhūtassa sāsane.
Dīpaṅkaro nāma jino, uppajji lokanāyako.
Uppajjante ca jāyante, bujjhante dhammadesane.
Caturo nimitte nāddasiṃ, jhānaratisamappito.'

"While I had reached the pinnacle of success and mastery in the hermit's dispensation (jhāna and abhiññā), the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, appeared.

Absorbed in the delight of meditative absorption (jhāna), I did not see the signs that appeared at these four occasions: when the Bodhisatta Dīpaṅkara was conceived, when he was born, when he attained Enlightenment, and when he preached the first sermon of the Dhammacakka."

Thus, the hermit Sumedha only briefly mentioned the appearance of Dīpaṅkara Buddha.
184:
286
Regarding the events such as the conception of the Bodhisatta Dīpaṅkara mentioned in the words of the hermit Sumedha, the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary states: 'Dīpaṅkaro nāma satthā loke udapādi, saṅkhepeneva tassāyamānupubbīkathā...' "The Teacher named Dīpaṅkara has appeared in the world; what follows is the sequential account of the life of that Dīpaṅkara Buddha in brief." After this introduction, the commentary describes the life of Dīpaṅkara Buddha from his time in the Tusita heaven onwards, as follows:

Counting back from this Bhadda Kappa, four incalculables and one hundred thousand aeons ago, in a single aeon called the Sāramaṇḍa Kappa, three Buddhas—(1) Taṇhaṅkara Buddha, (2) Medhaṅkara Buddha, and (3) Saraṇaṅkara Buddha—appeared in succession. After them, in an intermediate aeon (antarakappa) during the period of decline when the human lifespan was one hundred thousand years, while King Sudeva was reigning in the city of Rammāvatī...

The Bodhisatta Dīpaṅkara, having fulfilled the Perfections (pāramīs) and residing in the Tusita heaven, was approached by the devas from ten thousand universes who gathered and requested him to become a Buddha. Having accepted their request, he was conceived in the womb of Queen Sumedhā, the chief consort of King Sudeva, in the royal palace, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha under the constellation of Uttarāsāḷha. He was protected with great honor and guardianship, and after ten months had passed, he was born.
185:
287
At the time of the Bodhisatta Dīpaṅkara's conception and birth, the thirty-two great miraculous signs, such as the shaking of the ten thousand universes, became manifest.

(These thirty-two great signs always appear for all Bodhisattas at these four occasions: (1) when they are conceived, (2) when they are born, (3) when they attain Enlightenment, and (4) when they preach the first sermon of the Dhammacakka. These matters pertaining to all Bodhisattas will be written and described in full detail upon reaching the chapter on the Gotama Buddhavaṃsa. In this Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, however, even in the section on the conception of the Bodhisatta Dīpaṅkara, it describes in detail how those thirty-two great signs appeared and what specific benefits each sign would manifest in the future.)

Thereafter, Prince Dīpaṅkara grew up in comfort and, upon reaching maturity, he took over the administration of the kingdom and ruled as king. (a)

While ruling the kingdom, he resided for ten thousand years, rotating among three magnificent golden palaces: the Haṃsa Pāsāda, the Koñca Pāsāda, and the Mayūra Pāsāda. There were about three hundred thousand well-adorned female attendants. His chief consort was the princess named Padumā, and his son was Prince Usabhakkhandha.
186: While the Bodhisatta, Prince Dīpaṅkara, was enjoying royal splendor comparable to that of the devas in the three golden palaces mentioned earlier, he went out to enjoy the gardens. On his way, he successively saw the divine messengers—an old man, a sick man, and a dead man. Filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he returned from the garden and entered the city of Rammāvatī. When he wished to go out to the garden for the fourth time, he called the master of the elephants and commanded, “I shall go out to inspect the garden today; prepare the elephant-vehicles.” The master of the elephants replied, “Very well,” and prepared eighty-four thousand elephant-vehicles. At that time, Prince Dīpaṅkara, adorned with ornaments provided by the deva Vissakamma, mounted his royal elephant and, surrounded by eighty-four thousand elephants and a vast army, entered the garden. After dismounting and touring the garden, he sat upon a very cool and delightful stone slab and formed the intention to renounce the world. Then, a Great Brahmā from the Suddhāvāsa realm brought the eight requisites (parikkhāra) and appeared before the Bodhisatta. Seeing the eight requisites, the Bodhisatta asked, “What are these?” Upon hearing that they were the requisites of a monk, he removed his royal ornaments and entrusted them to the treasurer. Then, using his royal sword, he cut off his hair and threw it into the sky.
187:
At that moment, Sakka, the King of Devas, received the hair-relic in a golden casket and enshrined it in the Makuṭa Cetiya, made of emerald-blue (indanilā) stone and measuring three yojanas in height, on the summit of Mount Meru.

Thereafter, the Bodhisatta donned the robes offered by the Brahmā and threw his pair of lay garments into the sky. A Suddhāvāsa Brahmā received them and enshrined them in the Dussa Cetiya, measuring twelve yojanas, in the Suddhāvāsa realm.

When the news of Prince Dīpaṅkara’s renunciation spread, one crore (ten million) people followed his example and became monks. The Bodhisatta Dīpaṅkara, together with the one crore monks who followed him, practiced the difficult austerities (dukkharacariyā) in the forest for ten months. When the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha) arrived, the day he was to become Buddha, he entered a certain city for alms. On that day, the city dwellers had prepared undiluted milk-rice (pāyāsa) to offer to the devas, and they offered it to the Bodhisatta and his retinue of one crore monks.

After partaking of the milk-rice, the Bodhisatta spent the day in a Sal grove in that area. When evening came, he left his retinue of one crore monks and proceeded alone toward the site of the Mahābodhi tree.

## Attaining Buddhahood and Preaching the Dhammacakka

On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a wandering ascetic named Sunanda.
188:
As soon as he spread the grass at the foot of the Nyaung-kyat (Ficus retusa) tree, the Aparājita Throne (the Unconquered Seat), measuring fifty-three cubits, appeared.

(Regarding the measurement of fifty-three cubits for the throne, some sub-commentaries (Ṭīkā) written in the Pali language during the Ava period explain it as the height, while others explain it as the width. A detailed explanation will be provided when reaching the lineage of Gotama Buddha.)

Sitting in a cross-legged posture on the Aparājita Throne and resolving with fourfold effort at the foot of the Mahābodhi (Nyaung-kyat) tree, he conquered the army of Māra. In the first watch of the night, he attained Pubbenivāsanussati-ñāṇa (knowledge of past lives). In the middle watch, he attained Dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa (the divine eye, capable of seeing subtle and distant forms). In the last watch, he contemplated the Law of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) in both forward and backward orders—the way the wheel of Saṃsāra turns and the way it is broken. He then entered the fourth jhāna of Ānāpāna (mindfulness of breathing). Emerging from that jhāna, he contemplated the five aggregates. Seeing the fifty characteristics related to the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, he developed insight (vipassanā) up to the stage of Gotrabhū-ñāṇa. At the moment of dawn, he realized the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (Arahattamagga-ñāṇa) along with all the qualities of a Buddha, thus attaining the peerless state of Buddhahood in the three worlds.
189:
After becoming Buddha, he spent seven weeks at seven different locations (Satta-sattāha) near the Bodhi tree, experiencing the bliss of fruition (phala-samāpatti). Having accepted the request of the Great Brahmā to teach the Dhamma, he preached the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, at Sunandārāma. At that time, one hundred crore humans, devas, and Brahmās realized the Four Noble Truths.

At the time of his enlightenment and at the time of preaching the Dhammacakka, the thirty-two great omens appeared clearly.

The hermit Sumedha, being absorbed in the bliss of jhāna, did not know or see these great omens that occurred at the four stages: the conception, the birth, the enlightenment, and the first sermon of the Blessed Dīpaṅkara. (This was mentioned previously in the Sumedha-kathā.)

## Traveling on a Missionary Journey

After preaching the first sermon, the Blessed Dīpaṅkara traveled for the benefit of humans, devas, and Brahmās. While he was residing at the Sudassana Monastery in the city of Rammāvatī, the citizens invited him for alms. The details of how he traveled with four hundred thousand Arahants, how he gave the prophecy (byādita) to the hermit Sumedha on the way, how he arrived at the place of invitation and partook of the alms offered by the citizens of Rammāvatī, and how the earth shook violently through the power of the Dhamma while Sumedha was reflecting on the Perfections (pāramīs), have been fully described in the Sumedha-kathā.
190:
It was also described how the people were frightened by the earthquake and questioned the Blessed Dīpaṅkara, who explained, “There is nothing to fear; the earth shook because the hermit Sumedha is reflecting on the Dhamma.” Upon hearing this, many people went to the hermit Sumedha and gave him great praise. After receiving this praise, the hermit Sumedha entered the forest. What has not yet been written is as follows:

After the citizens of Rammāvatī had offered alms to the Blessed Dīpaṅkara and the four hundred thousand monks, they honored him with flowers and perfumes and assembled to listen to the Dhamma.

At that time, the Blessed Dīpaṅkara spoke to the multitude:

1. “Dānaṃ nāma sukhādīnaṃ, nidānaṃ paramaṃ mataṃ. Dibbānaṃ pana bhogānaṃ, patiṭṭhāti pavuccati.”
(Generosity is known as the supreme cause of the three types of happiness [human, celestial, and Nibbāna]. It is said to be the foundation for celestial enjoyments.)
Thus, he preached a very sweet and noble discourse on Generosity (Dāna-kathā). Then:

2. “Sīlaṃ nāmetaṃ idhaloka-paraloka-sampattīnaṃ mūlaṃ.”
(This Morality is the root of various attainments [sampatti] in this world and the next.)
In this way, he preached the discourse on Morality (Sīla-kathā), explaining the benefits and power of virtue in detail through many reasons.
191:
3. After preaching the discourse on Morality, the Blessed Dīpaṅkara preached the discourse on Heaven (Sagga-kathā) to show that by relying on this morality, one attains such celestial bliss. He taught that the heavenly realms are desirable, pleasant, and heart-uplifting; they are truly blissful, and one can find constant joy there. He explained that the Cātumahārājika devas enjoy celestial bliss for a period of nine million years by human reckoning, and so forth, regarding the virtues of the heavenly realms.

4. After thus attracting and softening the minds of beings with the discourse on Heaven to incline toward meritorious acts of generosity and morality, he continued by showing that even this heavenly bliss is impermanent and unstable. He taught that one should not have intense craving for this collection of heavenly bliss. He showed the faults, baseness, and impurity of sensual pleasures (kāma), and the benefits of renouncing and escaping from them, concluding the discourse with the Deathless Nibbāna.

In this manner, the Blessed Dīpaṅkara preached to the multitude, establishing some in the Refuges, some in the Five Precepts or Ten Precepts, some in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), some in the Fruits of Once-returning and Non-returning, some in all four Fruits of the Path, some in the Threefold Knowledge (Vijjā), some in the Six Higher Powers (Abhiññā), and some in the Eight Attainments (Samāpatti). He then departed from the city of Rammāvatī and entered the Sudassana Monastery.
192:
## Three Great Assemblies of Teaching

(a) After attaining Buddhahood, the Blessed Dīpaṅkara spent the seven weeks (Satta-sattāha, 49 days) near the Bodhi tree. In the eighth week, he accepted the request of the Brahmā and preached the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, at Sunandārāma, providing the deathless medicine of Dhamma to one hundred crore devas and humans.
(This was the first great assembly.)

(b) Later, the Blessed Dīpaṅkara, knowing that the wisdom of his son, Prince Usabhakkhandha, had matured, placed the Prince at the head and preached an exhortation (similar to the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta preached by our Buddha to his son Rāhula), providing the cool water of the deathless Dhamma to ninety crore devas and humans.
(This was the second great assembly.)

(c) Again, the Blessed Dīpaṅkara, after subduing the heretics near a great Sirīsa (Kukko) tree at the gate of the city of Amaravatī, performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire. He then resided on the Paṇḍukambala stone slab at the foot of the Parichattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Placing the deva who had been his mother, Queen Sumedhā, at the head, he preached the Abhidhamma, providing the cool water of the deathless Dhamma to ninety crore devas and Brahmās.
(This was the third great assembly.)
193:
## The Three Great Assemblies of Disciples
(1) The first assembly of the disciples of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara took place at Sunandārāma. At this first gathering, where Arahants from all directions specially assembled, one hundred thousand crores of Arahant noble ones met in harmony.
(This was the first great assembly of disciples.)
(2) The second assembly of disciples took place at the peak of Mount Nāradakūṭa. The circumstances were as follows:
On one occasion, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was wandering for alms accompanied by four hundred thousand monks. He arrived at Mount Nāradakūṭa, which was endowed with various wonders and was extremely delightful to the heart.
That mountain was possessed by a Yakkha named Naradeva. Every year, the people would regularly bring a human being as a sacrificial offering to this mountain-dwelling Yakkha.
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, seeing that those people were endowed with past merits and were worthy of refuge, ascended to the peak of Mount Nāradakūṭa alone, without calling the Sangha of monks. Then, the Yakkha became violently angry and, in an attempt to make the Buddha flee in terror, used all his power to threaten him by shaking the great mountain and other means. However, seeing the Buddha residing in perfect serenity without any harm, he thought: "This great monk is truly wonderful!"
194:
"He possesses great power and majesty. All the harm I intended for this great monk has only fallen back upon me. I have no other refuge but this great monk. Just as a person who has slipped and fallen on the ground must rely on that very ground to stand up, I too shall now take refuge in and serve this great monk."
Having had this thought, the Yakkha Naradeva prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, which were adorned with the one hundred and eight marks of the wheel. He confessed his offenses against the Buddha and took refuge in him. Thereafter, the Buddha preached the gradual discourse to the Yakkha Naradeva, beginning with the discourse on giving (dānakathā) and the discourse on virtue (sīlakathā). At the conclusion of the sermon, the Yakkha Naradeva, along with his ten thousand followers, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).
On the day the Yakkha Naradeva attained Stream-entry, people living throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa brought one person from each village to be offered as a sacrifice to the Yakkha Naradeva. Furthermore, they brought large quantities of sesame, rice, chickpeas, green grams, kidney beans, and so on, as well as butter, cream, oil, honey, and molasses. The Yakkha Naradeva returned all the offerings, such as rice, to the people and presented the humans brought for sacrifice to the Buddha.
Then, the Buddha called those people with the words 'Ehi Bhikkhu' (Come, monk), and having ordained them, he established them all in the fruit of Arahantship within only seven days.
195:
Residing in the midst of one hundred crore Arahants on the full moon day of Tabodwe (Māgha), the Buddha recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha at the great assembly of disciples endowed with the four factors.
Regarding the term 'Ehi Bhikkhu monk': It refers to a monk who does not need to seek or prepare a bowl, robes, etc., for ordination. As soon as the Buddha calls 'Ehi Bhikkhu' (Come, monk), the original appearance of a layman disappears, and the appearance of a monk of sixty years' standing clearly emerges.
In the context of the assembly of disciples endowed with four factors, the four factors are:
1. All the monks were 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks.
2. All those monks were possessors of the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā).
3. All those monks assembled without being summoned.
4. It was the full moon Uposatha day of the fifteenth.
These are the four factors.
This preceding account of the Yakkha Naradeva is the sequence of words found in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary.
In the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi text itself, it is preached only generally: "Furthermore, while the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was residing in seclusion at the peak of Mount Nārada, one hundred crore Arahants, who were pure and free from the defilements, assembled."
(This was the second great assembly of disciples.)
196:
(3) On another occasion, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara spent the rains retreat (vassa) at the peak of Mount Sudassana. At that time, the people living in Jambudīpa, according to their custom of holding a mountain-top festival every year at the end of the rains retreat, came to the peak of Mount Sudassana. Meeting the Buddha and hearing his Dhamma, they were filled with clear faith and joy and were ordained as monks. The Buddha preached the Dhamma to those monks again on the day of Mahāpavāraṇā (the full moon day of Thadingyut). All the new monks, by contemplating the formations of the three planes (tebhūmaka saṅkhāra) through the stages of insight and the path, reached the fruit of Arahantship. At that time, the Buddha performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony together with ninety thousand crore Arahants.
(This was the third great assembly of disciples.)
The ordinary Dhamma assemblies of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara resulted in the realization of the Four Noble Truths by ten thousand or twenty thousand beings. The number of individual beings who realized the Four Noble Truths is beyond counting.
At that time, the well-purified Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was widespread in all directions; it was known by many humans, devas, and brahmās; and it was full and prosperous with noble virtues such as sīla.
The Buddha Dīpaṅkara, who knew and saw the three worlds, was always surrounded by four hundred thousand Arahant disciples who possessed the six supernormal powers and were of great might.
197:
During the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, if there were those who had not yet reached the fruit of Arahantship but were still practicing as trainees (sekha) when they passed away from the human life, they were (all) considered regrettable.
The word (or Dispensation) of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was well-manifested and brilliant throughout the entire world. Having slain the enemies of defilements, it was always beautified by the noble Arahants who were unshaken by various objects, free from the stains of defilements, and whose taints (āsavas) were exhausted.
## Description of the City and Other Details
The birthplace of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was the city of Rammāvatī.
His father was King Sudeva, and his mother was Queen Sumedhā.
The pair of chief disciples were the Elder Sumangala and the Elder Tissa. His attendant was the Elder Sāgata.
The pair of chief female disciples were the Elder Nun Nandā and the Elder Nun Sunandā. The Bodhi tree where he attained enlightenment was the Pipphalī tree (Nyoung-kyat).
The chief male lay supporters were Tapussa and Bhallika. The chief female lay supporters were Sirimā and Soṇā.
The height of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was eighty cubits. Shining brilliantly like a...
198:
...great torch or a lampstand, and like a great Sal tree in full bloom, he was exceedingly beautiful.
(The benefit of describing the birthplace and other details is this: If these details were not shown, people might think, "The birthplace of this Buddha is not known, nor are his father and mother. He might be a deva, a Māra, a Yakkha, or a Brahmā. It is not extraordinary for such wonders to happen to devas or brahmās." Thinking it not wonderful, they might not consider the Dhamma preached as worthy of listening to or believing in. In that case, the realization of the Truth would not occur. When the birthplace, father, mother, etc., are shown, they think, "Even though he was a true human being, he possessed such power and majesty." Thus, beings listen to and believe in the Dhamma preached by the Buddha, and the realization of the Truth can occur. Therefore, the birthplace, father, mother, and so on are described.)
The natural aura of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara spread twelve yojanas in all directions (without any special creation by his psychic power). The lifespan of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was one hundred thousand years.
(This is the portion directly mentioned in the Pāḷi text.)
The additional details (Sambahulavāra) which, although not directly in the Pāḷi text, are explained in the Commentaries to be presented, are as follows:
199:
The three palaces used by the Bodhisatta Dīpaṅkara during his life as a layman were Haṃsa-pāsāda, Koñca-pāsāda, and Mayūra-pāsāda.
His retinue of women numbered three hundred thousand. His chief queen was named Padumā Devī. His son was Prince Usabhakkhandha. The number of years he reigned in the palace was ten thousand.
When he renounced the world, he did so by means of an elephant. When he became a Buddha, he resided at the place called Nandārāma.
The Buddha Dīpaṅkara remained for that long a duration, saving a great multitude of beings.
Together with his disciples and the Sangha, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, having illuminated the entire world with the three True Dhammas—namely, learning (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (paṭivedha)—and having saved the multitude of beings, reached the state of peaceful extinction, like a great blazing fire that has gone out.
## Spiritual Urgency (Saṃvega)
The power of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the entire retinue of four hundred thousand great Arahant disciples, and the marks of the wheel on the Buddha's feet—all these have ceased and vanished.
200:
302
Alas, all conditioned things are indeed void, lacking any stable essence.
## Construction of the Cetiya
In this manner, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, who had realized the Four Noble Truths without remainder, attained Parinibbāna at the Nandārāma (Nanda Garden). In that very garden, a Cetiya (relic stupa) for the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was constructed, using realgar and orpiment as fine earth, and ghee and butter as water. It stood thirty leagues (yojanas) in height. Within that great Cetiya, they enshrined the undivided relic (asambhinna-dhātu), which remains as a single mass without breaking into pieces, according to the natural custom of long-lived Buddhas. People from all over Jambudīpa came together in unity and completed the great Cetiya, decorating and adorning it with the seven kinds of jewels.
The Chronicle of Buddha Dīpaṅkara ends.

## 2. The Chronicle of Buddha Koṇḍañña
After the aeon (kappa) in which the Buddha Dīpaṅkara appeared had ended, and after the passing of one incalculable period (asaṅkhyeyya)—or many aeons so numerous they cannot be counted in figures—the Buddha Koṇḍañña appeared in a certain aeon.
(Although this type of incalculable period is so vast that it cannot be counted in figures, it is called a "Buddhanntara Asaṅkhyeyya" because it is marked only as the interval between the former Buddha Dīpaṅkara and the subsequent Buddha Koṇḍañña.)
201:
303
Regarding the appearance of the Buddha Koṇḍañña: The Bodhisatta Koṇḍañña, after fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) for sixteen incalculable periods and one hundred thousand aeons, resided in the Tusita heaven according to the custom of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of many devas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of Queen Sujātā, the chief consort of King Sunanda, in the royal city of Rammavatī.
(At the moment of conception, the thirty-two great omens appeared clearly as they always do.)
When ten months were complete, he was born. At the moment of birth, not only did the great omens appear as usual, but special and wonderful events pertaining to all Bodhisattas also occurred.
(All these will be written in detail when reaching the Chronicle of Buddha Gotama.)
## Reigning over the Kingdom
The Bodhisatta prince was named Prince Koṇḍañña because he belonged to the Koṇḍañña clan. When Prince Koṇḍañña reached maturity, he resided in three magnificent golden palaces named Sucira, Surucira, and Subha, which were extremely delightful. He reigned for ten thousand years, being entertained and served by Queen Ruci-devī, who possessed a pleasing and beautiful complexion, along with three hundred thousand dancers and female attendants.
202:
304
## The Great Renunciation
While reigning in this manner, when Queen Ruci-devī gave birth to a son named Vijitasena, the Prince saw the four great omens—an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and an ascetic. He then renounced the world and became an ascetic, departing on a chariot drawn by noble horses.
Following the example of the Bodhisatta Prince Koṇḍañña's renunciation, one hundred million people also became ascetics.
The Bodhisatta Koṇḍañña, together with those one hundred million ascetics, practiced the difficult austerities (dukkharacariyā) for ten months. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become a Buddha, he partook of the thick milk-rice (ghanā-pāyāsa) offered by the daughter of a merchant named Yasodharā from Sunanda village. He spent the day in the Sal grove in that area. When evening came, he left the company of the monks and proceeded alone to the site of the Mahābodhi tree. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by an Ajivika named Sunanda. As soon as he spread them at the foot of a Sālakalyāṇī tree (also known as the Nabhai tree), the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka), measuring fifty-seven cubits, appeared.
## Attaining Enlightenment
Sitting cross-legged upon that Aparājita Throne, he resolved with fourfold effort and conquered the army of Mara. In the first watch of the night, he attained the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), and in the middle watch, he attained the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa).
203:
305
In the last watch of the night, he contemplated the law of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) in forward and backward order. He then entered the fourth absorption of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-catuttha-jhāna). Emerging from that absorption, he contemplated the five aggregates. Upon seeing the fifty characteristics related to the arising and passing away of those five aggregates, he developed insight (vipassanā) up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). At the very moment of dawn, he realized the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) along with all the qualities of a Buddha, thus attaining the peerless state of Buddhahood in the three worlds.
## Three Great Assemblies of Dhamma
After becoming a Buddha, he spent seven weeks at the seven locations (satta-ṭṭhāna) near the Bodhi tree, passing the time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). In the eighth week, he accepted the request of the Great Brahma to teach the Dhamma. When he considered, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?", he saw the one hundred million monks who had followed him in renunciation. He thought, "I shall preach the Dhamma to those monks before all others." Then, considering "Where do those monks reside now?", he saw that they were staying in the forest of divine trees called Devavana near the city of Arundhavatī, eighteen leagues away from the Bodhi tree. Taking his bowl and robes, he traveled to that Devavana forest by psychic power in an instant.
At that time, the one hundred million monks saw the Buddha Koṇḍañña approaching from afar.
204:
306
With hearts full of great devotion, they fulfilled their duties by welcoming the Buddha, taking his bowl and robes, preparing his seat, and showing respectful service. They then sat in suitable places surrounding the Buddha.
Then, the Buddha preached to those one hundred million monks the Discourse on Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion (Dhammaccakkappavattana Sutta), which is the customary first sermon of all past Buddhas.
The Buddha Koṇḍañña—who was endowed with infinite psychic power, incomparable retinue and fame, innumerable virtues, a presence difficult for anyone to approach disrespectfully, patience like the thickness of the earth, virtue (sīla) like the mass of the ocean's waters, concentration (samādhi) as firm as Mount Meru, and wisdom (paññā) like the expanse of the sky—preached at all times the teachings of the Factors of Enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), which clearly demonstrate the faculties (indriya), powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), path factors (maggaṅga), and the truths (sacca) for the benefit of many beings.
In this first assembly of the Wheel of Dhamma, the realization of the Four Noble Truths (attainment of the Dhamma) occurred for one hundred billion devas and humans, with the one hundred million monks at the head.
(This is the first Dhammābhisamaya, the first great assembly where humans, devas, and Brahmas were made to know the Four Noble Truths.)
Later, on another occasion, at the great assembly for the preaching of the Maṅgala Sutta, devas and Brahmas from ten thousand world systems gathered in this single world system, creating subtle and small bodies (so that they could all fit).
205:
307
At that great assembly, a certain unnamed deity asked the Buddha the "Maṅgala Question" regarding which things in this world constitute the highest blessings (maṅgala) for prosperity and progress. Taking that deity as the primary listener, the Buddha preached the Maṅgala Sutta.
At that assembly of the Maṅgala Sutta, ninety billion devas and humans reached the Fruit of Arahatship. Those who reached the state of Stream-entry (Sotāpanna) and so forth were so numerous they could not be counted.
(This is the second Dhammābhisamaya, the second great assembly where humans, devas, and Brahmas were made to know the Four Noble Truths.)
On another occasion, while the Buddha Koṇḍañña was subduing the heretics by performing the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya) of water and fire, he preached the Dhamma while standing in the sky. At that time, eighty billion humans, devas, and Brahmas reached the Fruit of Arahatship. Those humans, devas, and Brahmas who were established in the three lower Fruits were so numerous they could not be counted.
(This is the third Dhammābhisamaya, the third great assembly where humans, devas, and Brahmas were made to know the Four Noble Truths.)

## Three Great Assemblies of Disciples
(1) There were also three assemblies of the disciples of Buddha Koṇḍañña. For the first assembly: After the Buddha Koṇḍañña had realized the Four Noble Truths and attained Buddhahood,

he observed the first rainy retreat (vassa) in the Canda Garden, depending on the city of Candavatī.
In that city of Candavatī, two youths—Bhaddaluṅga, the son of the wealthy Brahmin Sucindhara, and Subhaddaluṅga, the son of the Brahmin Yasodhara—heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha Koṇḍañña. With devoted hearts, they and ten thousand other youths became monks under the Buddha Koṇḍañña. (This is the second great assembly of disciples.)
(3) Later, on another occasion, while the Buddha Koṇḍañña was wandering through the countryside, he ordained King Udena along with his retinue of nine hundred million. When the monk Udena and his followers reached the Fruit of Arahatship, the Buddha Koṇḍañña recited the Ovāda-pāṭimokkha surrounded by nine hundred million Arahats led by the monk Udena.
(This is the third great assembly of disciples.)

## The Prediction of the Future Gotama Buddha
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Universal Monarch named Vijitāvī, ruling in the city of Candavatī. This Universal Monarch Vijitāvī, accompanied by a vast retinue, ruled and protected the earth righteously, within the boundaries of the universe up to the shores of the four oceans, without any need for punishment or weapons.

At that time, Koṇḍañña Buddha, accompanied by one hundred thousand billion (one hundred thousand times ten million) Arahats, was wandering through the countryside and eventually arrived at the city of Candavatī. When the Bodhisatta, King Vijitāvī, heard of the arrival of Koṇḍañña Buddha, he went out to welcome the Buddha, arranged a place for the Buddha to reside, and invited the Buddha along with the entire assembly of disciples for the next morning's meal. The following day, having prepared excellent food and offerings, he presented a great donation of alms-food to the assembly of one hundred thousand billion Arahats, with Koṇḍañña Buddha at their head.

After offering the meal and listening to the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), the Bodhisatta requested, "Venerable Sirs, please reside in this city of Candavatī for the three months of the rainy season to favor the many people." He then continuously offered an incomparable great donation to the assembly of monks led by Koṇḍañña Buddha throughout the entire three months of the rainy season.
208:
310
Then, Koṇḍañña Buddha gave the prediction to the Bodhisatta, saying: "In an aeon far distant from this one (three asankhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons hence), you shall surely become a Buddha." (The section regarding this prediction, including the practice of austerities and the full details of the prophecy, is clearly expounded in the Pali text just as it was for the prediction by Dīpaṅkara Buddha. However, since it has already been mentioned in the Story of Sumedha, it is not repeated here.)

After hearing the prediction, as the Buddha continued to preach the Dhamma, King Vijitāvī, the Bodhisatta, developed such great faith from hearing the Dhamma that, desiring to fulfill the great benefit of Buddhahood, he offered his vast kingdom and royal luxury to Koṇḍañña Buddha. He then ordained in the presence of the Buddha, studied the Three Pitakas, attained the eight meditative attainments and five superknowledges, and having reached the pinnacle of superknowledge, he was reborn in the Brahma realm at the end of his life.

## Description of the City and Others
The birthplace of Koṇḍañña Buddha was the city of Rammāvatī.
His father was King Sunanda, and his mother was Queen Sujātā.
The pair of chief disciples were the Venerable Bhadda and the Venerable Subhadda. His attendant was the Venerable Anuruddha.
209:
311
The pair of chief female disciples were the Elder Tissā and the Elder Upatissā. The Bodhi tree where he attained enlightenment was the Sālakalyāṇī (also known as the Trumpet flower tree or the Wood-apple tree).

The chief male lay supporters were Soṇa and Upasoṇa. The chief female lay supporters were the lay devotees Nandā and Sirimā.

Koṇḍañña Buddha was eighty-eight cubits in height and was as beautiful as the moon or the midday sun.

During the time of Koṇḍañña Buddha, the human lifespan was one hundred thousand years. Remaining for that duration, he rescued and liberated many beings, including humans, devas, and brahmas, from the current of saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna.

The three golden palaces used by the Bodhisatta Koṇḍañña during his life as a layman were Sucira, Suruci, and Subha.

There were three hundred thousand court ladies. His chief queen was named Rucidevī. His son was named Vijitasena. He reigned for ten thousand years.

When he renounced the world, he departed in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. After becoming a Buddha, he resided in the Candārāma (Canda Garden).
210:
312
Just as the sky is adorned and beautiful with stars and constellations, so too, during the time when the dispensation of Koṇḍañña Buddha flourished, this great earth was adorned and beautiful with Arahats who had exhausted their taints (āsavas) and were free from impurities. (This means the entire surface of the earth was covered with the glow of saffron robes.)

Those noble Arahats were incomparably sublime; they were never shaken or disturbed by the eight worldly conditions. They were difficult to approach for those who were arrogant. When those famous noble Arahats desired to attain Parinibbāna, they would fly into the sky to a height of about seven palm trees. (Like a flash of lightning entering a dark cloud), they would enter the Tejo-kasiṇa jhāna, and while displaying a great light, they would attain Parinibbāna in the sky as their bodies were consumed by the fire element.

## Saṃvega (Spiritual Urgency)
That incomparable and matchless power of Koṇḍañña Buddha, and his concentration infused with omniscience—all of that has ceased and vanished. Indeed, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are without any enduring essence and are merely empty.

## Construction of the Stupa
In this way, Koṇḍañña Buddha, who had realized the Four Noble Truths without remainder, attained Parinibbāna at the Candārāma (Canda Garden). In that very garden, using red arsenic and yellow orpiment as fine clay, and oil and ghee as water...
211:
313
...they constructed the Stupa of Koṇḍañña Buddha, which was seven yojanas in height.

According to the custom and nature of long-lived Buddhas, his relics remained as a single mass (asambhinnadhātu), not breaking into pieces, appearing like a golden statue. Having enshrined those unfragmented relics within the Stupa, all the people living in Jambudīpa completed the great Stupa, decorating it with the seven kinds of jewels.

The Chronicle of Koṇḍañña Buddha ends.
