## 3. The Chronicle of Maṅgala Buddha
After the end of the aeon in which Koṇḍañña Buddha appeared, and after the passing of an incalculable number of aeons (or so many aeons that they cannot be counted by numbers), in a certain aeon, four Buddhas appeared in succession: (1) Maṅgala Buddha, (2) Sumana Buddha, (3) Revata Buddha, and (4) Sobhita Buddha. Among them, the first to appear was Maṅgala Buddha.

## The Conception
The manner of Maṅgala Buddha's appearance is as follows: The Bodhisatta Maṅgala, after fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) for sixteen asankhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons, was residing in the Tusita heaven according to the custom of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world...
212:
314
...and was conceived in the womb of Queen Uttarā, the chief consort of King Uttara, in the capital city of Uttara, which was the most noble among all cities. (At the time of conception, the thirty-two great omens appeared as is the nature of Bodhisattas.)

## The Radiance of the Mother
From the time the Bodhisatta Maṅgala was conceived, the radiance from the Queen's body spread and remained within a circumference of eighty cubits, so bright that even the light of the moon and sun could not overcome it. The Queen did not need to use any other light, such as fire; she lived, moved about, and was attended to by her retinue by the light emanating from her own body.

## The Birth of the Bodhisatta
While many devas protected the pregnancy, when ten months were complete, he was born in the garden named Uttaramadhura, which was noble and delightful. (At the time of birth, the great omens appeared as usual, and extraordinary and wonderful events pertaining to all Bodhisattas also occurred.)

## Reigning over the Kingdom
When the Bodhisatta Prince Maṅgala reached maturity, he lived in three golden palaces: the highly famous Yasavanta, the very delightful Rucimanta, and the very glorious Sirimanta.
213:
315
In those three palaces, he enjoyed royal luxury comparable to divine bliss for nine thousand years, accompanied by Queen Yasavatī and a retinue of thirty thousand well-adorned dancers.

## Renunciation
When Queen Yasavatī gave birth to a son named Sīvala, the Prince saw the four great omens: an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a monk. He then renounced the world and became a monk, departing on the thoroughbred horse named Paṇḍara, which was well-adorned.

Following the example of the Bodhisatta Prince Maṅgala's renunciation, three crores (thirty million) of people also became monks.

The Bodhisatta Maṅgala, together with those thirty million monks, practiced austerities (dukkaracariyā) for eight months. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become a Buddha, he accepted and consumed the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of a wealthy man named Uttarā from the village of Uttara. He spent the heat of the day in the Sal grove in that area. When evening came, he left the assembly of monks and proceeded alone to the site of the Mahābodhi tree. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by an Ajivaka (naked ascetic) named Uttara. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Nāga (Bodhi) tree, the Aparājita Throne, fifty-eight cubits in size, appeared.
214:
## The Attainment of Buddhahood

Seated in the cross-legged posture upon the Aparājita Throne, having established the fourfold effort and conquered the hosts of Māra, He attained the knowledge of past lives (Pubbenivāsanussati-ñāṇa) in the first watch of the night, and the divine eye (Dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa) in the middle watch. In the last watch, He contemplated the Law of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) in both forward and backward order. Then, entering the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), and emerging from that jhāna, He contemplated the five aggregates. Seeing the fifty characteristics related to the arising and passing away of those five aggregates, He developed insight (vipassanā) up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (Gotrabhū-ñāṇa). Simultaneously with the rising of the dawn, He realized the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) along with all the qualities of a Buddha, and thus attained the peerless state of Buddhahood in the three worlds.

## The Extraordinary Bodily Radiance

The radiance of the Mangala Buddha was more extensive than that of other Buddhas. For other Buddhas, the natural radiance that emanates without being specially created by psychic power extends to eighty cubits or one fathom. 

However, for Mangala Buddha, it was not so; His natural bodily radiance shone constantly, day and night, pervading the ten thousand world systems (cakkavaḷa). Because of this brilliant radiance, all surrounding trees, the ground, forests, mountains, and oceans—even objects as dark as cooking pots—shone brilliantly as if they were wrapped in gold plates.
215:
The lifespan during which Mangala Buddha flourished was ninety thousand years, and throughout that duration, everything remained enveloped in this golden hue and light. During the era of that Buddha, there was no light from the moon, sun, stars, or constellations. Because there was no sunlight, the distinction between night and day was not apparent.

Even in the absence of sunlight, beings went about all their necessary activities solely by the radiance of the Buddha. They marked the distinction between night and day in the world by the blooming of flowers that usually open in the evening and by the chirping of birds that usually sing in the early morning.

One might ask: "Did other Buddhas not possess such power?" The answer is that they did. If those other Buddhas so desired, they could cause their radiance to pervade ten thousand world systems or even beyond. However, in the case of Mangala Buddha, by the power of His past aspirations, His bodily radiance constantly pervaded the ten thousand world systems without needing to be specially created by psychic power, just like the one-fathom natural radiance of other Buddhas.

## The Past Aspiration of Mangala Buddha

When the Mangala Buddha was a Bodhisatta, in a life similar to that of King Vessantara, He lived with His wife and children on a mountain resembling Mount Vaṅka.
216:
At that time, an ogre (yakkha) named Kharadāṭhika, having heard news of the Bodhisatta's great desire for almsgiving, disguised himself as a Brahmin, approached the Bodhisatta, and asked for the two royal children as a gift.

Then, the Bodhisatta, joyfully thinking, "I shall give my son and daughter to the Brahmin," gave the two children, causing the great earth, which is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick down to the water's edge, to tremble. 

The ogre, leaning against a backrest at the end of the walkway, devoured the two children like chewing on lotus stalks, even while the Great Being was watching. 

Although the Bodhisatta looked at the ogre and saw the blood gushing from the ogre's mouth like flames as he opened it, there was not even a hair's breadth of displeasure in His heart. Instead, great joy and satisfaction arose in the Bodhisatta's body as He thought, "This gift I have now given is a truly noble gift."

The Bodhisatta made an aspiration: "By the fruit of this almsgiving, in the future, may the radiance from my body shine forth in the same manner as this flow of blood." Based on that aspiration, when He became a Buddha, the natural radiance of that Mangala Buddha emanated from His body and pervaded the ten thousand world systems.
217:
Furthermore...

There was another past aspiration of the Mangala Buddha. When He was a Bodhisatta, having seen the stupa of a certain Buddha, He thought, "It is fitting that I should sacrifice my life for this Buddha." He then had His entire body wrapped in cloths soaked in ghee, just as one wraps a lamp wick. He filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, which was slightly flared at the rim, with ghee. Lighting a thousand wicks in that golden bowl, He carried it upon His head, set His entire body on fire, and spent the whole night circumambulating the noble stupa clockwise.

Although He strove in this manner until dawn, not even a single hair-pore of the Bodhisatta was affected by the heat; it was as if He were inside a lotus. Indeed, it is the nature of the Dhamma to protect those who practice it from danger. Therefore, the Buddha taught:

"Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ,
Dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahati.
Esānisaṃso dhamme suciṇṇe,
Na duggatiṃ gacchati dhammacārī."

(The Dhamma indeed protects him who lives by the Dhamma; the Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness. This is the advantage of Dhamma well-practiced: he who lives by the Dhamma does not go to a state of suffering.)

By the fruit of this aforementioned meritorious deed, the natural bodily radiance of the Mangala Buddha also remained pervading the ten thousand world systems.
218:
## Three Great Dhamma Assemblies

After becoming a Buddha, the Lord Mangala Buddha stayed near the Mahābodhi tree for the seven weeks (Satta-sattāha). Having accepted the request of the Great Brahma to preach the Dhamma, He considered, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He saw thirty million monks who had ordained following His example and who possessed strong supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit.

Thinking that He would preach the Dhamma to those monks before all others, He again considered where those monks were currently residing. He saw that they were living in the woods called Sirivana near the city of Sirivaḍḍhana, eighteen yojanas away from the Mahābodhi tree. Taking His bowl and robes, He traveled through the air in an instant to the Sirivana woods where those monks resided.

At that time, the thirty million monks, seeing the Mangala Buddha approaching, welcomed Him with great devotion, took His bowl and robes, prepared a seat, and performed respectful salutations. They then sat in suitable places surrounding the Buddha.

Then, the Buddha preached to those thirty million monks the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which is the discourse habitually preached by all past Buddhas. When this first discourse of the Wheel of Dhamma was preached, the thirty million
219:
monks attained the Fruit of Arahantship. The realization of the Four Noble Truths (attainment of liberation) occurred for one hundred billion devas and humans.

(This is the first great Dhamma assembly, known as the First Dhammābhisamaya, the first time He caused beings to realize the Four Noble Truths.)

When the Mangala Buddha was about to preach the Abhidhamma, He resided near the city of Citta. At the foot of a Champaka tree at the city gate, He performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) of fire and water to subdue the pride of the heretics, just as our Buddha performed the Twin Miracle near the mango tree planted by the gardener named Kaṇḍa at the gate of Sāvatthī. After subduing the heretics, He resided upon the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone throne at the foot of the Parichattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and preached the Abhidhamma to the devas and Brahmas.

At that time, the realization of the Four Noble Truths occurred for one hundred billion devas and Brahmas.

(This is the second great Dhamma assembly, known as the Second Dhammābhisamaya, the second time He caused devas and Brahmas to realize the Four Noble Truths.)

Before the Mangala Buddha appeared, in the city of Surabhi, a Great King named Sunanda fulfilled the duties that lead to the arrival of the Wheel Treasure and thus obtained the Wheel Treasure.

When the Mangala Buddha appeared, King Sunanda saw that the Wheel Treasure had sunk and receded from its original place.
220:
King Sunanda, feeling unhappy, asked the court chaplains and Brahmins, "Why has this Wheel Treasure, which appeared by the power of my merit, sunk and receded from its original place?"

Then the court chaplains and Brahmins replied:

"O Great King, the Wheel Treasure sinks and recedes from its place because the life of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) is near its end, or because the Universal Monarch has entered the monkhood, or because a Buddha has appeared in the world.

There is no question of Your Majesty's life ending; Your Majesty will live for a very long time.

In truth, the Mangala Buddha has now appeared in the world. Therefore, Your Majesty's Wheel Treasure has sunk and receded from its original place."

Hearing the report of the court chaplains and Brahmins, the Universal Monarch Sunanda, along with his retinue, bowed in respect to the Wheel Treasure and requested, "I shall first pay my respects to the Mangala Buddha by the power and majesty of you, the Wheel Treasure; during that time, may you, the Wheel Treasure, not disappear." Then, the Wheel Treasure remained in its original place.

Thereafter, King Sunanda, being greatly delighted, surrounded by a retinue thirty-six yojanas in circumference, [went to] the true blessing of the whole world...
221:
Having approached the Exalted Maṅgala Buddha, he pleased the Buddha and the community of monks with a great offering. He donated cloth for robes produced in the Kāsi country to one hundred thousand crore Arahants. After offering all necessary requisites to the Buddha, he sat in a suitable place to listen to the Dhamma. The son of that Universal Monarch, a prince named Anurāja, also sat down in the same manner as the king.

Then, the Exalted Maṅgala Buddha preached the Dhamma in the sequential order of discourse to the people, headed by King Sunanda. King Sunanda, along with a retinue of ninety crores, attained Arahantship endowed with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

At that time, the Buddha, observing the past meritorious practices of that assembly, saw the special merit from their previous lives which would allow them to be fully equipped with bowls and robes through psychic power (without having to seek them). He stretched out his right arm and said, "Ehi Bhikkhavo" (Come, monks). At that very moment, all those people had hair measuring two finger-breadths, were clad in and carried bowls and robes created by psychic power, and were endowed with the inspiring appearance of monks, like senior elders of a hundred years' standing. They then stood surrounding the Buddha.

(This is the third realization of the Dhamma, known as the third great Dhamma assembly [tatiya-dhammābhisamaya], where the Four Noble Truths were made known to beings.)
222:
## Three Great Assemblies of Disciples

On one occasion, while the Exalted Maṅgala Buddha was residing in the city of Mekhala, the youths Sudeva and Dhammasena, who were destined to be the chief disciples and each had a retinue of one thousand youths (according to the Sri Lankan commentary, ten thousand youths), became "Ehi Bhikkhu" monks in the presence of the Buddha. On the full moon day of Tabodwe (Māgha), having attained Arahantship along with their retinues, the Buddha recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the midst of one hundred thousand crore monks.

(This is the first great assembly of disciples.)

Again, in the midst of an assembly of one thousand crore monks who had entered the monkhood during the gathering of the royal relatives in the great garden named Uttara, He recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.

(This is the second great assembly of disciples.)

In the great assembly of monks headed by the monk Sunanda (formerly the Universal Monarch), He recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the midst of ninety crore monks.

(This is the third great assembly of disciples.)

## The Prophecy of Gotama Buddha's Enlightenment

During the time of that Exalted Maṅgala Buddha, our Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Suruci in the village of Suruci. He had reached the further shore (mastery) of the five scriptures: the Vedas, the dictionary known as Nighaṇḍu, the poetics known as Keṭubha, the grammar known as Akkharappabheda, and...
223:
...the chronicles and legends known as Itihāsa as the fifth.

(The details of how Itihāsa is the fifth scripture were explained extensively in the section on Sumedha Brahmin in the Sumedha-kathā.)

He was highly proficient and skilled in writing and reciting verses called Padaka. He was also highly proficient and skilled in writing and reciting prose called Veyyākaraṇa.

He was fully accomplished in wisdom, without deficiency, in the Lokāyata scripture which does not increase merit but only prolongs the world, and in the Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa scripture which describes various marks starting from the marks of a Great Man.

That Bodhisatta, Suruci the Brahmin, having approached the Buddha and heard the extremely sweet Dhamma, gained faith in the Buddha and established himself in the Three Refuges. He then invited the Buddha along with the community of disciples, saying, "Please accept my alms-food tomorrow."

When the Buddha asked, "Brahmin, how many monks do you wish to invite?", he replied, "Exalted One, how many monks are in your retinue?"

Since it was the time of the first assembly of disciples, the Buddha said, "There are one hundred thousand crore disciples." He then invited them, saying, "Exalted One, if that is so, please accept my alms-food along with all those monks." The Buddha consented by remaining silent.
224:
After inviting them for the next day's meal, the Bodhisatta Suruci Brahmin returned home and reflected:

"I am able to offer gruel, rice, and cloth for robes to this many monks. But how can there be enough seating and space?"

His reflection caused the Paṇḍukambala stone throne of Sakka, the King of Devas, situated on the summit of Mount Meru (which is eighty-four thousand yojanas high), to become hot. (Because of the Bodhisatta's reflection, Sakka's throne became hot; in common parlance, it is said that the stone throne became stiff.)

Then Sakka wondered, "Who wishes to displace me from this seat?" Looking with his divine eye, he saw the Bodhisatta Suruci Brahmin and thought, "This Bodhisatta has invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha and is reflecting on the seating. It is proper that I go there and take a share of the merit." Having so planned, he disguised himself as a carpenter, holding an adze and an axe, and appeared clearly before the Bodhisatta.

## Discussion about Building the Pavilion

Sakka the carpenter asked, "Does anyone have work to be done for a fee?" When the Bodhisatta saw Sakka the carpenter, he asked, "Young man, what kind of work can you do?" He replied, "There is no craft that I do not know...
225:
...whether someone wants a pavilion, a palace, or any other building such as a house, I am able to perform all the work they desire."

Then the Bodhisatta said, "If so, I have work to be done." When asked, "What should be done?", he replied, "I have invited one hundred thousand crore monks for tomorrow's meal. Can you, young man, build a pavilion for those monks to stay in?" He said, "If you can pay me a fee, I can build it." The Bodhisatta replied, "Young man, I can pay." He said, "If you can pay, very well, I shall build it." Then Sakka looked at a certain area of ground.

## A Jeweled Pavilion Arising from the Ground

The area of ground measuring twelve yojanas that Sakka looked at became a level surface like a kasiṇa disk. Then Sakka thought and looked, "Let a great pavilion, made of the seven jewels and adorned with magnificent, delightful decorations, arise from the ground in this area." At that very moment, the great jeweled pavilion emerged, breaking through the ground. In that pavilion, there were silver lotus-pots on golden pillars, golden lotus-pots on silver pillars, coral lotus-pots on ruby pillars, ruby lotus-pots on coral pillars, and lotus-pots made of the seven jewels on pillars made of the seven jewels.
226:
Then he thought and looked, "Let nets adorned with many golden bells hang down between the pillars inside the pavilion." As soon as he looked, nets adorned with many golden bells and small golden bells hung down. When stirred by a gentle breeze, a very sweet sound emerged, like the sound of the five-fold musical instruments. It was like the time when many devas gather to play and sing in the celestial realm.

Again, he thought, "Let celestial garlands of perfume, flowers, and foliage hang down in the spaces between." At that moment, celestial garlands of perfume, flowers, and foliage hung down.

He thought again, "Let seats for one hundred thousand crore monks, and also suitable, highly valuable rugs and bowl-stands for the monks, emerge breaking through the ground." At the moment of that thought, they emerged.

He thought again, "Let a large water jar appear in each and every corner." At the moment of that thought, the water jars appeared.

Sakka the carpenter, having created all these things, went to the Bodhisatta Suruci Brahmin and said, "Sir Brahmin, please come. After looking at your pavilion, please give me a suitable fee." When the Bodhisatta went and looked at the pavilion, even as he was looking, his entire body was continuously touched by the five-fold joy (pīti).
227:
## Giving the Great Offering (Mahādāna)

Then, the Bodhisatta, looking at the pavilion, had this thought: "This pavilion was not made by a human being. It must be that because of my meritorious desire to give a great offering and my virtues, Sakka's throne must have become hot. Because of that heat, Sakka, the king of devas, must have created this pavilion." He then thought again, "It is not proper for me to give an offering for only one day in such a pavilion. I shall give a great offering for seven days."

Indeed, no matter how great the quantity of external offerings may be, they are not able to satisfy the hearts of Bodhisattas. However, only when they give by cutting off their decorated heads, or by gouging out their extremely beautiful, bright, and clear eyes, or by extracting their hearts, do Bodhisattas feel satisfaction, joy, and fulfillment based on their acts of charity. This point should be firmly believed and noted by considering the Bodhisatta King Sivi, who, although he gave offerings at the five locations—the four city gates and the center of the city—spending five hundred thousand pieces of silver daily, was not satisfied until he gouged out both his eyes and gave them to Sakka, who had come in the guise of a Brahmin to ask for them. Therefore, the Bodhisatta Suruci Brahmin also thought, "I should give an offering to the one hundred thousand crore monks," and for seven days in that pavilion...
228:
He invited the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, to be seated and offered a specially prepared donation of milk-rice (pāyāsa) and beverages. 

In providing this milk-rice and beverage, humans alone were not sufficient; devas also participated, alternating with them. The area of twelve or thirteen leagues was also insufficient for all the monks to reside, so those monks (who did not find a place) created their own dwellings through their psychic power.

## Offering of Medicinal Requisites and the Triple Robes
On the final day of the donation, after having all the monks' alms-bowls washed clean, he filled the bowls with ghee, butter, oil, honey, and molasses for medicinal purposes and offered them along with a set of triple robes. Even the robes received by the most junior monk (saṅghanava) were worth one hundred thousand. 

## Receiving the Prophecy
Then, while the Buddha Maṅgala was delivering the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), He looked into the future with His Knowledge of the Future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa), considering: "This person is giving such a great donation; what will become of him in the future?" He saw that in a Bhadda-kappa one hundred thousand cycles and two asaṅkheyyas from now, he would surely become a Buddha named Gotama. Calling the Bodhisatta Suruci the Brahmin, He prophesied: "After this much time has passed, you will surely become a Buddha named Gotama."
229:
331
(The section regarding this prophecy is clearly taught in the Pāḷi text, including the practice of austerities and the complete prophecy, just as it was taught in the prophecy of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. However, since it has already been mentioned in the Sumedha-kathā, it will not be repeated here.)

Then, when the Bodhisatta heard the words of the prophecy from the Buddha Maṅgala, he was filled with joy and delight. He thought, "I will surely become a Buddha. What is the use of living in a household? I shall become a monk right now." He then renounced his great wealth as a wealthy Brahmin (Brāhmaṇa Mahāsāla) without any lingering attachment, as if it were a glob of spit. He became a monk in the presence of the Buddha Maṅgala, learned the Tipitaka, and developed the five super-knowledges (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti) within himself. Without losing his jhāna, he was reborn in the Brahma realm at the end of his life.

## Description of the City and Others
The birthplace of the Buddha Maṅgala was the city of Uttara.
His father was King Uttara, and his mother was Queen Uttarādevī.
His pair of chief disciples were the Venerable Sudeva and the Venerable Dhammasena. His attendant was the Venerable Pālita.
His pair of chief female disciples were the Venerable Sīvalā and the Venerable Asokā. The Bodhi tree where He attained enlightenment was the Nāga (Ironwood) tree.
230:
332
The noble male lay supporters were the wealthy merchant Nanda and the wealthy merchant Visākha. The noble female lay supporters were the laywomen Anulā and Sutanā.

The height of the Buddha Maṅgala was eighty-eight cubits. The radiance from His body, as previously mentioned, always shone beautifully throughout the ten thousand world systems. Occasionally, it reached not just ten thousand, but hundreds of thousands of world systems.

The lifespan during the time of the Buddha Maṅgala was ninety thousand years. Remaining for that duration, He rescued many beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—from the current of saṃsāra and brought them to the dry land of Nibbāna.

The three golden palaces used by the Bodhisatta Maṅgala during his life as a layman were the Yasavanta Palace, the Rucimanta Palace, and the Sirimanta Palace.

There were thirty thousand ladies-in-waiting. The chief queen was named Yasavatī, and the son was named Sīvala. He reigned for nine thousand years.

When He renounced the world, He departed riding the horse named Paṇḍara. After becoming a Buddha, He resided in the Uttarārāma (Uttara Garden).
231:
333
Just as it is impossible to count the waves in the great ocean, it is impossible to count the Arahant disciples of the Buddha Maṅgala.

During the entire time the Buddha Maṅgala, who brought the three types of people to Nibbāna, remained alive, there was no monk in His dispensation who died with defilements. (They all became Arahants and attained Parinibbāna.)

The Buddha Maṅgala, who had a great following and great fame, lit the lamp of Dhamma and rescued many people from the current of saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna. Then, like a great fire that has blazed and then gone out, or like the sun that has set, He showed the nature of impermanence, suffering, and non-self of all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) to humans, devas, and Brahmas, and entered Parinibbāna.

As soon as the Buddha Maṅgala attained Parinibbāna, the original radiance of the Buddha in the ten thousand world systems disappeared, and total darkness fell. In those world systems, there was intense weeping and lamentation among the people.

## Sense of Urgency (Saṃvega)
That incomparable and peerless power of the Buddha Maṅgala, and His concentration (samādhi) infused with Omniscient Knowledge—all of it has ceased and vanished. Indeed, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are without any solid core and are truly empty.
232:
334
In this way, the Buddha Maṅgala, who saw the Four Noble Truths without remainder, attained Parinibbāna in the great garden named Uttara (so named because it excelled other gardens, with all fruit trees bearing fruit and all flowering trees blooming). In that very garden, using realgar and orpiment as fine powder (mortar), and oil and ghee as water, they built a Cetiya for the Buddha Maṅgala, which was thirty leagues high.

According to the tradition of long-lived Buddhas, the unbroken relics (asambhinnadhātu), which remained as a single mass like a golden statue, were enshrined within the Cetiya. All the people living in Jambudīpa completed the great Cetiya, decorating it with the seven kinds of jewels.

The Chronicle of Buddha Maṅgala ends.

## 4. The Chronicle of Buddha Sumana
In this way, the Buddha Maṅgala had illuminated the ten thousand world systems of the birth-field (jāti-khetta), overcoming the various lights of the sun, moon, stars, devas, and Brahmas with the natural radiance from His body, so that there was no distinction between day and night. After He attained Parinibbāna, as if total darkness had been created all at once, the lifespan of the people, which was ninety thousand years, gradually decreased to ten years, then increased again to an asaṅkheyya, and then decreased again.
233:
335
When the lifespan decreased again and reached ninety thousand years, the Bodhisatta Sumana, having completed the perfections (pāramīs), was residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and Brahmas, he descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of Queen Sirimā, the consort of King Sudatta in the capital city of Mekhala.

When the Bodhisatta was conceived, the thirty-two great omens appeared as usual. When he was born after ten months, the same great omens appeared, along with the wonderful events associated with all Bodhisattas.

When the Bodhisatta Prince Sumana reached maturity, he lived in three golden palaces: (1) Canda, (2) Sucanda, and (3) Vaṭaṃsa. He enjoyed divine-like luxury and happiness for nine thousand years, reigning with his chief queen named Vaṭaṃsikā (so named because she was like a flower worn on the head of others), surrounded by six million three hundred thousand beautifully adorned attendants.

(Regarding these six million three hundred thousand attendants, it should be understood that they did not all serve at once, but were the total number of attendants designated to serve in shifts.)
234:
336
When Queen Vaṭaṃsikā gave birth to a son named Anupama, the Bodhisatta saw the four great signs—an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a monk. According to the nature of Bodhisattas, he renounced the world, riding an elephant adorned with ornaments provided by the devas, and became a monk. When the Bodhisatta Prince Sumana renounced the world to become a monk, thirty crores of people followed his example and also became monks.

The Bodhisatta Sumana, together with those thirty crores of monks, practiced the austerities (dukkharacariya) for ten months. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), he accepted and consumed the thick milk-rice offered by Anupamā, the daughter of the merchant Anoma from the village of Anoma. He spent the day in the Sal grove in that area. When evening came, he left his followers and proceeded alone to the site of the Mahābodhi tree. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by an ascetic (Ajīvaka) named Anupama. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the (Nāga) Bodhi tree, the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka) of thirty cubits appeared.

After sitting cross-legged on that Unconquerable Throne (as described in the previous Chronicle of Buddha Maṅgala), he blew away the army of Māra, attained Omniscient Knowledge, and became the Sammāsambuddha, the Supreme One of the three worlds. He then uttered the solemn inspired utterance (udāna) that is never omitted by any Buddha: "Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ..."

## Three Great Assemblies of Dhamma
After becoming a Buddha, the Buddha Sumana stayed near the Mahābodhi tree for the seven-seven (forty-nine days).
235:
After residing there and accepting the request of the Great Brahma to teach the Dhamma, He reflected, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" While reflecting, He saw the thirty crores (300 million) of monks who had ordained together with Him, as well as His half-brother Prince Sarana and the chaplain's son, the youth Bhavitatta, who were endowed with past merits to attain the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna. Seeing them, He thought, "I shall preach the Dhamma to them first." Then, He reflected again, "Where are those monks residing now?" and saw that they were staying in the Mekhala Park in the city of Mekhala, eighteen leagues away from the Great Bodhi tree. Taking His bowl and robes, He traveled through the air in an instant to the Mekhala Park where those monks resided.

At that time, the thirty crores of monks saw the arrival of Sumana Buddha. With hearts full of great devotion, they performed the duties of welcoming the Buddha, receiving His bowl and robes, preparing the seat, and paying respectful homage. They then sat in suitable places surrounding the Buddha.

Then, Sumana Buddha sent the park keeper to call His younger brother Prince Sarana and the chaplain's son Bhavitatta. To Prince Sarana and Bhavitatta, along with their thirty-seven crores of attendants, and to the thirty crores of monks who were His former companions in ordination, as well as to many other millions of devas and humans—to a total of one hundred thousand crores of humans, devas, and Brahmas—
236:
He preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which is the constant tradition of previous Buddhas. After preaching, He beat the great drum of the Deathless (Amata), which is the Dispensation of the Buddha, endowed with the nine-fold members and well-joined with the conch-shell of the Four Noble Truths.

To state specifically: After Sumana Buddha attained Omniscience and accepted the request of the Great Brahma, He acted accordingly. Desiring to liberate the venayyas (beings to be tamed) from the bond of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa), and to protect those venayyas whose jewels of merit were being stolen and destroyed by the thieves of defilements (kilesa), He constructed the great royal city of Nibbāna. This city was well-fortified with the walls of Virtue (Sīla), surrounded by the moat of Concentration (Samādhi), and beautifully adorned with the gate of Insight-knowledge (Vipassanā-ñāṇa), the door-leaves of Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension (Sati-sampajañña), and the pavilions of Meditative Attainments (Samāpatti). It was filled with noble persons who had attained the group of the Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma (Factors of Enlightenment).

After constructing the great royal city of Nibbāna, Sumana Buddha laid out the great main road of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna), which is perfectly straight, neat, beautiful, wide, and long, without any interruption. On both sides of that main road, He established the peaceful and pleasant great market-row of the Dhamma, displaying the many precious jewels known as the Four Fruits (Phala), the Four Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidā), the Six Supernormal Powers (Abhiññā), and the Eight Attainments (Samāpatti), so that those who desire them could joyfully purchase and use them with the capital of
237:
faith, energy, moral shame, and moral dread (Saddhā, Viriya, Hiri, Ottappa).

In this way, by constructing the City of Dhamma, opening the Great Market of Dhamma, and beating the Great Drum of Dhamma—which is the first great assembly of teaching the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta—Sumana Buddha granted the realization of the Dhamma to one hundred thousand crores of humans, devas, and Brahmas.

(This is the first great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma [Dhammābhisamaya].)

On another occasion, near a mango tree in the city of Sunandavatī, Sumana Buddha performed the wonderful and marvelous Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) of water and fire to subdue the intoxicated, aggressive, and arrogant pride of the heretics. He then administered the medicine of the Dhamma to humans, devas, and Brahmas. At that time, one hundred thousand crores of beings realized the Four Noble Truths.

(This is the second great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma.)

On another occasion, devas and Brahmas from ten thousand world-systems gathered with the humans, devas, and Brahmas of this world-system and engaged in a discussion regarding the attainment of Cessation (Nirodha-samāpatti). They asked, "How does one enter the attainment of Cessation? How does one become one who has reached Cessation? How does one emerge from the attainment of Cessation?" Being unable to decide on these points and matters concerning the attainment of Cessation, both humans and devas,
238:
up to the nine realms of the Fine-Material Brahmas (Rūpāvacara Brahma), were in doubt and divided into two sides. Then, King Arindama, who was a conventional deva (sammuti-deva) among humans, approached Sumana Buddha, the refuge of the three worlds, in the evening. When King Arindama asked the aforementioned questions regarding the attainment of Cessation, Sumana Buddha gave a clear explanation and preached the Dhamma. Through this, ninety thousand crores of humans, devas, and Brahmas realized the Four Noble Truths.

(This is the third great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma.)

## Three Assemblies of the Disciples

## The First Assembly (Paṭhama-sannipāta)

There were three great assemblies of the disciples (Sāvaka-sannipāta) of Sumana Buddha. Among these three, in the first assembly, Sumana Buddha spent the rainy season (vassa) depending on the city of Mekhala. At the end of the rainy season, on the first Pavāraṇā day of the full moon of Thadingyut, He performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony together with one hundred thousand crores of Arahants, all of whom were Ehi Bhikkhu monks.

(This is the first great assembly of the disciples.)

## The Second Assembly (Dutiya-sannipāta)

Thereafter, on another occasion, while He was residing on a golden mountain, one league in extent and made of pure gold due to the meritorious power of King Arindama, in a place not far from the city of Saṅkassa, He taught, demonstrated, and admonished ninety thousand crores of the king's men who had come accompanying King Arindama with the noble Dhamma.
239:
He caused them all to become Ehi Bhikkhu monks. On that very day, surrounded by the assembly of monks who had reached the Fruit of Arahantship, He recited the Pātimokkha in an assembly endowed with four factors.

(Regarding the four factors, although they are not explicitly mentioned in the Commentary here, according to the explanation of the Dīghanakha Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, Vol. 3, p. 146, they should be understood as: (1) It is the full moon day of Tabodwe; (2) The assembly of monks gathered of their own accord without being invited by anyone; (3) Those monks are all Arahants endowed with the six supernormal powers; (4) They are all Ehi Bhikkhu monks.)

(This is the second great assembly of the disciples.)

## The Third Assembly (Tatiya-sannipāta)

Thereafter, on another occasion, Sakka, the king of devas, came to visit and pay homage to Sumana Buddha. At that time, surrounded by eighty thousand crores of Arahants, Sumana Buddha recited the Pātimokkha.

(This is the third great assembly of the disciples.)

**********

## The Bodhisatta as a Naga King Receiving the Prophecy

During the time of Sumana Buddha, our Bodhisatta was Atula, a Naga King of great power and majesty. Hearing that "A Buddha has arisen in the three worlds," he left his abode in the Naga realm accompanied by his kin. To Sumana Buddha, who was surrounded by one hundred thousand crores of monks,
240:
he made offerings with celestial music and instruments, and gave a great donation of food and drinks. He also offered a pair of robes to each and every monk and established himself in the Refuges (Saranagamana).

Sumana Buddha also gave a detailed prophecy to Atula the Naga King, saying, "In the future, this Naga King will become Gotama Buddha."

(The manner of receiving the prophecy is exactly the same as the detailed account of the prophecy given by Dīpaṅkara Buddha.)

Upon hearing the prophecy of Sumana Buddha, the Bodhisatta Atula the Naga King felt exceedingly joyful and firmly resolved to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs) even more intensely.

## Description of the City, etc.

The city of birth of Sumana Buddha was the city of Mekhala.
His father was King Sudatta, and His mother was Queen Sirimā.
He ruled the palace for nine thousand years, and His three palaces were Canda, Sucanda, and Vaṭaṃsa.
His Chief Queen was Queen Vaṭaṃsikā, who had six million three hundred thousand attendants, and His son was Prince Anupama.
241:
The pair of Chief Disciples were the Venerable Sarana and the Venerable Bhavitatta, and His attendant was the Venerable Udena.

The pair of Chief Female Disciples were the Therī Soṇā and the Therī Upasoṇā, and the Bodhi tree under which He attained enlightenment was the Nāga (Ironwood) tree.

The noble male lay supporters were the wealthy merchant Varuṇa and the wealthy merchant Sarana, and the noble female lay supporters were Cālā and Upacālā.

The height of Sumana Buddha was ninety cubits. He resembled a great golden pillar prepared for worship, and He graced the ten thousand world-systems with His radiant body-aura.

The lifespan during the time of Sumana Buddha was ninety thousand years. Remaining for that duration, He rescued and liberated many humans, devas, and Brahmas from the current of the round of rebirths to the dry land of Nibbāna.

Having liberated those who were worthy of crossing over and being freed from the great ocean of Saṃsāra, and having caused those who were worthy of knowing the Four Noble Truths to realize them, Sumana Buddha entered Parinibbāna and passed away, just as the great moon sets.

Those noble ones who were Arahants with taints exhausted, and Sumana Buddha who was peerless in the three worlds, having caused the great peerless light of the Dhamma to shine and possessing great fame and reputation—
242:
344
The Buddha Sumana, along with many disciples who were Arahants, has attained Parinibbāna and passed away.

## Saṃvega (Spiritual Emotion)
That peerless golden knowledge of omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) of the Buddha Sumana, and the peerless Dhamma treasures such as the four Fruits (Phala) and the fourfold Analytical Knowledge (Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa)—all these have ceased and vanished. Indeed, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are without essence and are empty.

## Construction of the Stupa
Thus, the Buddha Sumana, who realized the Four Noble Truths without remainder and bore great fame, attained Parinibbāna in the great park named Aṅga. In that very park, using orpiment (manosilā) and realgar (haritāla) as fine powder, and oil and ghee as water, they built a Stupa for the Buddha Sumana, which was four leagues (yojanas) in height.

According to the custom and nature of long-lived Buddhas, the undivided relics (asambhinna-dhātu), which remain as a single solid mass without breaking into pieces, stood like a golden statue. Having enshrined those undivided relics within the Stupa, all the people living in Jambudīpa finished the great Stupa, decorating it with the seven kinds of jewels.

The Chronicle of Sumana Buddha ends.

## 5. The Chronicle of Revata Buddha
After the Buddha Sumana attained Parinibbāna, the human lifespan gradually decreased from 90,000 years to 10 years, then increased again to an incalculable age (asaṅkhyeyya), and then decreased again. When it reached 60,000 years, the Bodhisatta Revata, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), was dwelling in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the assembly of devas and brahmās, he descended to the human world and took conception in the womb of Queen Vipulā, the consort of King Vipula in the royal city of Sudhaññavatī. After ten months had passed, he was born from his mother's womb, like a golden hamsa bird emerging from Mount Cittakūṭa.

(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, the great omens and wonders appeared as previously mentioned.)

## Reigning over the Kingdom
When the Bodhisatta Prince Revata reached maturity, due to the power of his perfections and merit, he dwelt in three magnificent golden palaces: (1) Sudassana, (2) Ratanagghi, and (3) Āveḷa. He enjoyed divine-like pleasures for 6,000 years, being entertained and served by Queen Sudassanā and 33,000 attendants, while reigning over the kingdom.
244:
346
## The Great Renunciation
While reigning in this manner, when Queen Sudassanā gave birth to a son named Varuṇa, he saw the four great omens. According to the nature of Bodhisattas, adorned with ornaments provided by the devas, he departed for the great renunciation on a chariot drawn by noble horses. He was like the moon surrounded by stars, like Sakka, the king of devas, surrounded by the host of devas, or like Hārita Mahābrahmā surrounded by the host of brahmās. He went forth with a great fourfold army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. Upon reaching the forest, he handed over the ornaments he was wearing to the treasurer, cut off his hair with his royal sword, and threw it into the sky.

Sakka, the king of devas, received that sacred hair in a golden casket and established a great Stupa made of the seven jewels on the summit of Mount Meru in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

The Bodhisatta Prince donned the lotus robes offered by a Brahmā and became a monk; ten million men followed his example and also became monks.

The Bodhisatta Revata, together with those ten million monks, practiced austerities (dukkharacariyā) for seven months.

## Attaining Enlightenment
Having practiced austerities for seven months, on the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become a Buddha, he accepted the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of a wealthy man named Sādhudevī.
245:
347
After partaking of the meal, he spent the day in the Sāla grove in that area. When evening came, he left the accompanying monks and proceeded alone towards the site of the Mahābodhi tree. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by an ascetic named Varuṇindhara. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Mahābodhi Nāga tree, an Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka) measuring 53 cubits appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that throne and resolving with fourfold effort (vīriya), he dispersed the army of Māra as previously mentioned and attained the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha), the Lord of the Three Worlds, endowed with the Knowledge of Omniscience.

## Three Great Assemblies of Dhamma
After becoming a Buddha, the Buddha Revata stayed near the Mahābodhi tree for the seven weeks (satta-sattāha = 49 days). Accepting the request of the Great Brahmā to teach the Dhamma, he reflected, "To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?" He saw the ten million monks who had renounced with him, as well as other devas and humans who were endowed with past merits to attain the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna. Thinking, "I shall teach the Dhamma to them first," he reflected again, "Where are they living now?" Seeing that they were in the Varuṇa Grove, eighteen leagues away from the Mahābodhi tree, he took his bowl and robes and traveled through the air in an instant to the Varuṇa Grove where those monks resided.

At that time, the ten million monks saw the Buddha Revata coming from afar. With hearts full of devotion, they went out to meet the Buddha, took his bowl and robes, prepared his seat, and paid their respects with great reverence. Then, they sat in suitable places surrounding the Buddha. The Buddha Revata then preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which is the customary discourse preached by all previous Buddhas, to those ten million monks who had been his companions in renunciation. He established those ten million monks in the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala). The number of those who were established in the lower Paths and Fruits was countless.

(This was the first great assembly of Dhamma [Dhammābhisamaya].)

Later, on another occasion, in the city named Uttara—so called because it was superior to all other cities—a king named Arindama, who could conquer all enemies, was reigning. Hearing that the Buddha Revata had arrived at his city of Uttara, he went out to meet the Buddha accompanied by thirty million people. He invited the Saṅgha led by the Buddha for the next day's meal and offered a great alms-giving for seven days. He honored the Buddha with a great lamp offering spanning three gāvutas and sat near the Buddha. Then, the Buddha Revata preached a very wonderful Dhamma discourse in accordance with King Arindama's disposition. In that great assembly, ten billion devas and humans realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation.

(This was the second great assembly of Dhamma [Dutiyadhammābhisamaya].)

They asked, "Venerable sirs, where is the Buddha dwelling?" The monks replied, "Lay followers, the Buddha is dwelling in the attainment of cessation." After seven days had passed, they saw the Buddha emerging from the attainment of cessation and asked about the virtues and benefits of nirodha-samāpatti. The Buddha then preached to those people about the virtues and benefits of the attainment of cessation. At that time, one billion devas and humans were established in the Fruit of Arahantship.

(This was the first great assembly of disciples.)

## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha, the Brahmin Atideva, Receiving the Prophecy
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Atideva in the city of Rammāvatī, who had reached the pinnacle of mastery in the Vedic sciences taught by a lineage of teachers. Having met the Buddha Revata and heard his Dhamma...

## Description of the City, etc.

The birthplace of the Buddha Revata was the city of Sudhaññavatī; his father was King Vipula and his mother was Queen Vipulā.

His pair of female chief disciples were the Elder nuns Bhaddā and Subhaddā, and the Bodhi tree where he attained enlightenment was the Nāga (Ironwood) tree.

The Buddha Revata was eighty (80) cubits in height, and like a celestial banner-pole, he illuminated all directions. The natural radiance from his body spread for one yojana around him, day and night.

The lifespan during the time of the Buddha Revata was sixty thousand (60,000) years, and having remained for that long (four-fifths of the lifespan), he rescued many beings—humans, devas, and brahmas—from the current of saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna.

Having manifested the power of the ten knowledges of the Buddhas and revealed the deathless Dhamma to the world, the Buddha Revata attained Parinibbāna and was extinguished like a great flame when its fuel is exhausted.

## Sense of Urgency (Saṃvega)

That physical body of the Buddha, which was like a mass of jewels, and those ten peerless qualities of the Buddha—all have ceased and vanished. Indeed, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are void and without permanent substance.

Before his Parinibbāna, the Buddha Revata made a resolve: "After I am gone, so that all beings may reach the celestial realms and Nibbāna, let my relics not remain as a single mass but be divided and scattered into many pieces." He then attained Parinibbāna in the Nāgavana garden, not far from the city. The relics of the Buddha Revata, unlike the relics of long-lived Buddhas which usually remain as a single mass, were divided into pieces according to his resolve and were distributed throughout the island of Jambudīpa, where they were worshipped by humans, devas, and brahmas.

The Chronicle of the Buddha Revata ends.

## 6. The Chronicle of the Buddha Sobhita

After the Buddha Revata attained Parinibbāna, the human lifespan gradually decreased from sixty thousand (60,000) years to ten (10) years, then increased again to an asaṅkhyeyya, and then decreased again to ninety thousand (90,000) years. At that time, the Bodhisatta of the Buddha Sobhita...
252:
...after fulfilling the perfections for four asaṅkhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons, while residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas, he accepted the request of the devas and brahmas. He descended to the human world and took conception in the womb of Queen Sudhammā, the consort of King Sudhamma of the royal city of Sudhamma. After ten months, he was born in the Sudhamma garden, emerging from his mother's womb like the full moon emerging from a bank of clouds.

(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, the great omens and wonders appeared as previously described.)

## Reigning over the Kingdom

When Prince Sobhita reached maturity, he lived in three golden palaces: (1) Kumuda, (2) Naḷina, and (3) Paduma. He enjoyed celestial-like pleasures for nine thousand (9,000) years, attended by Queen Maṇilā and thirty-seven thousand (37,000) maidens, and reigned over the kingdom.

## Renunciation

While reigning in this manner, when Queen Maṇilā gave birth to a son named Sīha, he saw the four great omens. A great sense of urgency (saṃvega) arose in him, and he became a monk within the palace itself. He practiced mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) in the palace and, upon reaching the fourth jhāna...
253:
...he practiced asceticism (dukkharacariyā) for seven days within the palace itself.

Then, on the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he would become a Buddha, he partook of the milk-rice offered by Queen Maṇilā and made a firm resolve for his renunciation:

"Let this palace where I now reside, just as it is decorated, travel through the air while the people watch, and let it descend to the ground with the Mahābodhi tree at its center. Let these palace women also, when I am near the Mahābodhi tree, depart from the palace of their own accord without me having to say anything."

As soon as the thought arose, the Bodhisatta's palace rose into the sky, which was dark blue like collyrium, from within the palace of his father, King Sudhamma. The exterior of the palace, decorated with fragrant flower garlands, was as if the whole sky were adorned. It had a beautiful radiance like the sun, or like the liquid of molten red gold, or like the pleasant moon in the autumn month of Tazaungmon (Kattika). It was exceedingly bright and beautiful. There were also various wonderful golden bell-nets hanging down. When the gentle breeze blew, the sound produced by those golden bell-nets was like the sound of five types of musical instruments played by a very skilled...
254:
...musician, being very pleasant and delightful to the heart. With the sweet and melodious sound heard from afar, making beings prick up their ears, people at their doorsteps and crossroads stood and stared in amazement and praise. Traveling through the sky not too low and not too high, just above the treetops and forest canopies, it was as if enticing the people. With the brilliance of the various jewels and the trees and branches, it attracted the eyes of all, as if proclaiming the special merit of the Bodhisatta. 

The dancers and attendants who followed in that palace also sang songs with the sweet sound of the five noble musical instruments and uttered pleasant words of praise. The Bodhisatta's fourfold army, shining with the radiance of their ornaments and bodies, was like a great celestial army decorated with various dyed and fragrant flower ornaments, a sight one could never tire of. They surrounded the palace in the sky just as they would on the ground.

The palace traveled through the air and descended to the ground, centering on the Mahābodhi Nāga (Ironwood) tree, which was eighty-eight (88) cubits high, with a straight, large, and smooth trunk, and beautiful with buds and tender shoots.
255:
The dancers and attendants, without the Great Bodhisatta having to say anything, descended from the palace and departed of their own accord.

## Attaining Buddhahood

The Bodhisatta Sobhita, adorned with many virtues, attained the three knowledges (vijjā) during the three watches of the night while surrounded by a great multitude of people. The armies of Māra came to the Buddha Sobhita as they naturally do. The palace remained in that very place.

## Three Great Dhamma Assemblies

After becoming a Buddha, the Buddha Sobhita stayed near the Mahābodhi tree for the seven weeks (sattasattāha). Accepting the request of the Brahma king to teach the Dhamma, he reflected, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He saw his half-brothers, Prince Asama and Prince Sunetta, and thought, "These two princes have the special supporting conditions (upanissaya) of past merit to attain the paths and fruits. They are capable of understanding the deep and subtle Dhamma. Well then, I shall preach the Dhamma to these two princes." Having so planned, he traveled through the air in an instant, descended into the Sudhamma garden, and sent for the two princes through the gardener. When they arrived, surrounded by the two princes and their retinue, in the midst of a vast assembly of humans, devas, and brahmas from the highest heaven to the lowest hell...

When the sermon of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta was preached, countless humans, devas, and Brahmās realized the Four Noble Truths.
(This was the first great occasion of the realization of the Dhamma [Dhammābhisamaya].)

On another occasion, near the city gate of Sudassana, by a magnificent Pāṭalī tree, the Buddha performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire. Then, while seated upon the Paṇḍukambala stone seat at the foot of the Parichattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, He preached the Abhidhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, ninety billion devas and Brahmās realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation.
(This was the second great occasion of the realization of the Dhamma [Dutiyadhammābhisamaya].)

On another occasion, in the city of Sudassana, Prince Jayasena built a great monastery measuring one league in extent. Within that monastery, he had various excellent flowering and fruiting trees, such as the Asoka and Mahālekhā, planted closely together without any gaps. He then offered that great Jayasena monastery along with the park to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. At the ceremony of the monastery's dedication, the Sobhita Buddha preached a discourse on the great offering, praising the merit of the donation. During this, one hundred billion humans, devas, and Brahmās realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation.
(This was the third great occasion of the realization of the Dhamma [Tatiyadhammābhisamaya].)

## The Prediction of the Bodhisatta Gotama as the Brahmin Sujāta

## 7. The Chronicle of Anomadassī Buddha
After the aeon (kappa) in which the Sobhita Buddha appeared had ended, and after the passing of an incalculable number of empty aeons (suñña-kappa) in which no Buddha appeared, three Buddhas—(1) Anomadassī, (2) Paduma, and (3) Nārada—appeared in a single aeon. The first to appear was the Anomadassī Buddha.

The Bodhisatta Anomadassī fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for sixteen incalculables (asaṅkheyya) and one hundred thousand aeons. At the end of that period, while residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas, He accepted the request of the devas and Brahmās to become a Buddha. He descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of Queen Yasodharā, the Chief Queen of King Yasavā in the royal city of Candavatī.
262:
364
One unique feature was that as soon as the Prince Anomadassī entered the lotus-like womb of Queen Yasodharā, due to the power of the Bodhisatta's merit, a light shone and spread within a radius of eighty cubits, such that even the light of the sun and moon could not surpass it.

When ten months had passed, Queen Yasodharā gave birth to the Bodhisatta Prince Anomadassī in the Sucandana garden.
(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonders appeared as previously described.)

On the day of the naming ceremony, the wise men who were to give the name said: "Because many jewels fell from the sky like rain when the Bodhisatta was conceived, and because He is the cause for the appearance of peerless (anoma) treasures, let the Prince be named Anomadassī."

## Reigning over the Kingdom
When the Bodhisatta Prince Anomadassī reached maturity, He lived in three golden palaces: (1) Sirī, (2) Upasirī, and (3) Vaḍḍha. He enjoyed royal splendor comparable to divine bliss for ten thousand (10,000) years, being entertained and served by Queen Sirimā and twenty-three thousand (23,000) attendants.

365
## Renunciation
While He was thus reigning, when Queen Sirimā gave birth to a son named Upavāṇa, the Bodhisatta Prince Anomadassī saw the four great omens and renounced the world, departing on a golden palanquin to become a monk. When the Prince became a monk, three crores of men followed His example and also became monks. Surrounded by those three crore monks, the Bodhisatta practiced austerities (dukkharacariyā) with great effort for ten months.

## Attaining Buddhahood
After practicing austerities for ten months, on the full-moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day He was to become a Buddha, He entered the Brahmin village of Anupama for alms. He partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of a wealthy merchant named Anopamā. He spent the day in a Sal grove in that area. When evening came, He left the accompanying monks and proceeded alone to the site of the Mahābodhi. On the way, He accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by an ascetic (takkatuṃ) named Anoma. As soon as He spread the grass at the foot of the Ajjuna (Terminalia arjuna) tree, an Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita Pallanka) thirty-eight (38) cubits in size appeared. Sitting cross-legged upon that throne, He resolved with fourfold effort, defeated the army of Māra as previously described, and attained the state of a Sammāsambuddha, the Knower of All (Sabbaññū), the Supreme One of the Three Worlds.
264:
The Blessed One Anomadassī, having severed the ten long-reaching fetters (saṃyojana) that bind one to the cycle of rebirth, and having destroyed the kammas that cause wandering through the three realms of existence with the Path-knowledge (Magga-ñāṇa) known as the destruction of kamma (kammakkhaya), was able to preach the Eightfold Noble Path, the excellent way to reach Nibbāna, to the Indagū (beings) among Brahmas, devas, and humans.

That Blessed One Anomadassī was endowed with virtues that others could not disturb or shake, like the great ocean. He was endowed with virtues that made him difficult to approach by ordinary persons, like Mount Meru. He was endowed with infinite virtues, like the great sky. He was also graceful with the major and minor marks, like a Sal tree in full bloom.

Beings felt peaceful and joyful by beholding the Blessed One Anomadassī. Upon hearing the sound of the Dhamma he taught, they reached Nibbāna, the state free from death.

## Three Great Assemblies of Dhamma

After becoming a Buddha, the Blessed One Anomadassī stayed near the Mahābodhi tree for the seven-week period (forty-nine days). Having accepted the request of the Great Brahma to preach the Dhamma, he looked with the Buddha-eye, namely the knowledge of the inclinations and latent tendencies of beings (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of the degrees of maturity of the faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa).
265: While surveying the world, He saw three crores of monks who had renounced the world together with Him and were endowed with past merits for attaining the Path and Fruition. Thinking, "Where are they living now?", He saw them residing in the Sudassana Grove near the city of Subhavatī. He traveled through the air and descended into the Sudassana Grove. Surrounded by those three crores of monks and in the midst of an assembly of Devas and humans, He preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. In that great assembly, beings to the extent of one hundred crores realized the Four Noble Truths and were liberated. (This was the first great assembly of the Dhamma (Dhammābhisamaya).) Later, on another occasion, near the city of Osadhi, He performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire near a great Asana tree. Then, at the foot of the Parichattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, He sat on the Paṇḍukambala stone and rained down the golden rain of Abhidhamma teachings for the three months of the rainy season. At that time, eighty crores of Devas and Brahmas realized the Four Noble Truths and were liberated. (This was the second great assembly of the Dhamma (Dutiyadhammābhisamaya).) Later, on another occasion, in a great assembly where He analyzed and answered the questions of the Maṅgala-pucchā, seventy-eight crores of beings realized the Four Noble Truths and were liberated. ## The Prediction of the Bodhisatta Gotama as a Yakkha General

At the time when the Blessed One Anomadassī appeared, our Bodhisatta was a Yakkha General who ruled over many millions of Yakkhas with great power and majesty.

Inside that jewelled pavilion, he offered a great donation, including alms-food and drinks, for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.

At that time, while the Blessed One Anomadassī was delivering the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) concerning the alms-food to the Bodhisatta Yakkha General, he gave the prediction: "In the future, one asankheyya and a hundred thousand aeons from this world-cycle, this Yakkha General will surely become a Buddha named Gotama."

(The manner of giving the prediction is exactly as detailed as the prediction given by the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara.)

Upon hearing the words of prediction from the Blessed One Anomadassī, the Bodhisatta, with a heart full of extreme joy and awe, made an effort to further fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

## Details of the City, etc.

The birthplace of the Blessed One Anomadassī was the city of Candavatī; his father was King Yasavā, and his mother was Queen Yasodharā.

He reigned for ten thousand (10,000) years, and his three palaces were Siri, Upasiri, and Vaḍḍha.
268: The Chief Consort was Queen Sirimā, who had twenty-three thousand attendants. His son was Prince Upavāṇa. The vehicle He used to renounce the world after seeing the four great omens was a golden palanquin. He practiced austere practices (dukkharacariyā) for ten months. His pair of Chief Disciples were the Elder Nisabha and the Elder Anoma. His attendant was the Elder Varuṇa. His pair of Chief Female Disciples were the Nun Sundarī and the Nun Sumanā. The Bodhi tree under which He attained enlightenment was the Ajjuna (Thauk-kyan) tree. His noble male lay supporters were the wealthy merchant Nandivaḍḍha and the wealthy merchant Sirivaḍḍha. His noble female lay supporters were the laywoman Uppalā and the laywoman Padumā. The height of Anomadassī Buddha was fifty-eight (58) cubits. His radiance, like the rising sun, spread around for twelve yojanas. The lifespan during which Anomadassī Buddha appeared was one hundred thousand (100,000) years. He remained for that long (four-fifths of the lifespan), rescuing and saving the multitude of beings, including humans, Devas, and Brahmas, from the current of the cycle of rebirth to the dry land of Nibbāna. The dispensation of Anomadassī Buddha, consisting of the noble words of Dhamma, flourished and was beautiful with the Arahants who were unshakeable by the worldly conditions (tādi-guṇa),
269:
The world was then brightened and graced by the noble Arahants who were free from passion (rāga) and the impurities of mental defilements (kilesa).

## Samvega

That Blessed One Anomadassī, who was endowed with incomparable retinue and fame, and his pair of chief disciples, etc., who were endowed with matchless virtues—all of them have ceased and vanished. Indeed, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are without permanent substance and are merely empty.

## The Cetiya

The Blessed One Anomadassī, who had conquered the five Maras, attained Parinibbāna within the great monastery called Dhammārāma. The great Cetiya of the Blessed One Anomadassī, built within that monastery, was twenty-five yojanas high.

(It was in the presence of this Blessed One Anomadassī that the Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna made their aspiration to become chief disciples. This matter will become clear in the chapter on the Gotama Buddhavaṃsa above.)

The Chronicle of Anomadassī Buddha ends.
