## 8. Paduma Buddhavaṃsa

After the Blessed One Anomadassī attained Parinibbāna, the human lifespan gradually decreased from one hundred thousand (100,000) years to ten (10) years, then increased again to an asankheyya, and then...
270:
decreased again. When the human lifespan reached one hundred thousand (100,000) years, the Bodhisatta Paduma, having completed the fulfillment of the perfections, was dwelling in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the assembly of devas and Brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and took conception in the womb of Queen Asamā, the consort of King Asama of the royal city of Campaka. After ten months had passed, he was born in the Campaka Garden.

(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, the great omens and wonders appeared as previously described.)

When the Bodhisatta Prince was born, a heavy rain of Paduma lotuses fell from the sky throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa, as far as the ocean. Therefore, on the day of naming the Bodhisatta Prince, the wise omen-readers and all the relatives named him Prince Mahāpaduma.

## Reigning

When the Bodhisatta Prince Mahāpaduma reached maturity, he resided in the three golden palaces: (1) Nanduttara, (2) Vasuttara, and (3) Yasuttara. He was entertained and attended to by thirty-three thousand (33,000) female attendants, headed by Queen Uttarādevī. He enjoyed royal bliss similar to celestial pleasure for ten thousand (10,000) years and reigned over the kingdom.
271:
## Renunciation

While reigning in this manner, when Queen Uttarādevī gave birth to a son named Ramma, he saw the four great omens and renounced the world to become a monk, riding a chariot drawn by noble horses and adorned with celestial ornaments. Following the example of the Bodhisatta Prince's renunciation, ten million men also became monks. The Bodhisatta Paduma, together with the ten million monks, practiced asceticism (dukkharacariyā) with great effort for eight months.

## Attaining Buddhahood

After practicing asceticism for eight months, on the full moon day of Kason, the day he was to become a Buddha, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of the wealthy merchant Sudhanyavatī, named Dhanyavatī, a resident of the city of Dhanyavatī. He rested during the day in the Sal grove in that area. When evening came, he left his retinue of monks and proceeded alone to the site of the Mahābodhi tree. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a person named Titthaka. As soon as he spread the grass at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree (a Sona tree), the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita Pallaṅka) measuring thirty-eight (38) cubits appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that throne, he resolved with fourfold effort (vīriya). As previously described, he drove away the army of Mara and attained the state of the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Knower of All (Sabbaññū).
272:
## The Three Great Assemblies of Teaching

After attaining Buddhahood, the Buddha Paduma stayed for the seven-week period (forty-nine days) near the Mahābodhi tree (the Mahā-soṇa tree). Having accepted the invitation of the Great Brahmā to teach the Dhamma, he reflected, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He saw that the ten million monks who had ordained together with him were endowed with the past merits necessary to attain the Paths and Fruits. He thought, "I shall preach to them first." Then, reflecting on where those monks were currently residing, he saw that they were in the Dhananjaya Garden near the city of Dhanyavatī. Taking his bowl and robes, he traveled through the air in an instant to the Dhananjaya Garden where those monks resided.

At that time, the ten million monks saw the Buddha Paduma coming from afar. With hearts full of great devotion, they went out to welcome the Buddha, took his bowl and robes, prepared his seat, and performed the duties of respectful salutation. They then sat in suitable places surrounding the Buddha. Then, the Buddha Paduma, surrounded by the ten million monks who were his former companions in ordination, preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta—the discourse which all previous Buddhas had preached—in the midst of the assembly of humans, devas, and brahmās. At that time, one hundred crores of humans, devas, and brahmās attained the extraordinary Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits.

(This was the first great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma, the First Dhamma-abhisamaya.)
273:
Later, on another occasion, the Buddha Paduma, at a gathering of his relatives, caused his younger brothers, Prince Sāla and Prince Upasāla (the future Chief Disciples), along with their retinues, to be ordained. While he was preaching the Dhamma, ninety crores of devas and humans attained the extraordinary Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits.

(This was the second great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma, the Second Dhamma-abhisamaya.)

Later, on another occasion, the Buddha Paduma preached a discourse of instruction to his son, the Venerable Ramma. At that time, eighty crores of humans, devas, and brahmās realized the Four Noble Truths and were liberated.

(This was the third great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma, the Third Dhamma-abhisamaya.)

**********

## The Three Great Assemblies of Disciples

## The First Sannipāta

There were three great assemblies of disciples of the Buddha Paduma. In the first instance, a king named Subhāvitatta, along with a retinue of one hundred thousand, received ordination as 'Ehi Bhikkhu' in the presence of the Buddha Paduma. In that assembly, the Buddha Paduma recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.

(This was the first great assembly of disciples.)

## The Second Sannipāta

Later, on another occasion, the Buddha Paduma entered the Rains Retreat (vassa) depending on the city of Usabhavatī as his alms-resort. At that time,
274:
the Buddha Paduma preached the Dhamma to the multitude of city dwellers who came to pay homage to him. Many people in that city developed faith and were ordained as monks. Then, on the full moon day of Thadingyut (the Pavāraṇā day), the Buddha Paduma performed the Visuddhi-pavāraṇā together with the monks who had ordained from Usabhavatī and other monks, totaling three hundred thousand Arahants. (Visuddhi-pavāraṇā refers to the Pavāraṇā ceremony performed exclusively by Arahants.)

(This was the second great assembly of disciples.)

## The Third Sannipāta

The lay devotees who remained in that city without ordaining, having heard the discourse on the benefits of Kathina, offered Kathina robes. When they requested the Right-hand Chief Disciple, the Venerable Sāla, who held the title of Dhamma-senāpati (General of the Dhamma), to perform the Kathina ceremony, the Sangha bestowed the robe upon him through the formal act of Natti-kammavācā. Many monks then joined together to sew the robe so that it would be finished within a single day. As it was a communal task of the Sangha, the Buddha himself assisted by threading the needle where the monks were sewing the robes. When the sewing of the Kathina robes was completed, the Buddha Paduma set out on a journey together with the three hundred thousand monks. Later, on another occasion, the Buddha Paduma entered the Rains Retreat within a great forest similar to the Gosinga Sal forest. The people, after seeing the Buddha and his retinue residing in that forest and hearing the Dhamma, were filled with faith and devotion. When the Buddha called them with the words 'Ehi Bhikkhu',
275:
they became monks through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination. At that time, surrounded by two hundred thousand monks, the Buddha performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony.

(This was the third great assembly of disciples.)

(The accounts of the Second and Third Sannipātas are written according to the explanations in the Commentary. According to the current Pali text, the assembly of three hundred thousand Arahants who gathered to sew the Kathina robe for the Right-hand Chief Disciple, the Venerable Sāla, seems to be regarded as the Second Sannipāta. Although aware of this implication, the Commentator wrote and explained it differently from the Pali text, likely because he relied on the explanations of ancient teachers who knew the Buddha's intention, and because only assemblies for Pavāraṇā or the recitation of Ovāda Pātimokkha are mentioned as assemblies of disciples in the chronicles of previous Buddhas. Therefore, this book presents the account according to the Commentary's explanation.)

**********

## The Bodhisatta as a Lion King Receiving the Prophecy

While the Buddha Paduma was residing in that forest, our Bodhisatta was a lion king. Upon seeing the Buddha Paduma, who had entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) for seven days, he was filled with great devotion. He paid homage, circumambulated the Buddha clockwise, and being exceedingly joyful, roared three times.
276:
For seven days, without abandoning the rapture (pīti) centered on the Buddha, he did not go out to search for food. Sacrificing his very life, he remained respectfully attending to the Buddha. 

Then, after seven days, the Buddha emerged from the attainment of cessation. Seeing the lion king, he thought, "May this lion king also develop devotion toward the Sangha of monks." He then resolved, "Let the Sangha of monks come to this place." Immediately, many crores of monks arrived at that spot. The Bodhisatta lion king also developed a heart of devotion toward the Sangha. At that time, the Buddha Paduma, knowing the mind of the lion king, proclaimed the prophecy: "In the future, this lion king will surely become a Buddha named Gotama."

(The manner of receiving the prophecy is exactly the same as that received from the Buddha Dīpaṅkara.)

Upon hearing the prophecy of the Buddha Paduma, the Bodhisatta lion king purified his mind even further and firmly resolved to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs) to a higher degree.

## Details of the City, etc.

The birthplace of the Buddha Paduma was the city of Campaka. His father was King Asama, and his mother was Queen Asamā.

He reigned for ten thousand (10,000) years. His three palaces were the Nanduttara Palace,
277:
the Vasuttara Palace, and the Yasuttara Palace.

His Chief Queen was Uttarā, who had thirty-three thousand (33,000) female attendants. His son was Prince Ramma.

After seeing the four great omens, the vehicle in which he renounced the world was a chariot drawn by noble horses. He practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for eight months.

His pair of Chief Disciples were the Venerable Sāla and the Venerable Upasāla. His personal attendant was the Venerable Varuṇa.

His pair of Chief Female Disciples were the Venerable Rādhā and the Venerable Surādhā. The Bodhi tree under which he attained enlightenment was the Mahā-soṇa (Kyon-sha-gyi) tree.

His noble male lay supporters were the wealthy merchant Bhiyya and the wealthy merchant Asama. His noble female lay supporters were the lay devotees Ruci and Nandarāmā.

The height of the Buddha Paduma was fifty-eight (58) cubits. The rays emitted from his body radiated in all directions, moving and shimmering here and there according to his will.

The light of the moon, the sun, jewels, fire, and rubies would vanish when they encountered the radiance of the Buddha's body.
278:
The lifespan during the time of the Buddha Paduma was one hundred thousand (100,000) years. He remained for that long (four-fifths of the lifespan), rescuing and delivering many humans, devas, and brahmās from the current of saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna.

He enabled those with mature faculties to realize the Four Noble Truths during his lifetime without exception. To the remaining humans, devas, and brahmās, he preached the Dhamma of instruction so that they might realize the Four Noble Truths later. Then, the Buddha Paduma, along with many Arahant disciples, entered Parinibbāna and passed away.

Just as a serpent in the world sheds its old skin, or a tree sheds its old leaves, or a brilliantly shining fire is extinguished when its fuel is exhausted, the Buddha Paduma abandoned all internal and external conditioned things (saṅkhāra) and attained peaceful cessation.

In this manner, the Buddha Paduma, the conqueror of the five Maras, attained Parinibbāna within the great monastery named Dhammārāma. As he had resolved, his relics were distributed into many fragments and remained spread throughout the island of Jambudīpa, receiving the worship of humans, devas, and brahmās.

Here ends the Chronicle of Paduma Buddha.

## 9. Nārada Buddhavaṃsa

After the Blessed One Paduma attained Parinibbāna, the human lifespan gradually decreased from one hundred thousand (100,000) years to ten (10) years, then increased again to an asankheyya, and then decreased again. When the lifespan reached ninety thousand (90,000) years, the Bodhisatta Nārada, having fulfilled the perfections for four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons, was dwelling in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the assembly of devas and Brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and took conception in the womb of Queen Anomā, the consort of King Sudeva of the royal city of Dhanyavatī. After ten months had passed, he was born in the Dhanañjaya Garden.

(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, the great omens and wonders appeared as previously described.)

On the day the Bodhisatta Prince was to be named, just as the naming was about to take place, various kinds of clothing and ornaments suitable for human use fell spontaneously from the sky, like a heavy rain, from celestial wishing-trees (padesā-trees) throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. Therefore, the wise men who were to name him gave him the name Prince Nārada, based on the meaning: Nāra = suitable for humans, Da = one who gives.

## Reigning

When the Bodhisatta Prince Nārada reached maturity, he resided in the golden palaces: (1) Jita, (2) Vijita...
280: 382  (3) In the three golden palaces, such as the Abhirāma palace, he enjoyed royal bliss similar to celestial pleasure for nine thousand (9,000) years, being entertained and served by a retinue of one hundred and twenty thousand (120,000) court ladies, headed by Queen Vijitasenā.  ## Renunciation  While reigning in this manner, when Queen Vijitasenā gave birth to a son named Nanduttara, the Bodhisatta saw the four great omens. Surrounded by the fourfold army and adorned with various garments, ornaments, perfumes, and flowers, he went on foot to the auspicious garden. There, he removed his ornaments and handed them to the royal treasurer. He then cut his hair himself with his royal sword and threw it into the sky.  Sakka, the king of gods, received the hair in a golden casket and enshrined it in a great pagoda (cetiya) three leagues high, made of the seven kinds of gems, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven (on the summit of Mount Meru). The Bodhisatta prince put on the robes offered by a Brahmā and became a monk within that very auspicious garden. Following the example of the Bodhisatta prince, one hundred thousand men also became monks.  (One point to be specially noted here is that for Bodhisattas other than the Bodhisatta of Nārada Buddha, they saw the four great omens while wandering for pleasure within the auspicious garden. Having seen them...)
281: 383  ...and having gained a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), they did not renounce the world in the same garden where they usually wandered, but went to distant forests and mountains to renounce. Thus, for those Bodhisattas, the place where they saw the four great omens and the place where they renounced were different. Because of the long distance, they renounced by riding vehicles such as elephants, horses, or chariots.  However, for the Bodhisatta Prince Nārada, it should be noted that he saw the four great omens in the auspicious garden, gained spiritual urgency, and renounced in this very same garden. In the commentary, that garden is explained as the Dhananjaya Garden outside the city.  ## Attaining Buddhahood  The Bodhisatta of Nārada Buddha practiced asceticism (dukkara-cariyā) for seven days within that same auspicious garden. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become Buddha, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by Queen Vijitasenā. He spent the day in that same garden, and when evening came, he left his retinue of monks and went alone to the site of the Bodhi tree. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a gardener named Sudassana. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Mahābodhi Sona (Great Trumpet-flower) tree, the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka) measuring fifty-seven (57) cubits appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that throne and resolving with fourfold energy, he blew away and dispelled the army of Māra as previously described, and attained the state of a Fully Enlightened Buddha, the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Possessor of Omniscient Wisdom.

(The description of the Mahābodhi tree, the Great Trumpet Flower tree (Red Trumpet Flower tree), where Narada Buddha attained enlightenment, is explained in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary: "That Red Trumpet Flower tree is ninety cubits high, with a smooth and even trunk. It has various complete branches and twigs, with lush, thick, and expansive green leaves. It provides dense and cool shade. Because it is guarded by tree deities, no birds of any kind can fly or dwell in the Bodhi tree; it stands on the ground like a collyrium-stick, acting as the king of trees, extremely delightful and beautiful to behold, with all its branches adorned with crimson flowers. Thus, it is like a Rasāyana elixir of longevity to the eyes of gods and humans.")
## Three Great Assemblies of Dhamma
After attaining Buddhahood, Narada Buddha stayed near the Mahābodhi (Great Trumpet Flower) tree for the Satta-sattāha (forty-nine days). Accepting the request of the Great Brahma to teach the Dhamma, He reflected, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He saw that the one hundred thousand monks who had renounced the world together with Him were endowed with past merits for attaining the Path and Fruit. Deciding, "I shall preach to them first," He reflected again, "Where are those monks residing now?" Seeing that they were in the Dhanañjaya Garden, He took His bowl and robes and traveled through the air in an instant to the Dhanañjaya Garden where those monks were.
At that time, the one hundred thousand monks saw Narada Buddha coming from afar and, with hearts full of devotion, went out to welcome the Buddha and [take] His bowl and robes...
283: 385 (This was the first great assembly of Dhamma realization.) Later, at another time, a Naga king named Doṇa ruled on the banks of the Ganges River near the city of Mahādoṇa. He possessed great psychic power and majesty. He was revered and worshipped by the people. If the people living in that area did not make offerings and pay respect to the Naga king, he would cause destruction to their dwellings by either preventing rain entirely, causing excessive rain, or causing hailstorms. At that time, Nārada Buddha, who had seen the other shore of Nibbāna, perceived that if he personally went to discipline the Naga king Doṇa, many people who were endowed with past merits would certainly attain the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna. Thus, surrounded by many monks, he proceeded to the dwelling place of the Naga king. When the people saw the Buddha, they pleaded, "O Blessed Buddha of great glory, a fierce, venomous, and powerful Naga king rules and causes trouble in this place. Please do not proceed here, lest you be harmed by that Naga king." The Buddha, as if he did not hear their words,
284: 386 continued to proceed and sat upon the flower seat that had been prepared for the Naga king to be worshipped. The people gathered, thinking, "We shall now witness the battle between the Buddha, the King of Monks, and the Naga king Doṇa." When the Naga king saw the Buddha sitting on the flower seat prepared for himself, he could not restrain his anger and, manifesting himself, emitted smoke. The Buddha also emitted smoke through his psychic power. When the Naga king emitted flames, the Buddha also emitted flames through his psychic power. The Naga king became greatly exhausted by the smoke and flames emanating from the Buddha's body. Unable to bear the suffering, he thought, "I shall kill this monk with the force of my poison," and released his Naga poison. Although the poison released by the Naga was powerful enough to destroy the entire island of Jambudīpa, it was unable to ruffle even a single hair on the Buddha's body. Then the Naga king looked, wondering, "What is happening to this great monk?" and "What is the state of this great monk?" He saw the Buddha with a serene and radiant face, shining with the six-colored rays like the sun in the autumn month of Tazaungmon (Kattika) or like the full moon. He then thought, "This great monk is indeed of great power. Due to not knowing my own strength, I have committed an offense against him," and he took refuge in the Buddha. Then, Nārada Buddha, having disciplined the Naga king Doṇa, [addressed] the minds of the people gathered there...

To inspire faith, He performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire and preached the Dhamma. At that time, ninety crores of devas and humans were established in the Fruit of Arahantship.

## The Three Great Assemblies of Disciples
## The First Assembly
There were three great assemblies of the disciples of the Buddha Nārada. On the first occasion, in the city of Thullakoṭṭhita, two young brahmins named Bhaddasāla and Vijitamitta, who were destined to be the chief disciples, were searching for the great lake of the Deathless Dhamma when they saw the Buddha Nārada sitting boldly in the midst of the assembly. Seeing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the Buddha's body, they decided, "This person is indeed a Buddha who has opened and removed the roof of defilements in the world." Faith arose in them toward the Buddha, and they, along with their retinue, were ordained in the presence of the Buddha. When they reached the Fruit of Arahantship, the Buddha recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the midst of one hundred thousand crores of monks.
(This was the first great assembly of disciples.)

## The Second Assembly
Thereafter, on another occasion, the Buddha Nārada preached the Buddhavaṃsa discourse, starting from the time He made the aspiration for Buddhahood, along with the Nidāna, in the assembly of His relatives. At that time, ninety crores of Arahants gathered together.
(This was the second great assembly of disciples.)

## The Third Assembly
Thereafter, on another occasion, while He was admonishing the Naga king Mahādoṇa, a Naga king named Verocana, who had great faith, created a great gem pavilion measuring three gāvutas near the banks of the Ganges River. He invited the Buddha, along with the Saṅgha, to reside within that gem pavilion. He also invited the people of the countryside to come and see his pavilion of offering. He arranged a grand festival of worship with many Naga dancers in various forms and costumes, playing music, dancing, and singing, and offered a great donation to the Buddha Nārada and the Saṅgha.

When the meal was finished, the Buddha preached the discourse of appreciation (Anumodanā). Upon hearing the discourse, the people were so inspired with faith that they requested ordination from the Buddha. The Buddha then ordained them by saying, "Ehi Bhikkhu." At that time, in the midst of eight million Ehi Bhikkhu monks, the Buddha recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.
(This was the third great assembly of disciples.) **********

## The Bodhisatta as an Ascetic with Supernormal Powers Receiving the Prophecy
At that time, our Bodhisatta was an ascetic who had established a hermitage on the slopes of the Himalayas and lived there, having mastered the five supernormal powers (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti). Out of compassion for the noble ascetic Bodhisatta, the Buddha Nārada, surrounded by eighty crores of Arahants and ten thousand Anāgāmī lay followers, visited the Bodhisatta's hermitage.

The noble ascetic Bodhisatta, having the opportunity to behold the Buddha, was filled with joy. He created a hermitage for the Buddha and His retinue to reside in. Having invited the Buddha and His retinue to stay there, he spent the entire night praising the collection of the Buddha's virtues and listening to the Buddha's Dhamma. The next morning, he went to Uttarakuru (by supernormal power) and brought back food and other offerings, and he gave a great meal offering to the Buddha, the Saṅgha, and the lay followers.

In this manner, after giving great meal offerings for seven days, he brought red sandalwood of great value from the Himalayas and offered it in worship to the Buddha. Then, the Buddha Nārada, after preaching a discourse to the noble ascetic,

proclaimed the prophecy: "In the future, he will surely become a Buddha named Gotama."

Upon hearing the prophecy of the Buddha Nārada, the noble ascetic Bodhisatta gladdened his heart exceedingly and firmly resolved to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs) even further.

The birthplace of the Buddha Nārada was the city of Dhanyavatī. His father was King Sudeva, a Cakkavatti, and His mother was Queen Anomā.

He reigned for nine thousand (9,000) years, and His three palaces were Jita, Vijita, and Abhirāma.

His Chief Queen was Vijitasenā, who had forty-three thousand attendants, and His son was Prince Nanduttara.

Having seen the four great omens, He renounced the world on foot without using a vehicle and practiced austerities (dukkharacariyā) for seven days.

His pair of Chief Disciples were the Elder Bhaddasāla and the Elder Vijitamitta, and His attendant was the Elder Vāseṭṭha.

His pair of Chief Female Disciples were the Nun Uttarā and the Nun Phagguṇī. The Bodhi tree under which He attained enlightenment was the Mahāsoṇa (Trumpet flower) tree.

The Buddha Nārada was eighty-eight (88) cubits tall, appearing as majestic as a great golden pillar prepared for worship, gracing the ten thousand world-systems of the birth-field. all the Buddha-duties He had to perform, the Buddha Nārada, along with many Arahant disciples, entered Parinibbāna and ceased, ending the cycle of existence.

## Spiritual Urgency (Saṃvega)
That Buddha Nārada, who was equal only to the peerless Buddhas, and those noble Arahants, who were endowed with peerless power and majesty—all of them have ceased and vanished. Indeed, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are without stable essence and are only empty.

## The Stupa
Thus, the Buddha Nārada, the Conqueror of the five Maras, attained Parinibbāna in the city of Sudassana. In that very city, the great Stupa of the Buddha Nārada was built (as mentioned before), standing four yojanas high.

## 10. The Chronicle of the Buddha Padumuttara
(According to the verse: "One in Sāra, two in Maṇḍa, only three in Vara. Four are shown in Sāramaṇḍa, five in Bhadda. If not even one Buddha arises, it is a Suñña-kappa.")
An aeon (kappa) in which only one Buddha arises is called a Sāra-kappa. An aeon in which two Buddhas arise is called a Maṇḍa-kappa. An aeon in which three Buddhas arise is called a
291:
393
Vara-kappa. An aeon in which four Buddhas arise is called a Sāramaṇḍa-kappa. An aeon in which five Buddhas arise is called a Bhadda-kappa. An aeon in which not even one Buddha arises is called a Suñña-kappa. Among these types of aeons, the aeon in which the three Buddhas Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada arose is called a "Vara-kappa.")

Thus, after the end of the great Vara-kappa in which the three Buddhas Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada arose, and after the passing of many Suñña-kappas (one Asaṅkheyya) that cannot be counted in numbers, one hundred thousand aeons ago from this present aeon, the Buddha Padumuttara arose.

(Although that aeon was a Sāra-kappa because only the Buddha Padumuttara arose, it was like a Maṇḍa-kappa because it was endowed with special delightful qualities. In the aeon when the Buddha Padumuttara arose, only people with great merit and power were born.)

As for the account of the Buddha Padumuttara's arising: At the end of fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), the Bodhisatta Padumuttara was residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and Brahmas to become a Buddha, He descended to the human world into the womb of Queen Sujātā, the consort of King Ānanda of the capital city Haṃsavatī.
292:
394
He was conceived in the womb and, upon the completion of ten months, was born in the Maṅgala Garden in the city of Haṃsavatī.
(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonderful marvels appeared clearly.)
Because a rain of paduma lotuses fell when Prince Padumuttara was born, his relatives named him Prince Padumuttara at the naming ceremony.

## Sovereignty and Reign
When the Bodhisatta Prince Padumuttara reached maturity, he resided in three golden palaces: (1) Naravāhana, (2) Yasavāhana, and (3) Vasavattī. He enjoyed divine-like luxury for ten thousand (10,000) years, attended and entertained by one hundred and twenty thousand ladies-in-waiting, headed by Queen Vasudattā.

## The Great Renunciation
While reigning in this manner, when Queen Vasudattā gave birth to a son named Uttara, the Bodhisatta saw the four great omens. As soon as he resolved, "I shall perform the noble act of renunciation," the Vasavattī golden palace spun like a potter's wheel and ascended into the sky. Like a great celestial mansion or the full moon, it moved through the firmament and descended to the earth, centering itself at the Mahābodhi tree.
293:
395
The Bodhisatta prince descended from the palace and, donning the lotus robes offered by Brahmā, entered the monkhood at that very spot. The palace then returned to the kingdom and settled in its original location. Among the followers who accompanied the Bodhisatta, all the men, excluding the women, became monks.

## Attaining Buddhahood
The Bodhisatta Padumuttara, together with those fellow monks, practiced austerities (dukkharacariyā) for seven days. On the day of his enlightenment, the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of a wealthy man named Rucānandā in the market town of Ujjenī. After spending the day in the Sal forest, he went alone toward the Bodhi tree in the evening. He accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by an ascetic named Sumitta. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Mahābodhi (Salala/Pine) tree, the Unconquered Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka) measuring thirty-eight (38) cubits appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that throne and resolving with fourfold energy, he drove away the hosts of Māra as previously described. In the first watch of the night, he attained the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa); in the second watch, the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa); and in the third watch, he contemplated the law of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Then, rising from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), he applied the three characteristics to the five aggregates. Through the power of the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), he clearly perceived the fifty aspects and developed insight (vipassanā) up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). Finally, through the Noble Path (ariya-magga), he realized all the qualities of a Buddha.
294:
396
(This refers to the time after becoming a Buddha.) He uttered the solemn utterance (udāna) common to all Buddhas, starting with "Aneka-jāti saṃsāraṃ..." and ending with "taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā."

As soon as he became a Buddha, a rain of paduma lotuses fell throughout the ten thousand world systems, as if decorating everything.

Special Note:
After becoming a Buddha, the Blessed One Padumuttara remained on the Bodhi throne for seven days (the first seven-day period), enjoying the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). On the eighth day, as he moved his right foot toward the ground to step on it, extraordinary paduma lotuses, which normally grow in water, burst through the great earth and appeared under his feet.

Each petal of those paduma lotuses was nine cubits long; the stalk where the pollen rests was thirty cubits; the pericarp (the seed vessel) was twelve cubits; and each flower contained pollen equivalent to about nine water pots.

The Blessed One Padumuttara was fifty-eight (58) cubits in height. The span between his shoulders was eighteen cubits; his forehead was five cubits; and his hands and feet were eleven cubits each.

When the Blessed One, with his eleven-cubit feet, stepped upon the twelve-cubit pericarp—

As soon as he stepped, the pollen, equivalent to nine water pots, flew upward and covered his fifty-eight-cubit body, spreading over him like a sprinkling of red arsenic or orpiment powder. Based on this extraordinary event, the Buddha became renowned as the Blessed One Padumuttara.
(This is the tradition of the reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.)

## Three Great Assemblies of Dhamma
After becoming a Buddha, the Blessed One Padumuttara stayed near the Mahābodhi (Salala) tree for the seven seven-day periods (forty-nine days). Accepting the request of the Great Brahmā to preach the Dhamma, he reflected, "To whom should I preach first?" He saw Prince Devala and Prince Sujāta (the future chief disciples), who were endowed with past merits to attain the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna. Deciding to preach to them first, he reflected on their current location and saw they were in the city of Mithilā. Taking his bowl and robes, he traveled through the air in an instant to the garden of the city of Mithilā where the princes resided.

At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara sent the gardener to summon the two princes. The two princes discussed among themselves, "Prince Padumuttara, the son of our aunt, has attained Buddhahood and has arrived at our city of Mithilā. Let us now approach to pay our respects to the Blessed One."

Accompanied by their retinue, they approached the Blessed One Padumuttara, surrounded him, and sat in a suitable place.

Then, the Blessed One Padumuttara, appearing exceedingly majestic while surrounded by the princes like the full moon surrounded by stars, preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta—the discourse traditionally preached by all previous Buddhas—to the two princes and the devas and humans who had gathered to hear the Dhamma. At that time, one hundred billion (one hundred thousand koṭis) devas and humans attained the special realization of the Paths and Fruits.
(This was the first great assembly of the realization of Dhamma.)

Later, on another occasion, before the appearance of the Buddha Padumuttara, an ascetic named Sarada had gathered a multitude of followers of his own doctrine and was preaching teachings that lead to the lower realms. The Blessed One Padumuttara went to Sarada's assembly and preached the Dhamma, showing the danger of falling into hell. At that time, three million seven hundred thousand (3,700,000) devas and humans, including Sarada's primary disciples, attained the special realization of the Paths and Fruits.
(This was the second great assembly of the realization of Dhamma.)

Later, on another occasion, his father, King Ānanda, sent twenty ministers along with twenty thousand men (just as King Suddhodana sent messengers to our Buddha) to the Blessed One Padumuttara, who was residing in Mithilā, to invite him to come to his city of Haṃsavatī. The ministers, with their twenty thousand (20,000) attendants—

Surrounded by that assembly of monks, the Buddha traveled to the city of Haṃsavatī. Wishing to show favor and support to his father the King, he resided in that city.

At that time, just as our Buddha of the Gotama lineage traveled to the royal city of Kapilavatthu and preached the Buddhavaṃsa discourse in the assembly of his relatives, the Blessed One Padumuttara likewise preached the Buddhavaṃsa discourse while walking on a jeweled walkway in the sky before the assembly of his relatives. At that time, five million (5,000,000) devas and humans attained the special realization of the Paths and Fruits.
(This was the third great assembly of the realization of Dhamma.)

There were also three great assemblies of the disciples of the Blessed One Padumuttara. In the first instance, the Blessed One Padumuttara recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in an assembly of one hundred billion (one hundred thousand koṭis) monks on the full moon day of Tabodwe (Māgha) in a large garden also named Mithilā, near the city of Mithilā.
(This was the first great assembly of disciples.)

(This was the second great assembly of disciples.)

Later, on another occasion, while the Blessed One Padumuttara, the refuge of the three worlds, was traveling on a dhammaduta mission to protect and support the multitude of people so they might be liberated from the bonds of defilements, there was a great assembly of eight hundred billion (eighty thousand koṭis) monks who had renounced their homes in various villages, towns, and provinces to become monks.

## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha as Governor Jaṭila Receiving the Prophecy
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a provincial governor (Taing-kyat-min) named Jaṭila, who possessed many billions in wealth. He offered a great donation of food, hard and soft, along with sets of robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. At the end of the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) for the meal, the Blessed One Padumuttara gave the prophecy to the Bodhisatta Governor Jaṭila, saying, "In the future, one hundred thousand aeons from now, he will surely become a Buddha named Gotama."
(The manner of receiving the prophecy was as complete as the prophecy received from the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara.)

## Special Features during the time of the Blessed Padumuttara
When the Blessed Padumuttara appeared in the world, the heretical enemies (titthiyas) were displeased and suffered greatly; their power vanished, and they faded into obscurity. Not even a few people offered them respect or alms, and they were even driven out of the country.
Then, all those heretics gathered together and approached the Buddha, saying, "O Buddha of great exertion, may Your Excellence be our refuge and reliance."
The Blessed Padumuttara, who desired the welfare of all beings and possessed great compassion, established all those heretics who came before him in the Three Refuges and the five precepts of conduct.
In this way, the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Blessed Padumuttara was free and empty of heretical enemies. It was beautiful and adorned with Arahants who possessed the five kinds of mastery (vasībhāva) and were 'Tādi' (unshakable), being unaffected by worldly conditions.

The city where the Blessed Padumuttara was born was Haṃsavatī; his father was King Ānanda, and his mother was Queen Sujātā.
He reigned for ten thousand (10,000) years, and his three palaces were Naravāhana, Yasavāhana, and Vasavattī.
His Chief Queen was Vasudattā, who had forty-three thousand (43,000) attendants, and his son was Prince Uttara.

The vehicle in which he renounced the world after seeing the four great omens was a palace-vehicle (pāsāda), and he practiced austere practices (dukkharacariya) for seven days.
His pair of Chief Disciples were the Elder Devala and the Elder Sujāta, and his attendant was the Elder Sumana.
His pair of Chief Female Disciples were the Nun Amitā and the Nun Asamā, and his Bodhi tree was the Salala (Pine) tree.
His noble male lay attendants were the wealthy merchant Vitiṇṇa and the wealthy merchant Tissa, and his noble female lay attendants were...

The lifespan during the time of the Blessed Padumuttara was one hundred thousand (100,000) years, and he remained for that duration (specifically eighty thousand years, which is four-fifths of the lifespan), rescuing and delivering many beings—humans, devas, and brahmas—from the flood of Saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna.
The Blessed Padumuttara, having removed, cut off, and destroyed all doubts of all beings, and having rescued them from the flood of Saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna, attained final peace (Parinibbāna) along with his assembly of disciples (like a great fire that has shone brightly and then gone out), ending the cycle of existence.

## 11. The Chronicle of Sumedha
After the aeon (kappa) in which the Blessed Padumuttara appeared had ended, seventy thousand (70,000) empty aeons (suñña-kappa) passed where no Buddha appeared. Counting back from this present aeon, thirty thousand (30,000) aeons ago, in a single aeon, two Buddhas appeared: (1) the Blessed Sumedha and (2) the Blessed Sujāta. (It was a Maṇḍa-kappa.)
Of those two Buddhas, the Bodhisatta Sumedha, at the end of fulfilling his perfections, was dwelling in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of Queen Sudattā, the consort of King Sudatta of the royal city of Sudassana. After ten months had passed, he was born in the Sudassana auspicious park.
(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonders clearly occurred.)
## His Reign
When the Bodhisatta Prince Sumedha reached maturity, he lived in three golden palaces: (1) Sucandana, (2) Kañcana, and (3) Sirivaḍḍhana.
303:
405
He enjoyed celestial-like pleasures and reigned for nine thousand (9,000) years, being entertained and served by forty-eight thousand (48,000) attendants, headed by Queen Sumanā.
## His Renunciation
While he was thus reigning, when Queen Sumanā gave birth to a son named Punabbasu, he saw the four great omens and renounced the world to become a monk, riding an elephant. Following the example of the Bodhisatta prince, one hundred crore men also became monks.
## His Enlightenment
The Bodhisatta Sumedha, together with those one hundred crore monks, practiced austere practices (dukkharacariya) for fifteen days (eight months according to the Sri Lankan version). On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become a Buddha, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of a wealthy merchant named Nakulā from the village of Nakula. He spent the day in the Sal grove in that area, and when evening came, he left his attendant monks and proceeded alone. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by an ascetic named Sirivaḍḍha. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Mahānīpa (or Kadamba) Bodhi tree, the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka) measuring fifty-seven cubits appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that throne, he resolved with fourfold exertion, and as previously described...
304:
406
...he blew away and drove out the army of Mara and attained the state of a fully enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha), the supreme of the three worlds and possessor of omniscience.
## Three Great Teaching Assemblies
After becoming a Buddha, the Blessed Sumedha stayed near the Mahānīpa Bodhi tree for the seven-seven days (forty-nine days). Accepting the request of the Brahma King to teach the Dhamma, he reflected, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He saw his half-brothers, Prince Sarana and Prince Sabbakāma (the future Chief Disciples), who were endowed with past merits for attaining the Path and Fruit and were capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths, as well as the one hundred crore monks who had renounced the world with him. He thought, "I shall preach the Dhamma to them first." Reflecting further on where those monks were currently staying, he saw that they were in the Sudassana royal park near the city of Sudassana. Taking his bowl and robes, he traveled through the air in an instant to the place where those monks were.
At that time, those one hundred crore monks saw the Blessed Sumedha coming from afar. With hearts full of devotion, they went out to meet the Buddha, took his bowl and robes, prepared his seat, and performed the duties of respect. They then sat in suitable places surrounding the Buddha. Then, the Blessed Sumedha sent the park keeper to...

...summon Prince Sarana and Prince Sabbakāma. To those two princes, to the one hundred crore monks who had renounced the world with him, and to the devas and humans who had come to listen, he preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which is the customary first discourse of all previous Buddhas. At that time, one hundred thousand crore devas and humans attained the special Dhamma of the Path and Fruit.
(This was the first great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma.)
Later, at another time, the Blessed Sumedha entered the attainment of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) at dawn. While reflecting on beings who were ready for liberation, he saw the great ogre (yakkha) Kumbhakaṇṇa, who lived at the entrance of a great forest and had a terrifying appearance, eating humans and causing all travel to cease. The Buddha went alone without any companion to the ogre's mansion, entered, and sat upon the prepared seat.
Then, the ogre Kumbhakaṇṇa became as violently angry as a venomous cobra struck by a stick. To frighten the Buddha, he made his body extremely fierce, creating a head like a mountain and opening eyes as bright as the sun. He manifested fangs as long and wide as the front of a plow, a dark and sagging uneven dewlap, a hideous nose sunken in the middle and bulging at the ends, a mouth as wide and red as a mountain cave, and thick, bristly, coarse hair. With such an extremely ugly and terrifying form, he came and stood before the Buddha.
306:
Even though he caused a great rain of his own nine types of weapons—a rain of stones, a rain of mountains, a rain of fire, a rain of hot water, a rain of hot mud, a rain of hot ashes, a rain of weapons, a rain of burning coals, and a rain of hot sand—emitting smoke and flames, he was unable to make even a single hair of the Blessed One tremble. Therefore, thinking, "I will kill the Buddha by asking him questions," the demon Āḷavaka (Kumbhakaṇṇa) asked him questions just as the demon Āḷavaka had done. Then, the Sumedha Buddha tamed the demon Kumbhakaṇṇa by answering his questions.

Then, on the second day, it was the day appointed by the king who ruled the country near the demon's dwelling to hand over his son to the demon. Accordingly, the king had the people load carts full of rice and offered the prince along with the rice to the demon. At that time, the demon offered the prince, whom he was supposed to eat, to the Buddha. The multitude of people living at the edge of the forest, hearing the good news, approached the Buddha. In that assembly, the Sumedha Buddha preached a discourse suitable and appropriate for the demon, causing ninety billion beings to attain the vision of the Path (Magga-ñāṇa).

(This is the second great assembly of the Second Awakening - Dutiyābhisamaya.)

Thereafter, on another occasion, the Sumedha Buddha preached the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths to the assembly of devas and humans in the great Sirinandana Park near the city of Upakārī. At that time, eighty billion devas and humans attained the extraordinary Dhamma of the Path and Fruit.

(This is the third great assembly of the Third Awakening - Tatiyābhisamaya.)

## Three Great Assemblies of Disciples

## Paṭhama-sannipāta
There were three great assemblies of disciples of the Sumedha Buddha. In the first instance, the Blessed One traveled to the royal city of Sudassana. At that time, one hundred billion Arahants assembled.

(This is the first great assembly of disciples.)

## Dutiya-sannipāta
Thereafter, on another occasion, the Blessed One observed the rains retreat (vassa) on the mountain named Devakūṭa. When the retreat ended, during the celebration of the Kaṭhina ceremony, ninety billion monks assembled.

(This is the second great assembly of disciples.)

## Tatiya-sannipāta
Thereafter, on another occasion, the Blessed One went on a journey (cārikā). Eighty billion monks who were following him assembled.

(This is the third great assembly of disciples.)

## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha becoming the youth Uttara and receiving the Prophecy
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a youth named Uttara, who excelled all men in various virtues. He offered his accumulated wealth of eighty billion to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
308:
He made the offering to the Saṅgha. Then, having heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, he established himself in the Three Refuges and was ordained in the Buddha's Dispensation. After preaching the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), the Sumedha Buddha gave the prophecy, saying: "In the future, this youth Uttara will certainly become a Buddha named Gotama."

(The manner of receiving the prophecy is exactly the same in detail as when receiving the prophecy from the Dīpaṅkara Buddha.)

Upon hearing the prophecy of the Sumedha Buddha, the Bodhisatta Uttara greatly purified his mind and firmly resolved to further fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

Having been ordained in the Dispensation of the Sumedha Buddha, he mastered the ninefold Pariyatti Dhamma of the Buddha, including the Suttas and Vinaya, reaching the further shore of knowledge, and brought glory to the Buddha's Dispensation.

Without ever lying down, he practiced the monk's Dhamma diligently in the three postures of sitting, standing, and walking. He attained not only the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) but also the pinnacle of the five superknowledges (abhiññā), and at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma realm.

## Description of the City and Others
The birthplace of the Sumedha Buddha was the royal city of Sudassana. His father was King Sudatta, and his mother was Queen Sudattā.

He reigned for nine thousand (9,000) years. His three palaces were Sucandana, Kañcana, and Sirivaḍḍhana.
309:
The Chief Consort was Queen Sumanādevī, who had forty-eight thousand female attendants. His son was Prince Punabbasu.

After seeing the four great omens, he renounced the world on an elephant. He practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for fifteen days.

The pair of Chief Disciples were the Elder Saraṇa and the Elder Sabbakāma. His attendant was the Elder Sāgara.

The pair of Chief Female Disciples were the Elder Nun Rāmā and the Elder Nun Surāmā. The Bodhi tree where he attained enlightenment was the Mahānīpa (Great Nauclea) tree.

The noble male lay supporters were the merchant Uruvela and the merchant Yasavā. The noble female lay supporters were the laywoman Yasodharā and the laywoman Sirimā.

The height of the Sumedha Buddha was eighty-eight (88) cubits. The radiance from his body illuminated all directions, just like the moon that shines clearly, illuminating all the stars.

To give another example: just as the jewel-treasure of a Universal Monarch shines within a radius of one yojana, the radiance from the Buddha's body always shone and spread within a radius of one yojana.

The lifespan during the time of the Sumedha Buddha was ninety thousand (90,000) years. Having remained for that long (four-fifths of the lifespan), he saved many
310:
multitudes of humans, devas, and Brahmas, pulling them out from the current of Saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna.

The Dispensation of this Sumedha Buddha was well-interspersed with Arahants who were endowed with the three knowledges (vijjā) and six superknowledges (abhiññā), who had reached the peak of power, and who were truly virtuous ones of the Tādi quality, unshaken by worldly conditions. (This means Arahants were present everywhere.)

All those Arahants, who possessed immeasurable fame, were liberated from defilements and free from the four types of substrata (upadhi). Those disciples of the Buddha, who had many followers, displayed the light of wisdom and then attained Parinibbāna and became cooled.

## The Stupa
In this way, the Sumedha Buddha, having conquered the five Maras, attained Parinibbāna in the great park named Medhārāma. His relics, according to his resolution as mentioned before, were divided into fragments and remained spread throughout the island of Jambudīpa, receiving the veneration of humans, devas, and Brahmas.

Here ends the Chronicle of Sumedha Buddha.

## 12. Chronicle of Sujāta Buddha
After the Sumedha Buddha attained Parinibbāna, the human lifespan gradually decreased from ninety thousand (90,000) years to ten (10) years. It then increased again to an asankheyya (incalculable) period, and then decreased again. When it reached ninety thousand years, the Bodhisatta of Sujāta Buddha, having completed the fulfillment of the perfections, was dwelling in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and Brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of Queen Pabhāvatī, the consort of King Uggata in the royal city of Sumangala. He was born after ten months had passed.

(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonders clearly appeared.)

On the naming day, the wise men who were to give the name called him Prince Sujāta, based on the fact that all people throughout the island of Jambudīpa were happy in both body and mind when the Bodhisatta prince was born.

## Reigning over the Kingdom
When the Bodhisatta Prince Sujāta reached maturity, he lived in three golden palaces: (1) Siri, (2) Upasiri, and (3) Nanda. He was entertained and served by twenty-three thousand (23,000) female attendants, headed by Queen Sirinandā.
312:
He enjoyed happiness similar to divine bliss for nine thousand (9,000) years while reigning over the kingdom.

## Renunciation
While reigning over the kingdom, the Bodhisatta Prince Sujāta saw the four great omens. When Queen Sirinandā gave birth to a son named Upasena, he renounced the world riding the auspicious horse named Haṃsavaha and became a monk. Following the example of the Bodhisatta prince's renunciation, ten million men also became monks.

## Attaining Buddhahood
The Bodhisatta of Sujāta Buddha practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) together with those ten million monks for nine months. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesak), the day he was to become Buddha, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of the merchant Sirinandana from the city of Sirinandana. He spent the day in the Sal forest in that area. In the evening, he proceeded alone toward the Mahābodhi tree. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by an ascetic named Sunanda. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Mahābodhi (thorny bamboo) tree, the Aparājita Throne, measuring thirty-three (33) cubits, appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that throne and resolving with fourfold effort (vīriya), he blew away and drove out the army of Mara as previously described, and attained the state of a Fully Enlightened Buddha, the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Knower of All (Sabbaññū).
313:
## Three Great Assemblies of Teaching

After attaining Buddhahood, the Buddha Sujāta spent the seven-week period (sattasattāha) near the Mahābodhi (Great Bamboo) tree. Accepting the request of the Great Brahma to teach the Dhamma, He reflected, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He then saw Prince Sudassana, His younger half-brother, and Sudeva, the son of the chaplain, both of whom possessed the merit from previous lives to attain the Paths and Fruits (and were destined to be the Chief Disciples). Deciding to preach to them first, He traveled through the air and descended at the Sumangala Royal Garden near the city of Sumangala. He sent the gardener to summon Prince Sudassana and the youth Sudeva. With these two as the primary listeners, He preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the discourse which all previous Buddhas had traditionally preached, to the gathered devas and humans. At that time, eighty crores of devas and humans attained the special Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits.

(This was the first great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma.)

Later, on another occasion, the Buddha Sujāta performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire near a Sal tree by the gate of the Sudassana Garden to subdue the heretics. He then spent the rainy season (vassa) on the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone at the foot of the Parichattaka tree in Tāvatiṃsa Heaven, the abode of Sakka, the king of devas, and preached the Abhidhamma to the devas and brahmas.
314:
At that great assembly of Abhidhamma, three million seven hundred thousand devas and brahmas attained the special Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits.

(This was the second great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma.)

Later, on another occasion, the Buddha Sujāta went to the presence of His royal father in the city of Sumangala. At that time, six million devas and humans attained the special Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits.

(This was the third great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma.)

**********

## Three Great Assemblies of Disciples

## The First Assembly

There were three great assemblies of the disciples of the Buddha Sujāta. In the first assembly, the Buddha Sujāta preached the Dhamma to a multitude of people who had come to the great garden named Sudhamma near the city of Sudhammavatī. He then ordained six million men by the "Ehi Bhikkhu" formula and recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the midst of those monks.

(This was the first great assembly of disciples.)

## The Second Assembly

Later, on another occasion, when the Buddha Sujāta descended from Tāvatiṃsa Heaven, there was a great assembly of five million monks.

(This was the second great assembly of disciples.)
315:
## The Third Assembly

Later, on another occasion, having heard the good news that "Prince Sudassana, the Buddha's younger brother, has been ordained in the presence of the Buddha and has attained Arahantship," four hundred thousand men, inspired to follow his example, came to be ordained. The Venerable Sudassana, the Right-hand Disciple, led them to the presence of the Buddha Sujāta. The Buddha preached the Dhamma to them and ordained them as Ehi Bhikkhus. In that assembly of monks, which was endowed with the four factors, He recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.

(This was the third great assembly of disciples.)

## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha as a Universal Monarch Receiving the Prophecy

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). Upon hearing the news that "A Buddha has appeared in the world," he approached the Buddha and listened to the Dhamma. He then offered his kingdom and royal luxury, along with the seven jewels, to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and was ordained in the presence of the Buddha. All the people living throughout the island of Jambudīpa became lay attendants (kappiya). They collected all the taxes from the country and constantly offered the four requisites—robes, alms-food, dwellings, and medicines—to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
316:
At that time, the Buddha Sujāta gave the prophecy to the Bodhisatta, saying, "In the future, he will surely become a Buddha named Gotama."

(The manner of receiving the prophecy was as detailed as that of the prophecy given by the Buddha Dīpaṅkara.)

Upon hearing the prophecy of the Buddha Sujāta, the noble Bodhisatta greatly purified his mind and made a firm resolve to further fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

Having been ordained as a monk in the dispensation of the Buddha Sujāta, the noble Bodhisatta mastered the Pariyatti Dhamma of the Buddha, consisting of the nine divisions including the Sutta and Vinaya, and brought glory to the Buddha's dispensation.

Without ever lying down, he practiced the meditation of the Brahma-vihāras in the three postures of sitting, standing, and walking. He attained not only the eight meditative attainments (samāpattis) but also the pinnacle of the five super-knowledges (abhiññās), and at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma realm.

## Details of the City and Others

The birthplace of the Buddha Sujāta was the city of Sumangala. His father was King Uggata, and His mother was Queen Pabhāvatī.

He reigned for nine thousand (9,000) years. His three palaces were Sirisanda, Upasiri, and Nanda.
317:
The Chief Queen was Queen Sirinandā, who had twenty-three thousand (23,000) female attendants. His son was Prince Upasena.

The vehicle in which He renounced the world after seeing the four great omens was a horse. He practiced asceticism (dukkharacariyā) for nine months.

The pair of Chief Disciples were the Venerable Sudassana and the Venerable Sudeva. His attendant was the Venerable Nārada.

The pair of Chief Female Disciples were the Bhikkhunī Nāgā and the Bhikkhunī Nāgasamālā. The Bodhi tree under which He attained Enlightenment was the Mahāveḷu (Great Bamboo) tree.

(That bamboo tree had a solid and thick stem. It was so dense with leaves that there were no gaps for sunlight to pass through. The bamboo was straight, large in circumference, and very pleasant to look at. It grew as a single stalk from the base, which then branched out at the top, appearing as beautiful as a well-arranged peacock's tail. That bamboo tree had no thorns at all, and its hollow was not very wide. Its branches spread in the four directions and were so closely knit that it provided a pleasant, cool, and dense shade.)

The noble male lay supporters were the wealthy merchant Sudatta and the wealthy merchant Citta. The noble female lay supporters were the laywoman Subhaddā and the laywoman Padumā.

The height of the Buddha Sujāta was fifty (50) cubits. He was endowed with all excellent characteristics and all the glorious attributes of the physical body (rūpakāya).
318:
The bodily radiance of the Buddha Sujāta (which was equal only to the peerless radiance of previous Buddhas) emanated and spread in all directions as He wished. It was immeasurable, incomparable, and beyond any worldly analogy.

The lifespan during the time of the Buddha Sujāta was ninety thousand (90,000) years. Having remained for that long (four-fifths of the lifespan), He rescued and liberated many devas, humans, and brahmas from the current of saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna.

Just as the waves rising and moving in the ocean are marvelous, and just as the stars and constellations shining brightly in the sky are marvelous, so too was the dispensation of the Buddha Sujāta marvelous and beautiful with the presence of Arahants.

## Spiritual Urgency (Saṃvega)

That Buddha Sujāta, who was equal only to the peerless Buddhas of the past, and all the glorious virtues of that Buddha, have all ceased and vanished. Indeed, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are without permanent essence and are merely empty.

## The Stupa (Cetiya)

In this way, the Buddha Sujāta, the Conqueror of the Five Māras, passed into Parinibbāna within the great monastery named Silārāma.
319:
The great stupa of the Buddha Sujāta, built in that monastery (as mentioned before), was three gāvutas in height.

Here ends the Chronicle of the Buddha Sujāta.

## 13. The Chronicle of the Buddha Piyadassī

After the aeon (kappa) in which the Buddha Sujāta appeared had ended, eighteen hundred (1,800) aeons ago from this present one, there was a single 'Vara' kappa. In that aeon, three Buddhas appeared: (1) the Buddha Piyadassī, (2) the Buddha Atthadassī, and (3) the Buddha Dhammadassī. The following is the account of the first to appear, the Buddha Piyadassī.

At the end of fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), the Bodhisatta of the Buddha Piyadassī was dwelling in Tusita Heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of Queen Candā, the Chief Queen of King Sudatta in the royal city of Sudhaññavatī. After ten months had passed, he was born in the great garden named Varuṇa.

(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonders clearly appeared.)

On the day of his naming ceremony, because he displayed a special miracle that brought love and joy to all people, he was named Prince Piyadassī.
320:
## Reigning

When Prince Piyadassī reached the proper age, he lived in three golden palaces: (1) Sunimmala, (2) Vimala, and (3) Giriguhā. He was entertained and served by thirty-three thousand (33,000) female attendants, headed by Queen Vimalā. He enjoyed celestial-like luxury and reigned for nine thousand (9,000) years.

## Renunciation

While reigning, Prince Piyadassī saw the four great omens. When Queen Vimalā gave birth to a son named Kañcanāveḷa, he renounced the world in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses and became a monk. Following his example, ten million men also became monks.

## Enlightenment

The Bodhisatta of the Buddha Piyadassī practiced asceticism (dukkharacariyā) together with those ten million monks for six months. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become a Buddha, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of a brahmin named Vasabha from the brahmin village of Varuṇa. He spent the day in the Sal grove of that region. In the evening, he went alone to the Mahābodhi seat. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by an Ajivaka named Sujāta. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Mahābodhi (Kakudha) tree,

## Attaining Buddhahood
The Bodhisatta of Atthadassī Buddha, together with those ninety million monks, practiced austerities (dukkharacariyā) for eight months. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become Buddha, while the people were bringing sweet thick milk-rice (ghanapāyāsa) to offer to the Naga maiden named Sucindhara, the Naga maiden did not consume the milk-rice herself. Instead, she manifested herself to the many people who came to worship and offered the milk-rice along with the golden bowl to the Bodhisatta. After partaking of the milk-rice offered by the Naga maiden, he rested during the day in the Sal grove in that area. In the evening, he proceeded alone to the Mahābodhi seat. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of kusa grass offered by the Naga king named Mahāruci. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Mahābodhi (Champaka) tree, the Aparājita Throne, measuring fifty-three cubits, appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that throne and resolving with fourfold energy (viriya), he blew away and dispelled the army of Mara as previously mentioned, and attained the state of the All-Knowing Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Worlds.
## Three Great Assemblies of Dhamma
After attaining Buddhahood, Atthadassī Buddha stayed near the Mahābodhi (Champaka) tree for the Satta-sattāha (forty-nine days)...

There were three great assemblies of disciples of Atthadassī Buddha. In the first instance, in the city of Sucandaka, the prince named Santa and the chaplain's son named Upasanta (who were to become the Chief Disciples) realized that no essence could be found in the three Vedas or in various other beliefs. They stationed brave men along with four wise men at the four gates of the city, instructing them, "You must come and report to us if you see or hear of a wise monk or brahmin."
At that time, Atthadassī Buddha, the refuge of the three worlds, arrived at the city of Sucandaka during his travels along with his assembly of disciple monks. When the guards went to the prince and the chaplain's son and reported that the Buddha had arrived at Sucandaka...

On the seventh day, together with all the city dwellers, they listened to the Dhamma preached by the Buddha. Again, at the assembly of humans, devas, and Brahmas who arrived to listen to the Mahāmangala Dhamma...

## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha as Susīma Ascetic Receiving the Prophecy
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a wealthy Brahmin named Susīma in the city of Campaka, who was recognized and known by the whole world as a great virtuous man. After giving away all his wealth to the poor, the needy, the helpless, the orphans, and travelers, he went near the Himalayas and became a hermit. Developing the eight attainments and five superknowledges, he became a noble ascetic of great power and influence. He stayed waiting for the time when the Buddha would appear, preaching to the multitudes about the faultlessness of wholesome deeds and the faultiness of unwholesome deeds.
Later, when Atthadassī Buddha appeared in the world and was raining down the rain of the Deathless Dhamma in the midst of the eightfold assembly in the great city of Sudassana, the Bodhisatta Susīma the hermit heard the Buddha's Dhamma. He then went to the celestial realm and brought back divine flowers such as the Paduma lotus and the Parichattaka (coral tree) flower from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Desiring to show his own power and influence, he manifested himself clearly and...

Like a great rain falling over the four islands, he caused a great rain of flowers to fall in the four directions. Having constructed a great flower pavilion adorned with flowers all around, he decorated the top with garlands at the pinnacle of worship. He also adorned the golden nets and other structures with flowers. He worshipped the Buddha with a large umbrella made of Mandārava flowers (divine flowers). The Buddha Atthadassī then gave the prophecy to the Bodhisatta, the ascetic Susīma, saying: "In the future, one thousand eight hundred aeons from now, this ascetic Susīma will certainly become a Buddha named Gotama."
(The details of the prophecy are exactly as described in the chronicle of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara.)
Upon hearing the prophecy of the Buddha Atthadassī, the Great Being was filled with joy and, with a mind fearful of living heedlessly, he firmly resolved to fulfill the ten perfections more intensely.
## Description of the City and Other Details
The birthplace of the Buddha Atthadassī was the city of Sobhana. His father was King Sāgara, and his mother was Queen Sudassanā.
He reigned for ten thousand (10,000) years. His three royal palaces were the golden palaces of Amaragiri, Sugiri, and Vāhana.
340: The Chief Queen was Queen Visākhā, who had thirty-three thousand attendant ladies. His son was Prince Sela. The pair of Chief Female Disciples were the Venerable Dhammā and the Venerable Sudhammā. The Bodhi tree under which he attained enlightenment was the Campaka tree. The noble male lay supporters were the wealthy merchant Nakula and the wealthy merchant Nisabha. The noble female lay supporters were the laywoman Makilā and the laywoman Sunandā. The Blessed One Atthadassī, who was equal only to the peerless Buddhas, was eighty cubits in height. He was as beautiful as a Sal tree in full bloom or like the full moon, the king of the stars and constellations. The natural rays of the Blessed One Atthadassī, which were not created by supernatural power but were inherent, always spread and radiated for one yojana in the ten directions, above and below. (If he so desired and resolved, they could shine through hundreds of millions of world systems.) The Blessed One Atthadassī, who was supreme among all beings, was endowed with the five eyes...

## The Stupa
Thus, the Buddha Atthadassī, who had conquered the five Maras, attained Parinibbāna in the great monastery named Anoma. His relics, according to his resolution as mentioned before, were divided into many fragments and were distributed throughout the island of Jambudīpa, where they received the worship of humans, devas, and Brahmas.

## 15. The Chronicle of Dhammadassī Buddha
After the Parinibbāna of the Buddha Atthadassī (in that same aeon, which was a Vara-kappa because three Buddhas appeared, but could also be called a Maṇḍa-kappa because it was endowed with special, pure, and serene qualities), the human lifespan gradually decreased from one hundred thousand (100,000) years to ten years, then increased again to an incalculable (asaṅkheyya) period, and then decreased again to one hundred thousand years.
342:
When the lifespan reached one hundred thousand years, the Bodhisatta Dhammadassī, having fulfilled the perfections, was residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and Brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of Queen Sunandā, the consort of King Saraṇa in the capital city of Saraṇa. When ten months were complete, he was born in the royal park named Saraṇa.
(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great and wonderful omens clearly appeared.)
Just as the Bodhisatta prince was born, in the legal texts (Dhammasattha) used for deciding various disputes, the rulings that were not in accordance with justice disappeared of their own accord, and only those in accordance with justice remained. Therefore, when naming the prince, the relatives along with the wise men who interpreted the omens named him Prince Dhammadassī (Seer of the Dhamma).
## Reigning over the Kingdom
When Prince Dhammadassī reached maturity, he lived in three golden palaces: (1) Araja, (2) Viraja, and (3) Sudassana. He was entertained and attended to by forty-three thousand (43,000) maidens, headed by Queen Vicikoḷī. He enjoyed royal glory similar to divine bliss for eight thousand (8,000) years and reigned over the kingdom.
343:
## The Great Renunciation
While Prince Dhammadassī was reigning, he saw the four great omens. When his son, named Puññavaḍḍhana, was born to Queen Vicikoḷī, he was as delicate as a deva and enjoyed bliss like that of a deva. However, rising from his bed at midnight and sitting on his auspicious couch, he saw the distorted postures of the sleeping court ladies. He was struck with great urgency (saṃvega) and resolved to renounce the world. Immediately, the golden palace of Sudassana, where the Bodhisatta resided, rose into the air. Surrounded by the fourfold army, it traveled like a second sun or a divine mansion and landed on the ground near the Bimbijāla (Maccāphulla) Bodhi tree.
The Bodhisatta donned the lotus robes offered by a Brahma and became a monk. He descended from the palace and stood nearby. The palace then traveled through the air again and settled on the ground, keeping the Bodhi tree inside. The royal women and attendants descended from the palace and stayed at a distance of half a gāvuta (about 800 tas). Among the people gathered there, all the men, excluding the women, followed the Bodhisatta's example and became monks. Those who followed him into monkhood numbered one hundred thousand crores.
## Attaining Buddhahood
The Bodhisatta Dhammadassī practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for seven days. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become a Buddha,
344:
he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by Queen Vicikoḷī. He spent the day in a large jujube grove in that area. In the evening, he proceeded alone to the Maha Bodhi seat. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a barley-field guard named Sirivaḍḍhana. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Bimbijāla Bodhi tree, the Aparājita Throne, measuring fifty-three (53) cubits, appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that throne, he attained Buddhahood according to the method previously described.
## The Three Great Sermons
After becoming a Buddha, the Buddha Dhammadassī remained near the Bimbijāla Bodhi tree for the seven weeks (satta-sattāha = 49 days). Accepting the request of the Brahma King to teach the Dhamma, he considered, "To whom should I preach the Dhamma first?" He saw that the one hundred thousand crores of monks who had renounced with him were endowed with past merits to attain the Paths and Fruits. He decided, "I shall preach to them first." He saw that those monks were staying in the Migadāya (Deer Park) at Isipatana (so named because it was the place where those with mundane jhāna descended from the sky), which was eighteen (18) yojanas away from the Maha Bodhi tree. He traveled there in an instant.
At that time, the one hundred thousand crores of monks saw the Buddha Dhammadassī approaching from afar. With hearts full of great devotion, they performed the major and minor duties (as previously described).
345: ...and sat in a suitable place surrounding the Buddha. Then, the Buddha preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which all previous Buddhas had preached, to the devas and humans who had come to listen, starting with those monks. At that time, one hundred thousand crores of beings attained the special Dhamma of the paths and fruits. (This was the first great assembly of Dhamma realization.) Later, at another time, in the city named Tagara, a king named Sañjaya saw the faults in sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation and became a hermit. Following King Sañjaya's example, ninety crores of people became hermits. All those noble hermits attained the five mundane superknowledges (abhiññā) and the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti). Then, the Blessed One Dhammadassī, seeing that those hermits were endowed with past merits for attaining the paths and fruits, traveled through the air. Upon reaching the hermitage of the hermit Sañjaya, he stood in the air and preached a discourse suitable to the hermit's inclination and disposition, enabling those hermits to attain the vision of the Dhamma known as the path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). (This was the second great assembly of Dhamma realization.) Later, at another time, Sakka, the king of gods, wishing to hear the Dhamma with his retinue, approached the Buddha. When the Buddha preached the Dhamma, eighty crores of beings attained the special Dhamma of the paths and fruits. (This was the third great assembly of Dhamma realization.) *********

## The Three Great Assemblies of Disciples
## The First Assembly
There were three great assemblies of disciples of the Buddha Dhammadassī. For the first assembly, in the city of Saraṇa, the Buddha Dhammadassī caused his half-brothers, the future Chief Disciples Prince Paduma and Prince Phussadeva, to be ordained along with their retinues. He then spent the rainy season (vassa) in that city. At the end of the rainy season, he performed the Visuddhi-pavāraṇā in the midst of one hundred thousand crores of monks who had been ordained at the beginning of the vassa and had become Arahants during the vassa.

On another occasion, after the Buddha Dhammadassī had preached the Abhidhamma and descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to the human world, one hundred crores of monks assembled.
(This is the second great assembly of disciples.)
## The Third Assembly
On another occasion, at the Sudassanārāma monastery, the Buddha Dhammadassī preached on the benefits and power of the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). He designated the great disciple, the Arahant named Hārita, as the foremost (etadagga) in the practice of dhutaṅga. At that time, in an assembly of eighty crores of monks, the Buddha recited the Ovāda-pātimokkha.
(This is the third great assembly of disciples.)

## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha as Sakka Receiving the Prophecy
At that time, our Buddha-to-be was Sakka, the King of Devas. The pair of Chief Disciples were the Elder Paduma and the Elder Phussadeva, and the attendant was the Elder Sunetta.

## The Stupa
Thus, the Buddha Dhammadassī, who possessed great energy, attained Parinibbāna in the Sālārāma monastery in the city of Sālavatī. The great Stupa of the Buddha Dhammadassī, built within that very monastery, was three yojanas in height.
