## 16. The Chronicle of Buddha Siddhattha
After the aeon (kappa) in which the Buddha Dhammadassī appeared had ended, one thousand seven hundred and six (1,706) aeons passed. Counting back from this present aeon, ninety-four aeons ago, a single Buddha named Siddhattha appeared.

As for the account of that Buddha Siddhattha... in that ninety-fourth aeon, when the human lifespan had decreased from an incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) period and reached one hundred thousand years, the Bodhisatta Siddhattha, having fulfilled the Perfections (pāramīs), was residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the assembly of Devas and Brahmas to become a Buddha, He descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of Chief Queen Suphassā, the consort of King Udena of the royal city of Vebhāra.
350:
452
When ten months were complete, He was born in the garden named Vīriya.
(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and great wonders clearly appeared.)

When the Bodhisatta prince was born, because the great and small tasks undertaken by all people and the benefits they desired and longed for reached successful completion, on the naming day, the wise men who read the omens and the assembly of relatives named the Bodhisatta prince 'Prince Siddhattha'.

## Reigning over the Kingdom
When the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha reached the proper age, He lived in three golden palaces: (1) the palace named Koka, (2) the palace named Suppala, and (3) the palace named Kokanada. He was entertained and served by forty-eight thousand (48,000) attendants, headed by Chief Queen Somanassā. He reigned for ten thousand (10,000) years, enjoying prosperity and happiness equal to that of the devas.

## Renunciation
While reigning over the kingdom, the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha saw the four great omens. When His son named Anupama was born to Chief Queen Somanassā, He renounced the world on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, riding a golden palanquin.
351:
453
He went to the Vīriya garden and became a monk. Following the example of the Bodhisatta's renunciation, one hundred thousand (100,000) men also became monks.

## Attaining Buddhahood
The Bodhisatta Siddhattha, together with those one hundred thousand monks, practiced asceticism (dukkara-cariyā) for ten months. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day He was to become a Buddha, He partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the young brahmin woman named Sunettā from the village of Asadisa Brahmin. He spent the day in the great jujube grove in that area, and in the evening, He went alone to the Mahābodhi site. On the way, He accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a guard of a barley field named Varuṇa. As soon as He spread the grass at the foot of the Bodhi (Mahālekhā) tree, the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka) measuring forty cubits appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that throne, He attained Buddhahood according to the method previously described.

## The Three Great Dhamma Assemblies
After becoming a Buddha, the Buddha Siddhattha remained near the Bodhi (Mahālekhā) tree for the seven-week period (satta-sattāha = forty-nine days). Accepting the request of the Brahma King to preach the Dhamma, He reflected, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He saw that the one hundred thousand monks who had renounced the world together with Him were endowed with past merits to attain the Paths and Fruits. He decided, "I shall preach the Dhamma to them first."

At that time, the one hundred thousand monks saw the Buddha Siddhattha coming from afar. With hearts full of great devotion, they performed the major and minor duties (as previously described) and sat in suitable places surrounding the Buddha. Then, the Buddha, beginning with those monks, preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta—which all previous Buddhas were accustomed to preach—to the devas and humans who had come to listen. (This was the second great assembly of the realization of Dhamma.)

## The Three Great Assemblies of Disciples
## The First Assembly
There were three great assemblies of the Arahant disciples of the Buddha Siddhattha. On the first occasion, in the city of Amara, which was as beautiful and pleasant to look at as the Tāvatiṃsa heaven of the devas, the two brothers, Prince Sambhala and Prince Sumitta, who were destined to be the Chief Disciples, reigned together like the Licchavī kings of Vesālī in the time of our Buddha. At that time, the Buddha Siddhattha, seeing that these two kings were endowed with past merits to attain the Paths and Fruits, traveled through the air and descended in the middle of the city of Amara. He showed His footprints (pada-cetiya), which were to be revered and which pressed upon the ground with level soles adorned with the one hundred and eight marks of the wheel. He then went to the Amara garden and sat beautifully like a statue of pure gold on a stone slab.

Then, the two royal brothers saw the footprints (pada-cetiya) of the Buddha and followed the tracks to where the Buddha had gone. Together with their retinue, they approached the Buddha, paid homage respectfully, and sat surrounding Him. When the Buddha preached the Dhamma discourse that was in accordance with their inclinations and dispositions,

(This was the first great assembly of disciples.)

## The Second Assembly
Thereafter, on another occasion, in the midst of ninety koṭis (900 million) of monks who had renounced the world in the assembly of relatives in the city of Vebhāra, the Buddha recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.
(This was the second great assembly of disciples.)

## The Third Assembly

## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha becoming the Hermit Mangala and receiving the Prophecy
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Mangala in the city of Surasena, who was highly proficient and expert in the original Vedas and their various branches. Having given away his accumulated wealth, amounting to many koṭis, to the poor, the helpless, and others, and having a mind that delighted in solitude (viveka),
355:
After becoming a hermit and attaining the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), and while living endowed with powerful and sharp psychic potency that others could not overcome, he heard the news that "The Buddha Siddhāttha has appeared in the world." Having approached, revered, and paid homage to the Buddha, and upon hearing the Dhamma, he was filled with great devotion. By his psychic power, he brought a fruit from a Jambu (rose-apple) tree and offered it to the Buddha Siddhāttha, who was staying at the Surasena monastery, together with his retinue of nine hundred million monks, and thus delighted them with the Jambu fruits.

Then, the Buddha Siddhāttha, having accepted and partaken of the offered Jambu fruits, gave the prophecy: "This hermit Mangala, in the ninety-fourth aeon from this present one, will surely become a Buddha named Gotama."

(The manner of receiving the prophecy is exactly the same in detail as the prophecy received from the Buddha Dīpaṅkara.)

Upon hearing the prophecy of the Buddha Siddhāttha, the Bodhisatta Mangala the hermit, with a heart full of great devotion, firmly resolved to further fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

## Description of the City and Other Details
The birthplace of the Buddha Siddhāttha was the city of Vaibhāra. His father was King Udena, and his mother was Queen Suphassā.

He reigned for ten thousand (10,000) years. His three royal palaces were the golden palace named Koka, the golden palace named Uppala, and the golden palace named Kokanāda.
356:
The chief consort was Queen Somanassā, who had a retinue of forty-eight thousand (48,000) ladies-in-waiting. His son was Prince Anupama.

Having seen the four great omens, he renounced the world by means of a palanquin (litter) and practiced asceticism (dukkara-cariyā) for ten months.

The pair of noble chief disciples were the Elder Sambhala and the Elder Sumitta, and his personal attendant was the Elder Revata.

The pair of chief female disciples were the Elder Nun Sīvalā and the Elder Nun Surāmā. The Bodhi tree where he attained enlightenment was the Kanikāra (Mahālekhā) tree.

The noble male lay supporters were the merchant Suppiya and the merchant Samudda, and the noble female lay supporters were the laywoman Rammā and the laywoman Surammā.

The height of the Buddha Siddhāttha was sixty (60) cubits. He graced the ten thousand world systems like a great jeweled pillar arranged for worship.

The Buddha Siddhāttha, who was equal only to the peerless Buddhas of the past, who was without a rival, and who was endowed with the five types of vision, lived in the world for one hundred thousand years.

That Buddha Siddhāttha, while manifesting the extensive and manifold radiance of his body and his wisdom, and while causing his disciples to blossom with the paths and fruits (magga-phala), and while causing them to flourish beautifully with the two types of
357:
attainments (samāpatti), namely mundane and supramundane, entered Parinibbāna and attained final cessation together with many Arahant disciples, thus ending the cycle of existence.

## The Cetiya
In this manner, the Buddha Siddhāttha, the noble King of Monks, passed away into Parinibbāna in the great park named Anoma near the city of Kañcanaveḷu. Within that same great park, a great Cetiya of the Buddha Siddhāttha, made entirely of jewels and built according to the aforementioned method, stood four yojanas in height.

Here ends the Chronicle of the Buddha Siddhāttha.
**********
## 17. Chronicle of the Buddha Tissa
After the aeon in which the Buddha Siddhāttha appeared had ended, the immediately following aeon was a Suñña-kappa (empty aeon) in which no Buddha appeared. Having passed that empty aeon, counting back from this present aeon, in the ninety-second aeon, two Buddhas appeared: (1) the Buddha Tissa and (2) the Buddha Phussa. (This was a Maṇḍa-kappa.)

Regarding the history of the Buddha Tissa among those two Buddhas: In that ninety-second aeon, when the human lifespan decreased from an incalculable period (asaṅkhyeyya) and reached one hundred thousand years, the Bodhisatta Tissa, having fulfilled the perfections, was dwelling in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and Brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and
358:
was conceived in the womb of Queen Padumā, the chief consort of King Janasandha in the royal city of Khemaka. When ten months were complete, he was born in the park named Anoma.

(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and great wonders clearly appeared.)

The wise omen-readers and the relatives named the Bodhisatta prince 'Prince Tissa'. (In naming, there are two types: Anvatta-nāma [descriptive name] and Ruḷhī-nāma [conventional name]. A name given based on a specific reason or special meaning is called Anvatta-nāma. A name given for the sake of convenience without a specific reason or special meaning is called Ruḷhī-nāma. Here, the naming of the Bodhisatta as Prince Tissa should be understood as a Ruḷhī-nāma.)

## Reigning over the Kingdom
When the Bodhisatta Prince Tissa reached the proper age, he lived in three golden palaces: (1) the palace named Guhāsela, (2) the palace named Nārisaya, and (3) the palace named Nisabha. He enjoyed royal splendor comparable to celestial bliss for seven thousand (7,000) years, being entertained and attended to by thirty thousand (30,000) ladies-in-waiting, headed by Queen Subhaddā.

## Renunciation
While reigning over the kingdom, the Bodhisatta Prince Tissa saw the four great omens. When Queen Subhaddā
359:
gave birth to a son named Ānanda, he renounced the world riding the noble horse named Sonuttara and became a monk. Following the example of the Bodhisatta prince, ten million men also became monks.

## Attaining Buddhahood
The Bodhisatta Tissa, together with those ten million monks, practiced asceticism (dukkara-cariyā) for eight months. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become a Buddha, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of the merchant named Vīra from the market town named Vīra. He spent the day in the great pine forest in that area. In the evening, while proceeding alone to the Mahābodhi seat, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a guard of a barley field named Vijitasaṅgāma. As soon as he spread the grass at the foot of the Mahābodhi (Asana/Pitaunk) tree, an Unconquerable Seat (Aparājita-pallaṅka) measuring forty (40) cubits appeared. Sitting cross-legged upon that seat, he attained Buddhahood according to the method previously described.

## The Three Great Dhamma Assemblies
After becoming a Buddha, the Buddha Tissa stayed near the Mahābodhi tree for the seven-seven days (sattasattāha), forty-nine days. Accepting the request of the Brahma King to preach the Dhamma, he considered, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He saw that Prince Brahmadeva and Prince Udaya, who lived in the city of Yasavatī, together with their
360:
retinue, were endowed with past merits for attaining the paths and fruits. He traveled through the air in an instant and descended in the great park named Migadāya near the city of Yasavatī. He sent the park keeper to summon the two princes. When they arrived in his presence, with the two princes as the leaders of the assembly, he preached the Dhammacakka discourse, which all Buddhas of the past have preached, to the devas and humans who had come to listen. He spoke with a voice like that of a Brahma, sweet and pervasive, reaching throughout the ten thousand world systems. At the end of the discourse, one hundred crore humans, devas, and Brahmas attained the special Dhamma of the paths and fruits.

(This was the first great occasion of the realization of the Dhamma [Dhammābhisamaya].)

Thereafter, on another occasion, the ten million monks who had renounced the world together with the Bodhisatta Tissa (who had gone elsewhere when the Bodhisatta proceeded to the Mahābodhi tree), heard that the Buddha Tissa had preached the Dhammacakka discourse. They came to the Migadāya park near Yasavatī, paid respectful homage to the Buddha, and sat surrounding him. Then, the Buddha Tissa preached the Dhamma to the veneyyas (those ready to be tamed), with those monks at the head. Ninety crore beings, led by those ten million monks, attained the special Dhamma of the paths and fruits.

(This was the second great occasion of the realization of the Dhamma.)

Thereafter, on another occasion, many humans and devas discussed and debated, "What are the noble blessings (mangala) that lead to prosperity and success in the world?"
361:
However, they could not reach a consensus on the nature of blessings that everyone could accept. They held a meeting and submitted the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha then preached the Mangala Sutta to the assembly of devas and humans. At the end of the discourse, sixty crore devas and humans attained the special Dhamma of the paths and fruits.

(This was the third great occasion of the realization of the Dhamma.)
**********
## The Three Great Assemblies of Disciples
## The First Assembly (Paṭhama-sannipāta)
There were three great assemblies of the Arahant disciples of the Buddha Tissa. In the first assembly, the Buddha Tissa performed the Visuddhi Pavāraṇā on the full moon day of Thadingyut (Assayuja), surrounded by one hundred thousand Arahants who had become monks at the beginning of the rainy season in the city of Yasavatī and attained Arahantship during the Vassa.

(This was the first great assembly of disciples.)

## The Second Assembly (Dutiya-sannipāta)
Thereafter, on another occasion, in the city of Nārivāhana, Prince Nārivāhana, the son of King Sujāta, went out to welcome the Buddha Tissa when he arrived at the city of Nārivāhana during his travels. He invited the Buddha along with the Sangha and offered the Great Incomparable Alms (Asadisa-dāna) for seven days. After handing over his throne and royal wealth to his son, he requested the Buddha for ordination together with his retinue. The Buddha Tissa then called them with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' formula, and all of them...
362:
They all became 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks. As the news of King Nārivāhana’s renunciation spread in all directions, crowds of people from various places came and followed King Nārivāhana’s example by ordaining. At that time, the Buddha Tissa recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the midst of nine million monks.
(This was the second assembly of disciples.)
## The Third Assembly
Later, on another occasion, having heard the Buddha-vaṃsa discourse preached by the Blessed One at the gathering of his relatives in the city of Khemavatī (Khemaka), eight million people ordained in the presence of the Blessed One and attained Arahantship. Surrounded by those monks, the Buddha Tissa recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.
(This was the third assembly of disciples.)
**********
## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha Becoming the Ascetic Sujāta and Receiving the Prophecy
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a king named Sujāta in the city of Yasavatī. Having renounced his prosperous city, his vast wealth of many millions, and his retinue of people who always sought to approach him with affection—abandoning them all without hesitation as if they were mere grass or reeds—he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), being greatly afraid and terrified of the suffering of birth and so forth, and went forth into the forest.
363:
Having become an ascetic (even before the Buddha Tissa had appeared), he became a highly renowned ascetic of great psychic power and majesty. When he heard the news that 'The Buddha Tissa has appeared in the world,' his body was suffused with the five kinds of joy (pīti). Having approached and paid homage to the Buddha Tissa with great respect and humility, he thought, 'I shall now worship the Blessed One with divine flowers such as the Mandārava and Pāricchattaka flowers.' By means of his psychic power, he went to the celestial realm, entered the Cittalata Grove, and filled a large jeweled basket, about a gāvuta in size, with divine flowers such as Paduma lotuses, Pāricchattaka, and Mandārava flowers. Carrying them through the air, he worshipped the Blessed One with those extremely fragrant divine flowers.
Not only that—he also held a Paduma umbrella over the Blessed One’s head, which was like a parasol, with a handle made of rubies, a top of gold, and leaves of red rubies, fashioned with fragrant filaments, and stood worshipping in the midst of the fourfold assembly. At that time, the Buddha Tissa gave the prophecy to the noble ascetic Sujāta, the Bodhisatta: 'Ninety-two aeons from this present one, this ascetic Sujāta will surely become a Buddha named Gotama.'
(The manner of receiving the prophecy is exactly the same as that received from the Buddha Dīpaṅkara.)
Upon hearing the prophecy of the Buddha Tissa, the Bodhisatta Sujāta, with a heart full of great faith, firmly resolved to further fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).
364:
## Details of the City and Others
The birthplace of the Buddha Tissa was the city of Khemaka. His father was King Janasandha, and his mother was Queen Padumā.
He lived the household life for seven thousand (7,000) years. His three palaces were the golden mansions named Guhāsela, Nārisaya, and Nisabha.
His chief consort was Queen Subhaddā, who had a retinue of thirty thousand ladies-in-waiting. His son was Prince Ānanda.
The vehicle in which he renounced the world after seeing the four great omens was the noble horse named Sonuttara. He practiced asceticism (dukkharacariyā) for eight months.
His two chief male disciples were the Elders Brahmadeva and Udaya. His attendant was the Elder Samaṅga.
His two chief female disciples were the Elder Nuns Phussā and Sudattā. The Bodhi tree under which he attained enlightenment was the Asana (Pitauk) tree.
His chief male lay supporters were the wealthy merchants Sambhala and Sirimā. His chief female lay supporters were the laywomen Kisāgotamī and Upasenā.
The Buddha Tissa was sixty (60) cubits tall. He was beyond compare and without equal, appearing to those who saw him like the great Himavantā mountains.
365:
Endowed with incomparable psychic power and majesty, the lifespan of the Buddha Tissa was neither too short nor too long. The Buddha Tissa, endowed with the five kinds of eyes, remained in the world for a period of one hundred thousand years.
Having dispelled the darkness of ignorance, and having enjoyed a great reputation and fame that was especially praised even among those who are highly noble and praiseworthy, the Buddha Tissa, together with many Arahant disciples, attained Parinibbāna like a great bonfire that, after blazing brightly, has been extinguished.
## The Stupa
Thus, the Buddha Tissa, who had conquered the five Māras, attained Parinibbāna in the great monastery named Nandārāma near the city of Sunandavatī. In that very monastery, the great stupa of the Buddha Tissa, built according to the aforementioned method, was three leagues (yojanas) in height.
The Chronicle of the Buddha Tissa ends.

## 18. The Chronicle of the Buddha Phussa
After the Parinibbāna of the Buddha Tissa, in that same Maṇḍa-kappa, the human lifespan gradually decreased from one hundred thousand years to ten years, then increased again to an incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) period, and then decreased again. When the human lifespan reached ninety thousand (90,000) years, the Bodhisatta Phussa, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), was dwelling in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and Brahmās to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and took conception in the womb of Queen Sirimā, the consort of King Jayasena of the royal city of Kāsika. When ten months were complete, he was born in the garden named Sirimā.
(At the time of the Bodhisatta’s conception and birth, great omens and wonders clearly appeared.)
366:
## Living in the Palace
When the Bodhisatta Phussa reached the proper age, he lived in the three golden palaces: (1) Garuḷapakkhā, (2) Haṃsa, and (3) Suvaṇṇabhāra. He enjoyed a life of luxury similar to that of the devas for nine thousand (9,000) years, being entertained and attended to by thirty thousand (30,000) ladies-in-waiting, headed by Queen Kisāgotamī.
## Renunciation
While living in the palace, the Bodhisatta Phussa saw the four great omens. When his son, Prince Anupama, was born to Queen Kisāgotamī, he renounced the world by riding an elephant and became an ascetic. Following the example of the Bodhisatta prince, ten million men also became ascetics.
367:
## Attaining Buddhahood
The Bodhisatta Phussa practiced asceticism (dukkharacariyā) for six months together with those ten million monks. Then, leaving behind the group of monks who had followed him, he practiced the solitary life for seven days. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become a Buddha, he accepted and partook of the milk-rice offered by Sirivaḍḍhā, the daughter of a merchant from an unnamed town. He spent the day in a grove of Yindaik (or Indian Rosewood) trees in that area. In the evening, he went alone to the Great Bodhi tree. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the ascetic named Sirivaḍḍha. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Great Bodhi (Āmalaka) tree, an Unconquerable Seat (Aparājita-pallaṅka) thirty-eight (38) cubits in size appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that seat, he attained Buddhahood according to the aforementioned method.
## The Three Great Dhamma Assemblies
After becoming a Buddha, the Buddha Phussa stayed near the Great Bodhi (Āmalaka) tree for the seven-week period (sattasattāha = 49 days). Accepting the request of the Great Brahmā to preach the Dhamma, he reflected, 'To whom should I preach the Dhamma first?' He saw that the ten million monks who had ordained with him were endowed with past merits to attain the Paths and Fruits. He traveled through the air to the Migadāya forest called Isipatana near the city of Saṅkassa where those monks resided. In the midst of those monks, he preached the Discourse of the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta), as was the custom of previous Buddhas.
368:
One hundred billion devas and humans attained the special Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits.
(This was the first great Dhamma assembly.)
Later, on another occasion, King Sirivaḍḍha of the city of Bārāṇasī renounced his vast wealth and became an ascetic. Along with that king, nine million people also became ascetics. The Buddha Phussa went to the place where those ascetics were and preached the Dhamma. Nine million beings attained the special Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits.
(This was the second great Dhamma assembly.)
Later, on another occasion, the Buddha Phussa preached the Dhamma to his son, Prince Anupama. At that time, eight million devas and humans attained the special Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits.
(This was the third great Dhamma assembly.)
**********
## The Three Great Assemblies of Disciples
## The First Assembly
There were three great assemblies of the Arahant disciples of the Buddha Phussa. On the first occasion, Prince Surakkhita and Dhammasena, the son of the royal chaplain, who were to become the chief disciples and lived in the city of Kaṇṇakujja, went to meet the Buddha Phussa when he arrived at their city. Together with six million men, they welcomed him, paid homage respectfully, and invited him. After offering a great almsgiving for seven days, they heard the Buddha’s discourse and gained faith in the Blessed One. Those two...

Together with six million men, they renounced the world and attained Arahantship. In the midst of those six million Arahants, the Buddha Phussa recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.
(This was the first assembly of disciples.)
## The Second Assembly
Then, on another occasion, in the royal city of Kāsika, he preached the Buddhavaṃsa discourse to an assembly of his relatives, headed by his father, King Jayasena. Having heard that Buddhavaṃsa discourse, five million people became 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks and attained Arahantship. In that assembly of five million Arahants, the Buddha Phussa recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.
(This was the second assembly of disciples.)
## The Third Assembly
Then, on another occasion, many gods and humans discussed among themselves, "What are the noble blessings (Maṅgala) that lead to prosperity and progress in the world?" However, they could not reach a consensus or understand the nature of blessings that everyone could accept and delight in. Thus, they formed an assembly and requested the Blessed One. When the Blessed One preached the Maṅgala Dhamma to those gods and humans, four million people renounced the world and attained Arahantship upon hearing it. In the midst of those Arahants, the Blessed One recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.
(This was the third assembly of disciples.)
370: ## The Bodhisatta, King Vijitāvī, Becoming a Monk and Receiving the Prophecy. At that time, our Bodhisatta was a king named Vijitāvī in the city of Arindama. Having heard the Dhamma of the Buddha Phussa, he developed great faith in the Buddha. After offering a great donation, he renounced the kingdom and became a monk in the presence of the Buddha. He studied the Tipiṭaka well, became a master of the Tipiṭaka, and preached the Dhamma to the masses. He also perfectly fulfilled the Perfections of Virtue (Sīla Pāramī). Then, the Buddha Phussa, the noble leader and guide of the three worlds, gave a prophecy to the noble monk Vijitāvī, saying: "In the ninety-second aeon from this one, this monk Vijitāvī will surely become a Buddha named Gotama." (The manner of receiving the prophecy is exactly as detailed as the prophecy given by the Buddha Dīpaṅkara.) Upon hearing the prophecy of the Buddha Phussa, the noble monk Vijitāvī, with a heart full of great faith, firmly resolved to further fulfill the ten Perfections. Having become a monk in the dispensation of the Buddha Phussa, the Great Being mastered the nine-fold scriptures (Pariyatti) of the Buddha, including the Suttas and Vinaya, and brought splendor to the Buddha's dispensation.
371:
473
(Without ever lying down) he practiced the meditation on the four sublime states (Brahmavihāra) in the three postures of sitting, standing, and walking. He reached the pinnacle of not only the eight attainments but also the five super-knowledges, and at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma realm.
## Description of the City and Others
The birthplace of the Buddha Phussa was the city of Kāsika; his father was King Jayasena, and his mother was Queen Sirimā.
He reigned for 9,000 years, and his three palaces were Garuḷapakkha, Haṃsa, and Suvaṇṇabhāra.
His chief consort was Queen Kisāgotamī, who had 30,000 attendant ladies, and his son was Prince Anupama.
The vehicle he used to renounce the world after seeing the four great omens was an elephant, and he practiced austerities (dukkharacariyā) for six months.
His pair of chief disciples were the Elder Surakkhita and the Elder Dhammasena, and his attendant was the Elder Sabhiya.
His pair of chief female disciples were the Elder Cālā and the Elder Upacālā, and the Bodhi tree under which he attained enlightenment was the Sirīsa tree.
372:

His chief male lay supporters were the wealthy merchant Dhanañjaya and the wealthy merchant Visākha, and his chief female lay supporters were the laywomen Padumā and Nāgā.
The Buddha Phussa was 58 cubits tall, as radiant as the sun, and endowed with delightful qualities like the moon.
The lifespan during the time of the Buddha Phussa was 90,000 years, and he remained for that long (four-fifths of the lifespan), rescuing many beings—humans, devas, and brahmas—from the current of Saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna.
Having disciplined many beings and rescued many devas and humans from the current of Saṃsāra, the Buddha Phussa, who was endowed with incomparable retinue and fame, attained Parinibbāna and passed away along with many Arahant disciples.
## The Stupa
Thus, the Buddha Phussa, having conquered the five Maras, attained Parinibbāna in a large monastery named Sena near the city of Kusinārā. According to his resolution, the relics were dispersed into fragments as mentioned before and were enshrined throughout the island of Jambudīpa, receiving the offerings of humans, devas, and brahmas.
The Chronicle of the Buddha Phussa is finished.

## 19. The Chronicle of the Buddha Vipassī
After the aeon in which the Buddha Phussa appeared had ended, counting back from this present aeon, the Buddha Vipassī appeared in the 91st aeon. As for the account of that Buddha Vipassī...
In that 91st aeon, when the human lifespan had decreased from an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) to 80,000 years, the Bodhisatta Vipassī, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), was residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of Queen Bandhumatī, the chief consort of King Bandhuma in the royal city of Bandhumatī. When ten months were complete, he was born in the Migadāya (Deer Park) named Khema, which was a sanctuary for deer and thus worthy of being called a deer forest.
(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonders clearly appeared.)
## Great Extraordinary Feature
When the Bodhisatta prince was born, a divine white umbrella always remained spread over him, day and night, wherever he went or stayed, so that cold, heat, grass, dust, and dewdrops could not fall upon or afflict him. He was someone who was always loved and...
374:
476
...delighted in by all people. Without his feet touching the ground, he was passed from one lap to another and nurtured to growth.
## The Name Vipassī
Immediately upon his birth, the Bodhisatta possessed eyes born of the fruit of kamma (kamma-vipākaja), which had the power to see like divine eyes. With these eyes, the Bodhisatta could see clearly for one yojana all around, day or night, without any obstruction. Just as the devas in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven look with eyes that never blink, the Bodhisatta prince, from the time of his birth, never closed his eyes and always looked with open eyes. Based on this, he became famous by the name "Prince Vipassī."
Furthermore, one day, while his father, King Bandhuma, was judging a case in the court of justice, the prince was adorned and presented to the King. While King Bandhuma held his son on his lap and was fondling him, the ministers unjustly decided against the rightful owner of the property. The Bodhisatta prince let out a loud cry of dissatisfaction and grief. When the King said, "What is the reason for my son's behavior? Investigate it," they investigated but saw no other reason, thinking, "It must be because the court ministers decided unjustly." So, they decided the case justly, restoring the property to the rightful owner.
375:
477
When the case was decided justly, the Bodhisatta prince was satisfied and stopped crying. To test if the prince truly knew, they decided unjustly again. The Bodhisatta prince again let out a loud cry of dissatisfaction and grief as before. Then, King Bandhuma firmly believed, "The Bodhisatta prince truly knows what is just and what is unjust." From that time on, the King ruled and governed justly without negligence.
From then on, the name "Prince Vipassī" became even more famous, based on his ability to "investigate and clearly distinguish between what is just and what is unjust."
## Reigning over the Kingdom
When the Bodhisatta Vipassī reached maturity, he lived in three golden palaces: (1) Nanda, (2) Sunanda, and (3) Sirimā. He enjoyed divine-like luxury and happiness for 8,000 years, being entertained and served by 120,000 attendant ladies, headed by Queen Sudassanā (alternatively, Queen Sutanu).
## Appearance of the Four Great Omens
The Bodhisatta Vipassī one day called his charioteer and gave the order, "I wish to see the park grounds; I will go out to the park." While he was riding the chariot to the park, on the way...
376: Upon seeing the old man created by the devas (a strange sight for the Bodhisatta prince who had never seen an old person before), he asked, "Friend charioteer, what is this man doing? His hair and body are unlike those of others." The charioteer replied, "Your Majesty, this person is called an old man." Then the Bodhisatta, truly not knowing the state of an old man, asked, "Friend charioteer, what is an old man?" The charioteer replied, "Your Majesty, this person is indeed called an old man. He will not live much longer now." The Bodhisatta prince then asked, "Friend charioteer, am I also subject to old age? Am I unable to escape old age?" The charioteer replied, "Your Majesty, all of us, including yourself, are subject to old age; we cannot escape it." Then the Bodhisatta prince said, "Friend charioteer, if that is so, I no longer wish to see the garden. Return to the palace from this very spot." Upon returning to the palace, the Bodhisatta prince reflected, "Oh, the nature of birth (jāti) is truly loathsome and wearying. If birth exists, the nature of old age (jarā) will surely manifest without fail." He remained brooding and unhappy. When the Great King, his father, summoned the charioteer and learned the reason, he provided the Bodhisatta prince...
377: ...with even more fivefold sensual pleasures than before, hoping to prevent him from renouncing the world. After thousands of years had passed, on his second trip to the garden, he similarly saw a sick person on the way. As before, he did not proceed to the garden but returned to the palace and remained brooding and unhappy. When the King heard of this, he provided even more fivefold sensual pleasures. After thousands of years had passed, on his third trip to the garden, he saw a corpse on the way and returned to the palace as before. After thousands of years had passed, on his fourth trip to the garden, he saw a monk on the way. He questioned the charioteer about the monk, and upon hearing the explanation, he was greatly pleased and directed the chariot toward the monk. Upon reaching the monk, he inquired about the benefits and was so delighted with the state of monkhood that he called the charioteer and said, "Friend charioteer, take this chariot and return it to the palace. As for me, I shall ordain as a monk right here." He then sent the charioteer back. That day was the day Queen Sudassanā gave birth to a son named Samavattakkhandha.
378:
480
After sending the charioteer back, the Bodhisatta Vipassī shaved his hair and beard and put on saffron-dyed robes at that very spot, renouncing the world. (Although there is no mention here of how he obtained the bowl and robes, it should be understood that, according to the nature of Bodhisattas, the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas descended and offered them.)
At that time, 84,000 residents of Bandhumatī city heard the news of the Bodhisatta Vipassī's renunciation and followed his example by becoming monks themselves.
## Becoming a Buddha
While the Bodhisatta Vipassī was wandering through villages, market towns, cities, and kingdoms, accompanied by those 84,000 monks, he became weary of the great offerings of food made by the people in large pavilions at every place he reached. On the 14th day of the waxing moon of Kasone (Vesākha), eight months after his renunciation, a thought arose in the Bodhisatta's mind: "It is not suitable for me to live mixed with a retinue. It would be better if I lived alone, separated from this crowd." Having separated from the crowd, on the following day, the full moon day of Kasone (the day he would become a Buddha), he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of the wealthy merchant Sudassana. After spending the day in the nearby Sal forest, he proceeded to the Mahābodhi seat in the evening. On the way...
379:
Having accepted the eight handfuls of grass offered by the barley-field guard named Sujāta, as soon as they were spread at the foot of the Pāṭalī Bodhi tree, the Aparājita-pallaṅka (Unconquered Throne) measuring fifty-three cubits appeared.

The main trunk of that Pāṭalī Bodhi tree was fifty cubits high on the day the Bodhisatta arrived, and the branches extending upwards were also fifty cubits, making the total height one hundred cubits. On that very day, the Pāṭalī Bodhi tree was covered from its base to the top with flowers that were as evenly arranged as if they were sewn together, possessing an extremely fragrant scent. It was also filled with a divine fragrance. On that day, not only the Pāṭalī Bodhi tree but all the trees, shrubs, and creepers within the ten thousand world systems also bloomed.

Sitting cross-legged upon that Aparājita-pallaṅka and establishing the fourfold effort (viriya), He attained Buddhahood in the manner previously described.

## Three Great Assemblies of Dhamma

After becoming a Buddha, the Buddha Vipassī stayed near the Mahābodhi (Pāṭalī) tree for the Satta-sattāha (forty-nine days). Having accepted the request of the Great Brahma to preach the Dhamma, He considered, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He then saw that Prince Khaṇḍa, His half-brother, and Tissa, the son of the chaplain, who were destined to be the chief disciples, were endowed with past merits for attaining the Path and Fruition...
380: ...to attain the Paths and Fruits. Thinking, "I shall preach the Dhamma to them first," he traveled through the air in an instant to the Khema Deer Park (Migadāya), a sanctuary for deer near the city of Bandhumatī. He sent a gardener to summon the prince and the chaplain's son. When the two arrived, he began with excellent advice and instructions on the suitability of ordaining as monks. Then, together with the assembly of devas and Brahmas who had gathered at that moment, he preached the Discourse of the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) to the two of them, as is the custom of all previous Buddhas. Starting with the prince and the chaplain's son, countless devas and Brahmas attained the special Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits. In particular, Prince Khaṇḍa and Tissa, the chaplain's son, who were to be the chief disciples, became "Ehi Bhikkhu" monks in the presence of the Blessed One and soon became Arahants. (This is the first great assembly of the realization of Dhamma.) Subsequently, eighty-four thousand men of Bandhumatī City heard the news: "The Blessed One Vipassī has arrived and is staying in the Khema Deer Park near Bandhumatī. Prince Khaṇḍa and the youth Tissa, the chaplain's son, have also ordained in the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī." Following their example, they also ordained as monks. To those eighty-four thousand who had ordained following the example, the Blessed One Vipassī administered the deathless medicine of the Dhamma. (This is the second great assembly of the realization of Dhamma.)
381: The eighty-four thousand people who had been attendants and followers of the Blessed One Vipassī while he was still a prince had come to pay respects to Prince Vipassī early in the morning on the day he went to the fourth garden. Not seeing the prince at the palace, they went back for breakfast. After eating, they asked, "Where is the prince?" and hearing that he had gone to the garden, they set out, saying, "We shall see the prince at the garden." On the way, they met the charioteer whom Prince Vipassī had sent back. Upon hearing the news of Prince Vipassī's ordination, they discarded all the lay ornaments they were wearing right there, bought robes from the market, shaved their hair and beards, and ordained as monks. After ordaining, those eighty-four thousand monks who followed his example went to the Bodhisatta Vipassī and remained surrounding him. The Bodhisatta practiced asceticism (dukkara-cariyā) for eight months while surrounded by those monks. On the fourteenth day of the waxing moon of Kason, the day before he would become Buddha, he thought: "I am living mixed with followers. Just as I wandered with these eighty-four thousand people as my retinue while I was a prince, it is not suitable for me to live with them as my retinue now. What benefit is there for me in this group of followers?" Becoming weary of delighting in company, he planned, "I shall leave this group of followers this very day." Then he thought again, "There is no more time today. If I go today, all these monks...
382: ...will know. I shall go only tomorrow." For the next day, in a village similar in appearance to Uruvelā village of our Buddha's time, the villagers invited the Bodhisatta along with his retinue and prepared thick milk-rice to offer to the Bodhisatta and his eighty-four thousand followers. Then, on the following day, the Full Moon of Kason, the day he would become Buddha, the Bodhisatta Vipassī partook of the meal in that village together with the monks of his retinue and then returned to his forest monastery. Upon reaching the forest monastery, after the monks who followed his example had performed the duties toward the Bodhisatta and entered their respective places for the day and night, the Bodhisatta entered his small leaf-roofed hut and thought, "This is the most suitable time to leave." He came out, closed the door of the leaf-roofed hut, and headed toward the Mahābodhi seat. Those monks who followed his example also went to attend upon the Bodhisatta in the evening. They surrounded the leaf-roofed hut, hoping to see the Bodhisatta. After a long time had passed, they said, "It has been a long time; let us investigate." When they opened the door of the leaf-roofed hut and looked, they did not see the Bodhisatta. Thinking, "Where has the Bodhisatta gone?" they did not make any attempt to search for him at all, [thinking] "The Bodhisatta..."
383:
He seemed to desire to dwell alone, being weary of living in a group or company. Thinking, "We shall see the Bodhisatta only when he becomes a Buddha," they turned and wandered towards the interior of Jambudīpa.

Thereafter, those eighty-four thousand (84,000) followers heard the news, "Prince Vipassī has become a Buddha and has preached the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka)." Consequently, all those monks arrived in succession and assembled in the great Khema Migadāya park near the royal city of Bandhumatī. At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī preached the Dhamma to those eighty-four thousand followers, and all eighty-four thousand followers attained the special Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits.

(This is the Third Awakening, the third great assembly of Dhamma.)

**********
## Three Great Assemblies of Disciples
## Paṭhama Sannipāta
There were three great assemblies of the Arahant disciples of the Blessed One Vipassī. In the first assembly, the Blessed One Vipassī showed the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the midst of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand (168,000) monks, comprising the eighty-four thousand monks who had ordained following the Bodhisatta's example in the Khema Migadāya park, and the eighty-four thousand monks who had ordained following the example of the Chief Disciples-to-be, Prince Khaṇḍa and the Brahmin youth Tissa.

(This is the first great assembly of disciples.)
384:
## Dutiya Sannipāta
Thereafter, at another time, there was an assembly of one hundred thousand monks who had ordained after witnessing the Blessed One perform the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) of water and fire.

(This is the second great assembly of disciples.)

## Tatiya Sannipāta
Thereafter, at another time, three royal brothers, who were half-brothers of the Blessed One Vipassī, returned after suppressing a rebellion in the border regions. The Great King, their father, being pleased with his three sons, granted them a boon, saying, "Ask for any boon you desire." The royal brothers thought, "We have the opportunity to ask for a boon; we need no other boon but the privilege to serve our elder brother, the Blessed One." Having received permission from their father, they invited the Blessed One to their respective territories to perform acts of service and offerings. The Blessed One went there and, while accepting the offerings and honor of the three brothers, preached the Dhamma, whereby eighty thousand people became Ehi Bhikkhu monks and attained Arahantship.

The Blessed One Vipassī, surrounded by those eighty thousand Arahants in the Khema Migadāya park, showed the Ovāda Pātimokkha.

(This is the third great assembly of disciples.)
385:
## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha as Atula the Naga King Receiving the Prophecy
At that time, our Blessed One's Bodhisatta was Atula, a Naga King of great power and majesty. Surrounded by many millions of nagas and accompanied by celestial musical instruments, he approached the Blessed One Vipassī, the Chief of the Three Worlds. To perform an act of worship and honor to the Blessed One and the surrounding Saṅgha, he invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. He constructed a great pavilion adorned with the essence of jewels, as beautiful as the full moon and made of the seven kinds of gems. Within that pavilion, he seated the noble Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and offered a great alms-giving for seven days. He also offered to the Blessed One a golden throne (pallaṅka) inlaid with the seven kinds of gems, fit only for noble persons and adorned with all kinds of ornaments.

The Blessed One Vipassī, residing in the midst of the Saṅgha, preached the Dhamma of appreciation (Anumodanā) for that gift. At the conclusion, he gave the prophecy (Vyākaraṇa) to the Bodhisatta Atula the Naga King, saying: "In the ninety-first aeon from this present one, this Atula the Naga King will surely become a Buddha named Gotama."

(The manner of receiving the prophecy is as detailed as the prophecy received from the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara.)

Upon hearing the prophecy of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Bodhisatta Atula the Naga King, with a very clear and devout mind, firmly resolved to further fulfill the Ten Perfections (Pāramīs).
386:
## Description of the City and Other Details
The birthplace of the Blessed One Vipassī was the royal city of Bandhumatī. His father was King Bandhuma, and his mother was Queen Bandhumatī.

He reigned for eight thousand (8,000) years. His three palaces were Nanda, Sunanda, and Sirimā.

His Chief Queen was Sudassanā, who had one hundred and twenty thousand (120,000) attendants. His son was Prince Samavattakkhandha.

After seeing the four great omens, the vehicle in which he renounced the world was a horse-drawn chariot. He practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for eight months.

His pair of Chief Disciples were the Elder Khaṇḍa and the Elder Tissa. His personal attendant was the Elder Asoka.

His pair of Chief Female Disciples were the Elder Candā and the Elder Candamittā. The Bodhi tree where he attained enlightenment was the Pāṭalī (Thakhut) tree.

His noble male lay supporters were the merchant Punabbasumitta and the merchant Nāga. His noble female lay supporters were the laywoman Sirimā and the laywoman Uttarā.

The height of the Blessed One Vipassī, the leader of the three worlds, was eighty (80) cubits. His aura (byāma-pabhā) extended seven leagues (yojanas) all around, radiating here and there. (This refers to his natural physical aura.)
387:
The lifespan during which the Blessed One Vipassī appeared was eighty thousand (80,000) years. He remained for that duration (four-fifths of the lifespan), rescuing many beings—humans, devas, and brahmas—from the current of Saṃsāra and bringing them to the dry land of Nibbāna.

The Blessed One Vipassī liberated many devas and humans from the bonds of defilements (kilesas). For the worldlings (puthujjanas) other than the Noble Ones (Ariyas), he revealed and distinguished the Middle Way (Majjhima Paṭipadā) leading to Nibbāna from the two base paths that are not the way to Nibbāna.

Having shown the light of Dhamma and preached Nibbāna, the state free from death, the Blessed One Vipassī, like a great fire that has blazed brightly and then gone out, attained Parinibbāna and ceased along with his many Arahant disciples.

## Saṃvega
The noble power, the noble glory, and the noble physical body (rūpa-kāya) of the Blessed One Vipassī, adorned with the marks of the wheel and other signs—all have ceased and vanished. Indeed, all conditioned things (saṅkhāras) are without permanent essence and are only empty.

## The Stupa
In this way, the Blessed One Vipassī, the conqueror of the five Maras, attained Parinibbāna within the great park named Sumitta.
388:
The great stupa of the Blessed One Vipassī, built within that great park, was seven leagues (yojanas) in height.

The Chronicle of Vipassī Buddha ends.

**********
## 20. The Chronicle of Sikhī Buddha
After the aeon (kappa) in which the Blessed One Vipassī appeared had ended, for fifty-nine (59) aeons, no Buddhas appeared in the world. These were only empty aeons (suñña-kappa), devoid of the light of Dhamma and shrouded in the darkness of ignorance (avijjā). During this time, Devaputta Māra and Kilesa Māra acted as absolute monarchs in the world without any obstacles or thorns. Beings had to follow the will of these two Māras.

Passing those fifty-nine empty aeons, and counting back from this present aeon, thirty-one aeons ago, two Buddhas appeared: (1) the Blessed One Sikhī and (2) the Blessed One Vessabhū. (This was a Maṇḍa-kappa.)

Regarding the history of the first of those two Buddhas, the Blessed One Sikhī: in that thirty-first aeon, when the human lifespan had decreased from an incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) period to seventy thousand (70,000) years, the Bodhisatta Sikhī, having fulfilled the Perfections, was residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and took conception in the womb of Queen Pabhāvatī, the consort of King Aruna in the royal city of Arunavatī.
389:
When the ten months were complete, he was born in the park named Nisabha.

(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonders clearly appeared.)

On the day the Bodhisatta prince was named by the wise omen-readers and relatives, they named him Prince Sikhī because the crest (uṣṇīṣa) on his head was raised like the crest of a peacock.

## Reigning over the Kingdom
When the Bodhisatta Prince Sikhī reached maturity, he resided in three golden palaces: (1) Sucandaka, (2) Giri, and (3) Vasabha. He enjoyed pleasures equal to celestial bliss for seven thousand (7,000) years, served and entertained by twenty-four thousand (24,000) attendants headed by Queen Sabbakāmā.

## Renunciation
While reigning over the kingdom, the Bodhisatta Prince Sikhī saw the four great omens. When Queen Sabbakāmā gave birth to a son named Atula, he renounced the world by riding an elephant and became a monk. Following the example of the Bodhisatta prince, seven million men also became monks.
390:
## Attainment of Buddhahood

The Bodhisatta Sikhī, after practicing asceticism for eight months together with those seven million monks who had followed him, on the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), the day he was to become a Buddha, left the company of those monks. He accepted and partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of the merchant Piyadassī in the market town of Sudassana. Having spent the day in the young khadirā forest in that area, he proceeded alone towards the Mahābodhi seat in the evening. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the ascetic named Anomadassī. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Mahābodhi (White Mango) tree, the Aparājita Throne, thirty-two cubits in size, appeared.

The dimensions of that White Mango Bodhi tree were equal to the Sal tree Bodhi of the previous Buddha Vipassī. On the day the Bodhisatta reached it, the main trunk of that White Mango Bodhi tree was fifty cubits high, and the branches spreading upwards were also fifty cubits. The entire tree appeared as if covered with celestial scents and flowers. Not only with flowers, but it also appeared as if covered with fruits. On one side of that White Mango Bodhi tree, there were tender fruits; on another side, medium-sized fruits; and on another side, appropriately ripe fruits, which possessed an excellent taste as if filled with celestial essence, being complete in color, fragrance, and flavor, and were hanging here and there. Just like that White Mango Bodhi tree,
391:
on that day, all the fruiting and flowering trees within the ten thousand world systems bore fruit and blossomed.

The Bodhisatta, sitting cross-legged upon that Aparājita Throne and resolving with fourfold energy, attained Buddhahood in the manner previously described.

## Three Great Assemblies of Teaching

After becoming a Buddha, the Buddha Sikhī stayed near the Mahābodhi White Mango tree for the seven-week period (forty-nine days). Having accepted the request of the Great Brahma to preach the Dhamma, He reflected, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He saw that the seven million monks who had been his companions in renunciation were endowed with past merit for attaining the Path and Fruit. He traveled through the air and descended into the Migādaya Grove near the royal city of Arunavatī, where those monks resided. Sitting gracefully in the midst of those seven million monks, He preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which is the tradition of all previous Buddhas, to the devas and humans who had come to listen. At that time, one hundred billion devas and humans attained the special Dhamma of the Path and Fruit.

(This was the first great assembly of the Dhamma, the first Dhammābhisamaya.)

Thereafter, on another occasion, near the royal city of Arunavatī, He preached the Dhamma to Prince Abhibhū and Prince Sambhava, who were to become the Chief Disciples, along with their retinues and followers.
392:
He administered the nectar of Dhamma to ninety billion devas and humans.

(This was the second great assembly of the Dhamma, the second Dhammābhisamaya.)

Thereafter, on another occasion, near the city gate of Suriyavatī, by a campaka tree, He performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire to subdue the pride of the heretics and to liberate all the people from the bonds of defilements. While He was preaching the Dhamma, eighty billion devas and humans attained the special Dhamma of the Path and Fruit.

(This was the third great assembly of the Dhamma, the third Dhammābhisamaya.)

**********

## Three Great Assemblies of Disciples

## First Congregation (Paṭhama Sannipāta)

There were three great assemblies of the Arahant disciples of the Buddha Sikhī. In the first instance, the Buddha Sikhī presided in the midst of one hundred thousand Arahants who had renounced together with Prince Abhibhū and Prince Sambhava, and He recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.

(This was the first great assembly of disciples.)

## Second Congregation (Dutiya Sannipāta)

Thereafter, on another occasion, He presided in the midst of eighty thousand monks who had renounced during the great assembly of His relatives in the city of Arunavatī, and the Buddha Sikhī recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.

(This was the second great assembly of disciples.)
393:
## Third Congregation (Tatiya Sannipāta)

Thereafter, on another occasion, He presided in the midst of seventy thousand monks who had renounced when He tamed the noble elephant named Nepālaka in the city of Dhanañjaya, and the Buddha Sikhī recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.

(This was the third great assembly of disciples.)

**********

## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha becoming King Arindama and Receiving the Prophecy

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a great king named Arindama in the city named Paribhutta. When the Buddha Sikhī arrived at the city of Paribhutta, King Arindama, along with his retinue and followers, went out to welcome the Buddha. Having bowed and paid respects with great devotion, he invited the Buddha and, for seven days at the palace, he performed a great alms-giving in a manner consistent with his royal power, noble lineage, wealth, and the quality of his faith (so that no one could find fault).

Opening the storehouses where clothes were kept, he offered many millions (koṭis) of very costly garments to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. (In worldly terms, twenty sets of clothes are called one koṭi; however, here, ten sets of clothes should be understood as one koṭi. — From Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 3, 270.)
394:
Not only that, he also offered to the Buddha his royal state elephant, which was endowed with strength, beauty, auspicious marks, and speed, and was adorned with golden nets and golden flowers. (Having valued that elephant along with its ornaments, he then offered) allowable requisites (kappiya-vatthu) of equal value to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.

At that time, the Buddha Sikhī gave the prophecy to the Bodhisatta King Arindama, saying: "In the thirty-first aeon from this one, this King Arindama will surely become a Buddha named Gotama."

(The manner of receiving the prophecy is complete and detailed, just as the prophecy received from the Buddha Dīpaṅkara.)

Upon hearing the prophecy of the Buddha Sikhī, the Bodhisatta King Arindama, with a very clear and joyful mind, firmly resolved to further fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

## Details of the City, etc.

The birthplace of the Buddha Sikhī was the royal city of Arunavatī. His father was King Aruna, and His mother was Queen Pabhāvatī.

The number of years He reigned as a king was seven thousand (7,000). His three palaces were the Sucandaka Golden Palace, the Giri Golden Palace, and the Vasabha Golden Palace.

His Chief Queen was Queen Sabbakāmā, who had twenty-four thousand (24,000) attendants. His son was Prince Atula.
395:
The vehicle He used for His renunciation after seeing the four great omens was an elephant. He practiced asceticism for eight months.

His pair of Chief Disciples were the Elder Abhibhū and the Elder Sambhava. His attendant was the Elder Khemankara.

His pair of Female Chief Disciples were the Elder Nun Sakhilā and the Elder Nun Padumā. The Bodhi tree under which He attained enlightenment was the White Mango Bodhi tree.

His noble male lay supporters were the merchant Sirivaḍḍha and the merchant Nanda. His noble female lay supporters were the laywoman Cittā and the laywoman Suguttā.

The Buddha Sikhī was seventy cubits in height, resembling a great golden pillar prepared for worship, and was graceful with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

The natural aura of the Buddha Sikhī's body radiated and spread for three yojanas in all directions, day and night without interruption. (If He so desired, it could shine through as many world systems as He wished.)

The lifespan during the time of the Buddha Sikhī was seventy thousand (70,000) years. Remaining for that long (four-fifths of the lifespan), He rescued and liberated many beings—humans, devas, and brahmas—from the current of Saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna.
396:
Causing the great rain of Dhamma to fall and moistening beings, including devas, with the pure water of Dhamma discourse, He led them to Nibbāna, the end of the suffering of the round of rebirths. Then, together with many Arahant disciples, the Buddha Sikhī entered Parinibbāna and passed away.

## Sense of Urgency (Saṃvega)

The entire physical body (rūpakāya) of the Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks such as reddish fingernails and toenails, has all ceased and vanished. Indeed, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) have no stable essence; they are merely empty.

## The Stupa

The Buddha Sikhī entered Parinibbāna at the great grove named Assa near the city of Sīlavatī. The relics of the Buddha remained in a single mass, not dispersed. The people of Jambudīpa built and worshipped a great stupa three yojanas high, made of the seven kinds of jewels (as beautiful as Mount Meru).

The Chronicle of Sikhī Buddha ends.

**********

## 21. Chronicle of Vessabhū Buddha

After the Buddha Sikhī passed into Parinibbāna, in that same Maṇḍa-kappa aeon where two Buddhas appeared, the human lifespan gradually
397:
decreased to ten years, then increased again to an incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) period, and then decreased again. When the human lifespan reached sixty thousand (60,000) years, the Bodhisatta Vessabhū, having fulfilled the perfections, was residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of Queen Yasavatī, the consort of King Suppatīta of the royal city of Anoma. When ten months were complete, he was born in the grove named Anupama.

(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonders clearly appeared.)

Because he made a noble sound that delighted many people at the time of his birth, on the day he was named, the relatives and wise omen-readers named him Prince Vessabhū. (The "noble sound" refers to the three great utterances beginning with "Aggo hamasmi lokassa.")

## Reigning over the Kingdom

When the Bodhisatta Prince Vessabhū reached maturity, he lived in the three golden palaces: (1) Rucī Golden Palace, (2) Surucī Golden Palace, and (3) Rativaḍḍhana Golden Palace. He was entertained and attended by thirty thousand (30,000) ladies-in-waiting, headed by Queen Sucittā, for a period of six thousand (6,000) years.
398:
500
He reigned over the kingdom, enjoying prosperity and happiness equal to that of divine bliss.

## Renunciation

While the Bodhisatta Prince Vessabhū was reigning, he saw the four great omens. When his son, named Suppabuddha, was born to the chief queen Sucittā, he departed for the royal garden on a golden palanquin. There, he received the robes offered by Brahma and became a monk. Following the example of the Bodhisatta prince's renunciation, thirty-seven thousand men also became monks.

## Attaining Buddhahood

The Bodhisatta Vessabhū practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) together with those thirty-seven thousand monks for six months. On the full moon day of Kason, the day he was to become a Buddha, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by a lady named Sirivaḍḍhanā from the village of Sucitta. He spent the day in the Sāla grove in that area, and in the evening, he proceeded alone to the Mahābodhi site. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the Naga king named Narinda. As soon as he spread them at the foot of the Mahābodhi (Sāla) tree, the Aparājita-pallaṅka measuring forty cubits appeared.

(The dimensions and beauty of the Sāla Bodhi tree should be understood in the same manner as described for the Pāṭalī Bodhi tree of the Buddha Vipassī.)
399:
501
Sitting cross-legged upon that Aparājita-pallaṅka and establishing the fourfold effort, the Bodhisatta attained Buddhahood in the manner previously described.

## Three Great Assemblies of Dhamma

After becoming a Buddha, the Buddha Vessabhū stayed near the Mahābodhi (Sāla) tree for the Satta-sattāha (forty-nine days). Having accepted the request of the Great Brahma to preach the Dhamma, He considered, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He then saw that His two younger half-brothers, Prince Soṇa and Prince Uttara, who were destined to be the chief disciples, were endowed with past merits for attaining the Path and Fruition. He traveled through the air and descended at the great garden named Aruṇa near the city of Anupama. He sent the gardener to summon the two royal brothers. In the midst of those princes and their retinue, He preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, as is the custom of all previous Buddhas. Many devas and Brahmas also came and listened respectfully. In that great assembly of Dhamma, eighty koṭis of devas and humans attained the special realization of the Path and Fruition.

(This is the first great assembly of Dhamma, the first Dhammābhisamaya.)

Thereafter, on another occasion, while the Buddha Vessabhū was traveling on a dhammadūta journey to the large towns known as janapadas within the country, He preached the Dhamma in various places, and seventy koṭis of devas and humans attained the special realization of the Path and Fruition.

(This is the second great assembly of Dhamma, the second Dhammābhisamaya.)
400:
502
Thereafter, on another occasion, in the city of Anupama itself, the Buddha Vessabhū dispelled the complex and many erroneous wrong views, humbled the pride of the heretics, and hoisted the banner of the Noble Dhamma. In a great gathering of a human audience assembled in an area nine yojanas wide, and an immeasurable number of devas and Brahmas, He performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) of water and fire to increase the faith of devas and humans. He then nourished and comforted sixty koṭis of devas and humans with the ambrosia of the Dhamma. (This means sixty koṭis of devas and humans attained liberation.)

(This is the third great assembly of Dhamma, the third Dhammābhisamaya.)

**********

## Three Great Assemblies of Disciples

## First Sannipāta

There were three great assemblies of the Arahant disciples of the Buddha Vessabhū. In the first instance, in the assembly of the future chief disciples, the Elder Soṇa and the Elder Uttara, the Buddha Vessabhū recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the midst of eighty koṭis of Arahants on the full moon day of Tabodwe.

(This is the first great assembly of disciples.)

## Second Sannipāta

Accepting the request of the devas and Brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and took conception in the womb of the Brahmin lady named Visākhā, the beloved wife of the Brahmin Chaplain (Purohita) named Aggidatta, who was skilled in advising and explaining the causes and effects to King Khemankara in the royal city of Khemavatī. When ten months were complete, he was born in the Khema Park.
(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonders clearly appeared.)
Special Note:
As mentioned before, from the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara to the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Buddhas were only of the Khattiya (noble) caste; however, the Blessed One Kakusandha was born into the Brahmin caste.
407:

This occurred due to the worldly convention of the time. In the world, there are four castes: Khattiya, Brahmin, Vessa, and Sudda. Bodhisattas in their final existence are never conceived in the Vessa or Sudda castes because neither of these is ever held as the supreme or most esteemed in the world.
As for the Khattiya and Brahmin castes, sometimes the world esteems the Khattiya caste most highly, and sometimes it esteems the Brahmin caste most highly. When the people of the world offer respect, honor, and worship to kings, the Khattiya caste is the most noble in the world, and Bodhisattas are born only in that caste. When the people of the world offer respect, honor, and worship to Brahmins, the Brahmin caste is the most noble in the world, and Bodhisattas are born only in that caste.
Thus, Buddhas are born from either the Khattiya or Brahmin castes. Since the world more frequently regards the Khattiya caste as supreme, most Buddhas are born into that caste. The esteem for the Brahmin caste as supreme occurs only occasionally; therefore, Buddhas are born into the Brahmin caste only occasionally. Thus, as stated, it should be understood that birth as a Buddha from the Khattiya caste is frequent, while birth from the Brahmin caste is rare.

## 23. The Chronicle of Buddha Koṇāgamana
After the Buddha Kakusandha attained Parinibbāna, in this same Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), the human lifespan gradually decreased from forty thousand (40,000) years to ten years, then increased again to an asankheyya (incalculable period), and then decreased again. When the human lifespan reached thirty thousand (30,000) years, the Bodhisatta Koṇāgamana, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), was residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas. Accepting the request of the devas and brahmas to become a Buddha, he descended to the human world and took conception in the womb of the Brahmin mother named Uttarā, the beloved wife of the Brahmin named Yaññadatta, in the royal city named Sobhavatī. When ten months were complete, he was born in the garden named Subhavatī.

(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonders appeared clearly.)

When the Bodhisatta was born, because a great rain of gold fell heavily throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa, on the day of his naming, the wise omen-readers and all his relatives, taking the meaning "Gold has come from the sky,"

518
named the boy "Kanakāgamana." (Kanaka = gold; Āgamana = coming; Kanakāgamana = the boy for whom gold came from the sky.) From that name Kanakāgamana, as a long time passed, the letters were modified and it became the name "Koṇāgamana." (Alternatively) By the method of Nirutti (etymology), the initial 'Ka' of the word 'Kanaka' was changed to 'Ko', the small 'na' was changed to the large 'ṇa', and the final 'ka' was dropped; thus, even at the time of naming, they named him the boy "Koṇāgamana."
