...reached 20,000 (twenty thousand) years, the Bodhisatta Kassapa, having fulfilled the Pāramīs and residing in the Tusita heaven according to the nature of Bodhisattas, accepted the request of the devas and brahmas to become a Buddha. He descended to the human world and was conceived in the womb of the Brahmin lady named Dhanavatī, the beloved consort of the Brahmin named Brahmadatta, in the royal city of Bārāṇasī where King Kikī reigned. When ten months were complete, He was born in the Isipatana Migadāya forest.
(At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, great omens and wonders clearly appeared.)
On the day the Bodhisatta prince was named, the experts in signs and all the relatives named the noble Bodhisatta 'Kassapa', based on his descent from the Kassapa clan.
## Enjoying Worldly Splendor
When the Bodhisatta Kassapa reached maturity, he resided in three noble palaces: (1) Haṃsa Palace, (2) Yasa Palace, and (3) Sirinandā Palace. He enjoyed worldly pleasures similar to celestial bliss for 2,000 (two thousand) years, being entertained and attended to by 48,000 (forty-eight thousand) Brahmin women, headed by his consort, the Brahmin lady Sunandā.
424:
526
## Renunciation
While the Bodhisatta Kassapa was living as a householder, he saw the four great omens. When his consort Sunandā gave birth to a son named Vijitasena, a great sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in him, and the thought occurred: "I shall renounce the world this very day."
Immediately after that thought arose, the palace where the Bodhisatta resided spun like a potter's wheel and rose into the sky. Accompanied by a vast multitude of people, like the moon appearing in the autumn season surrounded by stars and creating a delightful radiance, the palace traveled as if adorning the sky, clearly demonstrating his merit and power, captivating the eyes and hearts of all onlookers, and making the treetops appear exceedingly beautiful. It then descended to the earth, centering itself at the foot of the Banyan Bodhi tree.
Then the Bodhisatta descended from the palace, stood on the ground, and after receiving the robes and requisites offered by a Brahma, he became a monk. The Bodhisatta's consort and the entire retinue of ladies descended from the palace and went to a place forty usabhas (about half a gāvuta) away, where they stayed in temporary dwellings like a great army. All the men who had followed the Bodhisatta followed his example and became monks.
425:
527
## Attaining Buddhahood
The Bodhisatta Kassapa practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) together with the monks who followed him for seven days. On the full moon day of Kason, the day he was to become Buddha, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by his consort, the Brahmin lady Sunandā. He spent the day in the great Khadira forest in that area. When evening came, he proceeded alone to the Mahābodhi tree. On the way, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a guard of a barley field named Soma. As soon as he spread the grass at the foot of the Mahābodhi (Banyan) tree, the Aparājita Throne, fifteen cubits in size, appeared. Sitting cross-legged on that throne and resolving with fourfold energy (vīriya), he attained Buddhahood according to the method mentioned before.
## Five Great Dhamma Sermons
(1) After becoming Buddha, the Blessed One Kassapa resided near the Mahābodhi (Banyan) tree for seven weeks (sattasattāha). Accepting the request of the Brahma King to preach the Dhamma, He reflected, "To whom should I preach the Dhamma first?" He saw that the ten million monks who had renounced the world together with Him were endowed with past merit for attaining the Path and Fruit. He traveled through the air in an instant to the Isipatana Migadāya forest in Bārāṇasī where those monks resided. Staying in their midst, He preached the Dhamma as was the custom of previous Buddhas...
426:
528
When the sermon of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta was preached, many devas and Brahmās arrived respectfully to listen. At that time, twenty billion (koṭis) devas and humans attained the special Dhamma of the Path and Fruit.
(This was the first great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma, the first Dhammābhisamaya.)

(2) Thereafter, on another occasion, while the Blessed One Kassapa was wandering on a journey from city to city, village to village, and market town to market town, preaching the Dhamma, ten billion devas and humans attained the special Dhamma of the Path and Fruit.
(This was the second great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma, the second Dhammābhisamaya.)

(3) Thereafter, on another occasion, while the Blessed One Kassapa was performing the Twin Miracle of water and fire near the great Pāṭalī (Padauk) tree near the gate of the city of Sundara and preaching the Dhamma, five billion devas and humans realized the Four Noble Truths and were liberated.
(This was the third great assembly of the realization of the Dhamma, the third Dhammābhisamaya.)

(4) After performing the Twin Miracle of water and fire in that manner, the Blessed One Kassapa resided in the celestial assembly hall named Sudhammā in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. With the deva who had been his mother as the chief listener, he preached the seven books of the Abhidhamma for the benefit of the devas and Brahmās from the ten thousand world systems who had respectfully come to listen. At that time, three billion devas and Brahmās realized the Four Noble Truths and were liberated.

(5) Thereafter, on another occasion, there was a celestial ogre (yakkha) who, like the ogre named Naradeva during the time of Kakusandha Buddha, possessed great power and majesty and was also known by the name Naradeva.
427:
529
This famous and powerful yakkha, Naradeva, would transform himself to perfectly match the appearance, voice, and mannerisms of the reigning king in various cities across the island of Jambudīpa. After killing and devouring the king, he would take over the palace and the entire country, ruling as king while continuing to kill and eat many people. He was also extremely given to sensual pleasures with women.

When the wise queen and the court ladies realized, "This king is not our lord the Great King, but is indeed an ogre," the yakkha felt great shame. He then killed and devoured all the women in the palace, moved to another city, and acted as king again in the same manner.

In this way, as the ogre Naradeva arrived at the city of Sundara, killing and eating people, the citizens, having already heard the news, were terrified of the danger of death and fled from their city to various places. At that time, the Blessed One Kassapa, seeing the fleeing citizens, went and stood directly in front of the ogre Naradeva. When the ogre Naradeva saw the Blessed One Kassapa standing before him, he shouted with a distorted and fierce voice, but he was unable to frighten the Blessed One. Instead, he approached the Blessed One for refuge and asked him questions and problems.

The Blessed One Kassapa answered the questions and problems satisfactorily, admonished the ogre, and
428:
530
preached the Dhamma. At that time, countless devas and humans who had respectfully come to listen to the Dhamma realized the Four Noble Truths and were liberated.

## The One Great Assembly of Disciples
Regarding the fact that there was only one great assembly of the Arahant disciples of the Blessed One Kassapa...
In the city of Bārāṇasī, a youth named Tissa, the son of the court chaplain, saw that the Bodhisatta youth Kassapa was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Having heard his father, the great chaplain Brahmin, say, "Such marks can only belong to one who will become a Buddha," he had no doubt. He thought, "This youth Kassapa will renounce the world in the great renunciation and become a Buddha. I shall become a monk under that Blessed One Kassapa and strive diligently to be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra)." Even before the Bodhisatta youth Kassapa renounced the world, Tissa went to the Himalayas and became a hermit (isi). The followers of this hermit Tissa numbered twenty thousand.

Later, when the hermit Tissa heard the news that "the youth Kassapa has renounced the world, become a monk, and has now attained Buddhahood," he came from the Himalayas with his twenty thousand followers. When he requested to become a monk in the presence of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Blessed One called them with the "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, monk) formula. Thus, he and his twenty thousand followers became Ehi Bhikkhu monks and attained the Fruit of Arahantship. In the assembly of these twenty thousand Arahants,
429:
531
on the full moon day of Tabodwe (Māgha), the Blessed One Kassapa recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha.
(This was the one great assembly of disciples.)

## The Bodhisatta of Gotama Buddha, the Youth Jotipāla, Becoming a Monk and Receiving the Prophecy
At that time, our Blessed One's Bodhisatta was a famous youth named Jotipāla. He was one who constantly recited the Vedas, held various mantras, and had mastered the three Vedas. He was supreme and proficient in the knowledge of Brahmins, including the science of marks (Lakkhaṇa) which describes the marks of a Great Man, and the ancient histories (Itihāsa), as taught by generations of teachers. He was fully studied and skilled, without deficiency, in the science of the earth (Bhūmivijjā) and the science of the sky (Ākāsavijjā).

Jotipāla the youth was a very dear friend of a potter named Ghaṭīkāra. The potter Ghaṭīkāra was a noble lay supporter of the Blessed One Kassapa, possessed of great respect and humility toward the Triple Gem, and was very famous as an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) lay disciple. That potter Ghaṭīkāra took the Bodhisatta Jotipāla and approached the Blessed One Kassapa.
430:
532
When Jotipāla the youth heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One Kassapa, he became a monk in the presence of the Blessed One. He was possessed of great and devoted energy, was skilled in all major and minor duties, and fulfilled the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Blessed One without any deficiency in the three trainings of Virtue (Sīla), Concentration (Samādhi), and Wisdom (Paññā).

Having fully studied and mastered the nine-fold Pariyatti Sāsana (scriptures) of the Blessed One as preached by Him, he graced the Dispensation of the Blessed One. Seeing the collection of wonderful qualities of the Bodhisatta monk Jotipāla, the Blessed One Kassapa gave the prophecy (byādita), saying: "In this very Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), this monk Jotipāla will surely become a Buddha named Gotama."
(The manner of receiving the prophecy is as complete as the prophecy received from the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara.)

Upon hearing the prophecy of the Blessed One Kassapa, the noble Bodhisatta monk Jotipāla, with a very clear and pure mind, firmly resolved to further fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

In this way, our incomparable Bodhisatta, the Lord of the Three Worlds, for the sake of the single desire to attain the Golden Wisdom of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), avoided all unwholesome deeds that should be avoided throughout the long round of rebirths. He practiced and strove with courage and sacrifice, without retreating, to fulfill the ten perfections to their peak, performing meritorious deeds difficult for ordinary people to do.

533
Note:
According to the Buddhavaṃsa Pāli mentioned, it might be understood that the potter Ghaṭīkāra easily took his friend, the Bodhisatta Jotipāla, to the Blessed One Kassapa. However, in reality, as he could not easily take him, it is preached in the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta (Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, 4. Rājavagga, 1) that he had to take him by force, even pulling him by the hair after repeatedly speaking to him. The detailed story of Ghaṭīkāra and Jotipāla should be taken from that Sutta.

## Description of the City, etc.
The birthplace of the Blessed One Kassapa was the royal city of Bārāṇasī, where King Kikī reigned. His father was the Brahmin Brahmadatta, and his mother was the Brahmin lady Dhanavatī.

The number of years he lived as a householder was two thousand (2,000). The three palaces in which he resided were Haṃsa, Yasa, and Sirinanda.

His consort was the Brahmin lady Sunandā, who had forty-eight thousand (48,000) attendants. His son was the youth Vijitasena.

After seeing the four great omens, the vehicle in which he renounced the world was the palace itself. He practiced austerities (dukkharacariyā) for only seven days.
432:
534
The pair of chief disciples were the Elder Tissa and the Elder Bhāradvāja. The attendant was the Elder Sabbamitta.

The pair of chief female disciples were the Elder Nun Anuḷā and the Elder Nun Uruvelā. The Bodhi tree under which he attained enlightenment was the Banyan (Nigrodha) tree.

The noble male lay supporters were Sumangala and the potter Ghaṭīkāra. The noble female lay supporters were the laywoman Vijitasenā and the laywoman Bhaddā.

The Blessed One Kassapa was twenty (20) cubits in height. He was as beautiful as a solid mass of lightning in the sky, or like the full moon surrounded by the host of planets and stars.

The lifespan during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa was twenty thousand (20,000) years. Having remained for that long (four-fifths of the lifespan), he rescued and liberated many beings—humans, devas, and Brahmās—from the current of the round of rebirths to the dry land of Nibbāna.

The Blessed One Kassapa created the great reservoir of the Pariyatti Dhamma for the sake of many beings, including humans, devas, and Brahmās. He provided the fragrant ointment of the Fourfold Purification of Virtue (Catupārisuddhi-sīla) so that beings could beautifully reflect upon their own minds. He had them wear the garment of the two qualities of Hiri (shame) and Ottappa (fear of wrongdoing). He distributed various flowers of the Dhamma, namely the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), for them to wear. He distinguished between blameworthy and blameless states, and wholesome and unwholesome states.
433:
535
In order that they may distinguish and contemplate, He set forth the great and true Dhamma, the stainless Knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa). Just as one might say to those wandering on the banks of a reservoir seeking Nibbāna, 'Look at and behold this array of Dhamma ornaments,' He established it well.

To the multitude of beings who received His instructions and advice, He gave the helmet of virtue—consisting of the Five Precepts, the Ten Precepts, and the Fourfold Purification Virtue (Catu-pārisuddhi-sīla)—so they might strike down and subdue the enemies of defilements. He caused them to be well-girded with the armor of the four and five mundane and supramundane Jhanas. He had them don the leather cloak of the Dhamma of mindfulness and clear comprehension (Sati-sampajañña). He bestowed upon them the complete military equipment of energy (Viriya), which possesses four noble factors. He gave them the shield of the four foundations of mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna), which can ward off and prevent various enemies of defilements. He ensured that His host of disciples held spears of insight-wisdom (Vipassanā-ñāṇa), which are exceedingly sharp. To those heroic disciples, He gave the sword of Path-wisdom (Magga-paññā), which had been sharpened on the whetstone of energy. To subdue and eliminate the entanglement of defilements, He bestowed the noble supramundane virtue. To enable them to adorn themselves beautifully, He made the four supramundane Fruits (Phala) into crest-flowers and gave them various ornaments such as the three types of higher knowledge (Vijjā) and the six supernormal powers (Abhiññā). Having fashioned a great bouquet of flowers consisting of the nine supramundane states (Lokuttara-dhamma), and together with that bouquet...
434:
536
...He gave the great white umbrella of the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala), which wards off and prevents the heat of unwholesome states. Having created and established the great Dhamma-flower of the Eightfold Path (Aṭṭhaṅgika-magga), which leads safely and peacefully to the city of Nibbāna, that Blessed One Kassapa, together with a great many disciples and Arahants, entered Parinibbāna and attained cessation.

## Saṃvega (Spiritual Emotion)
That Blessed One Kassapa, who was the repository of incomparable virtues and difficult for others to approach, has passed away. That noble Jewel of the Dhamma, which was so well-expounded by the Blessed One that it was worthy of being boldly invited with the words 'Come and see' and practiced, has disappeared. That noble Jewel of the Saṅgha, the many disciples who practiced that Dhamma well, has also passed away. All of it has ceased and vanished. Indeed, all conditioned things (Saṅkhāra), both physical and mental, are without solid essence; they are merely empty.

## The Cetiya
Thus, the Blessed One Kassapa, the conqueror of the five Maras and the teacher of gods and men, attained Parinibbāna in the great park named Setabya, near the city of Setabya within the kingdom of Kāsi. The people of Jambudīpa gathered in unity and, making the outer bricks worth ten million each and the inner filling bricks worth five million each...
435:
537
...(following the method previously mentioned), they built and worshipped a great Cetiya one yojana in height.

The Chronicle of Kassapa Buddha ends.

## Summary Verse of Receiving Prophecies
Thus, the summary of how our Noble Bodhisatta received the Definite Prophecy (Niyata-byādika) in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas, from Buddha Dīpaṅkara to Buddha Kassapa, is written and composed in the Dhamma-rāthī Pyo, verses (7, 8, 9) as follows:

If one counts four asankhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons, the names of the asankhyeyyas are Sela, Bhāsa, Jeyya, and Ruci—there are four. In the first asankhyeyya, Sela, during the Sāramanda kappa, four Buddhas appeared: Tanhankara, Medhankara, Saraṇankara, and Dīpaṅkara. (1) Although he encountered the first three leaders of gods and men, he did not receive the prophecy as he did not yet possess the eight required factors. Only later, as the hermit named Sumedha, renowned for his pure and bright wisdom, when the Beloved Buddha went for alms, he lay down at the Buddha's feet and received the resounding words of the prophecy.

(2) After the asankhyeyya named Sela had passed, in the Sāra kappa that arose, during the time of Buddha Koṇḍañña, the Bodhisatta was a noble Wheel-turning Monarch named Vijitāvī. Having gathered those from near and far and offered a great gift with a clear mind, he received the prophecy as before.

(3) After the Bhāsa asankhyeyya had passed, in the excellent Sāramanda kappa, when the glorious Buddha Maṅgala appeared, the Bodhisatta was a famous Brahmin named Suruci. Having offered a complete gift, he was graced with the prophecy.

(4) When Buddha Sumana, who bestows peaceful happiness, appeared next, the Bodhisatta was the mighty Naga king named Atula. Having offered pure gifts to the Great Buddha, he was granted the prophecy.
436:
538
(5) During the time of the noble Conqueror Revata, the Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Atideva. Having offered many gifts, he received the solemn prophecy that moved the whole island.

(6) Following him, during the time of the glorious Sobhita, the Bodhisatta was a young Brahmin named Ajita. Having offered a great gift, the prophecy was spoken.

(7) After that, when the Jeyya asankhyeyya had passed, in the Vara kappa, when the Knower of Truth Anomadassī appeared, the Bodhisatta was a leader of Yakkhas named Senādibba. Having encountered the Buddha and offered a magnificent gift, he was praised with the prophecy.

(8) Next was Buddha Paduma, the lamp of the world who conquered the five Maras. The Bodhisatta was then a lion in the forest. Having shown great devotion, he received the prophecy.

(9) Immediately following was the glorious Nārada. The Bodhisatta was then a hermit. Having encountered the Buddha and served Him greatly, he was given the prophecy with a resounding voice.

(10) After that, when the Ruci asankhyeyya had passed, in the Sāra kappa, when Buddha Padumuttara appeared with great majesty, the Bodhisatta was a wealthy man named Jaṭila. Having offered gifts, he was given the prophecy in the midst of the assembly.

(11) Thirty thousand aeons after that, in the Maṇḍa kappa, when Buddha Sumedha appeared, the Bodhisatta was a youth named Uttara. Having offered gifts with devotion, he received the prophecy again.

(12) Immediately following was the glorious Sujāta. The Bodhisatta was then a powerful Wheel-turning Monarch ruling over the four islands. Having offered a great gift, he was joyfully pointed out with the prophecy.

(13) After eighteen aeons had passed, in the Vara kappa, during the time of Buddha Piyadassī, the Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Kassapa. Having offered his wealth, he was once again showered with the prophecy.
437:
539
(14) After that, during the time of Buddha Atthadassī, the Bodhisatta was the hermit Susīma. Having performed offerings and worship, he was given the prophecy of success.

(15) Next, during the time of Buddha Dhammadassī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, the king of gods. Having worshipped with devotion, the prophecy was revealed.

(16) After four aeons had passed, in the Sāra kappa, when Buddha Siddhattha appeared, the Bodhisatta was a hermit of great power and fame named Maṅgala. Having encountered and offered gifts to the Buddha, the prophecy was repeated.

(17) After ninety-two aeons had passed, in the Maṇḍa kappa, when Buddha Tissa appeared, the Bodhisatta was a powerful king named Sujāta. Having offered a great gift with the aim of attaining the goal, he achieved the prophecy.

(22) After thirty aeons had passed, in this great Bhadda kappa, when the renowned Buddha Kakusandha appeared, the Bodhisatta was the famous King Khema. Having offered complete and abundant gifts, the prophecy was preached.

(23) When Buddha Koṇāgamana appeared, the Bodhisatta was King Pabbata. Having offered a great gift, he was praised and given the prophecy.

(b) Receiving the prophecy while being a Yakkha General in the presence of Anomadassī Buddha (1 life).

(Mnemonic): Five hermits, nine monks, five humans, two nagas, Sakka, Yakkha, and a Lion King; these are the twenty-four in number.
## The Rarity of Encountering the Sasana
In this way, considering that our Great Bodhisatta, during the period of four asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons of fulfilling perfections, encountered the Sasana only twenty-four (24) times from the Sasana of Dīpaṅkara Buddha to the Sasana of Kassapa Buddha, one should deeply contemplate the rarity of encountering the Buddha's Sasana and strive with renewed effort to ensure that the current era of the Sasana we are experiencing is not in vain.
442:
## The Difficulty of Attaining Monkhood
Considering that even the Great Bodhisatta, who had already received the definite prophecy (niyata-byākaraṇa) from Dīpaṅkara Buddha, encountered only twenty-four Sasanas (which can be said to be extremely few compared to the total time elapsed), and among those twenty-four Sasanas, he attained the state of a monk (bhikkhu) serving the Sasana in only nine (9) lives, it is clear how difficult it is to become a monk, according to the scriptural saying: “Pabbajitabhāvo dullabho = The state of a monk is hard to attain.” If it is so difficult even for those who have received the definite prophecy, it goes without saying how extremely difficult it is for other ordinary people; it should be noted as being exceedingly rare.
## The Dullabha Monk
Nowadays, some virtuous Buddhists, while performing their livelihood duties, take the opportunity when they find free time to become monks, intending to attain the rare state of monkhood within that free time so that it is not wasted. Such a monk is called a “Dullabha Monk.” The intended meaning is that, as previously shown, although they cannot remain as a monk permanently for a long time, they strive to attain the exceedingly rare state of monkhood temporarily.
If one does not contemplate this meaning, one might mistakenly think that in this world, only those who temporarily ordain during their free time are “Dullabha Monks,” and that the state of those who have been monks since childhood (those ordained from being a novice) is not “Dullabha.”
443:
Because of such a misconception, people tend to give more importance and make more offerings to “Dullabha Monks” than to those who have been monks since childhood (lifelong monks) from the age of twenty. In reality, if even the temporary state of a “Dullabha Monk” is attainable, then the state of a monk intended for a lifelong duration is even more difficult to attain; there is no need to say it specially, it should be noted as truly difficult.
## Government Service and Monkhood
Some people say:
“Because there is a disciplinary rule (Vinaya) stating, ‘Na bhikkhave rājabhaṭo pabbājetabbo = Monks, one in the king's service should not be ordained,’ even if government officials request, ‘I wish to ordain during my leave; please ordain me,’ the Saṅgha should not ordain them. Since this contradicts the Vinaya, government officials should not undertake the practice of being a ‘Dullabha Monk’ nowadays.”
This should not be said. In the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) on the Mahākhandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga, in the explanation of the Rājabhaṭavatthu, it is stated:
Even if one is in the king's service, it is proper to ordain those who have returned their salary and wages to the king; those who have handed over their position to a son or brother and informed the king, “I am no longer your servant”; those who have completed the work for which they were paid; and those who have been graciously and satisfactorily permitted by the authority (the king) himself, saying, “If you wish to ordain, then do so.”
444:
Based on this commentary's explanation, if pensioners nowadays wish to ordain permanently, they should do so after returning their pension to the government or after obtaining gracious permission from the government, saying, “If you wish to ordain, then do so.”
The disciplinary rule stating “One in the king's service should not be ordained” is intended to mean that those who seek refuge in the Sasana specifically to escape from being a king's servant should not be ordained. (This point can be understood by referring to the original Pali text of the Rājabhaṭavatthu.) The government officials who become temporary “Dullabha Monks” nowadays have not the slightest intention of escaping their service; they are even very worried that the authorities might be dissatisfied and dismiss them from service for becoming a “Dullabha Monk.” Therefore, if permission is obtained from the relevant authorities, there is no contradiction between the training rule in the Vinaya Mahāvagga and the current practice of becoming a temporary “Dullabha Monk.”
As stated in that training rule, even if someone enters the Sasana to escape from the king's service, if they are ordained, only the preceptor monks who ordain them incur a dukkaṭa offense, while the person ordained truly attains the state of a monk; this is clearly stated in the Vinaya texts.
There might be another point of view:
“Even the Great Bodhisatta, who had received the definite prophecy, became a monk only nine times despite encountering twenty-four Buddhas. Based on this, it is reasonable to say that monkhood is hard to attain. However, according to the Buddhavaṃsa Pali, when Dīpaṅkara Buddha entered Rammavatī City for alms, he was followed by four hundred thousand Arahants. Furthermore, among the three assemblies of disciples, the first assembly consisted of one hundred thousand koṭis of Arahants. Considering such a large number of Arahants, it would seem that becoming a monk is not that difficult.”
445:
This is another point to consider. In truth, when it is said that monkhood is hard to attain, it means that the coincidence of causes for attaining it is rare. The Great Bodhisatta found it difficult to attain monkhood because the conditions and opportunities for ordaining were not aligned every time he encountered a Buddha's Sasana. The vast number of Arahants in the time of Dīpaṅkara Buddha were noble individuals whose conditions and opportunities were fully aligned not only for becoming monks but also for becoming Arahants. In any matter, if the causes are not aligned, the result is difficult to arise. When the causes are aligned, the result is easy to arise.
The countless Arahants in the time of Dīpaṅkara Buddha became both monks and Arahants because all their causes were fully aligned, starting from the perfections (pāramīs) they had prayed for and fulfilled in previous lives to become Arahants in that very life. For example...
446:
“Manussattabhāvo dullabho = Human birth is hard to attain.” The difficulty is illustrated by the simile of the blind turtle in the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta (9) of the Suññata Vagga (3) in the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pali: “Suppose a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the ocean. If an easterly wind blows, it drifts west; if a westerly wind blows, it drifts east; if a northerly wind blows, it drifts south; and if a southerly wind blows, it drifts north, drifting aimlessly. In that ocean, there is a blind turtle whose both eyes are destroyed, and it surfaces only once every hundred years. It is very difficult for the head of that blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, to enter the hole of that yoke drifting aimlessly with the wind. Even more difficult than that, it is hundreds of times harder for a being who has once fallen into the states of misery (apāya) or ruin (vinipāta) to regain human birth.” This is how it was taught. In other Pali texts as well, the difficulty of attaining human birth is frequently taught.
While on one hand, it is taught that human birth is very hard to attain, on the other hand, in texts like the Apadāna Pali and Vimānavatthu Pali, it is taught that by merely offering a single flower, one can attain human and celestial bliss for many lives. This might lead one to think, “Becoming human is not difficult; it can happen easily.” However, as previously shown, the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta and others were taught for those whose causes and conditions for becoming human are not aligned, whereas for those whose causes and conditions are aligned...
447:
549
Just as it is taught in the Apadāna Pāli and other texts that many human lives can be obtained through the offering of even a single flower, the rarity of becoming a monk should be understood in the same way.

Regarding the human state, if one looks at the current world where the population is increasing and births are occurring daily, it might seem (without deep consideration) that being born human is not difficult. However, in truth, if one considers the beings in the four woeful planes (apāya)—not to mention all four, but just the animal realm alone—the species are countless and vast. If one compares the number of ants, which are constantly being born, with the human population, one will find that the number of ants is incomparably greater. Considering that the beings born in the four woeful planes are so numerous while those born in the human state are so few, it is evident how difficult it is to obtain human birth.

In the same way, regarding the state of a monk, it is difficult to enter and become a monk every time a Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana) appears in the world. In the Dispensation of each Buddha, there may be many who become monks and even reach Arahantship because their conditions and opportunities are perfectly aligned. However, one should not assume that becoming a monk is easy just because many happen to gather and meet during the time of a Buddha when conditions are favorable.

In another way, the state of a monk, which is included among the five rarities (dullabha), can only be achieved by one who is endowed with both: (1) Buddhuppāda-dullabha, encountering the extremely rare Dispensation of a Buddha; and (2) Manussatta-dullabha,
448:
550
obtaining the extremely rare human birth. Only a person who possesses both of these can become a monk. When the Dispensation is absent, even if one is human, there is no opportunity at all to become a monk. Even when the Dispensation is clearly present, if one is a deva, Sakka, Brahma, or a being in the woeful planes, there is no opportunity to become a monk. Thus, among the two rare conditions for obtaining the state of a monk, encountering the Dispensation, called Buddhuppāda-navama, is exceedingly difficult. The Dispensation can only shine and be present in the world when a Buddha is enlightened. For a Buddha to arise, even after receiving the definite prophecy (niyata-byādisa), He must fulfill the Perfections (pāramīs) without rest through the four types of development (bhāvanā) mentioned before, for at least four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons (kappas). Even when a Buddha has arisen and the Dispensation is shining, if one does not obtain human birth, or if one is human but faces other obstacles, one cannot become a monk. If this point is considered deeply, there is reason to say that becoming a monk is even more difficult than encountering the era of the Dispensation in the world.

For those who, supported by great merit, have encountered the rare Dispensation and obtained the rare human birth, the state of a monk—which is the resulting effect—is no longer extremely difficult since the two primary causes are already fulfilled. Just as the countless Arahants during the time of Dīpaṅkara Buddha seemed to obtain the state of a monk easily because they were endowed with the two difficult primary causes, it should still be understood and stated that the state of a monk is very difficult because obtaining its root causes—the era of the Dispensation and the human state—is extremely rare.
449:
551
**********
The Bodhisatta, the hermit Sumedha, before meeting Dīpaṅkara Buddha, even in his youth, performed the act of generosity (dāna) by giving away all his grand household possessions; the act of renunciation (nekkhamma) by leaving the human society for the forest; the act of virtue (sīla) by practicing pure morality as a hermit; and the act of tranquility meditation (samatha-bhāvanā) by striving to attain jhānas and higher psychic powers (abhiññā). After receiving the definite prophecy from Dīpaṅkara Buddha, he reflected on the ten perfections as previously shown and tirelessly cultivated the Perfection of Generosity (dāna-pāramī) and others through the four types of development until his life as King Vessantara, for a duration of four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons.

In thus fulfilling and developing the ten perfections (as mentioned in the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary and the Jātaka Commentary), regarding the Perfection of Generosity: the number of lifetimes and existences in which he fulfilled dāna-pāramī—such as when he was the brahmin Akitti, the brahmin Sankha, King Dhanañjaya, King Mahāsudassana, the chief chaplain Mahāgovinda, King Nimi, Prince Candakumāra, the wealthy merchant Visayha, King Sivi, and King Vessantara—is immeasurable. In particular, when he was the wise hare, sacrificing his own life to give to the brahmin (who was Sakka) is the Ultimate Perfection of Generosity (dāna-paramattha-pāramī).
450:
552
Regarding the Perfection of Virtue (sīla-pāramī), the number of lifetimes in which he fulfilled it—such as when he was the elephant king Sīlava, the naga king Campeyya, the naga king Bhūridatta, the elephant king Chaddanta, Prince Jayadisa, and Prince Alīnasattu—is immeasurable. In particular, when he was the naga king Sankhapāla, observing virtue at the cost of his life is the Ultimate Perfection of Virtue (sīla-paramattha-pāramī).

Regarding the Perfection of Renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī), the number of lifetimes in which he fulfilled it by renouncing the sovereignty of great kingdoms and entering the forest—such as when he was Prince Somanassa, Prince Hatthipāla, and the wise Ayoghara—is immeasurable. In particular, when he was King Cūḷasutasoma, renouncing the kingship already in his hands as if it were a drop of spit, without any attachment, and entering the forest is the Ultimate Perfection of Renunciation (nekkhamma-paramattha-pāramī).

Regarding the Perfection of Wisdom (paññā-pāramī), the number of lifetimes in which he fulfilled it—such as when he was the wise Vidhura, the wise Mahāgovinda, the wise Kudāla, the wise Araka, and the wise Mahosadha—is immeasurable. In particular, in the Sattubhasta Jātaka, when he was the wise Senaka, being able to point out the snake inside the leather bag (by the power of wisdom without looking with his eyes) is the Ultimate Perfection of Wisdom (paññā-paramattha-pāramī).

Similarly, regarding the Perfection of Energy (vīriya-pāramī) and others, the number of lifetimes in which he fulfilled and cultivated them is likewise immeasurable and countless.
451:
553
In particular, in the Mahājanaka Jātaka, Prince Mahājanaka's swimming across the great ocean is the Ultimate Perfection of Energy (vīriya-paramattha-pāramī).

In the Khantivādī Jātaka, being the hermit Khantivādī and being able to endure without anger even when King Kalābu cut off his limbs is the Ultimate Perfection of Patience (khanti-paramattha-pāramī).

In the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka, being King Sutasoma and returning to Porisāda to keep his word "I will return" truthfully, even at the risk of his life if Porisāda wished to kill him, is the Ultimate Perfection of Truthfulness (sacca-paramattha-pāramī).

In the Mūgapakkha Jātaka (Temiya Jātaka), not breaking his resolve even at the cost of his life, despite being tested in various ways, both gentle and harsh, for sixteen years, is the Ultimate Perfection of Resolve (adhiṭṭhāna-paramattha-pāramī).

In the Ekarāja Jātaka (or the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka), being able to develop loving-kindness even towards an enemy king (or towards wild beasts such as lions and tigers) is the Ultimate Perfection of Loving-kindness (mettā-paramattha-pāramī).

In the Lomahaṃsa Jātaka, being able to remain indifferent (equanimous) without hatred or affection, whether village children did various bad or good things such as spitting phlegm and saliva on him or worshipping him with flowers and perfumes, is the Ultimate Perfection of Equanimity (upekkhā-paramattha-pāramī). (The details of these ten Jātakas that reach the level of Ultimate Perfection should be noted from the Burmese translation of the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary.)

These lifetimes shown by the great commentators as the fulfillment of the ten perfections
452:
554
are merely selections from the Jātaka stories found in the Pāli texts. Upon further examination, among those Jātaka stories in the Pāli texts, all except five Jātakas are events that occurred within this present aeon (kappa).

The five Jātakas that did not occur in this aeon are:

1. Ekanipāta (1) Apaṇṇaka-vagga (3) Serivavāṇija Jātaka: (The Commentary states that this Jātaka occurred five aeons ago: "Atīte ito pañcame kappe bodhisatto serivaraṭṭhe serivanāmako kacchapuṭavāṇijo ahosi" = In the fifth aeon prior to this one, the Bodhisatta was a merchant of trinkets named Seriva in the kingdom of Seriva, traveling with his wares in a shoulder-bag.)

2. Ekanipāta (10) Litta-vagga (4) Lomahaṃsa Jātaka: (The Commentary states that this Jātaka occurred ninety-one aeons prior to this one: "Atīte ekanavutikappamatthake bodhisatto bāhirakaṃ tapaṃ vīmaṃsissāmīti ājīvakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā acelako ahosi" = Ninety-one aeons ago, the Bodhisatta, wishing to test the ascetic practices outside the Dispensation, took the renunciation of the Ājīvakas and became a naked ascetic.)
453:
555
3. Dukanipāta (2) Santhava-vagga (9) Araka Jātaka: (The Commentary states in the conclusion of this Jātaka that it occurred seven aeons ago: "Evaṃ bodhisatto aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke nibbattitvā sattasaṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe na imaṃ lokaṃ puna āgamāsi" = Thus the Bodhisatta, with his jhānas intact, was reborn in the Brahma realm and did not return to this human world for seven cycles of world-contraction and world-expansion.)

4. Catukkanipāta (5) Cūḷakuṇāla-vagga (6) Kesava Jātaka: This Jātaka occurred approximately five hundred and seventy aeons ago.

5. Sattakanipāta (1) Kukkura-vagga (10) Baka Jātaka: This Jātaka also occurred approximately five hundred and seventy aeons ago.

These Kesava and Baka Jātakas are stories that occurred in successive lives. To summarize the detailed account in the Commentary: first, in the Kesava Jātaka, he was the hermit Kesava, and upon his death, he became the great Baka Brahma. This Baka Brahma was first a great Brahma in the Vehapphala realm, living for five hundred great aeons (mahākappa). When he passed away from that realm, he was reborn in the Subhakiṇha realm and lived for sixty-four great aeons. Again, when he passed away from that realm, he was reborn in the Ābhassara realm for a lifespan of eight great aeons, at which time he held a wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi).
454:
It is mentioned in the Commentary. Considering this, after passing through 500 world-cycles (kappas) in the Vehapphala realm and 64 kappas in the Subhakiṇṇa realm—a total of 564 kappas—one reaches the Ābhassara realm. Regarding the adoption of wrong views upon reaching the Ābhassara realm, although there is no specific mention of which particular kappa among the eight kappas of the Ābhassara lifespan it occurred, it is estimated that the combined duration of both the Kesava Jātaka and the Baka Brahma Jātaka is approximately 570 kappas.

In this way, the teachers of old (ācariya-paramparā) held the belief that all Jātakas where the Commentator simply points out 'in the past' (atīte) without specifying the exact number of kappas by counting back from this present kappa, are Jātakas that occurred only within this present world-cycle (Mahā-bhadra-kappa). According to this view, the previous lives of the Bodhisatta mentioned in the Atthasālinī Commentary and the Pāṭha Jātaka Commentary, which are described only generally as 'in the past' (atīte), are Jātakas that occurred within this world-cycle. Even among the Jātakas that occurred within this world-cycle, not all can be fully described; the lives and Jātakas that occurred in this world-cycle are indeed very numerous. However, the Buddha only selected and taught those Jātakas that were relevant to the present circumstances and events; the remaining lives and Jātakas that were not taught are far more numerous.
455:
Considering that only a portion of the Jātaka stories that occurred in this world-cycle were taught as they coincided with relevant events, it is clear that the lives spent fulfilling perfections (pāramīs) that were not revealed are numerous. Furthermore, if one reflects on how countless the lives were during the four incalculable periods (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand world-cycles (kappa) spent fulfilling perfections—not to mention the lives before this world-cycle—the task of fulfilling perfections by the Great Bodhisattas appears as a matter that is truly awe-inspiring and daunting for ordinary people.

On the other hand, if one focuses on the Great Bodhisattas themselves, it should be well understood that these Great Beings who fulfilled the perfections are noble persons worthy of endless praise, being profoundly delightful and wondrous beyond words.

In this extremely vast sequence of lives spent fulfilling perfections, the life of King Vessantara was the final life. Before renouncing the world, while still a layman, the Bodhisatta Sumedha first performed the act of generosity (dāna) by giving away all his possessions. Later, after becoming a hermit (risi) and receiving the definite prophecy (niyata-byākaraṇa), when he reflected on the qualities that lead to Buddhahood, he firmly resolved to first fulfill the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī), starting with the verse 'Imaṃ tvaṃ paṭhamaṃ tāva' and so on. Thus, the Great Bodhisattas, in fulfilling the ten perfections, begin with the perfection of generosity and continue until the final life, such as that of King Vessantara.
456:
The perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī) is a quality that brings about the attainment of a noble existence (bhava-sampatti) and the attainment of all necessary wealth and requisites (bhoga-sampatti) in future lives (following one like a shadow that cannot be prevented until Nibbāna is reached). For the Great Bodhisattas, as leaders of those traveling through the journey of saṃsāra (as shown in the Anudīpanī section on the perfection of generosity), it is especially important for everyone wandering in saṃsāra to be endowed with generosity. Therefore, in the final life as Vessantara, he particularly fulfilled the act of generosity, concluding the series of lives spent fulfilling perfections. Having completed the perfections and awaiting the proper time to become a Buddha, he passed away from the life of King Vessantara and went to dwell in the Tusita heaven, the abode where previous Bodhisattas reside.

## The Eight Differences (Vematta-dhamma)
Although these eight differences (vematta-dhamma) are explained in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary at the end of the lineage of Gotama Buddha, in this Buddhavaṃsa text, they are presented at the end of the section on the Twenty-four Buddhas to avoid being too far removed from the lineage of Buddhas starting from Dīpaṅkara.

'Vematta' is a Pali word derived from the root word 'matta'. (Vi = distinct/various; Matta = measure/extent). Although the Buddhas, starting from Dīpaṅkara, are equal to one another in terms of their attributes (guṇa), there are eight measures or extents in which they differ from one another.
457:
The eight differences are:
1. Āyu-vematta = (Difference in lifespan)
2. Pamāṇa-vematta = (Difference in height)
3. Kula-vematta = (Difference in lineage)
4. Padhāna-vematta = (Difference in the manner of practicing austerities)
5. Rasmi-vematta = (Difference in the emission of rays)
6. Yāna-vematta = (Difference in the vehicle used for the Great Renunciation)
7. Bodhi-vematta = (Difference in the Bodhi tree of enlightenment)
8. Pallaṅka-vematta = (Difference in the size of the throne)
These are the eight.

Among these eight:
## (1) Āyu-vematta
Āyu-vematta refers to the difference in the lifespan of the Buddhas from one to another.

These nine Buddhas—Dīpaṅkara Buddha, Koṇḍañña Buddha, Anomadassī Buddha, Paduma Buddha, Padumuttara Buddha, Atthadassī Buddha, Dhammadassī Buddha, Siddhattha Buddha, and Tissa Buddha—appeared during an age when the lifespan was 100,000 years.

Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña, Anomadassī,
Noble Paduma, Uttara, Attha, and Dhammadassī,
Siddhattha, and Tissa—these nine glorious ones,
Appeared without fail in the age of a 100,000-year lifespan.
458:
These eight Buddhas—Maṅgala Buddha, Sumana Buddha, Sobhita Buddha, Nārada Buddha, Sumedha Buddha, Sujāta Buddha, Piyadassī Buddha, and Phussa Buddha—appeared during an age when the lifespan was 90,000 years.

Noble Maṅgala, Sumana, the Conqueror Sobhita,
Lord Nārada, Sumedha, the Conqueror Sujāta,
Piyadassī, and the one named Phussa—these eight noble Buddhas,
Appeared in the past for the sake of liberation during the 90,000-year lifespan.

These two Buddhas—Revata Buddha and Vessabhū Buddha—appeared during an age when the lifespan was 60,000 years.

Revata and Vessabhū—these two in the 60,000-year age.

Vipassī Buddha appeared during the 80,000-year lifespan; Sikhī Buddha appeared during the 70,000-year lifespan; Kakusandha Buddha appeared during the 40,000-year lifespan; Koṇāgamana Buddha appeared during the 30,000-year lifespan; Kassapa Buddha appeared during the 20,000-year lifespan; and our Buddha appeared during the 100-year lifespan.

Noble Vipassī and noble Sikhī—in those two glorious times,
80,000 years and 70,000 years, they appeared in due order.
Sandha, Gamana, Pa, and Ma—the four Buddhas of this Bhadda-kappa,
40,000, 30,000, 20,000, and the 100-year era—they appeared in due order.

One might ask: Since Buddhas are noble persons who have greatly accumulated the merits of the perfections to become a Buddha, should not their lifespans be equal?
459:
In this matter, the detailed explanation given in the Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta of the Mahāvagga should be understood in brief: In the world, the righteousness or unrighteousness of kings is the fundamental cause for the long or short life of beings. To elaborate: when kings are righteous, the whole world follows suit in righteousness. Consequently, the deities also practice righteousness and cause the rain to fall properly. Due to such causes, the fruits, flowers, leaves, and other food consumed by humans are rich in nutrients and essence, and the climate is favorable. As a result, humans are healthy and live long lives. When kings are unrighteous, the majority of people gradually become unrighteous as well. The deities do not cause the rain to fall properly, and thus the food such as fruits, flowers, and leaves in the human world lacks essence. Furthermore, because the climate is unfavorable, people suffer from many diseases and have short lifespans due to living in an unfavorable climate and consuming food lacking in nutrients.

According to this principle, Buddhas who appear in an era of long lifespans have long lives. Buddhas who appear in an era of short lifespans have short lives.

Although every Buddha possesses the kamma-potency that results in a long life due to the merit of their rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), their lifespans are unequal because they correspond to the age-cycle (āyu-kappa) in which they appear. As stated in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary:
'Upacitapuññasambhārānaṃ dīghāyukasaṃvattanikakammasamupe-tānampi buddhānaṃ yugavasena āyuppamāṇaṃ asamānaṃ ahosi'—
460:
—which means: Although they are endowed with the accumulation of merit and possess the kamma that leads to a long life, the lifespan of the Buddhas was unequal according to the age-cycle (āyu-kappa) in which they appeared.

To use a worldly analogy: just as a teak seed, which has the potential to last for a thousand years, will not last for a thousand years if planted in a parched, barren land where water is scarce and there is drought; similarly, for the Bodhisattas in their final existence, no matter how much their kamma has the potential to grant a long life, if they become a Buddha in an era of short lifespans—which is like the parched, barren land—their lifespan will be short in accordance with that age-cycle.

## The Period of the Age-cycle in which Buddhas Appear
Buddhas do not appear during the 'waxing age' (vivaṭṭa-ṭṭhāyī-kappa / increasing age) when the lifespan of beings is gradually increasing. The reason is that if Buddhas were to appear in the waxing age and preach about the nature of impermanence (anicca), etc., beings would not be able to listen or believe. In that waxing age, because the lifespan is increasing from one generation to the next, the minds of beings cannot perceive the nature of impermanence, suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta) of conditioned things (saṅkhāra). Therefore, Buddhas do not appear in the waxing age, but only in the 'waning age' (vivaṭṭa-kappa / decreasing age) when the lifespan is gradually decreasing.

Even in the waning age, during the times when the lifespan is very long (above 100,000 years) before it drops to the 100,000-year mark, as previously mentioned, the nature of impermanence of conditioned things...
461:
563
Even if the Dhamma were taught, beings would not be able to listen or believe; therefore, Buddhas arise only when the maximum human lifespan is one hundred thousand years. (They do not arise during the waning age when the lifespan is longer than that.) When the lifespan decreases from one hundred thousand years, the period in which they may arise extends down to a one-hundred-year lifespan. If the lifespan decreases below one hundred years, although the nature of conditioned things (saṅkhāra), such as impermanence (anicca), could be taught very clearly, the mental continuities of beings at that time would be so thick with defilements (kilesa) such as greed, hatred, and delusion that they would no longer be able to accept, listen to, or practice the Dhamma even if impermanence and other truths were taught. Thus, Buddhas do not arise during a waning age when the lifespan is below one hundred years.

In this way, Buddhas invariably arise only between a maximum lifespan of one hundred thousand years and a minimum of one hundred years. Although any time within this waning period between one hundred thousand and one hundred years is technically a time when they could arise, they actually arise during the specific lifespan that coincides with the maturity of the Great Bodhisattas' accumulation of perfections (pāramī). For Great Bodhisattas whose accumulation of perfections is mature, if their perfections are fully ripened and coincide with the one-hundred-thousand-year lifespan, they arise during that one-hundred-thousand-year period. For Bodhisattas who are still fulfilling their perfections and are not yet mature, they cannot arise at the one-hundred-thousand-year mark, but arise at the ninety-thousand, eighty-thousand, seventy-thousand, or sixty-thousand-year mark, etc., whenever their maturity of perfections coincides with the prevailing lifespan.
462:
564
In this Bhadda Kappa, Kakusandha Buddha arose during the forty-thousand-year lifespan; (then, after an interval of one antara-kappa) Koṇāgamana Buddha arose during the thirty-thousand-year lifespan; (then, after an interval of one antara-kappa) Kassapa Buddha arose during the twenty-thousand-year lifespan. Therefore, it might be said that our Gotama Buddha should have arisen (after an interval of one antara-kappa) during the ten-thousand-year lifespan. However, because the accumulation of perfections was not yet mature, he could not yet arise. Not to mention the ten-thousand-year lifespan, he could not yet arise at the five-thousand, one-thousand, or even five-hundred-year lifespan. The reason is that the task of fulfilling the perfections was only completed at the end of the life as King Vessantara. (Only in that life were the perfections matured and completed.) That life of King Vessantara occurred during a one-hundred-year lifespan. Because the task of fulfilling the perfections was completed (the perfections matured) only during the one-hundred-year lifespan, he had to arise during the one-hundred-year lifespan.

Regarding the phrase 'yugavasena' (by power of the age) found in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, I shall further present the remarks of the Great Teacher Aggamahāpaṇḍita U Lin... (The word 'yuga' denotes a pair or a set; a set of these four—Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—is called a Yuga. There are four Yugas: Kṛta Yuga, Tretā Yuga, Dvāpara Yuga, and Kali Yuga. Kṛta Yuga is also called Kata Yuga or Sacca Yuga. The word 'Kṛta' is a Sanskrit form and should be 'Cata' or 'Catu', meaning four. Within the period defined by this Kṛta Yuga, virtue is as upright and firm as an object with four legs.
463:
565
Thereafter, upon reaching the period of Tretā Yuga, virtue remains firm like an object with only three legs, yet it does not reach the level of Kṛta Yuga.

Thereafter, upon reaching the period of Dvāpara Yuga, virtue is like an object with two legs; it does not possess the same stable and good firmness as in Kṛta and Tretā Yugas. It begins to waver.

When Kali Yuga is reached, however, virtue declines and diminishes greatly, and only evil becomes powerful.

Among these four Yugas, the duration of Kṛta Yuga is 1,728,000 (one million seven hundred twenty-eight thousand) years. The duration of Tretā Yuga is 1,296,000 (one million two hundred ninety-six thousand) years. The duration of Dvāpara Yuga is 864,000 (eight hundred sixty-four thousand) years. The duration of Kali Yuga is 432,000 (four hundred thirty-two thousand) years.

At the beginning of the world, starting from Kṛta Yuga, when one Yuga ends, it transitions to the next; when the final Kali Yuga ends, it turns back again to the beginning, Kṛta Yuga. In this way, they appear and disappear through the rotation of the four Yugas. While the periods of these four Yugas were rotating, the time when Gotama Buddha arose occurred within the beginning of Kali Yuga.

In the Gotama Purāṇa, it is stated that in the year Gotama Buddha attained Parinibbāna, the Kali Yuga year was 2,570 (two thousand five hundred and seventy). According to that Gotama Purāṇa, if one wishes to know the current Kali Yuga year, one should add the current Sāsana year to 2,570 (the number of Kali Yuga years that had passed before the Buddha's Parinibbāna). (For example) In the Sāsana year 2500, which is the year 1318 ME, if one wishes to know which Kali Yuga year has been reached, one should add the current Sāsana year 2500 and 2570, knowing that the Kali Yuga year 5070 has been reached.

Thus, according to the secular teachers, within the divisions of the four Yugas, the author of the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary intends to say that Buddhas who arise during excellent Yugas like Kṛta Yuga have long lifespans, while Buddhas who arise during inferior Yugas have short lifespans. According to these words of the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, the meaning is simply that "Buddhas who arise when the lifespan in the world is long have long lives, and Buddhas who arise when the lifespan is short have short lives." This is the remark of the Great Teacher U Lin.

## (2) Pamāṇavematta
Pamāṇavematta means the difference in height (stature) between one Buddha and another.

Dīpaṅkara Buddha, Revata Buddha, Piyadassī Buddha, Atthadassī Buddha, Dhammadassī Buddha, and Vipassī Buddha—the height of these six Buddhas was eighty cubits.

Koṇḍañña Buddha, Maṅgala Buddha, Nārada Buddha, and Sumedha Buddha—the height of these four Buddhas was eighty-eight cubits.

Sumana Buddha's height was ninety cubits.

Sobhita Buddha, Anomadassī Buddha, Paduma Buddha, Padumuttara Buddha, and Phussa Buddha—the height of these five Buddhas was fifty-eight cubits.

Sujāta Buddha's height was fifty cubits.

Siddhattha Buddha, Tissa Buddha, and Vessabhū Buddha—the height of these three Buddhas was sixty cubits.

Sikhī Buddha's height was seventy cubits.

Kakusandha Buddha, Koṇāgamana Buddha, and Kassapa Buddha—the heights of these three Buddhas were forty, thirty, and twenty cubits respectively.

As for Gotama Buddha, his height was sixteen cubits (or) eighteen cubits.

(The reason for providing these two different measurements will be explained upon reaching the Buddhavaṃsa of Gotama.)

In this way, while the heights of the Buddhas differ from one another, it should be understood that climate (utu) and nutrition (āhāra) are the primary causes. Buddhas are only human Buddhas who must arise from among humans, and according to the nature of the people during the era in which they arise, their lifespan is equal to the natural lifespan of ordinary humans. During the time of Buddhas who arise in a one-hundred-thousand-year lifespan, the people generally live for one hundred thousand years. During the time of Buddhas who arise in a ninety-thousand-year lifespan, the people generally live for ninety thousand years. Thus, the length of the lifespan occurs in accordance with the human lifespan of that time.

However, the height of the physical body cannot be determined solely by the lifespan. That it cannot be so determined is known by considering that among Buddhas who arose during a one-hundred-thousand-year lifespan, Dīpaṅkara Buddha, Atthadassī Buddha, and Dhammadassī Buddha were only eighty cubits tall, while Koṇḍañña Buddha was eighty-eight cubits, and Anomadassī Buddha, Paduma Buddha, and Padumuttara Buddha were fifty-eight cubits, and Siddhattha Buddha and Tissa Buddha were eighty cubits; thus, height does not follow the lifespan. If even Buddhas with the same lifespan
467:
569
do not have the same height, then there is no need to mention the height of Buddhas whose lifespans differ.

In the Vinaya Piṭaka (2), Pācittiya Pāḷi (9), Ratana Vagga (10), Nanda Sikkhāpada, it is taught that the Buddha's younger brother, Ven. Nanda, was only four finger-breadths shorter than the Buddha; considering this, it should be believed that there were many others at that time who, though not equaling the Buddha's height, were nearly as tall as the Buddha. Therefore, it should be understood that the height of the Buddhas occurs in accordance with the general height of the people in the era in which they arise. It does not mean that the Buddha's height is exactly the same as the height of the people of those various eras.

The fundamental reasons why the height of the Buddhas occurs in accordance with the general height of the people are climate (utu) and nutrition (āhāra). When the whole world becomes unrighteous (excluding the Ariyas), starting from the unrighteousness of kings, one must depend on a disordered climate and food/nutrition that is low in essence (ojā); thus, the temperature-produced materiality (utuja-rūpa) and nutriment-produced materiality (āhāraja-rūpa) of the people of that era cannot grow or thrive as much as they should. Conversely, it should be known that when they are righteous, the utuja-rūpa and āhāraja-rūpa grow large and thrive.

## (3) Kulavematta
Kulavematta refers to the diversity of clans or castes among the Buddhas, which differs from one Buddha to another.
The three Buddhas—Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa—were born into the Brahmin caste, while the remaining twenty-two Buddhas were born into the Khattiya (warrior-noble) caste. When the people of the world regard the Khattiyas as supreme, the Buddhas are born into the Khattiya caste. When the people of the world regard the Brahmins as supreme, the Buddhas are born into the Brahmin caste.
## (4) Padhanavematta
Padhanavematta refers to the diversity of exertion, specifically the differing ways and durations in which the Buddhas practiced the austerities known as dukkharacariya.
These seven Buddhas—Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña, Sumana, Anomadassī, Sujāta, Siddhattha, and Kakusandha—practiced dukkharacariya for ten months.
These four Buddhas—Maṅgala, Sumedha, Tissa, and Sikhī—practiced dukkharacariya for eight months.
Buddha Revata practiced dukkharacariya for seven months, and Buddha Sobhita practiced dukkharacariya for four months.
469:
These three Buddhas—Paduma, Atthadassī, and Vipassī—practiced dukkharacariya for half a month (fifteen days).
These four Buddhas—Nārada, Padumuttara, Dhammadassī, and Kassapa—practiced dukkharacariya for only seven days.
Buddhas Piyadassī, Phussa, Vessabhū, and Koṇāgamana practiced dukkharacariya for six months.
Our Buddha Gotama, the Inconceivable Supreme Lord of the Three Worlds, practiced dukkharacariya for six years.
Just as there are reasons for the differences in lifespan (āyuvematta) and other factors previously shown, there must also be a reason for the variation in the duration of the practice of exertion called dukkharacariya. Upon seeking the specific cause, it should be said that it is due to kamma.
To clarify further, in the Pubbakammapilotika Buddhāpadāna of the Avaṭaphalavagga (10), Page 349 (39) of the first volume of the Apadāna Pali, it is stated: "Avacaṃhaṃ joti pālo, sugataṃ kassapaṃ tadā" and so forth. (Regarding the cause of the past unwholesome kamma for which our Bodhisatta had to practice dukkharacariya for six years): "In the time of Buddha Kassapa, I was a Brahmin youth named Jotipāla. I insulted Buddha Kassapa, saying, 'Where could this shaveling (bald-headed one) find
470:
the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscience? The knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscience is extremely difficult to attain.' By the fruit of that unwholesome verbal kamma, I had to practice the conduct of dukkharacariya for as long as six years in this final life where I was to become a Buddha." Thus, the Buddha himself preached.
Considering that the Pali Canon directly states that practicing dukkharacariya for six years was due to unwholesome kamma, it is evident that those Buddhas who practiced dukkharacariya for only seven days did so because of intense, sufficient, and powerful wholesome kamma. Therefore, it should be said that kamma is the primary cause for the variation in the duration of the practice of dukkharacariya.
Although the duration of the exertion (padhāna-vīriya) practiced just before becoming a Buddha differs, it should be understood that the effort of exertion (payatta-vīriya), which is included among the Sixfold Glory (Bhagavā attributes) upon becoming a Buddha, is identical among all Buddhas.
## (5) Rasmivematta
Rasmivematta refers to the diversity of rays, which is the difference in the emission of rays from one Buddha to another. The rays of Buddha Maṅgala pervaded and remained throughout ten thousand world systems. The rays of Buddha Padumuttara pervaded and remained for twelve yojanas all around. The rays of Buddha Vipassī pervaded and remained for seven yojanas all around.
471:
The rays of Buddha Sikhī pervaded and remained for three yojanas all around. The rays of Buddha Kakusandha pervaded and remained for ten yojanas all around. The rays of Buddha Gotama pervaded and remained for about four cubits, equal to the fathom (byāma) of his body. The rays of the remaining Buddhas were not constant but shone as brightly as they desired.
*Tatra rasmivemattaṃ ajjhāsayappaṭibaddhaṃ, yo yattakaṃ icchati, tassa tattakā sarīrappabhā pharati. Maṅgalassa pana niccampi dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharatūti ajjhāsayo ahosi.* (Sutta Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā, Sixth Council Edition, Page 18). *Tatra*, among those diversities (vematta). *Rasmivemattaṃ*, the diversity of rays. *Ajjhāsayappaṭibaddhaṃ*, is connected to the aspiration (ajjhāsaya) made while fulfilling the perfections. *Yo*, whichever Buddha. *Yattakaṃ*, as much as [he] desired the body rays to pervade while fulfilling the perfections. *Tassa*, of that Buddha. *Tattakā*, that much. *Sarīrappabhā*, the body rays. *Pharati*, pervade. *Maṅgalassa pana*, as for Buddha Maṅgala. *Niccampi*, even constantly. *Dasasahassilokadhātuṃ*, the ten thousand world systems. *Pharatūti*, "may [my] body rays pervade." *Ajjhāsayo*, the aspiration made while fulfilling the perfections. *Ahosi*, existed. (This is the meaning of the quoted Commentary Pali.) In its sub-commentary (Ṭīkā), it is explained that 'ajjhāsaya' refers to the prayer and aspiration (patthanā) made while fulfilling the perfections.
472:
If one seeks the reason why the emission of rays differs from one Buddha to another, it should be attributed to the kamma of the perfections they fulfilled. Regarding this, the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas) explained in the biography of Buddha Maṅgala, whose natural body rays pervaded ten thousand world systems:
"In a final life while fulfilling the perfections (similar to the life of King Vessantara for the Bodhisatta of Buddha Gotama), the Bodhisatta of Buddha Maṅgala lived with his wife and children on a mountain resembling Mount Vaṅkapabba. A demon named Kharadāṭhika, disguised as a Brahmin, came to ask for his son and daughter. The Bodhisatta of Buddha Maṅgala, thinking joyfully, 'I shall give,' donated his son and daughter. The demon Kharadāṭhika, leaning against a plank at the end of the cloister, crunched and ate the son and daughter right before the Bodhisatta's eyes, as if chewing a bundle of lotus stalks. Although the Bodhisatta saw the demon's mouth open and a stream of bright red blood flowing from it like a flame, he did not feel even a hair's breadth of displeasure. Instead, when he reflected, 'I have indeed given a great gift,' immense joy and rapture arose in him. He then made an aspiration: 'By the result of this merit, may rays emit from my body in this same manner in the future.' Because of that aspiration,
473:
when he became Buddha Maṅgala, his natural body rays pervaded and remained throughout ten thousand world systems."
Based on this explanation, it should be understood that the difference in the emission of natural body rays upon becoming a Buddha depends on whether or not there was a special past aspiration and merit. When it is said that the emission of rays (rasmivematta) differs, it refers only to the natural body rays (pakati-obhāsa). If a Buddha desires and creates them through psychic power, any Buddha can cause rays to appear and pervade as far as he wishes. In the realm of psychic power, there is no such thing as 'iddhivematta' (diversity in power) where one Buddha has less and another has more.
## Three Types of Rays
(1) Byāmappabhā Rays: These rays constantly emit from the natural body of the Buddha (our Buddha Gotama) and extend for one fathom (byāma) around the body. They are extremely dense and so concentrated that they are almost indistinguishable from the Buddha's body itself. If one looks at an electric bulb from about a bamboo's length away, there is a circle of light that appears as a ball of fire. Only by looking closely can one see the actual flickering shape of the flame. Similarly, the Buddha's body has a circle of rays extending one fathom; these are called 'Byāmappabhā rays.' It is an extremely thick and concentrated halo of light.
(2) Asītiniccalobhāsa Rays: These are the natural body rays that extend continuously from the Byāmappabhā rays
474:
up to a distance of eighty cubits.
(3) Disāpharaṇa Rays: These are the rays that pervade the infinite world systems due to the increased clarity of the blood and other elements when the Buddha contemplates the Paṭṭhāna or performs the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya).
## Two Classifications of Rays
The specific excellence of the visible form (vaṇṇa-dhātu) of the Buddha, which can be seen by the eyes of humans, devas, and brahmās, is called 'rays' (rasmī) in this context. According to Abhidhamma principles, the Byāmappabhā rays and the Asītiniccalobhāsa rays should be called kamma-born rays (kammaja) or temperature-born rays with kamma as a condition (kammapaccaya-utuja). This is because both types of rays have past kamma as their primary cause. The Disāpharaṇa rays should be called mind-born rays (cittaja) or temperature-born rays with mind as a condition (cittapaccaya-utuja), as they have the clarity of the mind as their primary cause. In this way, the distinctions among the rays should be understood.

## Two Types of Pallaṅka
In this context, the term Pallaṅka (Pali) or Pallaṅ (Burmese) is of two types: Ābhujana-pallaṅka and Āsana-pallaṅka. Among these two:

Ābhujana-pallaṅka should be understood as the act of sitting cross-legged, as found in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta and other texts: "Nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā" (He sits down having crossed his legs).

Āsana-pallaṅka should be understood as a special seat or platform for sitting. This Āsana-pallaṅka, being a special seat, is of many kinds, such as Seṭṭhi-pallaṅka (Merchant's throne), Rāja-pallaṅka (Royal throne), Nāga-pallaṅka, Deva-pallaṅka, Dhamma-pallaṅka, Bodhi-pallaṅka, and so on. Among these:

The type of throne belonging to the Merchant of Bārāṇasī, as mentioned in the Commentary on the Mayhaka Jātaka (No. 5) of the Suci Vagga (2) in the Chakka Nipāta: "Gaccha imaṃ amhākaṃ gharaṃ ānetvā mama pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā amhākaṃ paṭiyattabhattassa pattaṃ pūretvā dāpehi" (Friend, go, invite this Paccekabuddha to our house, seat him upon my throne, and having filled his bowl with the rice prepared for me, offer it to him), is called Seṭṭhi-pallaṅka. It refers to a special seat used by wealthy merchants.

That throne is located on the terrace of the Bodhimanda, which is a hundred cubits high. At a spot four cubits away from the eastern side of the base of the magnificent Bodhi tree, as soon as the Bodhisattvas scatter the eight handfuls of grass, due to the momentum of the merit of the perfections (pāramīs) they have fulfilled, from the surface of the earth...
