...the throne appears, adorned and beautiful with various kinds of jewels. This throne is called Bodhi-pallaṅka (Pali) or Bodhi-pallaṅ (Burmese) because it is the throne where the Bodhisattvas realize the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscience, known as Bodhi (becoming a Buddha).

## Views on the Height of the Throne
Regarding the throne, there are two differing views concerning the throne upon which Gotama Buddha attained enlightenment: one view states that it does not rise even an inch above the ground, while another view states that it rises fourteen (14) cubits above the ground. Among these two—

## The View of the Author of Maṇidīpa-ṭīkā
As soon as the eight handfuls of grass donated by Sotthiya the grass-cutter were scattered at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree, by the power of the perfections fulfilled over immeasurable aeons, the Aparājita-pallaṅka emerged from the earth. It was adorned with various jewels and was exceedingly delightful; it is of such a nature that no one in the three worlds is capable of creating it. In extent, it measures fourteen (14) cubits, with a corresponding length. However, because it has no base (legs), it remains on the ground without being detached from it (without rising). It is like the crest-jewel of the entire earth. Furthermore, because it is a place that cannot be broken, cracked, or destroyed, like a block of vajira (diamond), and because it is the place where the five Maras were conquered (without the Buddha being defeated), it is the Aparājita-pallaṅka. Being a throne situated near the Bodhi tree, it is called the Bodhi-pallaṅka. In the scriptures where it is stated "Cuddasahatthubbedho pallaṅko" (The throne is fourteen cubits in height)...
483:
585
The word 'ubbedha' denotes only width or extent; it does not denote height. Therefore, in the Pali phrase "cuddasahatthubbedho," the meaning should be taken only as a throne that is fourteen cubits wide. This is the statement found on page 149 of the first volume of the Maṇidīpa Ṭīkā. (The intention of the author of the Maṇidīpa Ṭīkā, Shin Ariyavaṃsa, is that the throne is fourteen cubits in width, with a length proportionate to it; it has no height and is level with the ground. It is not made of earth but is a jewel throne that emerged from the earth due to the power of the perfections.)

## The View of the Author of the Paritta-gyi Ṭīkā
However, the author of the Paritta-gyi Ṭīkā states: "The Bodhisatta received the eight handfuls of grass offered by the grass-cutter Sotthiya, ascended the terrace of the Bodhimanda, and while standing at the northeast corner of the Bodhi tree, held the grass by the tips and scattered them. Immediately, due to the majestic power of the merit of the perfections accumulated over many aeons, the Aparājita Throne emerged from the earth. It was composed of all kinds of jewels, and it was fourteen cubits in height and width, with a length suitable and proportionate to those fourteen cubits. It is the pinnacle of the entire earth. Because it appeared at a place four and a half cubits away from the Bodhi tree, it is called the Bodhi Pallanka."

Other teachers say: "The throne does not rise even a finger's breadth above the ground; it is level with the earth's surface. The phrase 'cuddasa hattho pallaṅko' refers only to the width of fourteen cubits. It does not refer to the height or depth."
484:
586
If the throne indeed had height (refer back to the Chronicle of Vipassī Buddha), according to the Pali text stating the dimensions of Vipassī Buddha's throne (tepaññāsa hattha), the throne of Vipassī Buddha would have to be fifty-three cubits high. The Pāṭalī Bodhi tree of that Vipassī Buddha had a trunk of fifty cubits and branches of fifty cubits, totaling one hundred cubits from the ground to the top of the tree. Thus, a throne fifty-three cubits high would (even before the Buddha sat upon it) exceed the fifty-cubit trunk by three cubits and would be positioned among the branches. On such a throne positioned among the branches, Vipassī Buddha, who was eighty cubits tall, would have to sit unbecomingly, giving his back only to the main branches instead of the trunk. Therefore, the throne has no height at all," so they explain.

The words of those teachers should be carefully considered. This is because the domain of the Buddhas is unthinkable and inconceivable. An example for reflection: on the surface of a mirror only a span wide, the reflection of a stupa ten or a hundred cubits high can appear. In such a case, the mirror does not grow larger, nor does the stupa become smaller, yet the appearance of the stupa on the mirror's surface is an inconceivable matter (lokavisaya acinteyya). Similarly, the Buddhas, without intentionally creating it through psychic power, can—if they so wish—reside in the four postures of reclining, sitting, standing, and walking even within a mustard seed. Therefore, the meaning should be taken that the domain of the Buddhas is an unthinkable and inconceivable matter.
485:
587
(This is the statement found in the explanation of the word 'Bodhipallaṅke' in the introduction to the Ratana Sutta in the Paritta-gyi Ṭīkā. The summary of the Paritta-gyi Ṭīkā author's intention is that the throne is fourteen cubits high and fourteen cubits wide, with a proportionate length, and it is a throne made entirely of jewels that emerged from the earth due to the power of the perfections.)

Which view is more appropriate? For this question, I shall briefly present the explanation of the Monywe Jetawun Sayadaw. (The details should be sought in the second volume of the Samantacakkhudīpanī.)

The summary of Monywe Sayadaw's explanation is as follows:
Regarding these two statements by the two Ṭīkā authors on whether the throne has height or not, the author of the Maṇidīpa, who holds that the throne is not high, argues that if it were high according to the statement that Vipassī Buddha's throne was fifty-three cubits, it would exceed the fifty-cubit trunk of the Bodhi tree and be positioned among the branches. (Could the throne alone be beautiful then?) He reasons that the eighty-cubit tall Vipassī Buddha would have to sit awkwardly and cramped (without having the trunk as a backrest), leaning only against the branches (which is unbecoming to behold), thus pointing out the fault in the existence of height.

The author of the Paritta-gyi Ṭīkā, however, holds: "The Buddha can stand even within a mustard husk along with the eight requisites; this is the inconceivable domain of a Buddha (Buddhavisaya acinteyya). The dimensions of Vipassī Buddha's throne, Bodhi tree, and stature are indeed matters that are unthinkable."
486:
588
Although both views of the two teachers are supported by evidence and one may note whichever one prefers, when considering what is logical:

The Maṇidīpa text was composed around the year 830 [Burmese Era]. The statement that the throne has no height did not appear in texts composed during the reigns of the kings of Sri Lanka, Bagan, Myinsaing, Sagaing, and Pinya before the Maṇidīpa appeared. Since this is a new statement that only arose with this new Maṇidīpa text, and because other texts do not say so, it is an isolated statement.

Furthermore, regarding the Buddha's stay at the Animisa station, where he gazed at the Bodhi tree and the golden throne for seven days, if the throne had no height, it would seem he was merely gazing at a place spread upon the ground.

Some teachers also say: "The word 'pallaṅka' denotes a place (seat) and also a throne with height. In this context, the word 'pallaṅka' denotes a place." Regarding that statement, if it were true that it only meant a place, the texts would only say "Bodhipallaṅke" etc.; they have never said "Bodhi-āsane" etc. If it were as those teachers say, it should have been said so, but it was not. When residing in other places (referring to a general seat), it appears with the word 'āsana' as in "paññattāsane nisīdi" (sat on the prepared seat), "āsanaṃ paññāpetvā" (having prepared a seat), "aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle paññatte āsane nisīdi" (sat on a seat prepared at the foot of a certain tree), etc. However, upon reaching the Bodhi tree, it does not appear with the word 'āsana' but only with the word 'pallaṅka', as in "pallaṅkañca bodhirukkhañca animisehi akkhihi olokay amāno sattāhaṃ vītināmesi" (he spent seven days gazing with unblinking eyes at the throne and the Bodhi tree) and "pallaṅkassa ca ṭhitaṭṭhānassa ca antarā" (between the throne and the place where he stood), etc. Therefore, it should not be taken as a mere 'āsana' spread upon the ground without rising even a finger's breadth.
487:
589
Since the word 'pallaṅka' is specifically used here, it should be taken as a throne with a specific height. If it were taken as a mere ordinary grass seat, it would render the special mention of the causal perfections (pāramī) meaningless. Because it is a special throne with a wondrous height, it is stated in the Vinaya Mahāvagga Commentary: "cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca upacitānaṃ pāramīnaṃ balādhigamaṭṭhānaṃ pallaṅkañca bodhirukkhañca" (the throne and the Bodhi tree, which are the places of attaining the power of the perfections accumulated for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons).

## This following statement should be noted with particular attention
It is explained in the Buddhavamsa Commentary that the thrones of Sobhita Buddha, Anomadassī Buddha, Padumuttara Buddha, and Phussa Buddha were thirty-eight cubits in dimension. It is stated in the Padumuttara Buddha section of the Buddhavamsa Commentary and the explanation of the Mahānidāna Sutta in the Sutta Mahāvagga Commentary (page 79) that when Padumuttara Buddha, after completing the Pallaṅka-sattāha (seven days on the throne), descended from the throne and lifted his right foot to step down, a Paduma lotus emerged, splitting the earth to receive him, with large petals of ninety cubits, filaments of thirty cubits, a pericarp of twelve cubits, and each stalk being twelve cubits. If the throne had no height, the throne would be low and the receiving lotus would be high, which would be inconsistent. It is only appropriate if one takes it that while descending from the thirty-eight cubit high throne, the twelve-cubit Paduma lotus appeared beneath his feet. If one were to take it that the throne had no height but only surface area,
488:
590
it would be inconsistent because the throne would be low and the lotus that bloomed later would be high. Furthermore, later learned teachers do not much favor the view that there is no height but only surface area. It is only because the author of the Maṇidīpa was a learned teacher of the scriptures that they do not criticize him severely.

In this manner and others, the Monywe Jetawun Sayadaw decided extensively (that the view that the throne has height is the appropriate one). (From Samantacakkhudīpanī, Vol. 2, p. 318 onwards.)

## The Decision of the Taungkhwin Sāsanabaing Sayadaw
Regarding this matter of "whether the throne has height or not," I shall further extract and present the decision of the Great Sangharāja Sāsanabaing Sayadaw, Visuddhasīlācāra Siripavara Dhammasenāpati, from the work "Guḷhatthavinicchaya."

Regarding the statement that the Buddha's throne is fourteen cubits, according to the view of Shin Ariyavaṃsa, the author of the Maṇidīpa, it is not height or depth from the ground but only width and extent. According to the view of Shin Tejodīpa, the author of the Paritta-gyi Ṭīkā, it is the depth and height from the ground. While these views differ, both teachers are eminent authors of scriptures, capable of citing Pali authorities and weighing logical consistency. They have exerted effort to convince many by providing measurements, logic, and traditional accounts to instill new wisdom in those with tender intellects. As seen in those various scriptures, the point to be considered through 'līnantara-codanā' (hidden criticism) is:

There are three types of thrones (pallaṅka):
489:
591
The throne is of three types:
(1) Ūrubaddhāsana-pallaṅka: the posture of sitting cross-legged with the thighs.
(2) Ṭhāna-pallaṅka: the place or site where one sits cross-legged with those thighs.
(3) Āsanavisesa-pallaṅka: a special kind of seat.

Among these, in the Pallaṅkavemattakathā of the Buddhavamsa Commentary, the meaning of Ṭhāna-pallaṅka appears only with the word 'vitthata', which denotes width and extent. Also, in the accounts of the sitting postures of the Buddhas starting from Koṇḍañña Buddha, they appear only with the words 'āyāma' and 'vitthata', which denote length, width, and extent.

Some teachers, however, follow the view of the Paritta-gyi Ṭīkā author and decide that "the throne is not width and extent, but only depth and height," because the word 'ubbedha' appears in the explanation of the fifth sutta of the Khajjanīyavagga in the Khandhavagga Saṃyutta Commentary and in the Catukka Aṅguttara Commentary as: "bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha cuddasahatthubbedhe ṭhāne tiṇasantharaṃ attharitvā" (having ascended the Bodhimanda and spread the grass mat at a place of fourteen cubits 'ubbedha'). The words of those teachers should be examined. Why? Because if it were indeed depth and height as explained by the word 'ubbedha', since the commentator further adds the phrase "tiṇasantharaṃ attharitvā" (spreading the grass mat) after the phrase "cuddasahatthubbedhe ṭhāne," it would lead to the fault of an undesirable meaning (aniṭṭhappasaṅga-dosa)—that he spread the grass to a height of fourteen cubits. He did not spread it to a height of fourteen cubits. Therefore, in this context, the word 'ubbedha' must be taken to mean 'vitthāra' (width and extent), as presented by the Maṇidīpa Sayadaw.
490:
This is consistent with the later words of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), which state, "having spread the grass mat." Therefore, one should only accept and decide upon the meaning that "the grass was spread over an area fourteen cubits wide."

In this matter, there is a question to be asked: If, as the Maṇidīpa teacher decided, the throne (pallaṅka) was not of a certain height but only of a certain width, would not the statement "the son of Māra marched with a great army on account of the throne" be in vain? (The implication is that if it were merely a common grass mat, there would be no need for the son of Māra to march with a great army to seize it.) This is the question that may be raised.

The answer is: It is not in vain. In truth, although the Great Buddha sat only upon a grass mat spread fourteen cubits wide, due to the meritorious perfections (pāramīs) he had fulfilled throughout many lives in saṃsāra, all beings—humans, devas, and brahmās—perceived him as if he were sitting upon the Aparājita Throne, exquisitely adorned with the seven kinds of gems. Therefore, it should be answered that it is not in vain.

For example, at the moment the Bodhisatta was born, the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās first received the newborn Bodhisatta with a golden net. From the hands of those Great Brahmās, the four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) received him with an antelope skin. From the hands of those four Great Kings, humans received him with a roll of white cloth. The Bodhisatta then freed himself from the hands of the humans and stood upon the earth. Devas and brahmās, holding the five regalia such as the white parasol, surrounded him and honored him by shading him with the white parasol and fanning him with the yak-tail whisk. Although he was a newborn of only a moment...
491:
When the Bodhisatta stood upon the earth and looked towards the eastern direction, thousands of universes (cakkavāḷas) became like a single open space (without any obstruction or concealment). The devas and brahmās residing in those places honored him with scents, flowers, and so on, and addressed him: "O Prince, in this world, there is no one even equal to you; how then could there be anyone superior? Indeed, there is none."

Having looked towards the ten directions in this manner and seeing no one equal to himself, he thought, "This is the supreme direction," and then took seven strides towards the north. He then fearlessly uttered the supreme words of proclamation beginning with "Aggo hamasmi" (I am the foremost). This is recorded in the Mahāpadāna Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya and its Commentary.

In this matter, a problem was raised. The question was: When the Bodhisatta stood upon the earth, walked towards the north, and fearlessly uttered the supreme words, did he walk on the ground or through the air? Did he walk with a visible body or an invisible body? Did he walk naked without clothes, or was he adorned? Did he walk as a tender young infant, or as a fully grown adult? (If) he walked as a fully grown adult at the time of birth, did he remain an adult afterwards as he was while walking, or did he become an infant again? (This problem has arisen before.)
492:
This problem, which arose beneath the Lohapāsāda in Sri Lanka, was answered by the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya as follows: The Great Man, who was the Bodhisatta, walked on the ground itself, but to the multitude of people, it appeared as if he were walking through the air. The Bodhisatta walked with a visible body, but to the multitude of people, it appeared as if he walked with an invisible body. The Bodhisatta walked naked, just as he was born, without clothes; but to the multitude of people, it appeared as if he were adorned. The Bodhisatta walked as a tender young infant; but to the multitude of people, it appeared as if he were a handsome adult of sixteen years of age. As for the Bodhisatta himself, he was an infant while walking and remained an infant after walking. To the multitude of people, however, he appeared as a handsome sixteen-year-old adult while walking, and only after he had finished walking did they perceive him as an infant.

When they heard this answer, the great assembly was delighted and rejoiced, saying, "Friends, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya has answered the problem as if the Buddha himself were answering it." This is recorded in the Commentary to the Mahāpadāna Sutta.

In the dispute over whether "the throne (pallaṅka) has height or only width," just as the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya answered regarding the Bodhisatta's seven strides to the north, it should be firmly and without doubt understood by way of logical reasoning (yukti-lakkhaṇāhāra) that: "The Buddha's throne was not of a certain height, but only of a certain width. However, due to the accumulation of meritorious perfections (pāramīs) fulfilled throughout many lives in saṃsāra, all humans, devas, and brahmās perceived it as if it were the golden Aparājita Throne, exquisitely adorned with the seven gems and of great height, and they perceived him as sitting upon that throne."
493:
This is the decision of the Taungkhwin Sāsanābaing Sayadaw. (From the first volume of the Guḷhatthavinicchaya, page 44.)

In this way, one should know the eight points of difference and variation among the twenty-five Buddhas, known as the Vematta-dhamma. Regarding these eight Vematta-dhamma, it is composed in the Dhammarāsī Pyo, verse 26, (3) Section on Nature, as follows:

In twenty incalculable (asaṅkheyya) aeons (kappas), having perfected the Dhamma-pāramīs and reached the time of enlightenment to become a Buddha, the Lords of the Three Worlds, the Kings of Dhamma, are complete in all graces. Among the eight kinds of differences, the first is the lineage (kula). They are always born into either the noble warrior (Khattiya) lineage or the renowned Brahmin (Brāhmaṇa) lineage, whichever is held in highest esteem in the world at that time. (Kula-vematta)

The radiance of their bodies (rasmi), which shines unceasingly and brilliantly, varies in extent, such as a fathom or a league (yojana); there is no equality, they differ. (Rasmi-vematta)

Even the lifespan (āyu) of those Buddhas is not fixed at a certain amount; it is not always the same and differs. (Āyu-vematta)
494:
Neither too white nor too thin, neither too small nor too bent, neither too lean nor too stout, the physical stature (pamāṇa) of their bodies is also not the same; they differ in height. (Pamāṇa-vematta)

At the time of their Great Renunciation, they depart using different vehicles (yāna), such as a pleasant horse, an elephant, a swift chariot, or a palanquin. (Yāna-vematta)

The duration of their great striving, the practice of austerities (dukkaracariyā), differs in terms of days, months, and years. (Padhāna-vematta)

The famous throne (pallaṅka), which arises from the earth with wondrous splendor like a flash of lightning and reaches towards the sky, also varies in height, being appropriate and fitting for the stature of each Buddha. (Pallaṅka-vematta)

The species of the Bodhi tree, the king of trees known as the cause of enlightenment, also differs; thus, all eight points are complete. (Bodhi-vematta)

## Here ends the first volume of the Mahā Buddhavaṃsa.
